_meta.purpose: Shield TSCM spectrum-survey signature catalog. Maps ADALM-Pluto / USRP B210 IQ features (band x bandwidth x modulation-class x duty) to covert-surveillance RF signatures for the identify.py matcher. Signatures are DISTINCT-on-the-air fingerprints, not per-product rows; the deep product intelligence lives in example_products / confirm_steps.
_meta.source: Assembled 2026-07-02 from a 62-agent web-grounded research + adversarial-verify + completeness-critic fleet, reconstructed from agent transcripts and de-duplicated. A signature match is a LEAD, not a finding.
_meta.license_note: sigidwiki content is CC BY-NC-SA. Product names are for internal identification only; keep third-party marketing copy and waterfall images out of client deliverables.
_meta.matcher_note: identify.py ranks a captured signal against these like sigidwiki_ref.json: band overlap + occupied bandwidth + modulation class + duty. mode/tscm are human context, not scored.
_meta.hardware_note: Stock ADALM-Pluto (AD9363) tunes 325-3800 MHz; AD9364 mod extends ~70 MHz-6 GHz. USRP B210 tunes 70 MHz-6 GHz. Neither sees <70 MHz (low-VHF/27-49 MHz toy bands) nor >6 GHz (UWB 6.5/8 GHz, 5G mmWave). NON-RF classes (optical/IR, acoustic/ultrasonic) are unreachable by any SDR and are flagged as such.

device_classes.device_class: Drone / RC surveillance UAS — control uplink + video downlink RF signatures (2.4 GHz & 5.8 GHz FHSS/OFDM, 900 MHz & 1.2/1.3 GHz long-range, plus WiFi drones and DroneID/RemoteID)
device_classes.summary: A surveillance drone almost never emits a single signal — it emits a control-link signature (uplink, narrowband FHSS/LoRa, sub-GHz or 2.4 GHz) AND a video-downlink signature (wideband, 5.8 GHz or 2.4 GHz analog/OFDM), and often a third RemoteID/DroneID beacon. These are DISTINCT on the air and each gets its own row: the control link is a low-bandwidth hopper you find by its hop pattern and duty; the video link is a fat continuous carrier (analog FM) or a ~10-40 MHz OFDM block (DJI OcuSync/Lightbridge, Walksnail Avatar, HDZero). Separated by BAND (900/1200/1300/2400/5200/5800 MHz), CHANNEL WIDTH, MODULATION (analog FM video vs OFDM digital vs LoRa vs GFSK/FHSS vs Wi-Fi), and protocol variant where the on-air picture genuinely differs. Consumer camera drones (DJI Mavic/Air/Mini, Autel) collapse control+video into one proprietary OcuSync/SkyLink OFDM+FHSS stack; FPV/custom builds split them across separate radios (ELRS/Crossfire control + analog or Walksnail/HDZero video). CRITICAL REACH: the two headline surveillance bands, 5.725-5.925 GHz (video) and 5.2 GHz, are ABOVE a stock ADALM-Pluto's 3800 MHz ceiling (stock Pluto = AD9363, 325-3800 MHz) — they need a B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) or an AD9364-modded/re-tuned Pluto with an external 5.8 GHz front end. A stock Pluto only reaches the 900 MHz, 1.2/1.3 GHz, and 2.4 GHz signatures. Nothing here is above 6 GHz, so a B210 covers the entire class. Massive legitimate-device overlap exists at 2.4 GHz (Wi-Fi/BLE) and 900 MHz (ISM telemetry, LoRa IoT, cordless), so band presence alone is never a detection — the hop signature, duty, and video-carrier shape are what identify a drone.

confirm_steps: Look for the SIGNATURE PAIR, not a single signal: a wideband video slab/carrier (analog fat FM or ~20-40 MHz OFDM) co-present with a narrow hopping control skirt in the same or a paired band. A lone fat carrier could be many things; the pair is the drone tell.

On the waterfall, check DUTY to split control from video: control links hop in short narrow bursts on a regular cadence (ELRS ~50-1000 Hz on 2.4 / up to 200 Hz on 900 is metronome-regular; FrSky/Crossfire have their own cadence); video is a steady continuous slab. RemoteID/DroneID is burst-then-silent (~600 ms period).

Distinguish analog vs digital video: analog FM shows a peaked center carrier with FM video sidebands and audio subcarrier; digital (DJI/Walksnail/HDZero) shows a flat-topped noise-like OFDM block with sharp band edges. Width helps: DJI 20/40 MHz, HDZero ~27 MHz (17 MHz narrow), analog ~17-18 MHz occupied.

For 5.8 GHz and 5.2 GHz you MUST use a B210 or a modded/downconverted Pluto — a stock Pluto (AD9363, 325-3800 MHz) simply cannot see these bands; confirm your front end reaches 5.9 GHz before concluding 'no drone.'

Try to decode DJI DroneID / Broadcast RemoteID (open-source demods exist — proto17/dji_droneid for the 2.4 GHz OFDM burst and for BLE/Wi-Fi-NAN ASTM F3411): a successful decode yields drone serial + operator GPS/home point — definitive identification and operator localization.

Correlate with motion: point a directional antenna and watch RSSI track a moving airborne source. A benign Wi-Fi AP or IoT sensor is stationary; a drone's downlink RSSI and Doppler shift move. This is the key discriminator against the huge 2.4 GHz/900 MHz false-positive pool.
Sweep the sub-GHz long-range bands (433, 900/915, 1.2-1.3 GHz) explicitly — covert long-range platforms deliberately avoid crowded 2.4/5.8 GHz. Don't stop at 2.4/5.8.

Time-correlate control and video: arming/flight begins when a continuous video slab appears alongside an active control hopper; both go quiet together on landing/disarm. Simultaneous on/off across two bands is strong confirmation.
false_positive_overlap: 2.4 GHz digital video and Wi-Fi-drone signatures are visually IDENTICAL to ordinary 802.11 Wi-Fi (routers, laptops, phones, cameras, IoT) and to Bluetooth/BLE — this band is the single biggest false-positive minefield. Band presence alone is never a detection.
5.8/5.2 GHz digital video overlaps 5 GHz Wi-Fi (802.11a/n/ac/ax APs, wireless HDMI, some baby monitors) and 5 GHz cordless — a 20/40 MHz OFDM slab here is often just a home/office AP.

900/915 MHz control and telemetry overlap LoRaWAN/IoT, LPWAN, 900 MHz cordless phones, some smart meters, ISM sensors, and cellular guard bands — ELRS/Crossfire/SiK hoppers look like generic 900 MHz ISM traffic.
433 MHz telemetry overlaps LPD433 remotes, ham 70 cm, car key fobs, TPMS, weather stations, garage doors — extremely crowded, low-confidence band on its own.
1.2-1.3 GHz analog video overlaps GPS L2 (1227 MHz), amateur 23 cm, ATC transponders/DME, and radiosondes — a legit FM-video-shaped carrier is the tell but adjacent services cause confusion.
ELRS/FrSky/Spektrum control-link FHSS/DSSS hops resemble Bluetooth classic hopping and other 2.4 GHz FHSS ISM devices (some wireless mics, industrial telemetry).
Broadcast RemoteID over BLE/Wi-Fi is, by design, indistinguishable at the RF layer from any other BLE beacon or Wi-Fi frame — only payload decode confirms it's a drone.
DJI/Autel OFDM downlinks resemble each other and resemble some proprietary wireless-video/streaming gear — cross-vendor shape overlap means timing/RemoteID decode is needed to attribute.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Threat framing for a bug sweep: a surveillance drone is a MOBILE, INTERMITTENT emitter — it is only on the air while flying, so a one-shot spectrum snapshot will miss it. Sweep continuously and, ideally, during the windows when overflight is suspected. The highest-value TSCM win here is decoding DJI DroneID or Broadcast RemoteID: those beacons transmit the operator's GPS position and the drone's home point IN THE CLEAR (DJI DroneID is unencrypted and reverse-engineered — proto17/dji_droneid, NDSS 2023), so a successful decode can localize the person flying it — flag this capability to the client. Practical detection reality: because 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz are saturated with Wi-Fi/BLE and 900 MHz with IoT, you cannot call a drone from band presence alone — you need the control+video signature PAIR, the moving-source RSSI/Doppler behavior, or a payload decode. Prioritize a purpose-built drone-detection front end or the B210 for 5.x GHz; a stock ADALM-Pluto (AD9363, 325-3800 MHz) blindly misses the two most common video bands (5.2/5.8 GHz) and will give a false 'all clear' if it is the only receiver. Long-range/covert operators deliberately use 433/900 MHz/1.2 GHz to stay off the crowded bands defenders watch, so include the sub-GHz sweep. Note legal/exposure angle for the client: intercepting/decoding another party's drone control or video may implicate wiretap/interception statutes and FAA rules on interfering with aircraft — passive detection and RemoteID reception are generally fine, but active jamming/takeover is federally prohibited and should be surfaced to counsel before any 'counter-drone' action is proposed.

signatures.name: 5.8 GHz analog FM video downlink (FPV VTX, 40-channel A/B/E/F/Raceband)
signatures.mode: Analog FM composite video (NTSC/PAL) on a single fixed channel, no hopping
signatures.tscm: Fat continuous FM carrier (~17-18 MHz occupied per channel, ~30 MHz channel spacing) with a bright center pilot and video sidebands; sits on one of the 40 standard channels (e.g. R1=5658, R8=5917, A1=5865, E1=5705). Stays put once armed — no hopping. Power 25 mW (indoor) to 600 mW-2 W (long range). Classic 'one drone, one continuous fat carrier' picture. The single most common cheap-spy-drone / FPV video signature. [above stock Pluto 3800 MHz ceiling — needs B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) or AD9364-modded Pluto + 5.8 GHz downconverter/front end; fully inside B210 range]

signatures.name: DJI OcuSync / O3 / O4 digital video downlink 5.8 GHz (20 MHz OFDM)
signatures.mode: OFDM digital HD video downlink, ~20 MHz occupied, AES-256, dynamic channel selection
signatures.tscm: Flat-topped ~20 MHz OFDM block (the downlink video carrier) that hops channel occasionally to dodge interference but is otherwise a solid continuous slab, distinct from analog's peaked FM. This is the DJI consumer/prosumer camera-drone downlink (Mavic 3, Air 3, Mini 4 Pro, etc.). Often paired with a co-band FHSS uplink (separate row). O3+/O4 can widen to ~40 MHz at 50 Mbps. [above stock Pluto 3800 MHz — needs B210 or modded Pluto + 5.8 GHz front end; inside B210 range]

signatures.name: DJI OcuSync / O3 / O4 digital video downlink 2.4 GHz (20 MHz OFDM)
signatures.mode: OFDM digital HD video downlink, ~20 MHz occupied, band-agile (auto-switches 2.4/5.8)
signatures.tscm: Same ~20 MHz OFDM slab as the 5.8 GHz variant but placed in 2.4 GHz ISM — DJI drones auto-select 2.4 when 5.8 is congested. Looks Wi-Fi-like in width but is continuous and steadier than bursty Wi-Fi/802.11 frames; center-band OFDM mass surrounded by a hopping control skirt. Heavy false-positive overlap with Wi-Fi here. [in stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz) — 2.4 GHz ISM reachable; also in B210 range]

signatures.name: DJI OcuSync / O4 digital video 50 Mbps wide mode (~40 MHz OFDM)
signatures.mode: OFDM 4K/high-bitrate mode, ~40 MHz occupied bandwidth
signatures.tscm: Wider ~40 MHz OFDM block used by O3+/O4 in 50 Mbps mode for 4K/high-bitrate video — a genuinely distinct occupied bandwidth from the 20 MHz mode, worth its own row for a matcher watching channel width. Solid continuous slab, dynamic channel. [above stock Pluto 3800 MHz — B210 or modded Pluto + front end]

signatures.name: DJI Lightbridge / Lightbridge 2 downlink (legacy Phantom/Inspire, ~10-20 MHz)
signatures.mode: OFDM downlink, older Lightbridge PHY, 2.4 and 5.8 GHz variants
signatures.tscm: Predecessor to OcuSync on Phantom 3/4, Inspire 1/2, older Matrice. OFDM downlink block similar in shape to OcuSync but distinct protocol timing; still widely in the field on used/second-hand surveillance platforms. Both 2.4 and 5.8 GHz builds exist. [2.4 GHz build in stock Pluto range; 5.8 GHz build above stock Pluto — needs B210/front end]

signatures.name: Walksnail Avatar HD digital video downlink 5.8 GHz (~20 MHz OFDM, bidirectional)
signatures.mode: OFDM digital HD FPV, two-way (retransmit) link
signatures.tscm: Caddx/Walksnail Avatar HD kit — closest DJI clone, bidirectional so you see a downlink OFDM slab plus a thinner uplink return. Common on custom/DIY surveillance and freestyle quads. ~20 MHz occupied; distinguishable from DJI mostly by protocol timing, not gross shape. [above stock Pluto 3800 MHz — B210 or modded Pluto + 5.8 GHz front end]

signatures.name: HDZero digital video downlink 5.8 GHz (~27 MHz, one-way low-latency)
signatures.mode: OFDM digital video, ONE-WAY broadcast (no uplink retransmit), ~27 MHz (17 MHz narrow mode)
signatures.tscm: HDZero occupies ~27 MHz in standard mode (wider than DJI's 20 MHz; a ~17 MHz narrow mode also exists) and is strictly one-way downlink — no return-path uplink slab, which distinguishes it from Walksnail/DJI on the air. Sits on analog-style 5.8 GHz channels. Low-latency race/freestyle system also used in DIY surveillance builds. [above stock Pluto 3800 MHz — B210 or modded Pluto + front end]

signatures.name: DJI OcuSync/Lightbridge FHSS control uplink 2.4 GHz (narrowband hopper)
signatures.mode: Frequency-hopping narrowband command/control uplink (RC to drone)
signatures.tscm: The narrow hopping 'skirt' around the OcuSync video slab — narrow (~1-2 MHz) bursts jumping across 2.4 GHz carrying stick commands. On a waterfall it's a scatter of short hops flanking the fat video block; the pair (fat OFDM + hopping skirt) is the DJI fingerprint. Present even when video is on 5.8 (band-split ops). [in stock Pluto range (2.4 GHz ISM) and B210 range]

signatures.name: DJI FHSS control uplink 5.8 GHz (narrowband hopper)
signatures.mode: Frequency-hopping narrowband control uplink, 5.8 GHz variant
signatures.tscm: Same DJI control hopper but in the 5.8 GHz band when the drone runs video on 2.4 (band-split) or both on 5.8. Narrow hops flanking/co-located with the OFDM video. Distinct band = distinct reach, so separate row. [above stock Pluto 3800 MHz — B210 or modded Pluto + front end]

signatures.name: DJI DroneID / RemoteID beacon 2.4 GHz (OFDM burst, ~10 MHz, hops)
signatures.mode: Proprietary OFDM identification burst (unencrypted), periodic
signatures.tscm: Short OFDM bursts (~9 OFDM symbols, ~10 MHz occupied / ~15.36 MHz with guard carriers) recurring on the order of every ~600 ms, hopping across frequency points in 2.4/5.8 GHz, broadcasting drone serial/operator GPS/home point in the clear (reverse-engineered by proto17/dji_droneid and NDSS 2023 research). TSCM-gold: decodable to reveal operator location. Distinct from the continuous video slab by its burst-then-silent duty. Broadcast RemoteID (ASTM/WiFi-NAN/BT) beacons from non-DJI drones look similar in the burst-duty sense. [in stock Pluto range (2.4 GHz); 5.8 GHz hop points need B210/front end]

signatures.name: Generic Broadcast RemoteID beacon — Wi-Fi NAN / Bluetooth 4/5 (2.4 GHz)
signatures.mode: ASTM F3411 Broadcast RemoteID over Wi-Fi Beacon/NAN or BLE advertising
signatures.tscm: FAA/EU-mandated RemoteID from compliant non-DJI drones and add-on modules (Dronetag, BlueMark, Cube). BLE advertising = narrow ~1-2 MHz bursts on the three BLE adv channels (2402/2426/2480); Wi-Fi NAN/Beacon = short 802.11 frames. Carries drone ID + operator position. Overlaps massively with every BLE beacon and Wi-Fi AP — identify by decoding the RemoteID payload, not by RF alone. [in stock Pluto range (2.4 GHz) and B210 range]

signatures.name: ExpressLRS (ELRS) control link 2.4 GHz (LoRa/FSK FHSS, up to 1000 Hz)
signatures.mode: LoRa / GFSK frequency-hopping RC control, packet rates 50-1000 Hz
signatures.tscm: Open-source FPV control link on Semtech LoRa/FSK radios — very regular, high-rate (up to 1000 Hz on 2.4 GHz) narrow (~0.8-1.6 MHz) chirps/bursts hopping across 2.4 GHz on a fixed FHSS sequence. Extremely consistent hop cadence distinguishes it from Wi-Fi's irregular bursts. Pairs with analog or digital video (separate rows). Dominant DIY/FPV control link. [in stock Pluto range (2.4 GHz) and B210 range]

signatures.name: ExpressLRS (ELRS) control link 900 MHz (LoRa FHSS, up to 200 Hz)
signatures.mode: LoRa frequency-hopping RC control, sub-GHz long-range, up to 200 Hz
signatures.tscm: Sub-GHz ELRS for penetration/extreme range — narrow LoRa chirps hopping across the US 902-928 MHz ISM band (868 in EU). Lower packet rate cap (~200 Hz) than 2.4. On a waterfall, distinctive LoRa upchirp shape. Overlaps with 900 MHz IoT/LoRaWAN and telemetry — distinguish by hop cadence tied to a controller and pairing with a video downlink. [in stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz covers 900 MHz) and B210 range]

signatures.name: TBS Crossfire / Tracer control link 900 MHz (FHSS, CRSF, long range)
signatures.mode: Proprietary FHSS RC control (Crossfire), sub-GHz, LoRa/FSK, up to 2 W
signatures.tscm: TBS Crossfire is the other dominant long-range control link — LoRa (50 Hz) / GFSK-style FHSS hops across 868/915 MHz, ~6.7-11 ms latency, up to 2 W for 10-100 km range. Distinct hop pattern/timing from ELRS. TBS Tracer is the same family on 2.4 GHz (separate row). Long-range = serious surveillance platforms. [in stock Pluto range (900 MHz) and B210 range]

signatures.name: TBS Tracer control link 2.4 GHz (FHSS, CRSF)
signatures.mode: Proprietary FHSS RC control (Tracer), 2.4 GHz
signatures.tscm: 2.4 GHz sibling of Crossfire — fast FHSS control hopping across 2.4 GHz ISM, lower latency than the 900 MHz Crossfire, shorter range. Narrow hops; pairs with analog/digital video. Distinguish from ELRS by hop timing signature. [in stock Pluto range and B210 range]

signatures.name: FrSky ACCST D16 / ACCESS control link 2.4 GHz (FHSS)
signatures.mode: FHSS RC control (FrSky ACCST/ACCESS), ~1-2 km, 14-20 ms
signatures.tscm: Legacy-but-common consumer/hobby RC control on FrSky Taranis/Horus/X-series radios — GFSK FHSS hopping across 2.4 GHz, moderate rate. Extremely widespread on older camera/hobby platforms. Narrow hopping bursts; distinguish by FrSky's specific hop cadence. Pairs with analog video typically. [in stock Pluto range and B210 range]

signatures.name: Wi-Fi FPV drone — combined control+video over 802.11 (2.4 GHz, ~20 MHz)
signatures.mode: 802.11 b/g/n Wi-Fi carrying app control + MJPEG/H.264 video (toy/mini drones)
signatures.tscm: Cheap phone-app 'spy' drones and mini quads run a soft-AP: standard ~20 MHz 802.11 OFDM with bursty beacon+data frames on a Wi-Fi channel (1/6/11). Looks EXACTLY like an ordinary Wi-Fi AP — the drone tell is a hidden/odd SSID (often vendor-named) plus a live high-bitrate video stream from a moving source. The hardest class to distinguish from benign Wi-Fi. [in stock Pluto range (2.4 GHz) and B210 range]

signatures.name: Wi-Fi FPV drone — combined control+video over 802.11 (5.8 GHz, ~20-40 MHz)
signatures.mode: 802.11 a/n/ac Wi-Fi soft-AP carrying control + video, 5 GHz
signatures.tscm: Same Wi-Fi-drone concept on 5 GHz (5.2 or 5.8 GHz) for cleaner spectrum/HD — 20 or 40 MHz 802.11 OFDM, bursty frames. Indistinguishable from a 5 GHz home AP by RF shape; identify via SSID/OUI and moving-source video. Common on mid-tier consumer camera drones' Wi-Fi mode. [above stock Pluto 3800 MHz (5.2/5.8 GHz) — B210 or modded Pluto + 5 GHz front end]

signatures.name: 1.2 / 1.3 GHz analog FM video downlink (long-range FPV)
signatures.mode: Analog FM composite video, sub-2 GHz long-range VTX (popular 1256/1280 MHz)
signatures.tscm: Long-range analog video for penetration/distance — a fat continuous FM carrier on 1080-1360 MHz (1256 and 1280 MHz most common), ~17-18 MHz occupied, 0.1 mW-800 mW. Distinct band from 5.8 GHz so its own row. Overlaps GPS L2 (1227), amateur 23 cm, and ATC/DME — a fat FM video carrier here is a strong drone tell. Favoured by longer-range/covert builds. [in stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz covers 1.2/1.3 GHz) and B210 range]

signatures.name: 900 MHz analog FM video downlink (long-range FPV, rare)
signatures.mode: Analog FM composite video on 900 MHz ISM, long-range
signatures.tscm: Least-common analog video band (big antennas, limited gear) but exists for max range/penetration — fat continuous FM carrier around 900-960 MHz. Heavy overlap with 900 MHz ISM (LoRa, cordless, cellular guard bands); a wide FM video-shaped carrier is the tell. Rare but a genuine distinct signature. [in stock Pluto range (900 MHz) and B210 range]

signatures.name: MAVLink telemetry radio — SiK 915 MHz (GFSK FHSS, bidirectional data)
signatures.mode: GFSK frequency-hopping bidirectional MAVLink telemetry (SiK radio)
signatures.tscm: ArduPilot/PX4 autonomous surveillance platforms carry a separate SiK telemetry radio (RFD900, HolyBro, 3DR-style) — GFSK FHSS on 915 MHz (433/868 regional), narrow ~250-500 kHz hops carrying bidirectional MAVLink (position, mission, camera). Distinct from control-link RC: it's a data/telemetry channel, often present alongside an ELRS/Crossfire stick link. Signals autonomous/waypoint ops. [in stock Pluto range (915 MHz) and B210 range]

signatures.name: MAVLink telemetry radio — 433 MHz variant (GFSK FHSS)
signatures.mode: GFSK FHSS bidirectional MAVLink telemetry, 433 MHz ISM (EU/global builds)
signatures.tscm: Same SiK/RFD telemetry link on the 433 MHz ISM band (common on non-US and export builds). Narrow GFSK hops around 433.05-434.79 MHz. Overlaps LPD433, ham 70 cm, car-key and weather-sensor traffic — the drone tell is continuous bidirectional data cadence tied to a moving platform. [in stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz covers 433 MHz) and B210 range]

device_classes.device_class: Covert body-worn transmitters & miscellaneous covert data links
device_classes.summary: This class covers the "wire" a person carries and adjacent low-profile covert data links, as distinct from fixed room bugs. On the air these break into four families: (1) classic crystal/PLL narrowband-FM analog body wires spread across the traditional surveillance segments - low-VHF ~30-50 MHz, 88-108 MHz (parasitic on FM broadcast), 108-136 MHz aircraft band, the "hot" 135-174 MHz law-enforcement/wireless-mic segment, 174-216 MHz, the very common 315/433/868 MHz ISM sub-GHz band, and UHF 380-512 MHz; (2) narrowband SSB/AM covert links (rarer, favored for range/low power); (3) digital/encrypted body wires in the 902-928 MHz ISM and 2.400-2.4835 GHz ISM bands, typically FHSS or narrow digital carriers with AES; and (4) burst / store-and-forward data bugs that digitize, compress, and dump audio in short bursts, including GSM/LTE cellular exfiltration. The key TSCM insight is that band + channel width + modulation + duty is the signature, not the make. A stock PlutoSDR (325-3800 MHz) reaches almost everything from 325 MHz up (including the extremely common 433/868 MHz ISM bugs) EXCEPT low-VHF (30-50 MHz) and the 88-108/108-136/135-325 MHz range, which need the AD9364 frequency-extension mod or a downconverter/upconverter; the B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) covers all of these natively (except below 70 MHz). The hardest targets are the intermittent SSB wires and the burst/store-and-forward devices, which are silent 99%+ of the time and demand long unattended spectrum logging rather than a walk-through sweep. Major honest caveat: nearly every band here is shared with legitimate LMR, wireless mics, IoT, cordless devices, remote controls, and cellular - analysis is about isolating an unexplained emitter near the protectee, not about a modulation being inherently hostile.

confirm_steps: Demodulate every suspect narrowband VHF/UHF/ISM carrier as FM (and also as USB/LSB for the SSB case) and listen: recovering live room/body audio, or hearing your own test tone/rustle correlated with the protectee's movement, confirms a voice wire. A carrier with LMR trunking control, CTCSS/DCS-only idle, or a short periodic data protocol (keyfob/TPMS/telemetry) is NOT a covert wire.

Localize with a near-field probe / directional antenna and RSSI: walk toward the suspected wearer or fixture - a covert wire's signal rises sharply within a meter or two. A signal that does NOT localize to the protected person/space is almost certainly a licensed background emitter.

Cross-check the frequency against licensed LMR/FCC ULS and known site systems: an FM/P25 voice carrier on a channel with no license on record and no operational reason to be at this location is the flag.

For 315/433/868 MHz suspects specifically, discriminate on DUTY: legitimate ISM devices (remotes, TPMS, sensors) transmit brief periodic bursts, while an audio wire holds a continuous voice-bearing carrier - a persistent carrier on 433.92 MHz near the protectee is a strong flag.

For 900 MHz / 2.4 GHz / 5.8 GHz digital suspects: capture IQ and inventory every legitimate device (Wi-Fi APs, BT/BLE, Zigbee, wireless mics, cordless). Anything left over after accounting for known devices - especially a carrier that tracks a person's movement - warrants teardown/physical search.

For FHSS suspects, use max-hold / persistence over minutes to reveal the hop comb across the full ISM band, then estimate hop rate and dwell; compare against known BT/BLE and cordless patterns to isolate an unexplained hopper.

For burst / store-and-forward and scheduled cellular exfil: run UNATTENDED wideband logging for 24-72 h with event capture; look for an isolated digital burst that repeats on a fixed schedule (e.g. every N hours) with no human activity behind it.

For GSM/LTE 'bug' suspects: use near-field cellular detection - identify a transmitting cellular emitter co-located with the protectee/room that has no legitimate phone/hotspot explanation; corroborate with a physical search of AC units, power strips, chargers, and outlets.

Confirm any find physically: RF localization narrows the location, but a TSCM confirmation is the recovered device in hand, not a spectral peak. Photograph, do not power-cycle, and preserve for chain of custody.

Demodulate every suspect narrowband VHF/UHF carrier as FM (and also as USB/LSB for the SSB case) and listen: recovering live room/body audio, or hearing your own test tone/rustle correlated with the protectee's movement, confirms a voice wire. A carrier with LMR trunking control, CTCSS/DCS-only idle, or a data protocol is NOT a covert wire.
false_positive_overlap: 150-174 MHz and 380-512 MHz narrowband FM voice is overwhelmingly legitimate business/public-safety LMR - a covert wire looks identical in modulation; only lack of signaling + localization + no-license separates them.
88-108 MHz carriers are almost all licensed FM broadcast; parasitic wires hide precisely by resembling them.

315/433/868 MHz ISM audio wires share the band with a huge population of keyfobs, TPMS sensors, weather stations, garage/gate remotes, and low-power telemetry - the discriminator is a continuous voice-bearing carrier vs. the brief periodic bursts of legit ISM devices.
174-220 MHz and 470-608 MHz overlap legitimate professional wireless microphones (theater, church, AV) - a body wire and a lav mic are the same signature.
900 MHz encrypted-digital and FHSS signatures are shared with Shure/Phenyx-class digital wireless mics, LoRa, cordless phones, SCADA telemetry, and IoT.
2.4 GHz digital and FHSS body wires are drowned in Wi-Fi, Bluetooth/BLE, Zigbee, RC, baby monitors, and video links - the most false-positive-prone band on the list.
5.8 GHz covert A/V overlaps 5 GHz Wi-Fi and FPV drone video.
GSM/LTE covert links are indistinguishable on spectrum from any nearby legitimate phone, hotspot, tablet, or wearable - near-field localization is the ONLY separator.
P25/DMR covert kits share their exact signature with legitimate encrypted public-safety and business digital radio.
Burst/store-and-forward blocks can resemble routine scheduled IoT check-ins, meter reads, or telemetry beacons.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Prioritize by how the target hides in TIME and BAND, not by exotic modulation. The continuous analog FM wires (VHF/UHF and the very common 315/433/868 MHz ISM bugs) are the easiest catch and should fall out of any competent walk-through sweep - the work there is discrimination (is this carrier a licensed LMR channel, a legit ISM burst, or an unexplained continuous wire near my protectee?), which means FM/SSB demod + localization + duty analysis + a license cross-check, never a bare peak. The genuinely hard members of this class are the ones that are silent almost all the time: SSB voice-operated wires (narrow, only present on speech), and above all the burst / store-and-forward and scheduled cellular-exfil bugs. Those defeat a one-pass sweep by design and require unattended 24-72 h wideband logging with scheduled-burst anomaly detection - build that logging mode into the app, because a real-time matcher alone will miss them. For every ISM-band digital suspect, the correct workflow is inventory-and-subtract: enumerate all legitimate emitters, then investigate the residue, especially any emitter whose RSSI tracks a person. Encryption (AES on P25/DMR and the 900 MHz/2.4 GHz digital wires) means you will confirm the SIGNATURE, never the content - set expectations accordingly. Reach: a stock Pluto (325-3800 MHz) misses the entire low-VHF/FM-broadcast/108-325 MHz swath where a large share of classic body wires live (and just misses 315 MHz), but DOES cover the extremely common 433/868 MHz ISM bugs - either add the AD9364 frequency-extension mod, pair a cheap RTL-SDR for a 24-1700 MHz first look, or use the B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) which covers everything here except below 70 MHz and 5G mmWave. Above 6 GHz is out of B210 entirely (not a concern for this class except mmWave 5G exfil). Finally, per TSCM firms, GSM/LTE bugs are cited as near-impossible without proper near-field cellular gear - flag to the client that a stock SDR sweep is necessary but not sufficient for cellular exfil, and recommend a dedicated near-field cellular detector as a companion tool.

signatures.name: Low-VHF analog FM body wire (30-50 MHz)
signatures.mode: Narrowband FM (crystal or free-running), 30-50 MHz low band
signatures.tscm: Single narrow FM carrier, 5-16 kHz deviation, voice audio recovered on FM demod. Older/foreign kits and long-range rural wires used this band for propagation. Carrier drifts with body movement/temperature on free-running units; crystal units are stable. [OUT of stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz) - needs AD9364 mod/downconverter or an HF/low-VHF front end. Below B210's 70 MHz floor too - requires a separate low-band receiver.]

signatures.name: FM-broadcast-band parasitic body wire (88-108 MHz)
signatures.mode: Wideband/narrowband FM hiding inside/adjacent to commercial FM broadcast
signatures.tscm: Cheap wires deliberately sit on or between FM stations so a normal FM radio can monitor them and they hide in broadcast clutter. Look for an unexpected carrier in a guard channel between stations, or a weak local signal much stronger near the protectee than the licensed station would be. Often free-running (audible drift). [OUT of stock Pluto range - needs AD9364 mod. In range for B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz). A cheap RTL-SDR also covers this band and is the fast first-look tool.]

signatures.name: Aircraft/VHF-gap analog body wire (108-136 MHz)
signatures.mode: Narrowband FM (occasionally AM) in the 108-136 MHz band
signatures.tscm: Classic surveillance segment noted as dense with devices. Any FM voice carrier here is anomalous because the licensed band is aeronautical AM - an FM voice bug stands out on the demod. Narrow (~12-16 kHz) carrier with recovered room/body audio. [OUT of stock Pluto range - needs AD9364 mod. In range for B210.]

signatures.name: Low-threat narrowband FM body wire, 135-150 MHz ('HOT' segment)
signatures.mode: Narrowband FM, 11.25/12.5 kHz channel, crystal or PLL
signatures.tscm: One of the densest historical body-wire/wireless-mic segments. Precise crystal/PLL carrier, 12.5 kHz-wide, clear voice on FM demod, no CTCSS/DCS or LMR signaling on a raw covert wire (distinguishes it from a licensed LMR channel that carries tones/PL). Fixed carrier that moves with the wearer's position (RSSI varies as the body moves). [OUT of stock Pluto range (below 325 MHz) - needs AD9364 mod. In range for B210.]

signatures.name: Analog FM body wire, 150-174 MHz VHF LMR segment
signatures.mode: Narrowband FM, 12.5 kHz (post-narrowbanding) or legacy 25 kHz
signatures.tscm: The core law-enforcement/professional body-wire band. Voice FM carrier, 12.5 kHz per FCC narrowbanding; legacy kits still 25 kHz-wide. Distinguish covert wire from licensed VHF LMR by absence of trunking control/PL tone and by localization to the protectee. Sub-audible CTCSS may be present on kits that use a squelch tone. [OUT of stock Pluto range (below 325 MHz) - needs AD9364 mod. In range for B210.]

signatures.name: Analog FM covert link, 174-216 MHz (high-VHF/TV band edge)
signatures.mode: Narrowband/medium FM in the high-VHF (old TV 7-13 / wireless-mic) band
signatures.tscm: Body wires and wireless mics extend up to ~220 MHz. Post-DTV this band is quieter, so an unexplained voice FM carrier is conspicuous. 15-25 kHz wide, voice on demod. Overlaps legitimate professional wireless-mic gear. [OUT of stock Pluto range (below 325 MHz) - needs AD9364 mod. In range for B210.]

signatures.name: Sub-GHz ISM covert audio wire (315 / 433 / 868 MHz)
signatures.mode: Narrowband FM (analog) or 2FSK/GFSK (digital) on 315/433.92/868 MHz ISM channels
signatures.tscm: The single most common cheap covert-audio-bug band worldwide - documented on TSCM threat-frequency lists. 433.92 MHz especially is packed with sub-$20 module-based analog FM and low-rate FSK audio wires; 315 MHz (US remotes) and 868 MHz (EU ISM) are the neighbors. Narrow carrier, voice on FM demod for analog units; digital units show a narrow 2FSK/GFSK carrier. Overlaps a huge population of legitimate 315/433/868 MHz keyfobs, TPMS, weather sensors, garage/gate remotes, and low-power telemetry - the discriminator is a CONTINUOUS voice-bearing carrier (bugs stream; most legit ISM devices burst briefly and periodically). [IN stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz) for 433/868 MHz; 315 MHz sits just below the 325 MHz Pluto floor and needs the AD9364 mod (or an RTL-SDR first look). All IN range for B210.]

signatures.name: Narrowband SSB/AM covert voice link (VHF/UHF)
signatures.mode: SSB (USB/LSB) or reduced-carrier AM, ~2.7-3 kHz voice
signatures.tscm: Rare but used where max range from minimal power/battery is needed - SSB puts all power in a 3 kHz-wide sideband, so the emission is very narrow and easy to miss with a coarse FFT. No carrier peak in SSB (suppressed carrier); shows as a narrow ~3 kHz smear that only appears when the wearer speaks (voice-operated). Demodulate as USB/LSB to recover intelligible speech. Frequency-agile hand-tuned units drift. [Partly in Pluto range where the carrier sits in 325-3800 MHz; VHF instances need the AD9364 mod. In range for B210 across the whole span (above 70 MHz). Narrow BW demands fine FFT resolution (small RBW) and patient dwell to catch.]

signatures.name: UHF analog FM body wire, 380-470 MHz
signatures.mode: Narrowband FM, 12.5 kHz, crystal/PLL, UHF surveillance band
signatures.tscm: Very common modern covert wire band (better antenna efficiency at body size than VHF). Precise narrow FM carrier, voice on demod, no LMR trunking/PL. Overlaps heavily with UHF business/public-safety LMR and covert police kits (Motorola XTS-class covert radios live here) - localization and 'no license on file' reasoning required. [IN stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz) and B210. Fully reachable with stock hardware.]

signatures.name: UHF analog FM body wire, 470-512 MHz
signatures.mode: Narrowband FM, 12.5 kHz, upper-UHF T-band segment
signatures.tscm: Same as the 380-470 wire but in the T-band shared with legacy public-safety/business LMR in major metros. Narrow FM voice carrier; distinguish from licensed LMR by lack of signaling and by RF localization to the person. [IN stock Pluto range and B210.]

signatures.name: P25 / digital-voice covert body wire (VHF/UHF)
signatures.mode: C4FM/CQPSK P25 Phase 1 (or DMR 4FSK) digital voice, often AES-256
signatures.tscm: Covert LEO kits (e.g. XTS2500-class covert radios) transmit encrypted P25/DMR. 12.5 kHz channel, characteristic 4-level FSK/C4FM constellation and ~4800 sym/s framing (P25 Phase 1 C4FM is literally a 4-level FSK on transmit; also demodulatable as CQPSK); encrypted payload is noise-like after the sync but the framing/duty is regular. PTT-driven so intermittent. Encryption blocks content recovery but the signature (band, 12.5 kHz, C4FM/4FSK, digital sync) is detectable. [UHF instances (380-512) IN stock Pluto/B210 range; VHF instances (136-174) need the AD9364 mod on Pluto, native on B210.]

signatures.name: 900 MHz ISM digital/encrypted body wire (narrow-channel)
signatures.mode: Narrow digital carrier (GFSK/PSK) in 902-928 ISM, often AES
signatures.tscm: Fixed-channel (non-hopping) digital wire sitting on one 900 MHz ISM channel. ~100-300 kHz wide digital carrier, flat noise-like spectrum, continuous while active. Shares the band with 900 MHz digital wireless mics (Shure ULX-D style), LoRa, cordless phones, and IoT - overlap is heavy. [IN stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz) and B210. Fully reachable.]

signatures.name: 900 MHz ISM FHSS digital/encrypted body wire (hopping)
signatures.mode: Frequency-hopping spread spectrum, GFSK, AES-encrypted, ~50-100 hops across 902-928
signatures.tscm: Hops pseudo-randomly across the whole 26 MHz ISM band; on a persistence/max-hold display it paints the entire band with a comb of short dwells. No single stable carrier - the giveaway is many brief bursts filling 902-928 with a regular hop rate. Overlaps cordless phones, some SCADA/telemetry, and hopping wireless mics. [IN stock Pluto range and B210, but capturing all hops needs the full 26 MHz span - stock Pluto (~20 MHz usable IQ) can't see the whole band in one shot; step/scan or use B210's wider capture. Max-hold sweeping recommended over single-dwell IQ.]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz ISM narrow-channel digital/encrypted body wire
signatures.mode: Narrow digital carrier (GFSK/QPSK/OQPSK), ~1-2 MHz, AES-encrypted digital audio
signatures.tscm: Fixed-channel 2.4 GHz digital wire (Endoacustica-class encrypted 2.4 GHz kits, ~500 m range). 1-2 MHz-wide noise-like digital carrier parked on one channel; continuous while transmitting. Massive false-positive overlap with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, Zigbee, wireless mics, RC, and video links - this is the single most crowded band on the list. [IN stock Pluto range (up to 3800 MHz) and B210 (up to 6 GHz). Reachable, but the crowded band means IQ + localization is essential, not just a peak.]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz ISM FHSS/adaptive-hopping digital body wire
signatures.mode: Frequency-hopping (Bluetooth-style adaptive or proprietary) GFSK, encrypted
signatures.tscm: Hops across the 2.4 GHz band like Bluetooth/BLE but carries a covert audio payload. On max-hold it fills 2400-2483.5 with short 1 MHz bursts. Nearly indistinguishable from legitimate Bluetooth/BLE traffic on spectrum alone - must correlate hop pattern/persistence with the presence of a person and rule out paired devices. [IN stock Pluto/B210 range. Same wide-span capture limitation as 900 MHz FHSS - step-scan or wide B210 capture; single 20 MHz Pluto IQ window misses most hops.]

signatures.name: 5.8 GHz ISM digital/encrypted body or video-audio wire
signatures.mode: Wideband digital (OFDM/QPSK) 5.8 GHz encrypted audio/video link
signatures.tscm: Higher-band covert kits (encrypted A/V transmitters) that moved up to 5.8 GHz to escape 2.4 GHz congestion. Wide (several-MHz to 20 MHz) OFDM/digital carrier, noise-like, continuous. Overlaps 5 GHz Wi-Fi, FPV drone video, and cordless. [OUT of stock Pluto range (>3800 MHz). IN B210 range (up to 6 GHz) - reachable only on the B210 front end, not stock Pluto.]

signatures.name: Burst / store-and-forward digital audio bug (VHF/UHF)
signatures.mode: Compressed digital burst (FSK/PSK), stored audio dumped in short packets
signatures.tscm: Digitizes and compresses audio, holds it, then transmits a brief burst - representative example ~3.6 s burst once every 6 hours. Silent >99% of the time, so a walk-through sweep almost never catches it. On a spectrogram it appears as an isolated rectangular block of digital energy at a fixed frequency, then nothing. Detection requires long unattended waterfall logging with event capture. [UHF bursts IN stock Pluto/B210 range; VHF bursts (130-325) need AD9364 mod on Pluto, native on B210. The real constraint is TIME/dwell (unattended logging), not front-end reach.]

signatures.name: Burst / store-and-forward bug in 900 MHz / 2.4 GHz ISM
signatures.mode: Compressed digital burst in ISM band (GFSK/DSSS), store-and-forward
signatures.tscm: Same store-and-forward behavior but hiding in ISM traffic, where a brief data burst is indistinguishable from routine IoT/Wi-Fi chatter. Short (sub-second to seconds) digital packets on a scheduled interval. Effectively invisible without correlating a repeating scheduled burst against an otherwise-quiet protected space. [IN stock Pluto range (to 3800) and B210. Requires long unattended logging and anomaly/schedule detection, not a single sweep.]

signatures.name: GSM / 2G cellular covert audio link (voice-call bug)
signatures.mode: GMSK GSM uplink burst, 200 kHz channel, TDMA framing
signatures.tscm: GSM 'bug' auto-answers or dials out and streams room/body audio over a normal cell call. Uplink is a 200 kHz GMSK carrier (GMSK is a form of FSK/MSK) with GSM's ~4.6 ms TDMA burst structure and 217 Hz frame buzz. Extremely common, cited by TSCM firms as impossible to find without correct gear. Near-field detection (a phone/module transmitting from the protectee's body/room with no legitimate reason) is the tell. [GSM-850/900/1800/1900 uplinks all IN stock Pluto range (325-3800) and B210. Reachable, but distinguishing a bug's uplink from any nearby legitimate phone requires near-field/localization, not spectrum ID alone.]

signatures.name: LTE / 4G-5G cellular covert data exfiltration link
signatures.mode: SC-FDMA/OFDM LTE uplink, 1.4-20 MHz resource blocks, encrypted
signatures.tscm: Modern cellular exfil bug (audio or bulk data) using an LTE module - cited as the most prevalent way to move large data covertly over an unmonitored protocol. Uplink SC-FDMA, variable-width resource-block allocation, bursty when streaming/uploading. Indistinguishable from any legitimate phone/hotspot on spectrum alone; near-field localization to an unexplained emitter is required. [Sub-3.8 GHz LTE bands IN stock Pluto range and B210; n77/n78 (3.3-4.2 GHz) partly exceed Pluto's 3.8 GHz ceiling, and mmWave 5G above 6 GHz is OUT of B210 entirely. For the common sub-3.5 GHz bands, reachable.]

device_classes.device_class: Cellular GPS vehicle/asset trackers (magnetic, OBD-II, hardwired, battery-covert) — detected on the cellular UPLINK only, not the GPS side
device_classes.summary: Cellular GPS trackers are the single most common covert TSCM find on vehicles, yet the GPS/GNSS receiver inside them EMITS NOTHING — it only listens to satellites. The ONLY detectable RF signature is the cellular UPLINK the device uses to phone location home: a 2G/3G/4G-LTE/LTE-M/NB-IoT/5G transmission on a standard carrier uplink band. The defining detection problem is DUTY CYCLE: most modern trackers are interval reporters (PSM/eDRX low-power modes) that sleep silent for minutes to hours (or a full day), wake for a few hundred ms to a few seconds, GNSS-fix, attach, dump a location packet, and drop back to sleep. Between reports the device is RF-invisible — a single spectrum sweep will almost always miss it. Effective detection requires DWELL: park the vehicle, leave a wideband monitor watching the LTE/NB-IoT uplink bands for a full report interval (30+ min, ideally hours), and catch the periodic burst. A moving vehicle in real-time (10-60 s update) mode is far easier to catch because it transmits almost continuously. The signatures below are organized by radio-access technology and uplink band because that is what the SDR actually sees; the thousands of tracker models collapse into this handful of on-air signatures. REACH NOTE: every uplink band in this class sits inside a stock ADALM-Pluto's 325-3800 MHz range EXCEPT 5G NR mid-band n77/n78 at 3.3-3.8 GHz, which is at or just past the Pluto's 3800 MHz upper edge. There is no sub-325 MHz gap — the lowest band here is 600 MHz. A B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) covers everything in this class, including n78.

confirm_steps: Understand the core trap first: the GPS receiver emits nothing. You are hunting the CELLULAR UPLINK, and most trackers sleep between reports. A one-pass sweep proves nothing — absence of signal is NOT absence of device.

DWELL, don't sweep. Park the vehicle in a quiet RF spot, set the SDR to watch the candidate uplink band(s) with a waterfall, and leave it running for at least one full report interval — 30-60 min minimum, ideally several hours or overnight — to catch a periodic burst. Log timestamps of any repeating bursts; a fixed inter-burst interval (e.g., every 60 s, 5 min, 60 min, 24 h) is the tracker tell.

Force the device to talk: drive the vehicle. Motion often triggers real-time/frequent reporting on motion-activated trackers, converting a silent interval reporter into a near-continuous uplink you can catch. Watch the LTE low-band (600/700/850) and AWS/PCS uplinks while moving.
Provoke a report: some units report on ignition-on, geofence-cross, or a shock/tow event. Cycle ignition, move the vehicle a few hundred meters, or bump it, and watch for a correlated uplink burst.

Correlate direction with a directional antenna / near-field probe. Once you see a repeating uplink burst, use a directional log-periodic or a near-field sniffer to walk the signal to its source location on the vehicle (wheel wells, bumpers, under seats, OBD-II port, behind trim, inside battery/fuse box).

Physically inspect the highest-probability mounts regardless of RF: OBD-II port (plug-in trackers report here and are trivial to find), under-hood/battery for hardwired units, steel surfaces for magnetic units (frame rails, wheel wells, inside bumpers, tow hitch, under spare tire).

Distinguish tech on the waterfall: 200 kHz constant-envelope GMSK TDMA burst = 2G; ~5 MHz noise-like = 3G WCDMA; SC-FDMA variable-RB burst = LTE Cat-1; ~1.4 MHz short burst = LTE-M; a single ~4 kHz pip or <180 kHz burst on a fixed raster = NB-IoT.

Rule out the phone/host vehicle: a modern car has its OWN embedded cellular modem (telematics/eCall) and the occupant's phone, both of which transmit on these exact bands. Confirm the burst source is NOT the head unit/TCU or a phone before declaring a covert tracker — geolocate the emitter physically.
For NB-IoT/single-tone suspects, use maximum FFT resolution (narrow RBW) and the longest dwell you can afford — these devices may transmit for only seconds per day.
If the suspected band is 5G n78 (3.5 GHz) or you need >3.8 GHz headroom, switch from a stock Pluto to a B210 (or equivalent) to stay in range and get enough instantaneous bandwidth.
false_positive_overlap: The occupant's own smartphone transmits on the IDENTICAL LTE/5G uplink bands — this is the #1 false positive. Any cellular uplink burst could be a phone in the vehicle.

The vehicle's own embedded telematics/eCall modem (GM OnStar, Ford, Toyota, BMW, etc.) is a factory-installed cellular tracker on these same bands — legitimate but indistinguishable on the air from a covert unit without physical location.

Legitimate fleet/insurance/teen-driver/usage-based-insurance (UBI) trackers and OBD-II dongles use exactly these signatures and are often installed with the owner's consent — presence of a cellular tracker is not proof of illicit surveillance.

Nearby vehicles, pedestrians, and buildings all radiate the same uplink bands — in any populated area the LTE uplink spectrum is crowded, so a random burst is meaningless without repetition + physical geolocation.
IoT devices unrelated to tracking (smart tolls, connected sensors, cellular alarm panels, e-readers, some smartwatches) also use LTE-M/NB-IoT bursts.
2G GMSK bursts in-band can be from femtocells, IMSI-catchers, or test equipment rather than a tracker.

In the US, a live 2G/3G uplink cannot connect to a shut-down macro network, so such a signal is more likely lab gear, a private base station, or a jammer than a functioning tracker — do not over-index on it as a tracker find.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Operationally, cellular GPS trackers are the highest-yield vehicle TSCM find and the easiest to physically discover (OBD-II and magnetic units especially), yet the WORST to find by RF sweep because of duty cycle. Do not rely on the spectrum analyzer alone: a thorough physical search of the OBD-II port, battery/fuse box, wheel wells, bumpers, undercarriage, and cabin (steel surfaces for magnets) will find more trackers than any single RF pass. Use RF to CONFIRM and geolocate an emitter and to catch battery units with no obvious mount. The decisive technique is a long dwell on the carrier uplink bands (a spectrum-monitoring recording left running through at least one report interval, better overnight) plus motion/ignition provocation to force a report. Always physically geolocate any suspicious uplink burst before concluding — the occupant's phone and the car's own factory modem live on the same frequencies. Interval/PSM/eDRX devices can be silent for a full day; the honest client message is that a clean single sweep does NOT clear a vehicle, and a combined physical + long-dwell RF search over time is required. Reach: everything in this class is in-band for a B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz); a stock ADALM-Pluto (325-3800 MHz) covers all 2G/3G/4G/LTE-M/NB-IoT and 5G low/mid bands EXCEPT it strains at the very top for 5G n78 (3.5-3.8 GHz) — use a B210 there. There is no sub-325 MHz gap in this class (lowest band is 600 MHz).

signatures.name: 2G GSM uplink 850 MHz (GMSK, legacy/imported tracker)
signatures.mode: GSM/GPRS uplink, GMSK modulation, 200 kHz carrier, 577 us TDMA bursts
signatures.tscm: Classic ~270 kbps GMSK constant-envelope burst on a 200 kHz channel; TDMA frame structure (8 timeslots, 4.615 ms frame). Location reports appear as short GPRS uplink bursts. In the US the 850 MHz 2G networks are shut down (2022) so a live signal here means an imported/rest-of-world tracker roaming, a private/femto GSM, or a stale device that will never connect — but MANY cheap trackers sold worldwide are still 2G-only. [In stock Pluto reach (824-849 MHz well within 325-3800 MHz). Easily seen on Pluto/B210.]

signatures.name: 2G GSM uplink 900 MHz (E-GSM, rest-of-world)
signatures.mode: GSM/GPRS uplink, GMSK, 200 kHz carrier, TDMA bursts
signatures.tscm: Same GMSK/200 kHz TDMA burst signature as 850 but on the European/global GSM-900 uplink. This is the single most common band for cheap imported magnetic trackers and covert 2G bugs worldwide. Live in most of the world; dead in the US/Canada. A GMSK burst here on a US vehicle = imported 2G tracker (or GSM audio bug). [In stock Pluto reach (880-915 MHz).]

signatures.name: 2G GSM uplink 1800 MHz (DCS, rest-of-world)
signatures.mode: GSM/GPRS uplink, GMSK, 200 kHz carrier, TDMA
signatures.tscm: GSM-1800 uplink; same GMSK/TDMA burst signature. Overlaps the LTE B3 uplink range, so a 200 kHz GMSK burst distinguishes it from wideband LTE SC-FDMA occupying the same spectrum. Global 2G band. [In stock Pluto reach (1710-1785 MHz).]

signatures.name: 2G GSM uplink 1900 MHz (PCS, legacy North America)
signatures.mode: GSM/GPRS uplink, GMSK, 200 kHz TDMA
signatures.tscm: North American PCS 2G uplink. Shut down in the US (2022). A live GMSK burst here is almost certainly NOT a working tracker connecting to a macro network — but note private/portable GSM base stations and some jammers/IMSI-catchers use this band, so treat with suspicion. [In stock Pluto reach (1850-1910 MHz).]

signatures.name: 3G UMTS/WCDMA uplink 850 MHz (legacy)
signatures.mode: UMTS/HSPA uplink, WCDMA, 5 MHz wide, spread-spectrum
signatures.tscm: 5 MHz-wide noise-like WCDMA spread-spectrum uplink. During a data session (location upload) it looks like a ~5 MHz raised noise floor rather than discrete bursts. US 3G is fully shut down (2022) so a live UMTS uplink means an imported/roaming device. Older 3G trackers exist but are being retired globally. [In stock Pluto reach (824-849 MHz); the 5 MHz occupied width fits within Pluto's ~20-56 MHz instantaneous BW.]

signatures.name: 3G UMTS/WCDMA uplink 1900/2100 MHz (Band 1/2, global)
signatures.mode: UMTS/HSPA uplink, WCDMA 5 MHz, spread-spectrum
signatures.tscm: WCDMA uplink on the global 2100 MHz (Band 1, 1920-1980 up) or NA 1900 band. 5 MHz noise-like spread-spectrum energy during upload. Still live in parts of the world; US retired. Distinguish from LTE by lack of SC-FDMA/OFDM structure and the characteristic ~3.84 Mcps spreading. [In stock Pluto reach (1920-1980 MHz).]

signatures.name: 4G LTE Cat-1 uplink, low-band 600 MHz (n71/B71)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, FDD, 1.4-10 MHz allocations
signatures.tscm: T-Mobile 600 MHz uplink (B71/n71), uplink 663-698 MHz (downlink 617-652). SC-FDMA single-carrier uplink; occupied width depends on resource-block grant (as narrow as 1.4 MHz for a small location packet). Low band = best building/foundry penetration, favored for deep-concealment trackers. Bursty during report, silent otherwise. [In stock Pluto reach (663-698 MHz). Nothing in this class goes below 325 MHz, so no sub-Pluto gap here.]

signatures.name: 4G LTE Cat-1 uplink, low-band 700 MHz (B12/B13/B14/B17)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, FDD, 1.4-10 MHz
signatures.tscm: 700 MHz uplink (AT&T B12/B17, Verizon B13, FirstNet B14). SC-FDMA uplink bursts. This is one of the MOST common bands for US covert trackers (Verizon/AT&T low-band coverage). Occupied bandwidth scales with data — a periodic location dump is often a very narrow (1.4-3 MHz) short burst. [In stock Pluto reach (698-716 MHz).]

signatures.name: 4G LTE Cat-1 uplink, 850 MHz (B5/B26)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, FDD
signatures.tscm: Cellular 850 (B5, uplink 824-849) / extended 850 (B26, uplink 814-849) LTE uplink. SC-FDMA. Shares spectrum with legacy 2G/3G 850 — distinguish LTE by SC-FDMA structure and variable RB-based bandwidth vs. the fixed 200 kHz GMSK of GSM. Common tracker band. [In stock Pluto reach (814-849 MHz).]

signatures.name: 4G LTE Cat-1 uplink, PCS 1900 (B2/B25)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, FDD
signatures.tscm: 1900 MHz PCS LTE uplink (B2, 1850-1910) / extended PCS (B25, uplink 1850-1915, includes G-block). SC-FDMA bursts. Widely used mid-band tracker uplink. [In stock Pluto reach (1850-1915 MHz).]

signatures.name: 4G LTE Cat-1 uplink, AWS 1700 (B4/B66)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, FDD
signatures.tscm: AWS uplink 1710-1755 (B4) / extended AWS-3 to 1780 (B66, uplink 1710-1780). SC-FDMA. Overlaps GSM-1800 range — again SC-FDMA vs GMSK distinguishes. Very common US tracker uplink (T-Mobile/AT&T AWS). [In stock Pluto reach (1710-1780 MHz).]

signatures.name: 4G LTE Cat-1 uplink, 2100 (B1, global)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, FDD
signatures.tscm: Global IMT 2100 uplink (B1). SC-FDMA. Primary band for rest-of-world/imported LTE trackers. Shares range with UMTS B1 — LTE has SC-FDMA structure, UMTS is spread noise. [In stock Pluto reach (1920-1980 MHz).]

signatures.name: 4G LTE Cat-1 uplink, 2600 (B7, global capacity)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, FDD, up to 20 MHz
signatures.tscm: 2600 MHz (B7, uplink 2500-2570) uplink, common global capacity band. Wider RB grants possible (up to 20 MHz). Less common for low-data trackers but present on high-report-rate/real-time devices. [In stock Pluto reach (2500-2570 MHz); 20 MHz occupied width may exceed Pluto instantaneous BW — capture center burst or use B210 for full span.]

signatures.name: LTE-M (Cat-M1) uplink, 1.4 MHz narrowband, half-duplex
signatures.mode: LTE-M Cat-M1, SC-FDMA within 1.4 MHz (6 RB) narrowband, HD-FDD
signatures.tscm: THE dominant modern low-power tracker uplink. Cat-M1 confines uplink to a 1.4 MHz (6 resource-block) narrowband anywhere within a host LTE band (600/700/850/AWS/PCS). Half-duplex FDD. Uses PSM/eDRX so it sleeps for the whole report interval then wakes for a short SC-FDMA burst. Very narrow, very brief — easy to miss on a sweep. Look for a ~1.4 MHz-wide short-lived SC-FDMA burst inside a carrier uplink block, repeating on a fixed interval. [In stock Pluto reach across all host bands (663-1980 MHz here). Narrow 1.4 MHz burst fits Pluto BW easily; the challenge is TIME not frequency.]

signatures.name: NB-IoT (Cat-NB1/NB2) uplink, single-tone 3.75 kHz
signatures.mode: NB-IoT SC-FDMA single-tone, 3.75 kHz subcarrier, 200 kHz channel raster
signatures.tscm: Extremely narrow single-tone uplink (3.75 kHz spacing, ~4 kHz occupied; single-tone can also use 15 kHz spacing) inside a 180 kHz NB-IoT resource block (200 kHz channel raster). Used by ultra-low-power multi-year asset trackers (container/trailer/equipment). Reports as infrequently as once/day, so it is on-air for seconds per DAY. This is the HARDEST signature in the class to catch — you need a narrow-RBW dwell on the specific NB-IoT anchor carrier for a very long window. A single near-CW pip that briefly appears and vanishes. [In stock Pluto reach by center frequency, but 4 kHz occupied width demands very narrow RBW/high FFT resolution and long dwell — a detection-time and resolution problem, not a tuning-range one.]

signatures.name: NB-IoT uplink, multi-tone (3/6/12 tones, 15 kHz)
signatures.mode: NB-IoT SC-FDMA multi-tone, 15 kHz subcarriers, up to 180 kHz within 180 kHz RB / 200 kHz carrier
signatures.tscm: NB-IoT multi-tone uplink using 15 kHz spacing — 3, 6, or 12 tones, up to ~180 kHz occupied (12 tones fill the full 180 kHz resource block within the 200 kHz NB-IoT carrier). Multi-tone always uses 15 kHz spacing. Slightly easier to see than single-tone due to wider footprint, but still infrequent bursts from a sleeping device. Look for a sub-200 kHz SC-FDMA burst on a fixed NB-IoT raster, repeating on a long interval. [In stock Pluto reach by frequency; still a long-dwell detection problem due to the interval duty cycle.]

signatures.name: 5G NR uplink, low-band n71/n5/n25/n26 (NSA/SA)
signatures.mode: 5G NR uplink, CP-OFDM or DFT-s-OFDM (SC-FDMA), 15/30 kHz SCS, FDD low-band
signatures.tscm: Newest RedCap/5G trackers use NR low-band uplink (n71 600, n5 850, n25/n26 PCS/ext-850). Uplink is DFT-s-OFDM (SC-FDMA-like) or CP-OFDM. For small location packets the grant is narrow, but NR numerology (30 kHz SCS) and SSB timing distinguish it from LTE. Still rare in consumer trackers as of 2026 but emerging (RedCap = the 5G answer to Cat-1/Cat-M). [In stock Pluto reach (663-915 MHz).]

signatures.name: 5G NR uplink, mid-band n77/n78 (3.3-3.8 GHz)
signatures.mode: 5G NR TDD uplink, CP-OFDM/DFT-s-OFDM, 30 kHz SCS, wide channel
signatures.tscm: C-band / 3.5 GHz NR uplink (TDD, so uplink and downlink share the channel in time). Unlikely for a low-power covert tracker (power-hungry, poor penetration) but possible on high-bandwidth real-time asset units. TDD structure and wide occupied bandwidth are the tells. [At/just past the stock Pluto's 3800 MHz upper edge — n78 tops out at 3800 (right at the limit) and performance degrades near the edge. Use a B210 (up to 6 GHz) for reliable capture. This is the ONLY band in the class that strains a stock Pluto's range.]

signatures.name: Real-time / high-rate LTE uplink (continuous-ish reporting mode)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, frequent RRC-connected reporting (1-60 s updates)
signatures.tscm: Not a new band — a DUTY-CYCLE variant. When a tracker is in live/real-time mode (theft-in-progress, active surveillance, powered OBD-II/hardwired device with no battery constraint), it stays RRC-connected and transmits every 1-60 s or holds the connection continuously. This is the EASY case: near-continuous SC-FDMA uplink energy on a carrier band while the vehicle moves. A powered OBD-II or hardwired tracker has no reason to sleep, so it often lives here. Rising, repeating uplink bursts that correlate with vehicle motion are the signature. [In stock Pluto reach across listed bands. This mode is the one you CAN catch in a normal sweep because it is on-air often.]

device_classes.device_class: Cellular "SIM" audio bugs (call-to-listen / auto-dial covert GSM/LTE/5G eavesdropping devices)
device_classes.summary: A cellular SIM bug is a stripped-down cellphone/modem (transmitter + mic + SIM, often a battery) hidden in an everyday object. The operator calls the bug's number (call-to-listen) or the bug auto-dials/streams on VOX (auto-dial), and the room audio rides the mobile network — unlimited range. On the air, a SIM bug IS a phone: it emits exactly the standard cellular UPLINK signature for whatever radio it carries. So the signatures below are just the cellular uplink emissions the SDR can see, one row per genuinely distinct band x channel-width x modulation x duty combination. There is NO magic "bug waveform" — the entire TSCM problem is duty/behavior/context, not modulation. Two facts dominate reach: (1) a stock PlutoSDR tops out at 3800 MHz (325-3800 stock; the AD9364 firmware/clock mod extends ~70 MHz-6 GHz, unguaranteed/uncalibrated at the edges), so most low/mid cellular UPLINK (GSM 850/900, LTE/5G bands below 2.7 GHz uplink) is in reach, but n41 (2496-2690 TDD) and 5G n77/n78 (3.3-3.8/3.3-4.2 GHz) sit at or past the stock edge; (2) a B210 covers 70 MHz-6 GHz so it reaches all sub-6 cellular uplink but NOTHING mmWave (5G FR2 24-40 GHz) is reachable by either radio. Critically, a SIM bug transmits on the UPLINK band (mobile-to-tower), which is the LOWER of each FDD duplex pair — sweep the uplink sub-bands, not the downlink you'd see from a cell tower (for TDD bands like n41/n78, uplink and downlink share the frequency and alternate in time). The device is receiver-quiet between transmissions: a dormant call-to-listen bug is RF-silent until called, so a single spectrum snapshot misses it — you must either dwell for a periodic registration/paging-response burst or force it to transmit (call the suspected number / create noise to trip VOX) while watching the uplink bands.

Endoacustica GPS car tracker with audio recorder + GSM bug (combined locator + listen)
'USB wall charger' GSM bug — SIM inside a functional USB mains charger (spy-shop form-factor family)
'Mains plug / socket' voice-activated GSM SIM listening device (mains-plug form factor)
GSM power strip / triple-plug / power-adapter bug (concealment form-factor family)
OBD2 GPS tracker with built-in microphone + GSM/GPRS listen-in (Amazon 'OBD2 GPS Tracker Spy' family) — plugs into car OBD-II port
Spy Equipment UK 'GSM Car Bug' (hardwired 12 V car listen device)
SpyEquipmentUK GSM listening device line

confirm_steps: Identify the UPLINK sub-bands for your region and dwell there, not the downlink — an FDD bug transmits mobile-to-tower on the LOWER band of each duplex pair (e.g. US: GSM850 UL 824-849, PCS UL 1850-1910, AWS UL 1710-1755, 700 UL 698-716/777-787). For TDD bands (B41/n41 2496-2690, C-band NR n78 3.3-3.8) uplink shares the frequency with downlink and appears only in the UL time slots.

Do NOT rely on a single snapshot. A call-to-listen bug is RF-silent until called. Either (a) dwell for minutes to catch periodic registration/tracking-area-update/paging-response bursts, or (b) actively provoke: make noise / motion to trip VOX auto-dial, or call the suspect SIM number if known, while watching the uplink waterfall for a synchronized burst.

Correlate emission with audio/motion you create. Clap or speak on a schedule; a VOX auto-dial bug's uplink bursts will track your stimulus. This behavioral correlation is far more decisive than any modulation ID.

Use near-field to localize: with a small loop/antenna, walk the room while the device is transmitting (provoked) — signal strength peaks at the concealment (power strip, charger, OBD port, wall socket, clock). A non-linear junction detector (NLJD) finds the dormant electronics even when RF-silent; combine RF + NLJD + physical search.

Match the burst envelope to the generation: spiky 577 us/4.615 ms pulse train = 2G GSM (200 kHz); smooth continuous 5 MHz haystack = 3G WCDMA; scheduled intermittent SC-FDMA blocks (1.4-20 MHz) = LTE/5G; a razor-thin 180 kHz or 3.75/15 kHz sliver with long gaps = NB-IoT alert bug.

Physically inspect the likely hosts: open/inspect power strips, USB chargers and charging cables, OBD-II port, wall sockets, lamps, clocks, power banks — look for a SIM card, an unexplained antenna, or a mic port. Presence of a SIM in a device that has no reason to have one is near-conclusive.

Check reach before trusting a 'clean' sweep: confirm whether your Pluto is stock (325-3800 MHz — misses 5G n78/n77 C-band UL at/above 3.8 GHz) or AD9364-modded (~70 MHz-6 GHz, uncalibrated at the edges). For C-band/3.5 GHz uplink prefer a B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz). Note B41/n41 (2.5-2.69 GHz) IS within stock Pluto range. Neither radio sees mmWave FR2 (24-40 GHz).

If you can, capture with an IMSI-catcher-aware tool or a cellular scanner to log which ARFCN/EARFCN/NR-ARFCN and cell the device attaches to; an unexpected device registering to a tower from inside the swept room is strong corroboration (note legal constraints on active cellular interception).
Consider a portable RF-shielded (Faraday) bag/room test: seal the suspect object; if a previously-heard uplink burst pattern disappears when the object is bagged, the emitter is inside it.
false_positive_overlap: Every ordinary cellphone, smartwatch, and tablet in or near the room emits the exact same uplink signatures — there is NO modulation-level difference between a bug and a legitimate phone. Discrimination is entirely behavioral/contextual.

Legitimate IoT devices flood the same bands: cellular GPS trackers, fleet OBD dongles, alarm-panel cellular backups, smart meters, e-readers, connected cars, cellular routers/hotspots, vending telemetry, medical alert pendants — all transmit GSM/LTE/Cat-M/NB-IoT uplink bursts identical to a bug.

NB-IoT/LTE-M smart meters and sensors produce exactly the thin narrowband low-duty sliver a store-and-forward alert bug produces — a 180 kHz sliver alone means nothing without locating it to a suspicious host.

A powered-off or dormant bug produces ZERO RF, so absence of a signal never clears a room — this is a false-NEGATIVE trap, the mirror of the false-positive problem. Pair RF with NLJD + physical search.

2G GSM bursts can be confused with any legacy M2M/telematics still on 2G (alarm dialers, older trackers) — though in networks that have sunset 2G, a live GSM uplink is anomalous enough to be a useful flag by itself.
Nearby legitimate femtocells/small cells and Wi-Fi-calling handoffs can create uplink activity uncorrelated with room occupants, mimicking an auto-dial bug's 'unattended' pattern.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Bottom line for the matcher: do not try to fingerprint a 'bug waveform' — there isn't one. A SIM bug is a phone; the rows above are just standard cellular UPLINK emissions. The matcher should (1) key on the UPLINK sub-bands (LOWER half of each FDD pair; UL time-slots for TDD bands like n41/n78), (2) score DUTY/behavior and location-correlation, not modulation identity, and (3) never mark a room clean on RF alone. The two decisive discriminators are: an uplink emitter that transmits without a human handling a phone (unattended auto-dial / call-to-listen), and an uplink emitter co-located with an object that has no business containing a cellular radio (power strip, USB charger, OBD dongle, wall socket, clock). Provoke-and-correlate (VOX/noise, or calling the SIM) plus near-field localization plus NLJD plus physical teardown is the real workflow; the SDR sweep only narrows band and confirms activity. Reach reality: stock Pluto (325-3800 MHz) covers all US low/mid uplink including B41/n41 2.5-2.69 GHz but stops at the 5G C-band (n78) edge; a B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) covers all sub-6 uplink; neither sees mmWave FR2. Legally, capturing/decoding cellular content is regulated (Wiretap Act / local equivalents) — passive spectrum energy detection and localization are the safe TSCM moves; leave content interception to law enforcement.

signatures.name: GSM 850 uplink (2G, GMSK)
signatures.mode: GSM/GMSK, 0.3 GMSK, 270.833 kbps, TDMA 8 slots/frame
signatures.tscm: Classic 200 kHz GMSK carrier over the full 824-849 MHz uplink block. TDMA burst = 577 us active in a 4.615 ms frame; a call-to-listen bug in a call holds one uplink timeslot, so you see a strong ~577 us pulse recurring every 4.615 ms (one slot lit) — the textbook GSM 'buzz' (this is the interference heard in nearby speakers). Frequency-hopping may smear the carrier across the band. Look for the periodic burst envelope, not a steady tone. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: GSM 900 / E-GSM uplink (2G, GMSK)
signatures.mode: GSM/GMSK, TDMA 8 slots/frame, E-GSM extension 880-890
signatures.tscm: Same 200 kHz GMSK / 577 us-per-4.615 ms TDMA burst as GSM850; primary 2G band outside the Americas and the default for cheap quad-band bug modules. Bursty uplink pulse train is the tell. E-GSM adds the 880-890 lower extension (P-GSM proper is 890-915). [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: GSM 1800 (DCS) uplink (2G, GMSK)
signatures.mode: GSM/GMSK 1800, TDMA 8 slots/frame
signatures.tscm: Identical GMSK/TDMA structure at 1.8 GHz. Quad-band bug modules (850/900/1800/1900) fall back here where 900 is congested. Same 200 kHz bursty envelope, just an octave up. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: GSM 1900 (PCS) uplink (2G, GMSK)
signatures.mode: GSM/GMSK 1900, TDMA 8 slots/frame
signatures.tscm: North American 2G PCS uplink. Same 200 kHz GMSK burst. Note most US carriers have sunset 2G/GSM — a live GSM uplink burst in the US is itself suspicious (few legit phones still use it), which paradoxically makes cheap 2G bugs EASIER to flag on-air even though the SIM may fail to register. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: UMTS/WCDMA 850 uplink (3G, band 5)
signatures.mode: WCDMA/UMTS, QPSK/HPSK, 3.84 Mcps, 5 MHz carrier
signatures.tscm: 5 MHz-wide spread-spectrum, noise-like flat-topped block, near-continuous during a call (power-controlled, so amplitude breathes with fast TPC). No TDMA burst structure — a smooth 5 MHz haystack distinguishes 3G from 2G's spiky bursts. 3G is being decommissioned in many regions, so a live WCDMA uplink is increasingly anomalous. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: UMTS/WCDMA 1900/2100 uplink (3G, bands 2/1)
signatures.mode: WCDMA/UMTS, 3.84 Mcps, 5 MHz carrier (B2 1850-1910 UL, B1 1920-1980 UL)
signatures.tscm: Same 5 MHz spread-spectrum haystack as 3G850, at PCS/IMT uplink. Continuous-during-call, power-controlled. B1 uplink 1920-1980 is the global 2100 IMT pairing; B2 1850-1910 the US PCS pairing. Distinguish from LTE by the fixed 5 MHz width and absence of LTE's SC-FDMA resource-block granularity. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LTE uplink 1.4 MHz (SC-FDMA, narrow)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, 1.4 MHz (6 RB), QPSK/16QAM
signatures.tscm: Smallest LTE channel. SC-FDMA (single-carrier FDMA) uplink looks like a contiguous OFDM-ish block but with lower PAPR. Scheduled: the phone only transmits when granted resource blocks, so uplink is BURSTY/intermittent tied to talk activity + periodic SRS/PUCCH. Freq range spans low LTE UL bands (B12/13/14/17 ~700, B5 850, B8 900). A tiny 1.4 MHz block is common on low-cost IoT-grade bug modems. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LTE uplink 3-5 MHz (SC-FDMA)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, 3 MHz (15 RB) / 5 MHz (25 RB), QPSK/16/64QAM
signatures.tscm: Mid-width LTE uplink across low+mid bands (700/850/900/1700 AWS/1900/2100). Scheduled SC-FDMA — bursty envelope keyed to uplink grants; between talk you still see periodic PUCCH/SRS pips. The most common width for a modern 4G audio bug streaming compressed audio (needs little bandwidth). Width + SC-FDMA flatness + scheduled bursts distinguish from continuous 3G. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LTE uplink 10 MHz (SC-FDMA)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, 10 MHz (50 RB)
signatures.tscm: 10 MHz uplink allocation, low/mid bands incl. B7 2500-2570 UL, B4/AWS 1710-1755, B2/B25 1850-1915. Scheduled bursts. A 10 MHz bug is overkill for audio but common because it just uses whatever the carrier assigns. Wider haystack, same scheduled/bursty behavior. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LTE uplink 15-20 MHz (SC-FDMA, wide)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, 15 MHz (75 RB) / 20 MHz (100 RB)
signatures.tscm: Widest single-carrier LTE uplink. Same scheduled SC-FDMA bursts, just a 20 MHz-wide envelope. Reachable on low/mid uplink bands with stock Pluto/B210; the wide occupied bandwidth makes the intermittent grant bursts obvious on a waterfall. Note carrier aggregation can stack multiple such blocks. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LTE Band 7 / high mid uplink (2.5-2.57 GHz)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink B7 2500-2570 (FDD)
signatures.tscm: Called out separately because it is the top FDD LTE UPLINK band an operator commonly sees — still inside stock Pluto's 3800 MHz ceiling and B210's 6 GHz. Scheduled SC-FDMA bursts. Above this, TDD bands (n41) push uplink energy into the 2.5-2.69 GHz shared block. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LTE B41 / 5G n41 uplink (2.5-2.69 GHz, TDD)
signatures.mode: LTE/NR TDD B41/n41 2496-2690, SC-FDMA/DFT-s-OFDM uplink in the UL portion of the TDD frame, up to 100 MHz aggregate
signatures.tscm: TDD band: uplink and downlink share 2496-2690 MHz and alternate in time, so you see uplink energy only during the UL slots (bursty at the TDD frame cadence, typically a downlink-heavy DDDSU-type pattern). Still within stock Pluto's 3800 MHz ceiling and B210's 6 GHz — the summary's earlier phrasing that n41 sits 'at or past the stock edge' referred to reachability margin, but 2.5-2.69 GHz is comfortably below 3.8 GHz and fully sweepable. A common US mid-band for modern 4G/5G bug modems that grab whatever the carrier assigns. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LTE-M (Cat-M1) uplink 1.4 MHz
signatures.mode: LTE-M / eMTC, SC-FDMA within a 1.4 MHz (6 RB) narrowband, QPSK/16QAM
signatures.tscm: IoT variant of LTE confined to a 1.4 MHz narrowband inside a host LTE carrier. Very low duty — an IoT-grade auto-dial bug may register then transmit tiny bursts, with long dormant gaps and possible PSM (power-save mode) sleeping for minutes/hours. Coverage-enhancement repetition makes bursts LONGER and more repetitive than normal LTE. Easy to miss on a snapshot; needs long dwell. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: NB-IoT uplink 180 kHz / single-tone 3.75-15 kHz
signatures.mode: NB-IoT NPUSCH, SC-FDMA, 180 kHz carrier; single-tone 3.75 or 15 kHz, or multi-tone 15 kHz
signatures.tscm: The narrowest cellular uplink — a 180 kHz carrier, and in single-tone mode an astonishingly thin 3.75 kHz or 15 kHz sliver that looks almost like a CW-ish line on a waterfall. Extreme low duty with heavy repetition/coverage extension: transmissions can last seconds but occur rarely. NB-IoT can't carry a real-time voice call (too little throughput) so it appears on store-and-forward / trigger-alert bugs (motion/VOX SMS alert, short recorded-clip upload) rather than live listen. Very easy to overlook; a thin persistent sliver in an NB-IoT uplink deployment warrants dwell. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: 5G NR sub-6 (FR1) uplink, 5-20 MHz (CP-OFDM/DFT-s-OFDM)
signatures.mode: 5G NR FR1 uplink, DFT-s-OFDM or CP-OFDM, 15/30 kHz SCS, 5-20 MHz shown
signatures.tscm: NR uplink on low/mid FDD bands (n5 850, n8 900, n12/n71 600-700, n66/n2/n25 ~1.9 GHz) is reachable by stock Pluto (<3.8 GHz) and B210. Looks like a wider, more flexible LTE — scheduled bursty uplink, DFT-s-OFDM (single-carrier-like, low PAPR) for coverage. Distinguishing NR from LTE on a waterfall alone is hard; both are scheduled OFDM bursts. Treat as 'modern cellular uplink.' [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: 5G NR n77/n78 (C-band/3.5 GHz) uplink, TDD wideband
signatures.mode: 5G NR FR1 TDD n78 3300-3800 (n77 to 4200), CP-OFDM/DFT-s-OFDM, up to 100 MHz, 30 kHz SCS
signatures.tscm: C-band NR. TDD, so uplink and downlink share the frequency and alternate in time — you see uplink energy only in the UL portion of the TDD frame (bursty at the slot cadence). Very wide (up to 100 MHz). n78 sits AT the stock Pluto ceiling (3800 MHz) — effectively out of a stock Pluto and needs the AD9364 mod (or a B210); n77 3800-4200 is fully past the stock edge. A B210 (to 6 GHz) covers all of n77/n78. Most modern 5G phones/bugs will still fall back to sub-3 GHz bands, so you can often catch the same device lower down. [needs-AD9364-mod]

signatures.name: 5G NR FR2 mmWave uplink (24-40 GHz)
signatures.mode: 5G NR FR2 mmWave, 50-400 MHz carriers, beamformed
signatures.tscm: Listed for completeness / honesty: OUT OF RANGE for both a stock Pluto AND a B210 (both stop at 6 GHz). Highly beamformed and short-range; essentially never used by a covert audio bug (no cheap mmWave bug modules exist, and mmWave barely penetrates a wall/enclosure). Requires a dedicated mmWave front end / downconverter. Flag as not-reachable rather than sweepable. [above-6GHz-out-of-range]

device_classes.device_class: nRF24L01 / proprietary 2.4 GHz GFSK links (wireless HID, keystroke loggers, covert data)
device_classes.summary: This class is a family of low-cost, proprietary (non-Bluetooth, non-Wi-Fi) 2.4 GHz GFSK transceivers — Nordic nRF24L01/nRF24LE1/nRF24LU1+, MOSART, Signia, and Microsoft's 2.4G silicon — that live in the 2400-2525 MHz ISM band on a 1 MHz channel raster. On the air they are NOT distinguished by vendor or by product; a Logitech Unifying mouse, a MOSART keyboard, and a covert nRF24 keystroke logger all emit the SAME handful of PHY signatures. What genuinely differs on the air is the DATA RATE (which sets occupied bandwidth and FM deviation: 250 kbps ~ <300 kHz, 1 Mbps ~ 1 MHz, 2 Mbps ~ 2 MHz), the DUTY/hopping pattern (single fixed sniff channel vs. Enhanced ShockBurst ACKed micro-bursts vs. Logitech-style channel agility vs. adaptive multi-channel), and a few band-edge/whole-band-sweep behaviors. So the distinct signatures below are organized by PHY variant + emission pattern, not by brand. For TSCM this is a HIGH-VALUE covert-exfil class the starter catalog missed: a hardware keylogger with an nRF24 backhaul looks identical to a benign wireless mouse dongle, and the whole band is squarely inside a stock PlutoSDR's 325-3800 MHz tuning range (the 2400-2525 MHz band is fully reachable; the challenge is the ~2 MHz-wide, sub-millisecond bursts, not the tuning). CRITICAL false-positive note: this band is shared with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth/BLE, Zigbee, and thousands of ISM toys — a bare GFSK burst at 2.4 GHz is NOT by itself evidence of surveillance; it must be characterized by burst timing, channel behavior, and correlation with keyboard/mouse activity.
