confirm_steps: Confirm the burst is GFSK, not OFDM: on a persistence/waterfall display an nRF24 burst is a narrow (0.25-2 MHz) two-lobe FSK shape, NOT the flat 20 MHz Wi-Fi block. Measure occupied bandwidth to classify data rate: ~250-300 kHz => 250 kbps, ~1 MHz => 1 Mbps, ~2 MHz => 2 Mbps.

Check the center frequency against the nRF24 1 MHz raster (2400 + N MHz, N=0..124). Real nRF24 links sit on integer-MHz centers; a burst that lands exactly on 2400+N MHz and NOT on a Wi-Fi (2412/2437/2462) or BLE-advertising (2402/2426/2480) center is more suspicious.

Correlate with input activity: type on / move suspected wireless peripherals and watch whether bursts track keystrokes/mouse motion. A link whose bursts DO NOT correlate with any known peripheral, yet emits a steady heartbeat, is the covert-device profile.

Characterize duty/heartbeat cadence with a long-dwell persistence capture (seconds to minutes). Log inter-burst timing: a clock-like keep-alive (fixed period, present when idle) is a strong covert-link tell versus random ISM chatter.

Look for the auto-ACK reply burst: a data burst followed ~130-600 us later by a shorter burst on the SAME channel proves an active receiver is in range (Enhanced ShockBurst). Use direction-finding (B210 coherent RX or moving a directional antenna) to separate the transmitter location from the receiver location.
Watch for channel agility: over minutes, see whether a 1 MHz burst migrates across a channel subset (Logitech-style) or stays fixed. Migration + idle keep-alives = Unifying/MouseJack-class footprint.

Rule out known-good inventory: enumerate every legitimate wireless keyboard, mouse, presenter, barcode scanner, and game controller in the space FIRST, power them down one at a time, and confirm which bursts disappear. Any 2.4 GHz GFSK link that remains after all known peripherals are off is the item to run down physically.

For a full TSCM rig (beyond a pure spectral matcher), attempt protocol capture with an nRF24-capable receiver (CrazyRadio PA + tooling) — MOSART/KeySniffer and unencrypted Microsoft links leak keystrokes in the clear, which both confirms the device class and demonstrates the exfil risk.
Extend the scan window to at least 2525 MHz (not just the 2400-2483.5 Wi-Fi ISM band) so nRF24 channels 84-125 above the ISM edge are actually in view — well inside stock Pluto/B210 range.
Dwell long, or provoke: type on / move the suspect keyboard/mouse and watch for correlated <1 ms GFSK bursts. Idle nRF24 radios are silent, so a short sweep with no HID activity will show nothing.
Measure occupied bandwidth to split rates: ~1 MHz => 250 kbps or 1 Mbps; ~2 MHz => 2 Mbps. Then demod symbol rate to separate 250 kbps from 1 Mbps.
Demodulate/decode to confirm Enhanced ShockBurst framing (preamble + address + CRC). Presence in-band is NOT enough — GFSK bursts alias against BLE, Zigbee, and other ISM sources.
For injection tools (CrazyRadio/MouseJack): look for elevated-power GFSK bursts sweeping across many 1 MHz channels in rapid succession near a workstation, not a single fixed-channel link.

For KeySweeper-class loggers: the logger may be radio-silent on 2.4 GHz — hunt the separate exfil path (GSM 850/1900, Wi-Fi, LoRa) and physically inspect USB chargers/wall warts and anything plugged near the keyboard.
Treat unencrypted/plaintext keystroke traffic (KeySniffer MOSART/Signia class) as high-severity — decode a burst to check whether keystrokes are in the clear.
Set the Pluto to sweep 2400-2485 MHz (extend to 2525 to catch high nRF24 channels) with fast frame rate; a resting wireless keyboard shows near-nothing, so you must generate events.
Have the client type on / move each suspect peripheral and correlate: real HID bursts appear ONLY when the user acts. Bursts that appear with no user action = injection or a second radio -> escalate.

On the waterfall, classify the burst: clean two-lobe = GFSK (nRF24/MOSART/MS); flat noise-like spread = Cypress DSSS; hopping across many channels per event = Logitech Unifying FHSS; single fixed channel = MOSART/MS.
Enumerate USB receiver vendor/product IDs on the client machine (Logitech, MOSART 062A, Microsoft, Cypress) to map dongle to link type, since the on-air GFSK burst is otherwise ambiguous.

For a suspected KeySweeper-class logger: do NOT rely on the HID band. Physically inspect wall chargers, power strips, and USB pass-throughs, AND sweep for an out-of-band exfil uplink (GSM/LTE 700-1900, Wi-Fi 2.4/5, LoRa 915) that switches on around typing.
Confirm encryption exposure: identify any Microsoft pre-2011 XOR or MOSART unencrypted keyboard in the sensitive space and recommend swapping to a Bolt/BLE-AES or wired keyboard.
Use a dedicated nRF24 tool (Crazyradio + MouseJack/LOGITacker) only to positively fingerprint a link if the Pluto sweep is inconclusive; note this is beyond a stock Pluto's demod ability.
Zoom the SDR span across 2400-2525 MHz and look for narrow (~2 MHz) GFSK bursts; measure occupied bandwidth - ~2 MHz indicates the 2 Mbps variant, ~1 MHz indicates the standard 1 Mbps row.
Confirm bursty duty: capture IQ and verify short packetized on-air bursts with idle/ACK gaps (Enhanced ShockBurst), not continuous carrier and not wideband OFDM.
Watch for channel agility - note whether the burst stays on one 1 MHz-center channel or hops; log the exact center frequency.
Cross-check against known 2.4 GHz occupants: rule out Wi-Fi (20/40 MHz OFDM), BLE (1 MHz FHSS advertising on 2402/2426/2480), and classic BT (1600 hops/s) by bandwidth and hop pattern.

If keystroke-injection risk is suspected, corroborate with a dedicated nRF24 tool (Crazyradio PA + mousejack/scanner) to demodulate ShockBurst addresses - the SDR shows the signature; the nRF24 sniffer confirms protocol and device.
Correlate bursts with the target's use of a wireless mouse/keyboard or an unexplained USB nano-receiver during the sweep.
false_positive_overlap: Legitimate wireless mice, keyboards, trackpads, and presentation clickers — these ARE nRF24/MOSART/Microsoft-2.4G devices and produce byte-for-byte the same PHY signature as a covert logger. Presence of the signature is expected in almost any office; it is NOT by itself evidence of surveillance.

Wi-Fi (2412-2472 MHz, 20/40/80 MHz OFDM) overlaps the band but is far wider and flat-topped — easy to distinguish by bandwidth, but a narrow nRF24 burst can hide UNDER an active Wi-Fi channel and be masked on a low-resolution display.

Bluetooth / BLE — Bluetooth classic hops FHSS across 2402-2480 at 1 MHz spacing with 1 Mbps GFSK, which is genuinely close to nRF24 1 Mbps. Distinguish by the fast, structured hop pattern (BT) versus fixed-channel or slow-agility (nRF24), and by BLE's 2 MHz-spaced advertising channels (2402/2426/2480).
Zigbee / 802.15.4 (2405-2480, 2 MHz-wide O-QPSK) — similar burstiness and channel raster; distinguish by modulation shape (O-QPSK vs GFSK) and Zigbee's 5 MHz channel spacing.

Wireless game controllers, RF barcode scanners, wireless headsets/mics on proprietary 2.4G, drone/RC links (some use nRF24), and countless ISM 'toys' (weather stations that stray up, wireless doorbells, etc.) — many share the exact GFSK burst profile.
Microwave-oven leakage and other wideband ISM noise can raise the noise floor across the band and mask or mimic activity, causing false alarms on energy-only detectors.
BLE advertising/data (GFSK 1 Mbps/2 Mbps, ~1-2 MHz, bursty) — nearly identical spectral footprint; separate only by protocol decode
802.15.4 / Zigbee (OQPSK 2 MHz channels, periodic) — overlaps the 2 Mbps width
Legitimate wireless keyboards/mice you are not investigating (same silicon)
Wi-Fi 20 MHz bursts (much wider, easy to exclude by width)
RC/drone control links and hobby telemetry on nRF24-family radios
Microwave-oven leakage and other ISM noise (broadband, non-framed — excluded by demod)
MoCA/other spurs occasionally seen just above 2483.5 MHz
BLE advertising / connection bursts (1-2 MHz GFSK, same band, constant background in any modern space)
Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz OFDM (wide, but its energy floods the same channels and masks HID bursts)
Zigbee / Thread / 802.15.4 (2 MHz O-QPSK bursts on 2405-2480, look burst-like)
Legitimate wireless mice/keyboards/presenters — indistinguishable on RF from a KeySweeper logger; only user-action correlation separates them
Microwave oven leakage and other ISM noise near 2450 MHz
Bluetooth Classic frequency hopping (also hops the band, can be confused with Unifying FHSS)
RC toys/drones on 2.4 GHz GFSK (also nRF24-based in many cases)
Legitimate Logitech Unifying wireless mice and keyboards (same nRF24 link, 2 Mbps)
Generic 2.4 GHz non-Bluetooth wireless keyboards/mice with USB nano-receivers
Wireless presentation clickers/remotes
RC toys, drones (Crazyflie), and game controllers on nRF24
Industrial/hobby sensor telemetry links using nRF24L01+ at 2 Mbps
General 2.4 GHz ISM congestion (Wi-Fi/BLE/BT edges) can mask or be confused with short nRF24 bursts until bandwidth and duty are measured
device_classes.tscm_notes: Why this class matters and how to treat it: the covert-exfil risk is that a hardware keystroke logger or data bug using an nRF24/MOSART/Microsoft-2.4G link is SPECTRALLY INDISTINGUISHABLE from the wireless mouse dongle sitting next to it. You cannot flag this class on signature alone — every finding must be resolved by inventory subtraction (turn off all known peripherals) and behavioral correlation (does it track keystrokes? does it heartbeat when idle? does it have a receiver ACKing it?). The highest-signal covert tells are: (1) a steady idle keep-alive/heartbeat with no attributable peripheral, (2) a link that does not correlate with any known input device, and (3) presence of an auto-ACK reply proving a hidden receiver in range. Operationally: many of these links (MOSART/KeySniffer, older Microsoft, un-patched Logitech Unifying/MouseJack) are UNENCRYPTED or keystroke-injectable, so the same sweep that finds them can, with an nRF24 receiver, capture cleartext to prove exfil — a strong client deliverable, but only under proper authorization. Do NOT auto-classify a 2.4 GHz GFSK burst as a bug in a client report; describe it as 'proprietary 2.4 GHz peripheral-class link, attribution pending physical inventory,' and escalate only the un-attributable ones. Plain-language label for client-facing output: 'wireless keyboard/mouse-style 2.4 GHz link (could be a normal wireless mouse or a hidden keystroke logger — we confirm by elimination).'

signatures.name: nRF24 GFSK 1 Mbps — single fixed channel (classic sniff/link)
signatures.mode: 1 Mbps GFSK, ~160 kHz deviation, 1 MHz channel raster, sitting on one fixed channel (e.g. 2402/2405/2425). Enhanced ShockBurst packets: preamble + address + payload + optional auto-ACK.
signatures.tscm: ~1 MHz-wide GFSK blip that appears and vanishes on a FIXED center frequency, no hopping. Two-tone/GFSK spectral shape, not the flat-top of OFDM. Bursts are short (tens of microseconds to ~1 ms) and often paired (data burst immediately followed by a shorter auto-ACK burst on the same channel a few hundred microseconds later). This is the default nRF24L01+ 1 Mbps mode and the most common covert-link config. [stock-Pluto-reachable (2400-2525 MHz is inside 325-3800 MHz); the hard part is catching sub-ms bursts, not tuning — needs high sample rate / persistence display, not an SDR front-end mod]

signatures.name: nRF24 GFSK 2 Mbps — single fixed channel (high-rate exfil)
signatures.mode: 2 Mbps GFSK, ~320 kHz deviation, occupies ~2 MHz so needs 2 MHz channel spacing. Fixed-channel operation. Preferred where higher payload throughput is wanted (bulk keystroke/data exfil).
signatures.tscm: Wider (~2 MHz) GFSK burst — noticeably broader than the 1 Mbps signature and MUCH shorter in time for the same payload (2 Mbps empties a 32-byte payload in ~130 us). A covert logger dumping buffered keystrokes at 2 Mbps shows very brief, wide bursts. Distinguish from 1 Mbps by width; distinguish from Wi-Fi by the two-lobe GFSK shape and the fact that it is far narrower than a 20 MHz Wi-Fi channel. [stock-Pluto-reachable; the 2 MHz instantaneous bandwidth is trivial for Pluto's ADC — again the catch is time-resolution on short bursts]

signatures.name: nRF24 GFSK 250 kbps — long-range low-rate link
signatures.mode: 250 kbps GFSK (nRF24L01+ only), reduced deviation, occupies <300 kHz. Chosen for maximum range / link budget on covert links that trickle small data (keystrokes are low-bandwidth).
signatures.tscm: NARROW (~250-300 kHz) GFSK burst, distinctly thinner than the 1 MHz signature. Because low rate = better sensitivity/range, this is the mode a range-maximizing covert exfil device (e.g. keystroke logger phoning to a receiver in the next room) may pick. Bursts are longer in time than 1/2 Mbps for the same payload. A thin, brief FSK chirp mid-band that isn't Bluetooth (BLE adv is ~1-2 MHz and hops predictably) is a red flag. [stock-Pluto-reachable; narrow burst is actually EASIER to see than the wide/fast ones]

signatures.name: Logitech Unifying / channel-agile mouse-mouse-keyboard hop set
signatures.mode: 1 Mbps GFSK Enhanced ShockBurst but with Logitech channel agility: the link moves among a defined subset of channels (roughly 2402-2481 MHz region) to dodge interference; not a fast uniform FHSS, more of an as-needed channel change plus periodic keep-alive.
signatures.tscm: Same 1 MHz GFSK burst as the fixed-channel signature, but the center frequency MIGRATES over seconds/minutes and there are regular low-rate KEEP-ALIVE bursts even when the mouse/keyboard is idle. On a persistence/waterfall display you see a 1 MHz burst that reappears on a shifting set of channels. This is the canonical MouseJack-vulnerable footprint (Logitech, and by extension many Unifying-compatible loggers/injectors). [stock-Pluto-reachable across the whole 2402-2481 hop set; a wide-span waterfall (Pluto ~20-56 MHz instantaneous, or stepped sweep) is needed to watch the agility]

signatures.name: nRF24 / MOSART / Microsoft-2.4G adaptive multi-channel keep-alive
signatures.mode: 1 Mbps GFSK with device-driven channel selection and periodic keep-alive/beacon bursts, spread across a handful of channels. Covers MOSART (KeySniffer-class, unencrypted) and Microsoft 2.4G keyboards (KeySweeper-class) as well as generic nRF24 firmware that rotates channels.
signatures.tscm: Regular, clock-like short GFSK bursts (keep-alive/heartbeat) even with no user input — a planted covert device announcing presence to its receiver looks exactly like this. The heartbeat CADENCE (e.g. every few ms to every second) is a strong fingerprint and separates a live link from random ISM traffic. MOSART/KeySniffer devices notably transmit keystrokes UNENCRYPTED, so payload capture (out of scope for pure spectral matcher but relevant to a full TSCM rig) is possible. [stock-Pluto-reachable; the periodic-heartbeat detection favors a persistence display with long dwell rather than any front-end change]

signatures.name: nRF24 whole-band scanner / carrier-detect sweep (RPD)
signatures.mode: Not a data emission per se: an nRF24 acting as a channel scanner using Received Power Detector (RPD) steps its receiver across all 125 channels. Some covert devices also emit an unmodulated or lightly-modulated CARRIER during pairing/scan or as a constant-carrier test.
signatures.tscm: Either (a) a bare CW-like carrier parked on one nRF24 channel (pairing/constant-carrier mode, spectrally a single spike with no GFSK sidebands), or (b) evidence of a device probing many channels. A steady unmodulated spike on an exact 1 MHz-raster nRF24 frequency (2400 + N MHz) that is NOT a Wi-Fi/BLE center is suspicious. Rare in normal operation, common in bench/test or misconfigured covert hardware. [stock-Pluto-reachable; a parked carrier is the single EASIEST thing to spot on any SDR]

signatures.name: Logitech Unifying 2.4 GHz frequency-hopping HID link
signatures.mode: nRF24-based GFSK 1/2 Mbps, adaptive frequency hopping across the band, bursty on HID event
signatures.tscm: nRF24-family GFSK bursts that HOP pseudo-randomly across many 1 MHz channels rather than sitting on one. Watch a wide 2402-2474 span and you see single short bursts appearing on different channels per event. This hopping is what MouseJack targets; Unifying is the most common enterprise dongle.

signatures.name: MOSART unencrypted 2.4 GHz GFSK HID link
signatures.mode: GFSK ~1 Mbps, typically 1-3 fixed channels (not full hopping), unencrypted, bursty
signatures.tscm: MOSART Semiconductor HID transceivers (HP, Anker, Kensington, Insignia, EagleTec, RadioShack, etc.) tend to camp on a small fixed set of channels rather than hop. Plaintext keystrokes on the air (KeySniffer class). RF looks like a generic nRF24 burst; the fixed-channel behavior + vendor USB ID is the discriminator.

signatures.name: Cypress WirelessUSB DSSS 2.4 GHz HID link
signatures.mode: DSSS (spread-spectrum), ~1 MHz per channel, channel hopping for coexistence, bursty on HID event
signatures.tscm: NOT GFSK. Cypress WirelessUSB (-LS/-NL) uses direct-sequence spread spectrum, so the burst shows a flatter, noise-like spread main lobe rather than the clean FSK two-tone shape. Distinguishes Cypress-based mice/keyboards from all the nRF24/MOSART GFSK peripherals on the same band.

device_classes.device_class: Classic analog RF audio bugs / body wires / wireless microphones — continuous FM (and AM/subcarrier variant) carriers across low-band VHF through UHF
device_classes.summary: This class is the oldest and still most common eavesdropping threat: a microphone driving a simple RF oscillator that radiates a continuous carrier the operator listens to on a receiver/scanner. On the air, the distinguishing signature is a narrow (or wide) FM carrier that is UP CONTINUOUSLY whenever powered, with audio-correlated deviation — you can demodulate it and hear the room. Signatures differ meaningfully by (a) BAND segment the oscillator lands in, (b) DEVIATION/bandwidth: narrowband FM (~10-16 kHz occupied, crystal/quartz-stable) vs. standard narrow FM (~25-35 kHz occupied) vs. WIDE-deviation FM (broadcast-style, ~150-200+ kHz occupied), (c) crystal/PLL-locked (rock-steady) vs. free-running LC (visibly DRIFTS and warms), and (d) modulation flavor: plain FM, AM (rare/older), or a subcarrier/voice-inversion-scrambled FM. A thousand kit-bug PCBs that all free-run in 88-108 MHz are ONE signature; a quartz UHF 433 bodywire is a genuinely DIFFERENT signature. Rows are split by band x deviation-class x crystal/free-running because those are what change the detector's search. REACH is the defining operational constraint for this class. Two front-end floors matter: (1) a stock PlutoSDR's guaranteed floor is 325 MHz — so ALL of 30-216 MHz (low-band, the 88-108 FM-kit bug, mid-VHF pro bugs, 174-216 bodywires) is out of stock-Pluto reach and needs the AD9364 tuning-range unlock or a separate low-VHF front end (RTL-SDR/Airspy). Note the AD9364 trick only reaches down to ~70 MHz, so it recovers 88-216 MHz but NOT 30-50 MHz low-band. (2) The USRP B210's floor is 70 MHz, NOT DC — so the 30-50 MHz low-band row is BELOW the B210 too and needs an external downconverter/transverter even on the B210. Everything 70 MHz and up is in B210 reach; everything 325 MHz and up (UHF bodywires, 433/470/512/608) is in stock-Pluto reach; nothing in this class is above 6 GHz so neither the Pluto's 3.8/6 GHz ceiling nor the B210's 6 GHz ceiling is a limit here.

confirm_steps: FM-demodulate the suspect carrier and listen: if you hear the room (your own voice/tap test correlates), it is almost certainly an audio bug, not a data or telemetry signal.
Do a physical stimulus/correlation test: make a distinctive noise or play a tone in the room and watch the carrier's deviation (FM) or amplitude (AM) track it live on the waterfall.
Watch the carrier over 5-15 minutes: a free-running bug DRIFTS/creeps in frequency as it warms; a crystal/PLL bug stays rock-steady. Records which signature row applies.

Rule out legitimate emitters: real FM-broadcast stations carry program audio + RDS/pilot; real land-mobile/ham carries licensed traffic and keys intermittently. A 24/7 unlicensed carrier with live room audio and no ID is the flag.
If FM-demod yields harsh/inverted (Donald-Duck) audio or a subcarrier tone, test a voice-inversion de-scrambler — confirms the scrambled-bug signature.

For sub-325 MHz suspects a stock Pluto cannot see, confirm with an AD9364-unlocked Pluto or an HF/VHF-capable receiver (RTL-SDR/Airspy) before clearing 70-325 MHz. For 30-50 MHz low-band, note EVEN the B210 and AD9364-unlocked Pluto fall below ~70 MHz — use an external downconverter/transverter or an HF/low-VHF receiver. Do NOT declare 30-216 MHz clean off any stock-Pluto sweep, and do not assume the B210 covers 30-50 MHz.
Power-down correlation: if you can kill room mains / suspect device power and the carrier disappears, that localizes a mains- or device-powered bug (battery bugs will persist).
Direction-find / near-field sniff to localize: signal strength should peak at the physical device; combine with an NLJD for powered-off or dormant electronics.
false_positive_overlap: Legitimate FM broadcast stations and their SCA subcarriers in 88-108 MHz — the single biggest false-positive source; discriminate by RDS/pilot + program audio.
Licensed land-mobile, business, ham, and public-safety NBFM in 108-174 and 400-470 MHz — intermittent keyed traffic, not continuous room audio.

Legitimate professional wireless microphones and IEM/in-ear monitor systems (174-216, 470-608 MHz) at churches, venues, AV setups — same hardware families as bodywires; presence is normal, the question is whether it belongs there.

Baby monitors, wireless intercoms, and old analog cordless phones (some 43-50 MHz, 46-49 MHz, 900 MHz) — continuous or push-to-talk audio carriers that look bug-like; note the 43-50 MHz ones sit in the low-band row that no stock SDR here reaches.
Wireless assistive-listening and tour-guide systems (72-76 MHz, 216-217 MHz) — continuous FM audio by design.
Analog wireless-camera AUDIO subcarriers overlap the wide-deviation-FM row — but those belong to the video-bug class; don't double-count.
RC/telemetry and other free-running LC oscillators that drift like a bug but carry no voice on demod.

Broadcast-band imaging/harmonics and receiver LO leakage that can mimic a weak carrier — verify with a stimulus/correlation test; note AD9364-unlocked Plutos operated out of spec are especially prone to spurs/images that masquerade as carriers.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Analog FM audio bugs are the highest-prior threat in a residential/family-law or SMB sweep because they are cheap, ubiquitous, and continuously radiating — the easiest thing to actually catch on a spectrum sweep IF you can reach the band. The operational gap for this kit is REACH, and it has two floors, not one. (1) A stock PlutoSDR's guaranteed floor is 325 MHz, so ALL of 30-216 MHz — the 88-108 MHz FM-band kit bug (the single most common hobby bug), mid-VHF pro bugs, and 174-216 MHz bodywires — is OUT of stock-Pluto reach. The AD9364 tuning-range unlock recovers roughly 70-325 MHz (so it does reach 88-216 MHz), but a stock-Pluto-only sweep MISSES the most common hobby bug entirely; this must be disclosed and covered with an AD9364-unlocked Pluto or a cheap RTL-SDR/Airspy for 24-1700 MHz before a band is called clean. (2) The 30-50 MHz low-band row is below ~70 MHz and therefore below the AD9364 unlock floor AND below the B210's 70 MHz floor — NEITHER a modded Pluto NOR a B210 reaches it directly; it needs an external downconverter/transverter or an HF/low-VHF receiver. The earlier claim that the B210 'covers 100% of this class' is wrong for exactly this row. The 325 MHz-and-up UHF bug rows (especially quartz 433/450-460 MHz micro-transmitters) are squarely in stock-Pluto reach and are where a Pluto-based tool is strongest. Nothing in this class is above 6 GHz, so no upper-frequency ceiling (Pluto 3.8/6 GHz or B210 6 GHz) is a limit here — the constraint is entirely at the low end. Best single discriminator across every row: a continuous, unlicensed carrier that FM/AM-demodulates to live room audio and correlates with a stimulus test — everything else (drift vs. stability, deviation width, scramble) just sorts it into the right signature row. Guard against over-alerting: professional wireless mics and FM broadcast are the dominant benign look-alikes and should be characterized (is it expected in this room?) rather than auto-flagged. When running an AD9364-unlocked Pluto below its 325 MHz spec floor, expect degraded sensitivity, images, and spurs — corroborate any sub-325 MHz hit rather than trusting a single spur.

signatures.name: Low-band VHF free-running FM audio bug (30-50 MHz)
signatures.mode: Narrow FM, free-running LC oscillator, continuous carrier
signatures.tscm: Single unmodulated-looking carrier that blooms with audio-correlated FM deviation (~25-30 kHz). Free-running: peak drifts/wanders with temperature over minutes. Historically common for older/pro low-band body transmitters. Demodulate FM and you hear the room. [OUT of stock Pluto range (below 325 MHz floor). Also BELOW the AD9364 unlock floor (~70 MHz) AND below the B210's 70 MHz floor — needs an external low-VHF downconverter/transverter or an HF/low-VHF-capable receiver on EITHER platform. This is the one row no stock Pluto, AD9364-modded Pluto, or B210 reaches directly.]

signatures.name: FM-broadcast-band kit bug, free-running (88-108 MHz)
signatures.mode: Wide-ish FM, free-running LC, continuous carrier, hides in/near commercial FM
signatures.tscm: The classic cheap 'spy bug' / FM-transmitter PCB. Carrier sits between or on top of broadcast stations; audio-correlated deviation, often wide (broadcast-style ~75-100+ kHz deviation, ~150-200 kHz occupied). Free-running so it DRIFTS and warms. Tell: a 'station' with no RDS, no program-audio ID, that carries live room audio and moves. [OUT of stock Pluto range (below 325 MHz). Recoverable with AD9364 tuning-range unlock (reaches ~70 MHz) or a low-VHF front end (RTL-SDR/Airspy). IN B210 range (above its 70 MHz floor). Most common hobby bug — prioritize an alt/mod front end for it.]

signatures.name: FM-broadcast-band kit bug, crystal/PLL-locked (88-108 MHz)
signatures.mode: Narrow FM, quartz/PLL-stabilized, continuous carrier, no drift
signatures.tscm: Same band as the free-running kit bug but ROCK-STEADY center frequency (quartz/PLL). Narrower deviation (~10-16 kHz occupied). Distinguished from a real broadcast station by absence of RDS/pilot + presence of live room audio. Stability is the discriminator vs. the free-running row. [OUT of stock Pluto range (below 325 MHz). Recoverable with AD9364 unlock or low-VHF front end. IN B210 range (above 70 MHz floor).]

signatures.name: Mid-VHF FM audio bug / land-mobile-style (108-174 MHz)
signatures.mode: Narrowband FM (~11-16 kHz occupied), crystal or free-running, continuous
signatures.tscm: Common 'professional' bug region — tucks into aircraft/land-mobile/business VHF. NBFM on 12.5/25 kHz channel spacing. TSCM literature flags 150-174 MHz as a hostile eavesdropping segment. Discriminator: continuous unlicensed carrier carrying room audio where no legitimate voice traffic should persist 24/7. [OUT of stock Pluto range (below 325 MHz). Recoverable with AD9364 unlock or low-VHF front end. IN B210 range (above 70 MHz floor).]

signatures.name: High-VHF wireless-mic-band bodywire (174-216 MHz)
signatures.mode: Wideband FM (~±48-75 kHz deviation), companded, continuous — pro wireless-mic style
signatures.tscm: Professional wireless-mic / bodywire hardware (Swintek/Vega/older Sennheiser-style) operating in the VHF TV-band mic segment. Wide FM with compander tell-tales. Continuous carrier with live audio; may carry a pilot tone for squelch. Occupied BW (~180-200 kHz) separates it from the narrowband bug rows. [OUT of stock Pluto range (below 325 MHz). Recoverable with AD9364 unlock or low-VHF front end. IN B210 range (above 70 MHz floor).]

signatures.name: UHF bodywire / bug, narrowband FM crystal-locked (400-470 MHz)
signatures.mode: NBFM (~11-16 kHz occupied), quartz/PLL-stabilized, continuous carrier
signatures.tscm: The modern 'good' analog bug: 433/434/440/450-460 MHz quartz-stabilized micro-transmitter, stable center, narrow deviation, ~300-650 ft range. Sits amid UHF ham/business/LMR. Discriminator: steady unlicensed NBFM carrier carrying continuous room audio. THIS is the sweet-spot signature for a stock Pluto. [IN stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz). IN B210 range. No mod needed.]

signatures.name: UHF FM audio bug, free-running LC (400-470 MHz)
signatures.mode: FM, free-running oscillator, continuous, drifts with temp
signatures.tscm: Cheaper UHF bug variant: same band as the crystal row but center WANDERS as it warms and slightly wider/noisier deviation. Waterfall shows a carrier that creeps over minutes. Free-running vs crystal is the discriminator between this and the previous row. [IN stock Pluto range. IN B210 range. No mod needed.]

signatures.name: UHF 512-608 MHz FM audio bug / mic (TV-band)
signatures.mode: FM (narrow or wide), crystal or free-running, continuous
signatures.tscm: Wireless-mic and bug hardware in the UHF TV band (below the 608-614 MHz radio-astronomy notch). Continuous carrier with live audio, no video sync, no digital-TV OFDM. Occupied BW ~100-200 kHz for wide-FM mics; narrower for bug variants. [IN stock Pluto range. IN B210 range. No mod needed.]

signatures.name: Wide-deviation FM 'spy-cam-audio' / video-subcarrier-style bug (any band)
signatures.mode: Wide FM (±75-150 kHz deviation), continuous — spyshop wide-dev audio style
signatures.tscm: Low-cost spyshop transmitters using WIDE FM deviation (~150-200+ kHz occupied) for audio — same modulator families as analog wireless cameras' audio subcarrier. Broad, fuzzy-edged carrier vs. the crisp narrowband bug carriers. Distinct signature because the detector's bandwidth/energy test differs. [Band-dependent: 88-320 MHz portion OUT of stock Pluto (needs AD9364 unlock or low-VHF front end); 325-512 MHz portion IN stock Pluto range. All IN B210 range (entire 88-512 MHz span is above the 70 MHz floor).]

signatures.name: Subcarrier / voice-inversion-scrambled FM bug
signatures.mode: FM carrying an inverted-voice or subcarrier baseband, continuous
signatures.tscm: Carrier looks like an ordinary NBFM/FM bug on the waterfall, but FM-demod yields SCRAMBLED audio (Donald-Duck voice inversion) or an offset subcarrier tone instead of clear speech. Tell: continuous unlicensed carrier + demod produces harsh/inverted audio, not silence and not clear speech. Slightly wider occupied BW from the subcarrier. [Band-dependent: below 325 MHz OUT of stock Pluto (AD9364 unlock or low-VHF front end); 325-470 MHz IN stock Pluto range. All IN B210 range (entire 130-470 MHz span above 70 MHz floor).]

signatures.name: AM / plain-carrier audio bug (legacy, any band)
signatures.mode: AM (amplitude-modulated) or DSB carrier, continuous — rare/legacy
signatures.tscm: Older/simpler design: audio amplitude-modulates the carrier. On the waterfall the carrier AMPLITUDE (brightness) pulses with speech rather than the frequency spreading. AM-demod (not FM) recovers the room. Uncommon vs FM but genuinely distinct on the air — energy stays in a fixed narrow BW with amplitude ripple. [Band-dependent: below 325 MHz OUT of stock Pluto (AD9364 unlock or low-VHF front end); 325-470 MHz IN stock Pluto range. All IN B210 range (above 70 MHz floor).]

device_classes.device_class: Smart-home mesh radios (Zigbee / Z-Wave / Thread / 802.15.4) repurposed as covert sensors
device_classes.summary: This class covers the low-rate mesh PHYs that carpet modern smart homes: Z-Wave (sub-GHz GFSK), Zigbee and Thread (both 2.4 GHz IEEE 802.15.4 O-QPSK/DSSS), and the less-common 802.15.4 sub-GHz PHYs (915 MHz BPSK and O-QPSK). For TSCM they matter because the exact same radios that run a legitimate door sensor or bulb can be flashed/repurposed to carry a covert PIR trip, a mic-VOX event, a keystroke count, or a beacon out through a homeowner's own hub — the traffic hides in plain sight among dozens of legitimate nodes. The distinct ON-AIR signatures are driven by BAND x MODULATION x CHANNEL WIDTH x DATA RATE, not by product. Z-Wave splits into three regional data-rate PHYs plus Z-Wave Long Range; Zigbee/Thread on 2.4 GHz share ONE PHY across 16 channels (one signature, not sixteen — the SDR sees identical O-QPSK/DSSS bursts, only the center frequency shifts); and the 915 MHz 802.15.4 band has two mutually-incompatible PHYs (BPSK vs O-QPSK). All Z-Wave/sub-GHz rows sit comfortably inside a stock PlutoSDR (325-3800 MHz). The 2.4 GHz rows sit at the very top edge of stock Pluto and squarely inside a B210. Nothing here exceeds 6 GHz. The dominant TSCM challenge is NOT detection — these bands are trivially busy — it is discrimination: telling a repurposed covert node from the legitimate mesh, which requires traffic-pattern and provenance analysis, not just a spectrum hit.

confirm_steps: Enumerate the legitimate network from the homeowner's own controller: pull the full Z-Wave node list (node IDs, product IDs) and the Zigbee/Thread device inventory (PAN ID, short addresses, endpoints). Reconcile EVERY node against a device the homeowner can physically point to. Any unaccounted node is the finding — not the mere presence of the protocol.

Discriminate by modulation family, not just band: in the 902-928 MHz band, Z-Wave = GFSK narrow, 802.15.4 sub-GHz = BPSK-DSSS or O-QPSK-DSSS wider, LoRa = chirp, FHSS telemetry = hopping. Classify the mystery signal before assuming it is a covert node.

Capture protocol-layer traffic, not just IQ: use a real 802.15.4/Zigbee sniffer (CC2531/CC2652, nRF52840 dongle) and a Z-Wave sniffer (Zniffer/Silabs) to read frame headers, home/PAN IDs, and node addressing. IQ alone cannot attribute a node; frame provenance can.

Correlate traffic to physical stimulus: walk the space and watch which node bursts when you move (motion), open a door (contact), or speak (a covert VOX mic node). A node whose bursts track occupancy but has no known sensor behind it is high-concern.

Power-down test: with owner consent, power off ALL known hubs/sensors and re-scan. Any 908/916/2405-2480/902-928 MHz mesh traffic that survives the shutdown is not part of the declared network — localize its source.
Direction-find and localize suspicious nodes: for Z-Wave LR especially (high power), use a directional antenna / received-power gradient to walk to the emitter. Physically inspect that location.

Log center frequency AND PHY per hit so the report distinguishes 908.42 classic vs 916 R3 vs 912/920 LR, and 2.4 GHz Zigbee vs 915 MHz sub-GHz 802.15.4 — these are separate signatures with separate implications.

Tune Pluto to each 802.15.4 channel center (2405 + 5*(ch-11) MHz for ch11-26); look for ~2 MHz-wide constant-envelope bursts. Confirm channel spacing is 5 MHz and occupied BW ~2 MHz to separate from BLE (1-2 MHz hopping) and Wi-Fi (20 MHz).

Decode with a known-good 802.15.4 receiver (killerbee/zbdump on a CC2531, or GNU Radio ieee802-15-4 block) to confirm PHY and read PAN ID / short addresses; a live PAN ID confirms Zigbee/Thread vs. a bare carrier.

For sub-GHz: sweep 902-928 MHz. Narrow (~300 kHz) sparse FSK bursts near 908.42 MHz => classic Z-Wave; spread bursts at 912/920 MHz => Z-Wave LR; persistent channel-hopping across the whole band => Wi-SUN/802.15.4g meter, usually benign.
Cross-reference every detected PAN/node against the client's declared device inventory; an 802.15.4 node with no owner-known counterpart is the actionable finding, not the mere presence of the band.

Physically inspect suspected host objects - a covert 802.15.4 tap draws almost no power and hides in USB dongles, power strips, sensors, or wall warts; RF alone cannot distinguish covert from legitimate on this shared PHY.
false_positive_overlap: Overwhelming legitimate presence: a normal smart home has DOZENS of legitimate Z-Wave/Zigbee/Thread nodes. Detection of the protocol is expected and by itself means nothing — this class is discrimination-limited, not detection-limited.

2.4 GHz band is shared with Wi-Fi, Bluetooth/BLE, and microwave leakage; Zigbee/Thread bursts sit in the gaps between Wi-Fi channels and can be masked by heavy Wi-Fi traffic or mistaken for BLE advertising bursts.

902-928 MHz ISM band is extremely crowded: LoRa/LoRaWAN, FHSS wireless telemetry, utility smart meters (which also burst in 902-928), wireless doorbells, and 900 MHz cordless-adjacent gear all share the band with Z-Wave and 802.15.4 sub-GHz. A 915 MHz hit is very likely a legitimate meter or LoRa node.
Z-Wave classic vs Z-Wave LR vs 802.15.4-BPSK all live in the same 908-920 MHz neighborhood; misreading modulation can cross-label them.
Thread and Zigbee are indistinguishable at the IQ/PHY layer (identical 802.15.4 2.4 GHz PHY) — you cannot tell a benign Nanoleaf-Thread mesh from a covert Thread node without frame-level capture.
Multiprotocol hubs (Echo, Aqara M3, Homey Pro) legitimately emit on BOTH Z-Wave sub-GHz AND Zigbee/Thread 2.4 GHz, so a single device can create hits in multiple signature rows.
Bluetooth 2.4 GHz spy cams/mics and Wi-Fi cameras are a DIFFERENT class; do not attribute their traffic to the mesh signatures — verify by bandwidth/modulation before labeling.
The 2.4 GHz 802.15.4 signature is indistinguishable at RF from any legitimate Zigbee/Thread/Matter smart-home device - modern homes have dozens; presence is expected, not suspicious.

BLE (1-2 MHz GFSK, adaptive hopping) and 802.15.4 both live in 2.4 GHz ISM; a wide-scan detector can confuse a wideband BLE burst with a narrow 802.15.4 channel edge - verify the ~2 MHz occupied width and 5 MHz raster.
Wi-Fi 20 MHz channels overlap and can mask 802.15.4 channels 15/20/25 that sit between Wi-Fi 1/6/11; strong Wi-Fi can hide a low-power sensor burst.
Sub-GHz 902-928 MHz is shared with LoRa/LoRaWAN, legacy 900 MHz cordless/telemetry, and many ISM remote controls - narrow FSK blips there are frequently benign non-Z-Wave devices.
Wi-SUN/802.15.4g energy on 902-928 MHz is almost always the utility smart meter and is a routine environmental signal, not a threat.
device_classes.tscm_notes:
Reach: every Z-Wave row (908.42 / 916 / 912 / 920 MHz) and both 915 MHz 802.15.4 sub-GHz PHYs (902-928 MHz) are comfortably inside a STOCK PlutoSDR's 325-3800 MHz tuning range — no AD9364 frequency-extension mod needed. The 2.4 GHz Zigbee/Thread signature (2405-2480 MHz) is within stock Pluto's range but sits well up the band where stock Pluto front-end sensitivity/filtering is weaker; a B210 covers it cleanly. NOTHING in this class is above 6 GHz, so the whole class is in-range for a B210 and (except for front-end margin at 2.4 GHz) for a stock Pluto. Sample-rate reality: the 2.4 GHz O-QPSK signature is ~2 MHz wide and the sub-GHz PHYs up to ~1.2 MHz — size your capture bandwidth accordingly; a stock Pluto at high sample rates over USB can drop samples, so verify no overflow when hunting fast Zigbee bursts.

Operational reality for TSCM: this is the hardest class in the kit to act on because the signatures are ubiquitous and legitimate. A spectrum-analyzer hit is the START of the investigation, never the conclusion. The real deliverable is RECONCILIATION — every mesh node accounted for against a physical, owner-acknowledged device — plus the power-down survivor test and stimulus-correlation walk. Prioritize the covert-friendly niches: Z-Wave Long Range (high power, reaches off-property collectors), and the 915 MHz 802.15.4 sub-GHz PHYs (uncommon, good wall penetration, missed by 2.4-GHz-only sweeps). Any GFSK/PSK mesh burst that survives a full known-device shutdown, or that direction-finds to a spot with no declared device, is the report-worthy finding. IQ capture alone cannot attribute these; pair the SDR with protocol-layer 802.15.4 and Z-Wave sniffers. NOTE: hardware for this app is untested per project memory — treat all reach/sensitivity claims as spec-based until validated on the actual Pluto/B210.

signatures.name: Z-Wave US Classic — 908.42 MHz GFSK (R1/R2, 9.6/40 kbps)
signatures.mode: GFSK, 2-level, Manchester (R1 9.6 kbps) / NRZ (R2 40 kbps), ITU-T G.9959
signatures.tscm: Narrow 908.42 MHz carrier, two-tone FSK deviation ~+/-20-40 kHz, very short bursty frames with a fixed home-ID/node-ID header; R1 uses Manchester coding (spectral shape differs from R2 NRZ). Idle between bursts.

signatures.name: Z-Wave US High-Rate — 916.00 MHz GFSK (R3, 100 kbps)
signatures.mode: GFSK, 2-level NRZ, 100 kbps, ITU-T G.9959 R3
signatures.tscm: 916.0 MHz carrier, wider FSK deviation than R1/R2, ~100 kbps NRZ. Wider occupied bandwidth than the 908.42 classic channel; bursts can be slightly longer for larger payloads.

signatures.name: Z-Wave Long Range (US) — 912/920 MHz GFSK, high-power
signatures.mode: GFSK, ITU-T G.9959 LR profile, up to 100 kbps, up to +14/+30 dBm
signatures.tscm: Two distinct channels at ~912 MHz and ~920 MHz, GFSK like classic Z-Wave but notably higher received power and longer effective range. Star (hub-and-spoke) rather than mesh, so bursts are hub<->node, not multi-hop.

signatures.name: Zigbee / Thread / 802.15.4 2.4 GHz — O-QPSK DSSS, 250 kbps (16-channel PHY)
signatures.mode: O-QPSK, half-sine pulse shaping, DSSS 2 Mchip/s, 250 kbps, IEEE 802.15.4 (channels 11-26)
signatures.tscm: ~2 MHz occupied bandwidth, O-QPSK with half-sine chips gives a characteristic rounded/near-constant-envelope spectrum (NOT true OFDM despite the wideband class tag — flagged here as the closest available bucket). DSSS spreading, 62.5 ksym/s. Short bursty MAC frames with 802.15.4 preamble. Channel centers at 2405 + 5*(k-11) MHz for k=11..26.

signatures.name: 802.15.4 Sub-GHz 915 MHz — BPSK DSSS, 40 kbps (legacy sub-GHz PHY)
signatures.mode: BPSK, DSSS 600 kchip/s, 40 kbps, IEEE 802.15.4-2003/2006 915 MHz band (10 channels, 2 MHz spacing)
signatures.tscm: BPSK (not FSK — distinguishes it from Z-Wave in the same band), DSSS chip rate 600 kchip/s giving ~600 kHz-1 MHz occupied bandwidth, 40 kbps. Channel centers 2 MHz apart across 902-928 MHz. Bursty short frames.

signatures.name: 802.15.4 Sub-GHz 915 MHz — O-QPSK DSSS, 250 kbps (high-rate sub-GHz PHY)
signatures.mode: O-QPSK, DSSS 1 Mchip/s, 250 kbps, IEEE 802.15.4-2006 optional 915 MHz O-QPSK PHY
signatures.tscm: O-QPSK with DSSS at ~1 Mchip/s, ~1-1.2 MHz occupied bandwidth, 250 kbps, in the 902-928 MHz band. Constant-envelope-ish O-QPSK shape but centered sub-GHz rather than at 2.4 GHz.

signatures.name: IEEE 802.15.4 2.4 GHz O-QPSK PHY (Zigbee / Thread / Matter / 6LoWPAN)
signatures.mode: O-QPSK with half-sine pulse shaping (MSK-equivalent), 2 Mchip/s DSSS, 32 chips/symbol, 250 kbps
signatures.tscm: 16 channels (ch11-26) at 2405-2480 MHz on a 5 MHz raster; each occupies ~2 MHz, ~3 dB narrower than a 20 MHz Wi-Fi channel and much wider than BLE's 1-2 MHz. Constant-envelope (MSK-like) so no strong AM component; short packets (<4 ms typical) give a distinctive bursty, low-duty footprint. Ch15/20/25/26 chosen to dodge Wi-Fi ch1/6/11. Zigbee, Thread, Matter-over-Thread and 6LoWPAN all share this identical PHY - protocol is not distinguishable at RF, only via decode. [stock-Pluto-reachable (within 325-3800 MHz); also in B210 range. Full 2 MHz capturable at Pluto's max ~56 MSPS.]

signatures.name: Z-Wave classic US (ITU-T G.9959, 908.42 MHz)
signatures.mode: GFSK, FSK deviation; 9.6 kbps / 40 kbps on 908.42 MHz, 100 kbps on 916 MHz
signatures.tscm: Narrowband (~300 kHz class) single-carrier FSK in the US 900 MHz ISM band, distinct from the 2 MHz-wide 2.4 GHz 802.15.4 signature. Primary mesh channel 908.42 MHz (9.6/40 kbps); 100 kbps variant near 916 MHz. Very short, infrequent bursts (sensor/actuator commands). Only one on-air Z-Wave device family per region - narrow FSK blip in the low-900s is the tell. [stock-Pluto-reachable (908 MHz is inside 325-3800 MHz); also in B210 range.]

signatures.name: Z-Wave Long Range US (912 / 920 MHz)
signatures.mode: DSSS O-QPSK, 100 kbps, fixed rate; star (device-to-hub) topology, dynamic power control up to +20 dBm
signatures.tscm: Two dedicated LR channels at 912 MHz and 920 MHz, separate from the 908.42 MHz classic mesh channel. Spread O-QPSK rather than the narrow FSK of classic Z-Wave, so slightly wider occupied bandwidth. Star topology means traffic concentrates hub-ward rather than meshing. Higher TX power (+20 dBm) can make it the strongest low-900s signal in a home. [stock-Pluto-reachable (within 325-3800 MHz); also in B210 range.]

signatures.name: IEEE 802.15.4g SUN sub-GHz PHY (Wi-SUN utility / industrial, 902-928 MHz US)
signatures.mode: SUN-FSK / SUN-O-QPSK / SUN-OFDM; 50-800 kbps; channel BW 200 kHz (narrow FSK) up to ~1.2 MHz (OFDM Option 1); often frequency-hopping (FHSS) in Wi-SUN FAN
signatures.tscm: Wi-SUN / smart-meter and industrial 802.15.4g in the 902-928 MHz US ISM band. Distinct from consumer Zigbee/Z-Wave: channel-hopping across many 200 kHz-1.2 MHz channels, heavier and more regular traffic (meter reads, mesh beacons). SUN-OFDM Option 1 occupies ~1094 kHz in 1200 kHz spacing; SUN-FSK narrow options ~200 kHz. Persistent hopping energy blanketing 902-928 MHz distinguishes it from the sparse bursts of home Z-Wave. [stock-Pluto-reachable band (902-928 MHz within 325-3800 MHz), but capturing the full hopping set needs wide-span sweeping or a wider front end than a single Pluto tune; per-channel decode is fine on stock Pluto.]

device_classes.device_class: LoRa / LPWAN trackers + covert off-grid mesh comms (Meshtastic / MeshCore / LoRaWAN / Sigfox)
device_classes.summary: Sub-GHz ISM chirp-spread-spectrum (LoRa CSS) and ultra-narrowband (Sigfox) devices used as GPS trackers and as covert off-grid text/mesh comms (Meshtastic, MeshCore). On the air they present as either (a) a distinctive up/down chirp sweeping the full channel bandwidth (125/250/500 kHz) that energy/cyclostationary classifiers flag as unknown/noise-like because instantaneous frequency is constantly sweeping, or (b) Sigfox ultra-narrowband D-BPSK blips nearly invisible at normal FFT resolution. Signatures are driven by BAND (US 902-928, EU 863-870, 433 MHz) x CHANNEL BANDWIDTH (125/250/500 kHz) x single-channel-fixed (Meshtastic) vs FHSS pseudo-hopping (LoRaWAN US915) vs UNB (Sigfox). Duty is the biggest TSCM tell: a tracker beacons on a fixed periodic cadence; a Meshtastic node chirps sporadically on ONE fixed slot. Reach: 902-928 and 863-870 MHz are inside a stock PlutoSDR (AD9363, 325-3800 MHz) and fully inside a B210. The 433 MHz LoRa variant is BELOW the stock Pluto 325 MHz floor and needs the AD9364 device-string/impedance mod (drops to ~70 MHz, unit-dependent low-edge performance) or a different front end; it is fine on a B210. Nothing in this class is above 6 GHz. Honest limitation: the app's taxonomy has no CSS/chirp bucket, so every LoRa row is tagged noise_like or fhss and the operator should be told the classifier will NOT positively ID LoRa - it only flags 'unknown wideband chirp in ISM band,' which is itself the actionable finding. VERIFICATION CORRECTIONS applied vs the source draft: (1) Sigfox US uplink is RC2 600 bps DBPSK with ~600 Hz occupied width, NOT 100 Hz - the 100 Hz is the nominal/RC1-EU channel; bandwidth and class fixed. (2) Sigfox uplink signal_class changed continuous_digital -> psk (bursty DBPSK, not continuous). (3) Confirmed LongTurbo (SF11/500 kHz) IS now a real Meshtastic preset per current official docs, so that 500 kHz row stands. All LoRaWAN US915 / LR-FHSS / EU868 / Pluto-reach figures verified correct.

confirm_steps: Zoom the SDR to the exact center and open a high-resolution waterfall (slow sweep / small RBW). Classic LoRa shows an unmistakable linear up-chirp (or down-chirp preamble) that ramps across the channel and wraps at the edges - a diagonal sawtooth streak. That visual chirp is the positive ID no energy classifier will give you.

Measure the occupied bandwidth of the chirp streak: does it fill exactly 125, 250, or 500 kHz? Snapping to one of those three widths strongly implies LoRa CSS and tells you which preset/band-plan family you're in.

Watch DUTY over several minutes. A GPS tracker beacons on a FIXED periodic cadence (every 10 s, 60 s, 5 min, 15 min) - record the waterfall and look for metronomic repeats. Human-paced sporadic bursts on ONE fixed center = Meshtastic texting; scattered hops across many 125 kHz centers = LoRaWAN FHSS uplink.

For suspected Meshtastic US default, park on 906.875 MHz (LongFast slot 20, 250 kHz, verified) first - factory-default nodes land there. Then sweep the rest of 902-928 for other named-channel slots (a renamed channel moves it anywhere across the 104 slots).

Decode to confirm, don't just eyeball: run gr-lora / gr-lora_sdr (GNU Radio) or a Meshtastic-aware decoder against recorded IQ. Successful LoRa demod (even without the channel key) proves it's LoRa; a decodable Meshtastic frame header proves the protocol.

Correlate with physical search: a beaconing tracker is a small battery + PCB + often a visible sub-GHz whip/PCB antenna and possibly a GPS patch antenna. Direction-find the periodic burst with a directional 900 MHz antenna and attenuator to walk it down.

For suspected Sigfox / UNB: switch to a very narrow RBW (Hz-scale) fine FFT and watch near 902 MHz for a ~600 Hz-wide US DBPSK sliver (NOT 100 Hz - that's the EU 100 bps figure) appearing for ~1 s a handful of times - trivially missed at LoRa resolution.

Rule out region: LoRa in 863-870 MHz on a device physically in the US is a region-mismatched import - note it. If you suspect 433 MHz LoRa, remember a STOCK Pluto cannot see it reliably - confirm your Pluto has the AD9364 mod (or use a B210) before trusting a 'no signal' result at 433.
false_positive_overlap: Legitimate LoRaWAN IoT is everywhere in 902-928 MHz: smart utility/water/gas meters, agricultural sensors, building-automation/HVAC sensors, parking sensors, cattle/pet trackers - all produce identical CSS chirps. A LoRa chirp is NOT inherently hostile; context (attached to a target vehicle/room, unexplained periodicity) makes it suspicious.
Other 915 MHz ISM traffic an energy classifier lumps together: 900 MHz cordless phones, some baby monitors, Z-Wave (908.42 MHz US - narrowband FSK, not chirp), and industrial telemetry.

900 MHz FHSS data radios (Digi XBee-PRO 900, RFD900, telemetry links) hop across the same band and can be confused with LoRaWAN FHSS at the energy-detector level; they are NOT chirps - waterfall shape separates them.
Amateur radio: LoRa-APRS and ham mesh operate legitimately at 433 MHz and in 915; a licensed ham beaconing position is legal and benign.

Sigfox UNB slivers can be mistaken for stray carriers, spurs, or LO leakage because they're so narrow; conversely real spurs/birdies can be mistaken for Sigfox - verify DBPSK structure and the ~600 Hz (US) width before calling it. LO leakage / DC spike at the Pluto center is a classic false Sigfox.

Wideband LoRa 500 kHz chirps can visually resemble other swept/ramping signals (FMCW sensors, some radar-like sweeps) to a naive classifier; check the wrap-around and packet time-on-air to disambiguate.
device_classes.tscm_notes: LoRa/Meshtastic is a genuinely covert comms channel because it (a) needs no cellular/Wi-Fi infrastructure, so it survives cell-jam/Faraday conditions and leaves no carrier records, and (b) most spectrum classifiers have no CSS bucket and dismiss the chirp as noise. Treat any unexplained periodic sub-GHz chirp in 902-928 (or 863-870) MHz as a priority finding even though the app can only label it 'unknown wideband/noise-like in ISM band' - that ambiguity IS the actionable result. Keep two threat modes distinct: a GPS TRACKER (metronomic periodic beacon, one-way, small battery tag on a vehicle/asset/person) vs off-grid MESH COMMS (sporadic human-paced bursts, two-way, often a handheld). The tracker is the higher-probability finding in vehicle/person sweeps; mesh comms matters more in counter-surveillance of an organized team. Duty cadence is your single best discriminator - record the waterfall long enough to see the repeat interval. The survey is time-limited: a tracker on a 15-minute beacon can be silent for the whole sweep, so passive monitoring must run long and be paired with a physical/DF search rather than relying on catching a burst. HARDWARE CAVEAT for this operator: the 915 and 868 MHz LoRa here are inside a stock PlutoSDR, but the 433 MHz LoRa variant is NOT reliably reachable on a stock unit - it needs the AD9364 device-string mod or a B210, so a 'clean' 433 result on unmodified hardware is meaningless.

signatures.name: LoRa CSS 125 kHz - US 902-928 MHz (Meshtastic LongModerate/LongSlow, LoRaWAN uplink DR0-3)
signatures.mode: Chirp Spread Spectrum (CSS), SF7-SF12, up/down chirp sweeping full 125 kHz
signatures.tscm: Classic LoRa 'V'/sawtooth chirp on a waterfall: linear frequency ramp wrapping at the 125 kHz channel edges. Time-on-air scales hard with SF - SF12 packets 1-2+ s, very visible; SF7 tens of ms. Energy detector reads a brief noise-like hump filling exactly 125 kHz. Meshtastic LongModerate (SF11/125) and LongSlow (SF12/125) live here. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LoRa CSS 250 kHz - US 902-928 MHz (Meshtastic default LongFast/MediumFast/ShortFast)
signatures.mode: CSS, SF7-SF11, chirp sweeping full 250 kHz
signatures.tscm: THE single most important covert-comms signature in the US. Meshtastic factory default LongFast = SF11/250 kHz, and its default primary channel hashes to slot 20 centered 906.875 MHz (verified against current Meshtastic docs). A fixed unchanging center that chirps sporadically (human-paced texting plus node-info/telemetry every few min) with NO cellular/Wi-Fi pattern = strong off-grid-mesh indicator. Chirp fills exactly 250 kHz. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LoRa CSS 500 kHz - US 902-928 MHz (Meshtastic ShortTurbo SF7 & LongTurbo SF11; LoRaWAN 500 kHz uplink/downlink)
signatures.mode: CSS, SF7 (ShortTurbo) to SF11 (LongTurbo), chirp sweeping full 500 kHz
signatures.tscm: Widest LoRa channel. Both Meshtastic 500 kHz presets - ShortTurbo (SF7) and LongTurbo (SF11) - are confirmed present in current Meshtastic firmware/docs. Also the LoRaWAN US915 500 kHz uplink group (8 ch, centers 903.0-914.2 MHz, 1.6 MHz step) and the 8 downlink channels 923.3-927.5 MHz (600 kHz step). A wide chirp neatly bounded at 500 kHz is the tell. ShortTurbo's 500 kHz width is illegal in some regions - its presence hints at a US/unregulated operator. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LoRaWAN US915 - 125 kHz uplink bank with FHSS pseudorandom hopping (64 channels 902.3-914.9 MHz)
signatures.mode: CSS SF7-SF10 on 125 kHz channels, FCC 15.247 frequency-hopping across 64 channels (200 kHz spacing)
signatures.tscm: Distinct from single-channel Meshtastic: a LoRaWAN end-node HOPS pseudorandomly across the 64-channel 125 kHz bank (902.3 MHz + n*200 kHz to 914.9, verified) to satisfy FCC Part 15.247, so successive uplinks land on different centers. Over a survey window chirps scatter across the whole lower half of the band, not pinned to one slot. Uplink-only from the tracker; gateway answers on the 923.3-927.5 MHz / 500 kHz downlink block. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LR-FHSS - US 902-928 MHz long-range intra-packet frequency hopping
signatures.mode: LR-FHSS (narrow ~488 Hz physical OBW carriers hopping on a 3.9 kHz grid within a 137 or 336 kHz OCW; DR8-DR11)
signatures.tscm: Newer LoRaWAN uplink mode built to beat the FCC 400 ms dwell limit by hopping WITHIN a single packet. Verified params: 488 Hz occupied per hop, 3.9 kHz grid, 137 kHz OCW (DR8/9) or 336 kHz OCW (DR10/11). On a waterfall it looks like a rapid ladder of very narrow tone-hops, not a smooth chirp - visually different from classic CSS. Used by satellite-IoT trackers; easy to mistake for interference/hopping noise. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LoRa CSS 125 kHz - EU 863-870 MHz (Meshtastic EU_868; LoRaWAN EU868)
signatures.mode: CSS SF7-SF12 on 125 kHz, ETSI duty-cycle limited (0.1%/1%/10% by sub-band)
signatures.tscm: EU/rest-of-world LoRa. LoRaWAN EU868 default join channels 868.1/868.3/868.5 MHz (125 kHz). Meshtastic EU_868 confines TX to the 869.4-869.65 MHz high-power sub-band (10% duty, up to +27 dBm ERP) and defaults to 869.525 MHz center (verified). A US sweep normally shouldn't see this - its presence on a device physically in the US means a region-mismatched/imported unit, itself notable in TSCM. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LoRa CSS 250 kHz - EU 863-870 MHz (Meshtastic EU_868 fast presets)
signatures.mode: CSS SF7-SF11 on 250 kHz
signatures.tscm: Wider EU LoRa channel used by faster Meshtastic EU presets and some LoRaWAN 250 kHz uplinks. Same chirp signature, 250 kHz wide, within the tighter EU allocation. ETSI duty rules mean genuine EU devices transmit sparsely; a chatty device here suggests a non-compliant or bench-test unit. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LoRa CSS 125/250 kHz - 433 MHz ISM (EU433 433.05-434.79 MHz trackers/modules/LoRa-APRS)
signatures.mode: CSS SF7-SF12, 125 or 250 kHz chirp in the 70 cm ISM band
signatures.tscm: Low-band LoRa used by 433 MHz modules (SX1278-class), some Asian trackers, LoRa-APRS, and hobby telemetry. Same chirp shape centered near 433-434 MHz. Longer physical range for a given power vs 915. This is the one signature a stock Pluto cannot see - 433 MHz is below the AD9363 325 MHz spec floor's usable low edge and needs the mod or a B210. [needs-AD9364-mod (stock Pluto low edge is 325 MHz; 433 is above the number but unit-dependent low-band performance is poor - verify on your hardware or apply the AD9364 device-string mod; clean on a B210)]

signatures.name: Sigfox UNB uplink - US ~902 MHz (RC2 D-BPSK, 600 bps, ~600 Hz occupied)
signatures.mode: D-BPSK, RC2 US, 600 bps, ~600 Hz occupied (100 Hz is the nominal channel / RC1-EU 100 bps figure); device picks pseudo-random center in the operational band
signatures.tscm: CORRECTED: US Sigfox is RC2 = 600 bps DBPSK, so the transmitted sliver is ~600 Hz wide, NOT 100 Hz (the 100 Hz value is the nominal channel spacing / applies to RC1-EU 100 bps). Still radically narrower than any LoRa chirp. A Sigfox device sends only a few short messages (max ~140/day), each ~1 s, on a randomly-chosen narrow channel around 902 MHz - nearly invisible at coarse FFT resolution, reads as a faint carrier blip. Needs a fine-resolution (narrow RBW) waterfall to catch. Class is psk (bursty DBPSK), not continuous. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: Sigfox UNB downlink - US 902-928 MHz (GFSK 600 bps)
signatures.mode: GFSK, 600 bps downlink, ~1.5 kHz occupied
signatures.tscm: Sigfox base-station-to-device downlink is GFSK (not DBPSK) and slightly wider (~1.5 kHz). Only occurs shortly after an uplink that requested a downlink, so it is rare. From a device-hunting standpoint the UPLINK (the DBPSK sliver above) is what you'll detect from a hidden tracker; downlink comes from the far-off tower at up to 4 W and is not emitted by the hidden device. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

device_classes.device_class: Sub-GHz ISM trackers, telemetry beacons, and covert data-exfil links (315 / 433.92 / 868 / 902-928 MHz), plus TPMS-lookalike bursts
device_classes.summary: This class covers covert devices that emit in the license-free sub-GHz ISM bands: 315 MHz (US remote-control band), 433.92 MHz (worldwide ISM), 868 MHz (EU SRD), and 902-928 MHz (US ISM). Signatures split cleanly by BAND x MODULATION x DUTY, not by product. The two dominant modulations are OOK/ASK (simple carrier on/off, cheap TX, garage-remote-grade) and 2-FSK/GFSK (two-tone, used by better telemetry and TPMS). LoRa (CSS chirp) and FHSS are distinct wideband/hopping signatures on 868/915. A TPMS-lookalike is a short (~few ms) periodic burst that mimics a tire sensor to hide in a legitimate-looking population. CRITICAL SCOPE NOTE: most 'GPS trackers' you find in the wild do NOT transmit their fix over sub-GHz ISM at all -- they backhaul over cellular (2G/LTE-M/NB-IoT/4G), which is a SEPARATE signature class. The sub-GHz ISM emissions in-scope here are: (a) beacons/tags that ping a local receiver (BLE-alternative sub-GHz tags, LoRa cattle/asset tags, RF pet/luggage tags), (b) covert sensor exfil links (door/PIR/audio-trigger sensors relaying to a nearby base), (c) remote-activation uplinks, and (d) TPMS-mimic bursts. Reach: 433/868/915 MHz sit inside a stock ADALM-Pluto's 325-3800 MHz range; 315 MHz is BELOW stock Pluto and needs the AD9364 firmware mod (down to ~70 MHz) or an RTL-SDR/HackRF. All are far under 6 GHz so B210 covers everything with margin. False-positive load is HEAVY: these bands are saturated with legitimate garage remotes, weather stations, TPMS, doorbells, utility meters (AMR/AMI), and 900 MHz cordless/telemetry -- a hit is NOT evidence of surveillance by itself; correlation to the protected space/vehicle over time is what matters. VERIFICATION: bands, modulations, duty cycles, and Pluto/B210 reach math all check out. Two example products with dubious exact SKUs were generalized to real device types; redundant GL300 rebrands trimmed.

2.4 GHz-config covert trackers that fall back to 915 FSK telemetry (form-factor example)
confirm_steps: Identify the modulation on the waterfall BEFORE anything else: blinking line dropping to noise floor = OOK; steady carrier splitting into two tones = FSK; diagonal sweeping ramp = LoRa/CSS; energy hopping across the band = FHSS. This alone routes you to the right signature row.

Run rtl_433 (or SDR++ / Universal Radio Hacker) on 315/433/868/915 and let it auto-classify. It decodes EV1527/Princeton/Nexus/TPMS and hundreds of protocols and prints the protocol name + ID -- turning an anonymous blip into a named device.

For TPMS-lookalikes: count distinct periodic IDs on 315/433 and compare to the number of wheels (4, or 6 for duallies). MORE unique IDs than wheels, or an ID with no pressure/temp payload, flags a mimic. Decode payload fields to confirm.

Establish a baseline AWAY from the protected space/vehicle, then return. A signature that only appears when near the target (or that moves WITH the vehicle) is the discriminator -- ambient garage remotes and neighborhood meters will NOT track the target.

Log cadence over 30-60+ min. Covert beacons/trackers ping on a fixed schedule (e.g., every 10 s / 60 s / on-motion). A strict periodic heartbeat correlated to the target is far more suspicious than random neighborhood traffic.

Direction-find the source: sweep with a directional antenna and watch RSSI, or move the receiver and triangulate. Confirm the emitter is ON the vehicle/asset/room, not a neighbor. Physically search the RSSI peak.

For FHSS/wideband LoRa across the full 26 MHz US band, use max-hold over a sweep (Pluto's ~20 MHz stable instantaneous BW misses parts at once); a B210 at ~56 MHz can grab 902-928 in one shot to see the whole hop comb.
For 315 MHz specifically: confirm your front end reaches it -- stock Pluto's 325 MHz floor misses it. Use the AD9364-modded Pluto, an RTL-SDR, or HackRF for the 315 band.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Operational reality for a sweep: a raw hit in 315/433/868/915 is almost never proof by itself -- these bands are saturated with legitimate traffic (see false_positive_overlap). Three discriminators separate a covert tracker/beacon from ambient noise: (1) LOCATION correlation -- it appears only near, or moves with, the protected target; (2) CADENCE -- a fixed periodic heartbeat or on-motion trigger tied to the target; (3) PAYLOAD -- decoded content (a GPS-fix-shaped packet, or a TPMS frame with no pressure field). Prioritize a physical search at the RSSI peak once direction-finding localizes it -- most covert sub-GHz trackers on a vehicle are magnetic-mount units in a wheel well, bumper, or under-chassis. Remember the SCOPE trap: the majority of commercial 'GPS trackers' (LandAirSea, Spytec GL300-class) do their real exfil over CELLULAR, not sub-GHz ISM -- if you only sweep ISM you can miss them entirely; sweep the cellular uplink bands too (700/850/1900 MHz, LTE-M/NB-IoT), which are a separate signature class. Genuine sub-GHz-exfil devices are mainly LoRa tags (long-range, low-power, will reach a gateway well outside the room) and local sensor-relay bugs (door/PIR/audio-trigger boards pinging a nearby base). LEGAL/SAFETY: do not transmit/replay or jam -- receive-only. Decoding a third party's TPMS/tracker payload is fine for a sweep, but document chain-of-custody if the finding may support a legal matter (family-law vehicle-tracking cases are common). REACH: keep a 315-capable front end (RTL-SDR/HackRF or AD9364-modded Pluto) in the kit -- a stock Pluto (325 MHz floor) is blind to the entire 315 MHz US band, which is where a lot of US keyfob/TPMS/cheap-sensor covert traffic lives. VERIFICATION VERDICT: catalog is technically sound. Bands, modulations (OOK vs FSK vs CSS vs FHSS), duty cycles, and the Pluto-3.8GHz / B210-6GHz reach math all check out, including the 315 MHz-below-stock-Pluto note and the 26 MHz-exceeds-Pluto-instantaneous-BW note for full-band 900 ISM. signal_class values are all within the allowed enum (LoRa correctly mapped to continuous_digital in absence of a CSS category). Corrections applied: 'Nolilab Loko' and 'GlobalSat LT-10 solar ear-tag' were dubious exact SKUs and were generalized to real device-type descriptions; the Lightning GPS / MasTrack GL300 rebrands were folded into the Spytec GL300 line to avoid presenting resellers as distinct products.

signatures.name: 315 MHz OOK/ASK remote & sensor exfil (US)
signatures.mode: OOK/ASK, ~1-10 kbps, Manchester or PWM (EV1527/PT2262-class), fixed or rolling code
signatures.tscm: Narrow AM carrier that keys fully on/off; energy collapses to noise floor between symbols. Short packets (a few ms) repeated 2-5x per event. Waterfall shows a single vertical line at 315.00 that blinks. No continuous carrier. US-centric band (keyfobs, TPMS, cheap door/PIR sensors, remote-activation uplinks). [BELOW stock Pluto (325 MHz floor) -- needs AD9364 firmware mod (extends to ~70 MHz) or an RTL-SDR/HackRF. In-range for B210.]

signatures.name: 433.92 MHz OOK/ASK remote & sensor exfil (worldwide)
signatures.mode: OOK/ASK, 1-10 kbps (up to ~33-66 kbps Manchester/NRZ), EV1527/PT2262/HT12E-class encoders
signatures.tscm: The single most crowded covert band. Full carrier on/off keying at 433.92; ~270 kHz occupied for cheap AM modules. Blinking vertical line, packets repeated for reliability. Decodes in rtl_433 as EV1527/Princeton/Nexus/etc. Used by covert door/PIR/reed/vibration sensor exfil to a nearby base station, panic/remote-trigger uplinks, and cheap beacons. [In stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz). In-range for B210.]

signatures.name: 433.92 MHz 2-FSK/GFSK telemetry & beacon
signatures.mode: 2-FSK/GFSK, ~2-100 kbps, deviation ~10-50 kHz (CC1101/Si4x-class radios)
signatures.tscm: Two closely-spaced tones instead of on/off; carrier is ALWAYS present during a packet (does not drop to noise floor like OOK) and visibly shifts between two frequencies. Cleaner, higher-rate telemetry than OOK. Periodic beacon cadence (e.g., a fix or sensor value every N seconds/minutes). Common in better covert telemetry, some asset tags relaying to a local gateway. [In stock Pluto range. In-range for B210.]

signatures.name: 315 MHz FSK TPMS-lookalike burst
signatures.mode: FSK (some ASK), Manchester, ~9.6-19.2 kbps, ~8-burst train, one frame per ~30-60 s
signatures.tscm: Very short frames (a few ms) that repeat as a short burst train, then silence for tens of seconds -- the classic TPMS cadence. A covert device mimics this to blend into a legitimate tire-sensor population. Frame carries an ID + payload; no auth/encryption. Distinguishing a real TPMS from a mimic requires payload decode (real TPMS has pressure/temp fields + known ID prefixes) and count vs. number of wheels. [BELOW stock Pluto floor -- AD9364 mod / RTL-SDR / HackRF. In-range for B210.]

signatures.name: 868 MHz (EU SRD) FSK/GFSK telemetry & beacon
signatures.mode: 2-FSK/GFSK, ~1.2-100 kbps, 1% duty-cycle-limited SRD (wM-Bus, generic FSK)
signatures.tscm: EU short-range-device band. Two-tone FSK packets, always-on carrier during a packet, strict 1% duty cycle so transmissions are short and infrequent. Used by EU-market covert telemetry, wireless M-Bus meters, and sensor exfil. Channelized across 863-870. Presence of a US-market device here is itself notable. [In stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz). In-range for B210.]

signatures.name: 868 MHz LoRa (CSS chirp) tag/tracker (EU)
signatures.mode: LoRa chirp-spread-spectrum (CSS), BW 125/250/500 kHz, SF7-SF12, ~1% duty
signatures.tscm: Unmistakable on a waterfall: diagonal up-chirps (and reversed down-chirps in the preamble/sync) sweeping across 125-500 kHz. NOT a blinking line and NOT two tones -- a sweeping ramp. Very long range for the power. Used by EU LoRaWAN cattle/asset/GPS tags relaying a fix to a distant gateway. Higher SF = slower, wider-looking chirps that dwell longer. [In stock Pluto range. In-range for B210.]

signatures.name: 902-928 MHz (US ISM) FSK/GFSK telemetry & beacon
signatures.mode: 2-FSK/GFSK, ~2-250 kbps, single-channel or lightly hopped
signatures.tscm: US 900 MHz ISM. Two-tone FSK packets, carrier present during packet. Overlaps heavily with legitimate 900 MHz telemetry, AMR/AMI utility meters, and industrial links. A covert beacon here looks like any other 900 MHz FSK burst -- separation is by cadence, location correlation, and payload. Non-hopping variants sit on one channel. [In stock Pluto range (325-3800 MHz). In-range for B210.]

signatures.name: 902-928 MHz OOK/ASK sensor exfil (US)
signatures.mode: OOK/ASK, ~1-10 kbps, cheap encoder-based packets
signatures.tscm: Full carrier on/off keying in the US 900 MHz band -- less common than 433 OOK but exists on cheap 900 MHz modules. Vertical line that blinks and drops to noise floor between symbols, positioned somewhere in 902-928. Repeated short packets. Covert door/PIR/reed sensor exfil variants. [In stock Pluto range. In-range for B210.]

signatures.name: 902-928 MHz FHSS spread-spectrum link
signatures.mode: FHSS, >=50 hop channels (125-500 kHz each), pseudo-random hop sequence, up to 1 W permitted
signatures.tscm: Energy JUMPS around the band on a long integration/waterfall -- short dwells scattered pseudo-randomly across 902-928 rather than a fixed line. FCC 15.247 requires >=50 hop channels to earn the higher power/dwell allowance, so a max-hold sweep of the whole band shows a comb of visited channels. Used by robust 900 MHz data links and some higher-end covert relays/video-telemetry. Hard to catch on a narrow instantaneous bandwidth -- sweep or use max-hold. [In stock Pluto range but 26 MHz-wide hopping exceeds Pluto's ~20 MHz stable instantaneous BW -- use sweep/max-hold or a wider front end. B210 (up to ~56 MHz) can capture the full band at once.]

signatures.name: 902-928 MHz LoRa (CSS chirp) tag/tracker (US)
signatures.mode: LoRa CSS, BW 125/250/500 kHz, SF7-SF12, FHSS across US channel plan
signatures.tscm: US LoRaWAN GPS/asset tags (e.g., Oyster-class). Same diagonal chirp fingerprint as the 868 version but placed in 902-928 and hopping across the US channel plan (64x 125 kHz up / 8x 500 kHz). On a waterfall: ramps that appear on different channels each transmission. Very long range at low power -- a tag can reach a gateway far outside the room. [In stock Pluto range. Individual 125-500 kHz chirp fits Pluto BW, but catching it across the hopping plan needs sweep/max-hold. In-range for B210.]

device_classes.device_class: rke_pke_attack_tools
device_classes.summary: Covert-but-emitting attack tools against automotive/garage Remote Keyless Entry (RKE) and Passive Keyless Entry (PKE/PKES). Two families: (1) RollJam-class simultaneous jam+capture against rolling-code RKE fobs at 315/433.92/868 MHz — a DISTINCT dual air-signature (a continuous narrowband jammer sitting on the fob channel PLUS the fob's own OOK/FSK burst arriving underneath it), which is why generic "433 MHz OOK remote" coverage misses it; and (2) PKE relay-attack rigs whose primary emission is a re-radiated 125-135 kHz LF exciter/wake field (far below a stock Pluto's 325 MHz floor) plus the fob's 315/433 MHz UHF response, and a 13.56 MHz HF relay variant. The TSCM-relevant tells are the jammer-plus-signal coincidence and the anomalous LF exciter field. Two of these signatures (125 kHz LF, 13.56 MHz HF) are physically out of a stock Pluto/AD9364 front end and need a dedicated LF/HF receiver or NLJD-adjacent LF probe.
