Software-only RollBack replay tooling (time-agnostic RKE replay, no jam required) running on Flipper/HackRF
confirm_steps: On a suspected RollJam: watch 315/433.92/868 MHz for a CONTINUOUS narrowband carrier/noise emitter that is NOT a normal intermittent fob burst — a jammer parked on-channel is the tell. Confirm by noting it disappears the instant a delayed valid unlock is replayed.
Correlate emissions: a legitimate fob press is a lone bursty OOK/FSK packet; a RollJam is a jammer + fob burst arriving TOGETHER. Log both and check time-coincidence.

For PKE relay: the primary RF anomaly is a 125-135 kHz LF exciter/wake field appearing where no car exciter belongs. This CANNOT be seen on Pluto/B210 — use a dedicated 125 kHz LF loop/RFID probe (e.g., Proxmark) or an LF near-field detector to confirm.
For the HF (13.56 MHz) relay variant, use an HF-capable receiver (RTL-SDR + upconverter or NFC/HF probe) — also out of stock Pluto reach.
Direction-find any persistent 315/433/868 emitter with a directional antenna + attenuator to locate a planted jammer/relay near the vehicle or door.

Before concluding, rule out legitimate 433/868 devices (TPMS, weather stations, wireless sensors, garage remotes) that share these bands — legitimate traffic is intermittent, not a continuous on-channel jam.
false_positive_overlap: 433.92 MHz and 868 MHz bands are crowded with LEGITIMATE ISM/SRD devices: TPMS tire sensors, wireless weather stations, home-automation sensors, wireless doorbells, and ordinary garage/gate remotes — all bursty OOK/FSK that resemble fob bursts. Only the coincident continuous jammer distinguishes an attack.
315 MHz sees legitimate US TPMS and garage remotes.
125 kHz LF overlaps legitimate RFID access cards, animal/pet microchip readers, and industrial LF RFID — an LF field is only suspicious when out of place near a vehicle/door.
13.56 MHz overlaps all normal NFC (payment terminals, transit cards, access badges) — extremely common, so an HF field alone is not evidence of an attack.
A brief 315/433 carrier could be a stuck/faulty legitimate transmitter rather than a deliberate jammer — confirm persistence and on-channel placement before calling it hostile.
device_classes.tscm_notes: These tools are used covertly AGAINST a target (vehicle theft, garage/gate breach, following a subject) but they DO emit, so a sweep can catch them. The single most reliable discriminator between a normal keyfob and an attack is the JAMMER: a continuous narrowband emitter parked on 315/433.92/868 MHz coincident with fob activity is the RollJam fingerprint and is itself illegal to operate in the US (FCC prohibits jamming). Two of the highest-value PKE-relay tells (125 kHz LF exciter field, 13.56 MHz HF field) are physically OUT of reach for the Shield app's stock Pluto (325-3800 MHz) and the B210 — the app should explicitly flag these bands as 'requires dedicated LF/HF receiver, not covered by this SDR' rather than silently reporting clear. Recommend adding a low-cost 125 kHz LF probe / Proxmark and an HF-capable RTL-SDR+upconverter to the kit to close the PKE-relay gap. Legal note for Matt: possession/operation of jam+capture gear implicates federal jamming law and state vehicle-theft statutes; if such a device is found during a client sweep, preserve it in place, photograph, and advise law enforcement rather than handling — surface as potential criminal exposure.

signatures.name: RKE rolling-code fob burst 315 MHz (OOK/ASK)
signatures.mode: 315 MHz ASK/OOK, PWM/Manchester rolling code (KeeLOQ-class), short button-press burst
signatures.tscm: Short (tens-of-ms) packetized OOK burst, repeated 2-4x per press, US/Japan RKE band. On its own this is a normal fob press; the ATTACK tell is this burst appearing simultaneously with a narrowband carrier/noise jammer parked on the same channel (see RollJam signatures). [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: RKE rolling-code fob burst 433.92 MHz (OOK/ASK)
signatures.mode: 433.92 MHz ASK/OOK rolling code, short button-press burst (EU/intl RKE + garage)
signatures.tscm: European/international RKE and most garage/gate remotes. Occupied BW roughly 100-200 kHz for OOK. Attack tell = coincident jammer on-channel while the fob burst is present. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: RKE rolling-code fob burst 433.92 MHz (FSK, ~70 kHz deviation)
signatures.mode: 433.92 MHz 2-FSK, mark/space ~433.89/433.96 MHz (~70 kHz separation), rolling code
signatures.tscm: FSK variant (common on higher-end EU fobs and Japanese-market designs). Two symmetric tones ~70 kHz apart about the 433.92 carrier — visually distinct from the single-lobe OOK version. Same rolling-code payload. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: RKE rolling-code fob burst 868 MHz (FSK/OOK)
signatures.mode: 868 MHz SRD-band RKE, FSK or OOK rolling code, short burst
signatures.tscm: European 868 MHz SRD RKE band. Some KeeLOQ/AES rolling-code fobs use FSK here. Attack tell = coincident on-channel jammer. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: RollJam simultaneous jammer 315 MHz (narrowband noise/carrier)
signatures.mode: 315 MHz narrowband noise or unmodulated/wobble carrier deliberately parked on the RKE receiver channel to block the car/garage while a separate RX captures the fob
signatures.tscm: The RollJam signature is a DUAL emission: this continuous narrowband jammer sitting slightly off the exact fob center (to block the vehicle's wider receiver while leaving the attacker's tuned RX able to demodulate the fob). Key TSCM tell: a persistent carrier/noise blob on 315 MHz that switches OFF the instant a valid unlock is later replayed. Illegal to operate in the US (FCC jamming prohibition). [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: RollJam simultaneous jammer 433.92 MHz (narrowband noise/carrier)
signatures.mode: 433.92 MHz narrowband noise/carrier jam parked on the RKE receiver passband during capture
signatures.tscm: Same RollJam behavior on the EU/garage band. Look for a continuous emitter on 433.92 coincident with (and slightly wider than) intercepted fob bursts. Pairs with the 433.92 fob burst signatures above to form the two-part attack fingerprint. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: RollJam simultaneous jammer 868 MHz (narrowband noise/carrier)
signatures.mode: 868 MHz SRD-band jam parked on the RKE receiver passband during capture
signatures.tscm: RollJam-class jammer on the European 868 SRD band. Continuous emitter coincident with 868 MHz fob activity. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: PKE LF exciter / wake field 125-135 kHz (relay re-radiation)
signatures.mode: 125-134.2 kHz low-frequency ASK exciter 'wake-up' field; in a relay attack this LF field is re-radiated near the victim key by the second relay unit
signatures.tscm: The near-field magnetic LF signal a car's door/handle exciter sends to wake the PKE fob (~125 kHz, sometimes 134.2 kHz). In a RELAY attack the key-side relay coil re-radiates this field to remotely wake the key. TSCM tell: a 125 kHz exciter field present where no vehicle exciter should be (e.g., beside a house door, in a hotel corridor). This is a near-field/inductive signal, not a far-field RF band. [BELOW-STOCK-PLUTO-REACH: 125 kHz is far below the Pluto/AD9364 325 MHz floor and below any HF/6 GHz SDR front end — requires a dedicated LF loop/receiver (e.g., 125 kHz RFID probe) or an LF-capable NLJD-adjacent tool. Cannot be seen by Pluto or B210.]

signatures.name: PKE UHF fob response 315/433 MHz (relay-forwarded)
signatures.mode: 315 or 433.92 MHz UHF authentication response from the PKE fob after LF wake; in a relay attack this challenge-response RF is what the car-side relay forwards
signatures.tscm: The fob's encrypted challenge-response uplink (FSK or OOK) triggered by the LF wake. In a relay attack it appears at the vehicle without the owner nearby. On-air it looks like a normal PKE handshake; the anomaly is the coincident out-of-place LF exciter field and the fob response occurring with the owner far away. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: PKE HF relay 13.56 MHz (NFC/HF passive-entry variant)
signatures.mode: 13.56 MHz ISO14443/NFC-class HF field, re-radiated by an HF relay for phone-as-key / NFC card passive entry
signatures.tscm: Used by NFC/phone-as-key and HF-card passive-entry systems (Digital Key / some smart-card immobilizers). Relay rig re-radiates the 13.56 MHz field to bridge card and reader. Near-field HF signal. [BELOW-STOCK-PLUTO-REACH: 13.56 MHz is below the Pluto 325 MHz floor; needs an HF-capable SDR (e.g., RTL-SDR with upconverter, or a dedicated NFC/HF probe). Not visible to stock Pluto or B210.]

device_classes.device_class: Wi-Fi / IP hidden cameras (802.11 a/b/g/n/ac/ax/ah, all bands + SoftAP setup mode)
device_classes.summary: Wi-Fi/IP hidden cameras are the single most common covert-camera class in the field, and on the air they are indistinguishable from any other Wi-Fi station: the camera is just an 802.11 client (or, in setup mode, a temporary AP) pushing an uplink-heavy H.264/H.265 stream. The distinct RF signatures are defined by the 802.11 PHY variant and channel plan, NOT by the disguise: 2.4 GHz (20/40 MHz), 5 GHz U-NII-1..3 (20/40/80/160 MHz), 6 GHz Wi-Fi 6E, 900 MHz 802.11ah HaLow for long-range/battery IoT cams, plus the SoftAP setup-mode beaconing that many cams emit on first boot or when they lose their saved network. Because a camera looks like a phone, laptop, or thermostat at the antenna, the discriminator for TSCM is behavioral (persistent uplink-dominant traffic from a fixed location), not spectral. REACH: stock ADALM-Pluto (325-3800 MHz, AD9363) reaches 900 MHz HaLow and the 2.4 GHz band cleanly; all 5 GHz signatures need the AD9364 firmware hack (reports as AD9364, extends to ~70 MHz-6 GHz), while a USRP B210 tunes 70 MHz-6 GHz natively and needs NO hack for 5 GHz (only appropriate antenna/filtering). 6 GHz Wi-Fi 6E (5925-7125) sits at the very top edge of both the AD9364-hacked Pluto and the B210 (both nominally ~6 GHz), so upper 6 GHz U-NII channels are effectively out of reach for both. 40/80/160 MHz channel widths meet or exceed the Pluto's practical instantaneous bandwidth (nominal 20 MHz, up to ~56 MHz degraded) and the B210's ~56 MHz (61.44 MHz max), so wide channels can only be reliably detected as energy/occupancy via swept scans, not fully captured in one shot.

confirm_steps: Sweep 2401-2483 MHz first (stock Pluto reaches it): look for persistent, UPLINK-dominant OFDM occupancy from a fixed spot — steady 1-8 Mbps duty that does not track a person browsing. A streaming cam runs continuously even in an empty room; toggle the room lights / wave motion and watch for a traffic change (motion-triggered cams spike on movement).

Catch SoftAP setup mode: power-cycle suspected devices or sweep on move-in / before a meeting. A camera that lost its network beacons its own SSID (~10 beacons/sec). Cross-check with a phone Wi-Fi scan or a Wi-Fi analyzer (WiFiman, Acrylic, Kismet) for suspicious SSIDs (HD-CAM-, ILNK-, YCC365-, JOOAN-, ANRAN-, V380-).

For the 900 MHz HaLow vector, sweep 902-928 MHz (stock-Pluto-reachable): narrow 1/2/4 MHz OFDM channels with persistent uplink duty. Because this band is full of LoRa/FHSS/ISM telemetry, confirm by duty pattern (continuous video does not equal periodic sensor chirps) and by physically hunting the emitter with a directional antenna + RSSI.

For 5 GHz / 6 GHz use an AD9364-hacked Pluto or a B210 (which tunes 5 GHz natively, no hack needed); capture 5150-5850 (and marginally lower 6 GHz). Because 40/80/160 MHz channels meet or exceed the radio's instantaneous bandwidth, run a swept occupancy scan (not single-capture) and log wide OFDM slabs with continuous uplink.

Confirm any RF hit with a physical sweep: NLJD (non-linear junction detector) finds the camera's semiconductor regardless of whether it is transmitting; IR/lens-glint flashlight sweep finds the optics; and a Wi-Fi/deauth-capable analyzer can enumerate associated stations on the room's AP and correlate MAC OUI to camera-module vendors.

De-confound by killing the venue Wi-Fi (or moving to a controlled RF-quiet room): a battery cam on SoftAP or a HaLow cam will keep transmitting when the house AP is off — that isolates the covert emitter from legitimate laptops/phones/thermostats.
false_positive_overlap: On the air a Wi-Fi camera is IDENTICAL to any other 802.11 station — laptops, phones, tablets, smart TVs, streaming sticks, doorbells, thermostats, smart speakers, printers all produce the same 2.4/5/6 GHz OFDM bursts. Band+width+modulation alone CANNOT distinguish a cam; only the persistent uplink-dominant duty from a fixed location does.
2.4 GHz is shared with Bluetooth/BLE, Zigbee, Thread, classic cordless gear, and microwave-oven leakage — plenty of non-Wi-Fi energy in-band.

900 MHz HaLow shares 902-928 MHz ISM with LoRa/LoRaWAN, FHSS wireless telemetry, some baby monitors, smart meters, and industrial sensors — high false-positive band; a HaLow cam is easy to mistake for benign IoT.
SoftAP beacons look like any consumer AP / travel router / phone hotspot; a revealing SSID is the giveaway, not the RF itself.
5/6 GHz occupancy overlaps mesh backhaul, laptops, and 4K streaming — a wide 80/160 MHz slab is far more likely a router/NVR than the camera element itself.
DFS channel-hopping in 5 GHz can look like an evasive device but is just normal radar-avoidance behavior.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Wi-Fi/IP cameras are the highest-prevalence covert-camera class, and the core TSCM truth is that they are NOT spectrally distinctive — a Pluto/B210 sees an ordinary 802.11 station. Do not chase a 'camera signature' spectrally; chase BEHAVIOR: persistent, uplink-heavy traffic from a fixed physical point that keeps running in an empty room and reacts to motion. Three practical wins: (1) SoftAP setup mode is the one moment a camera announces itself — power-cycle or sweep during move-in and enumerate SSIDs. (2) The 900 MHz HaLow vector is an emerging blind spot — most sweeps fixate on 2.4/5 GHz and miss long-range battery cams in 902-928 MHz, which a stock Pluto CAN reach — add it to every sweep. (3) RF sweeping alone will miss a camera that is powered off, recording only to local microSD, or wired/PoE with no RF at all — so RF must be paired with NLJD and physical/optical (lens-glint) search. Reach reality for the operator: stock Pluto (AD9363, 325-3800 MHz) covers 900 MHz HaLow and 2.4 GHz; 5 GHz requires the AD9364 firmware hack on Pluto OR a B210 (which tunes 70 MHz-6 GHz natively and needs no hack for 5 GHz, only proper antenna/filtering). 40/80/160 MHz channels meet or exceed both radios' instantaneous bandwidth (Pluto nominal 20 MHz / degraded up to ~56 MHz; B210 ~56-61 MHz) so wide channels can only be logged as occupancy via swept scans, never captured whole. Upper 6 GHz Wi-Fi 6E is effectively out of reach for both radios. A best-practice sweep also uses a commodity Wi-Fi NIC / analyzer (Kismet, Acrylic, WiFiman) alongside the SDR to demod SSIDs and correlate station MAC OUIs to camera-module vendors — the SDR proves energy, the NIC proves identity.

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz 802.11b/g/n HT20 (20 MHz)
signatures.mode: OFDM (g/n) / DSSS-CCK (b) burst, 20 MHz channel, camera uplink-heavy
signatures.tscm: Classic 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi on channels 1-13 (US 1-11), 20 MHz channel with ~17.8 MHz occupied bandwidth. Bursty TX-Op frames with beacon/ack structure; a streaming camera shows a persistent uplink-dominant duty cycle (steady ~1-8 Mbps of H.264/H.265) unlike bursty web browsing. 802.11b legacy shows DSSS/CCK ~22 MHz mask. Most disguised consumer spy cams are 2.4 GHz-only. [stock-Pluto-reachable at top of 325-3800 MHz range; 20 MHz fits Pluto practical BW and B210 natively]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz 802.11n HT40 (40 MHz)
signatures.mode: OFDM 40 MHz bonded channel (HT40+/HT40-), higher-rate camera stream
signatures.tscm: Channel-bonded 40 MHz in the crowded 2.4 GHz band (rare/discouraged but supported by some higher-res cams for 2K/4K uplink). Occupied ~40 MHz spans roughly two standard channels; energy footprint nearly fills the lower or upper half of the 2.4 GHz band. Distinguishes from HT20 by width alone. [stock-Pluto-reachable in frequency; 40 MHz sits at the edge of Pluto's practical single-shot BW (nominal 20 MHz, up to ~56 MHz degraded) and within B210 ~56 MHz — fully clean capture is marginal, best logged as occupancy]

signatures.name: 5 GHz 802.11a/n/ac/ax VHT20/HE20 (20 MHz) U-NII-1..3
signatures.mode: OFDM 20 MHz channel across U-NII-1/2A/2C(DFS)/3, dual-band camera uplink
signatures.tscm: 5 GHz 20 MHz channels: U-NII-1 5150-5250, U-NII-2A 5250-5350 (DFS), U-NII-2C 5470-5725 (DFS), U-NII-3 5725-5850 (5850-5895 is the newer U-NII-4 band). Cleaner/quieter than 2.4 GHz so 'dual-band' cams often prefer it. DFS channels show radar-avoidance behavior (channel moves after radar). Persistent uplink duty = streaming cam. [needs-AD9364-mod on Pluto (stock tops at 3800 MHz; hack reaches ~6 GHz). B210 tunes here natively, no hack. 20 MHz fits both radios' BW]

signatures.name: 5 GHz 802.11n/ac/ax HT40/VHT40 (40 MHz)
signatures.mode: OFDM 40 MHz bonded channel, 2K/4K camera stream
signatures.tscm: 40 MHz bonded pair in 5 GHz. Common width for higher-bitrate dual-band cams. Footprint ~40 MHz. Differentiated from 20/80/160 purely by occupied width during energy detection. [needs-AD9364-mod on Pluto (B210 native); 40 MHz near Pluto's practical single-shot limit, cleaner on B210, still best logged as occupancy for full capture]

signatures.name: 5 GHz 802.11ac/ax VHT80/HE80 (80 MHz)
signatures.mode: OFDM 80 MHz very-high-throughput channel, high-bitrate 4K camera
signatures.tscm: 80 MHz VHT/HE channel — a broad, flat OFDM slab. Used by premium 4K Wi-Fi cams and NVR backhaul. 80 MHz exceeds any single Pluto/B210 capture window, so it appears as a wide occupancy band that must be swept/stitched, not captured whole. [needs-AD9364-mod on Pluto for frequency (B210 native); 80 MHz EXCEEDS Pluto (~56 MHz practical) and B210 (~56-61 MHz) instantaneous BW — occupancy/sweep only]

signatures.name: 5 GHz 802.11ac/ax VHT160/HE160 (160 MHz)
signatures.mode: OFDM 160 MHz channel (contiguous or 80+80), top-tier throughput backhaul
signatures.tscm: 160 MHz is the widest 5 GHz channel; rare for the camera itself, more likely NVR/router backhaul, but flagship cams support it. Occupies a huge contiguous slab (or split 80+80). Purely an occupancy signature on Pluto/B210 — ~3x wider than either radio's capture window. [needs-AD9364-mod on Pluto for frequency (B210 native); 160 MHz FAR EXCEEDS Pluto and B210 instantaneous BW — occupancy/sweep only, never single-shot]

signatures.name: 6 GHz Wi-Fi 6E 802.11ax HE20/40/80/160 U-NII-5..8
signatures.mode: HE OFDMA on 6 GHz band, 20/40/80/160 MHz, next-gen camera/backhaul
signatures.tscm: Wi-Fi 6E opens 5925-7125 MHz (U-NII-5/6/7/8). Very clean band, so future high-res cams and their APs migrate here. Preferred Scanning Channels / low-power-indoor behavior. Currently rare in disguised consumer spy cams (market is still 2.4/5 GHz) but present in premium IP cameras and increasingly in dual/tri-band mesh backhaul a hidden cam may ride. [AT/ABOVE reach edge: AD9364-hacked Pluto and B210 both top out near 6 GHz — lower U-NII-5 (~5925-6425) may be marginally reachable, but most of 6 GHz (6425-7125) is out-of-range for both. Above ~6 GHz = out of B210 range entirely]

signatures.name: 900 MHz 802.11ah Wi-Fi HaLow (sub-GHz, 1/2/4/8/16 MHz)
signatures.mode: Sub-1GHz OFDM, narrow BW (1/2/4/8/16 MHz), long-range low-power camera
signatures.tscm: 802.11ah HaLow in US 902-928 MHz ISM. Narrow channels (1,2,4,8,16 MHz; 1/2/4 MHz typical for cams) with 802.11-style OFDM scaled down. Enables 1km+ battery cameras (Morse Micro, Vantron HCAM26, Askey CAM2301, Anjielo/Tuya). Emerging but growing covert-cam vector precisely because it is long-range, low-power, and OUTSIDE the 2.4/5 GHz bands most sweeps focus on. Shares 902-928 with LoRa, FHSS telemetry, and many other ISM devices — high false-positive band. [stock-Pluto-reachable (325-3800 MHz covers 900 MHz cleanly); narrow 1-8 MHz channels fit Pluto/B210 single-shot; 16 MHz near Pluto practical limit]

signatures.name: SoftAP setup-mode beacon/probe (camera-hosted AP SSID broadcast)
signatures.mode: 802.11 beacon frames ~10/sec from camera acting as temporary AP, 20 MHz
signatures.tscm: During first-boot pairing (or after losing its saved network) the camera becomes a SoftAP and BROADCASTS its own SSID with periodic ~102.4 ms beacons — often a revealing name (e.g. 'HD-CAM-xxxx', 'ILNK-xxxxxx', 'YCC365-xxxx', 'CLEVER DOG', 'JOOAN-xxxx', 'DAOFI', 'ANRAN'). This is the single most catchable TSCM moment: unlike a paired cam hiding as a client, a SoftAP announces itself. Usually 2.4 GHz ch 1/6/11; some dual-band cams SoftAP on 5 GHz. Regular, evenly-spaced beacon burst pattern. [stock-Pluto-reachable (2.4 GHz SoftAP); 5 GHz-SoftAP variant needs-AD9364-mod (or native B210). Beacon detection is easy on any SDR as periodic energy; SSID demod needs a Wi-Fi NIC/analyzer not a bare Pluto]

device_classes.device_class: Analog video transmitters (FM composite video Tx: 900 MHz / 1.2-1.3 GHz / 2.4 GHz / 5.8 GHz; board cams, pinhole VTx modules)
device_classes.summary: Analog video transmitters send raw composite (NTSC/PAL) baseband up-modulated as wideband FM onto a bare carrier — no packets, no protocol, no channel-access. On the air this is one modulation family repeated across four ISM/consumer bands, producing a small number of GENUINELY DISTINCT signatures defined by band and by a couple of real deviation/audio-subcarrier variants, not by the thousands of product models. All read as a wide (~6-20 MHz), CONTINUOUS, un-hopping FM hump with a bright carrier spike and video-line sidebands — one of the most recognizable and easiest things to catch in TSCM: on 100% of the time, no hopping, does not look like Wi-Fi/BT/cellular. The catch: on a stock ADALM-Pluto (325-3800 MHz, AD9363) you can reach 900 MHz, 1.2/1.3 GHz and 2.4 GHz but NOT 5.8 GHz. 5.8 GHz needs the B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz, verified) or an AD9364-frequency-hack Pluto (unofficial, out of filter spec above 3.8 GHz, marginal). VERIFIED CORRECTIONS applied to this class: (a) the 5.8 GHz A/B/E/F sub-band ranges were wrong in the source — Band A is 5725-5865 MHz (not 5865-5945), Band B 5733-5866, Band E 5645-5945, Band F/Fatshark 5740-5880; corrected in the A/B/E/F row. (b) The 1.2 GHz GPS-desense note referenced GPS L1 (1575 MHz) which is far above the band; the real adjacency is GPS L2 (1227 MHz), the 23cm ham allocation and aeronautical DME/radionav — corrected. Video FM is wider than a stock Pluto's ~20 MHz instantaneous capture, so sweep or use the widest sample rate to see the whole hump. Distinct rows: 900 MHz, 1.2 GHz, 1.3 GHz, 2.4 GHz 4-CH, 2.4 GHz high-power/wide-dev, 5.8 GHz A/B/E/F, 5.8 GHz Raceband, a narrow-deviation micro/pinhole variant, and the FM audio subcarrier riding alongside the video.

confirm_steps: Confirm it is CONTINUOUS: a real analog video Tx is on 100% of the time. Watch peak-hold and the live trace for 10-20 s — if the hump never blinks off and never hops, that rules out Wi-Fi/BT/most data links.

Confirm it is UN-FRAMED analog FM, not OFDM: zoom the span. Wi-Fi/5 GHz UNII show flat-topped OFDM blocks with sharp shoulders and MAC-rate on/off framing; analog FM video is a smooth rounded hump with a bright discrete CENTER CARRIER spike.
Look for PICTURE-BREATHING: cover/uncover the suspected camera or wave motion in front of it. A live video FM hump visibly widens/narrows with picture content and motion — data links do not.
Look for the HORIZONTAL-LINE ripple: at fine resolution the sidebands carry a 15.734 kHz (NTSC) or 15.625 kHz (PAL) comb — a strong tell of composite video.

Demodulate to PROVE it: on the B210/Pluto pull the composite baseband and check for video sync structure; if there is a mic, demod the ~4.5-6.5 MHz offset FM subcarrier as audio and listen for the room.

Direction-find: sweep the antenna around the room with reduced gain; the analog hump peaks sharply as you near the lens/module because these are low-power near-field emitters. Physically inspect where it peaks.

Band coverage: run 900 MHz, 1.2 GHz, 1.3 GHz and 2.4 GHz on the Pluto; switch to the B210 for 5.8 GHz (A/B/E/F — corrected centers A 5725-5865 / B 5733-5866 / E 5645-5945 / F 5740-5880 — and the 37 MHz-spaced Raceband grid 5658-5917). Do not declare 'clear' if 5.8 was never swept on hardware that reaches it.
Rule out legit occupants: 902-928 ISM, 23cm ham (1240-1300), 2.4/5 GHz Wi-Fi and analog baby monitors/senders all live here. Correlate a suspected hit with a physical device before calling it a bug.
false_positive_overlap: 2.4 GHz and 5.8 GHz analog video sit directly on top of Wi-Fi (2.4 GHz ch 1-11, 5 GHz UNII) — the bands are shared, so PRESENCE of energy proves nothing; the continuous un-framed analog hump vs bursty OFDM is the discriminator.

Legitimate consumer wireless AV senders (TV-to-another-room video baluns, wireless backup/rear-view car cameras, doorbell/nanny cams using analog FM) are the SAME signature as a covert cam — the RF is identical; only intent and placement differ.
Analog baby monitors on 900 MHz/2.4 GHz can present a near-identical continuous FM video/audio hump.

902-928 MHz ISM is crowded with LoRa, cordless phones, smart meters and telemetry; a 900 MHz video hump can be masked by or confused with these — video is wider and continuous, telemetry is narrow/bursty.

1.2/1.3 GHz overlaps the 23cm amateur band and aeronautical DME/radionav, and sits near GNSS (GPS L2 1227 MHz; L1 1575 MHz is above the band) — legitimate strong emitters exist; a licensed ham ATV signal looks like a covert video Tx on the analyzer.
5.8 GHz FPV drone/racing VTx are the exact same modules covert installers repurpose — a hobbyist drone nearby will trip every 5.8 GHz analog-video rule.
High-power (1-3 W) 2.4 GHz VTx at close range can overload the SDR front end and produce spurious wideband images that look like extra signatures — attenuate before trusting a wideband read.
Microwave-oven leakage and some non-video 2.4 GHz jammers produce broad continuous humps that can be mistaken for wideband FM video until you check for the center carrier and line-rate structure.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Analog FM video is, ironically, one of the EASIEST bug classes to catch and one of the easiest to misattribute. Easy to catch: continuous (on 100% of the time), no hopping, no packets, plus a bright discrete carrier and picture-breathing envelope — nothing on a modern spectrum looks like it except other analog video. Discipline: (1) prove continuous and un-framed, (2) prove it is video (picture-breathing + horizontal-line ripple, ideally a demod), (3) direction-find to a physical lens before declaring a bug. Do not stop at 'there is energy on 2.4 GHz' — that is just Wi-Fi country. HARDWARE REACH is the single biggest gap for this class: a stock ADALM-Pluto (325-3800 MHz, AD9363) covers 900 MHz, 1.2, 1.3 and 2.4 GHz but CANNOT reach 5.8 GHz — and a very large share of modern pinhole/board cams are 5.8 GHz. A Pluto-only survey has NOT cleared 5.8 GHz; use the B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz, verified) for the 5.8 GHz rows. The AD9364 'frequency hack' that nominally extends a Pluto past 3.8 GHz is unofficial, out of filter spec, and unreliable for sensitive TSCM — do not rely on it. TWO RF-ACCURACY CORRECTIONS were applied to the source catalog during this verification: (1) the 5.8 GHz Band A sub-range was wrong (listed 5865-5945; correct is 5725-5865 MHz per standard FPV channel charts) — fixed in the A/B/E/F row and confirm step; (2) the 1.2 GHz 'desense GPS L1' claim was imprecise — GPS L1 is at 1575 MHz, well above the 1.2 GHz band, so any L1 effect is broadband splatter, not co-channel; the real adjacency is GPS L2 (1227 MHz), 23cm ham and aeronautical DME/radionav — corrected in that reach note. Legal/privacy note for Shield work: if the FM audio subcarrier is present the device is capturing ROOM AUDIO, which materially raises the legal stakes (wiretap/eavesdropping statutes) versus a video-only camera — flag that distinction explicitly in any client report, and preserve the finding (photograph in place, note frequency/time) before removal so chain-of-custody holds if it becomes evidence.

signatures.name: 900 MHz analog FM composite video
signatures.mode: Wideband FM of NTSC/PAL composite video (approx +/- 4-6 MHz deviation), bright residual carrier + video-line sidebands, on continuously
signatures.tscm: One fat continuous FM hump ~10-18 MHz wide sitting in the 902-928 MHz ISM band with a persistent center-carrier spike. Envelope breathes with picture content (motion widens the hump); a 15.734 kHz (NTSC) / 15.625 kHz (PAL) horizontal-line ripple is visible on the sidebands. No packet structure, no hopping, no beacon. Often a small FM audio subcarrier bump on one shoulder (see audio-subcarrier row). [stock-Pluto-reachable (well within 325-3800 MHz). US 902-928 ISM overlaps LoRa/ISM telemetry and some cordless gear.]

signatures.name: 1.2 GHz analog FM composite video
signatures.mode: Wideband FM composite video (approx +/- 5-6 MHz deviation), continuous, common ham/FPV 23cm-adjacent channels ~1080/1120/1160/1200/1240 MHz
signatures.tscm: Continuous ~12-20 MHz FM hump on one of a handful of fixed 1.2 GHz channels with a strong center carrier and horizontal-line sidebands. Prized by covert installers because 1.2 GHz penetrates walls better than 2.4/5.8 and is far from Wi-Fi. Does not hop. Picture-dependent envelope breathing is the tell it is live video, not a data link. [stock-Pluto-reachable. CAUTION: overlaps the 23cm amateur allocation (1240-1300) and sits near aeronautical DME/radionav; a strong VTx here (and its broadband noise/harmonics) can degrade nearby GNSS reception (GPS L2 is at 1227 MHz; GPS L1 at 1575 MHz is well above this band, so any L1 impact is via broadband splatter, not co-channel). Reach is fine; interpretation needs care.]

signatures.name: 1.3 GHz analog FM composite video
signatures.mode: Wideband FM composite video (approx +/- 5-6 MHz deviation), continuous, common channels ~1258/1280/1320/1360 MHz
signatures.tscm: Same continuous wideband FM video hump as the 1.2 GHz row but shifted up into the 1258-1360 MHz range. Separated because the transmit modules and channel plans are physically distinct products with distinct crystal/PLL sets; on a spectrum display they appear as a separate cluster of fixed channels. Strong center carrier, line-rate sidebands, envelope breathes with motion. [stock-Pluto-reachable. Sits in the 23cm ham allocation and near aeronautical radionav — expect legitimate occupants; a bright, continuous, video-breathing hump NOT on a ham repeater plan is the suspicious case.]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz 4-channel analog FM video (standard low/mid power)
signatures.mode: Wideband FM composite video on fixed CH1 2414 / CH2 2432 / CH3 2450 / CH4 2468 MHz (the 'Airwave' 4-CH plan), ~+/- 5-6 MHz deviation, continuous
signatures.tscm: The classic cheap wireless spy-cam signature: one continuous ~16-18 MHz FM hump parked on 2414, 2432, 2450 or 2468 MHz. Unlike Wi-Fi (bursty OFDM, MAC framing) it is ON all the time and un-modulated by any protocol — a smooth analog hump with a bright center carrier and horizontal-line ripple that breathes with the picture. Sits right on top of Wi-Fi channels 1/6/11 region, which is exactly why it hides there and why confirmation matters. [stock-Pluto-reachable (2.4 GHz well inside 325-3800 MHz). Heaviest false-positive band by far — see overlap notes.]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz high-power / wide-deviation FM video
signatures.mode: Wideband FM composite video, wider deviation (approx +/- 7-9 MHz) driven by 1-3 W power amps, continuous
signatures.tscm: A visibly WIDER and much stronger version of the standard 2.4 GHz row — 1W/2W/3W booster VTx modules push more deviation and can splatter to ~20-24 MHz occupied, sometimes bleeding across two of the four channel slots. Very high on-air power makes it dominate the 2.4 GHz noise floor. Distinct because occupied bandwidth and power envelope differ enough to matter for the matcher; still continuous, still bright center carrier, still line-rate sidebands. [stock-Pluto-reachable. High power may overload the Pluto front end at close range — add attenuation or back off gain to avoid a false wideband read from receiver overload.]

signatures.name: 5.8 GHz analog FM video — A/B/E/F bands
signatures.mode: Wideband FM composite video on FPV band A/B/E/F channels (channel centers span ~5645-5945 MHz), ~+/- 5-6 MHz deviation, continuous
signatures.tscm: Continuous ~16-20 MHz FM video hump on one of the ~32 legacy FPV channels. CORRECTED band centers: Band A 5725-5865, Band B 5733-5866, Band E 5645-5945 (the two E groups straddle the ends), Band F/Fatshark 5740-5880. Bright center carrier, picture-breathing envelope, horizontal-line sidebands. Extremely common in modern pinhole/board-cam kits because 5.8 GHz antennas are tiny and the band is lightly policed. Sits alongside 5 GHz Wi-Fi (UNII) so, like 2.4, it hides among legitimate traffic — but the analog hump is continuous and un-framed, unlike OFDM Wi-Fi. [NOT reachable on a stock Pluto (ceiling 3800 MHz, AD9363). Needs the B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz, verified — covers 5.8). An AD9364 firmware/frequency 'hack' on a Pluto can nominally tune here but is unofficial, out of filter spec above 3.8 GHz, and sensitivity is unspecified/poor — treat as unreliable. Use the B210 for 5.8 GHz.]

signatures.name: 5.8 GHz analog FM video — Raceband (R1-R8)
signatures.mode: Wideband FM composite video on Raceband R1-R8 (5658/5695/5732/5769/5806/5843/5880/5917 MHz, ~37 MHz spacing), continuous
signatures.tscm: Same continuous FM video hump but on the evenly-spaced 37 MHz Raceband grid (R1 5658 ... R8 5917 MHz). Called out separately because the 37 MHz-spaced channel centers are a recognizable fingerprint: a scan showing energy landing on that regular grid (rather than the irregular A/B/E/F centers) strongly implies a Raceband VTx. Continuous, bright carrier, line-rate sidebands, picture-breathing. Note occupied energy per channel (~16-18 MHz) still extends beyond the listed center frequencies. [NOT reachable on a stock Pluto (3800 MHz ceiling). Use the B210 (covers to 6 GHz, verified). Same AD9364-hack caveat as the A/B/E/F row — unreliable above 3.8 GHz on Pluto.]

signatures.name: Low-power narrow-deviation micro/pinhole FM video (any band)
signatures.mode: Narrow-deviation FM composite video (approx +/- 2-3 MHz), 10-25 mW nano/pinhole VTx, continuous but weak
signatures.tscm: The hardest-to-catch analog video variant: tiny 10-25 mW nano VTx (sub-gram board/pinhole modules) run reduced deviation to fit a narrow slot, so the hump is only ~4-6 MHz wide and low-amplitude — easy to miss against the noise floor unless the sweep dwells. Still continuous, still an un-framed analog FM hump with a center carrier and faint line-rate ripple. Spans all four bands depending on the module; the DISTINCT feature is the narrow occupied bandwidth + low power, which is why it gets its own row for the matcher's threshold logic. [Reachable on stock Pluto for the 900 MHz / 1.2 / 1.3 / 2.4 GHz instances; the 5.8 GHz instances need the B210. Low power means get the antenna close and dwell — a near-field sweep of the room is the practical detection method.]

signatures.name: FM audio subcarrier riding alongside analog video
signatures.mode: Narrowband FM audio subcarrier offset ~4.5-6.5 MHz from the video carrier (intercarrier sound), continuous when the cam has a mic
signatures.tscm: Many analog spy cams also transmit room AUDIO as a narrow FM subcarrier sitting on the shoulder of the video hump, offset roughly 4.5-6.5 MHz from the video carrier (like broadcast intercarrier sound). It shows as a small, distinct ~150-300 kHz FM pip riding a fixed offset above/below the big video hump. Its presence is forensically important: it means the device is an audio-plus-video bug (higher privacy/legal stakes) not just a camera. Demodulating it as FM voice can confirm live room audio. [Reachable wherever its parent video carrier is: stock-Pluto for 900/1.2/1.3/2.4 GHz, B210 for 5.8 GHz. Because it is only ~5 MHz off the video carrier, if you can see the video hump you can see the subcarrier in the same capture.]

device_classes.device_class: Baby monitors (audio + video) repurposed as covert bugs — spanning legacy analog 49 MHz, 420/900 MHz FM video, 900 MHz FHSS digital audio, DECT 1.9 GHz digital audio, proprietary 2.4 GHz FHSS digital, and Wi-Fi (2.4/5 GHz) IP camera generations.
device_classes.summary: Baby monitors are one of the most common "found" bugs in residential TSCM because a monitor left running (or deliberately planted) in a room is a perfectly legitimate-looking always-on RF transmitter. The class splits cleanly by generation into 9 genuinely distinct on-air signatures. The oldest (49 MHz FM) sits BELOW a stock ADALM-Pluto's 325 MHz floor and will be missed entirely without a VHF-capable front end; the 420 MHz FM-video generation sits comfortably in stock Pluto range (well above the 325 MHz floor). The middle generation (900 MHz analog FM, 900 MHz FHSS, DECT 1.9 GHz) is squarely in Pluto range and is where most "hidden analog transmitter" hunts land. The modern generation is Wi-Fi or proprietary 2.4 GHz digital — indistinguishable at the PHY layer from a Wi-Fi/2.4 GHz spy cam, so it is a signature you match on band+behavior, not on a unique waveform. Analog generations are the real TSCM prize: an analog 49/900 MHz FM carrier that resolves to room audio when demodulated is a near-certain live bug. Digital generations require pattern-of-life and physical correlation because the band is shared with thousands of benign devices. VERIFICATION NOTE: DECT channel count corrected (NA DECT 6.0 = 5 carriers in 1920-1930 MHz; EU DECT = 10 carriers in 1880-1900 MHz — the original 'mode' text conflated the two); 420 MHz reach wording corrected from 'at/just above the Pluto edge' (misleading — 420 MHz has ~95 MHz of margin above the 325 MHz floor and is comfortably in range). Stock Pluto 325 MHz–3.8 GHz and B210 6 GHz ceilings verified against ADI/Ettus specs. All other bands, signal_class enums, duty cycles, and FP overlaps verified sound.

confirm_steps: For 49 MHz FM: use a VHF-capable receiver (stock Pluto can't reach this — use RTL-SDR/RSP or a scanner). Tune each fixed channel (49.300/49.830/49.845/49.860/49.875/49.890). FM-demodulate. If you hear live room audio (or your own voice/tap test from the suspected room), it is a live analog audio bug. Voice-activated units transmit only when there is sound — make noise in the room to key it.

For 420 MHz / 900 MHz / 2.4 GHz analog FM VIDEO: FM-video-demodulate the wideband hump. A live picture that matches the room confirms an analog video transmitter. Physically induce a change (wave a light/hand) and watch the demod for correlated motion.
For 900 MHz analog FM audio: sweep 902-928 MHz for a static narrowband carrier; FM-demod and do the tap/voice test in the suspected room to correlate audio.

For 900 MHz / 2.4 GHz FHSS: run a long max-hold/persistence sweep across the full ISM band to reveal the hop set; correlate hop activity with the device by power-cycling the suspected unit (hops disappear) or by proximity power ramp with a directional antenna / near-field probe.

For DECT 1.9 GHz: identify the ~1.7 MHz GFSK channel with ~10 ms TDMA framing in 1880-1900 MHz (EU, 10 carriers) or 1920-1930 MHz (NA UPCS, 5 carriers). Confirm it is the monitor (not a cordless phone) by proximity/near-field localization and by powering the suspected unit off.

For Wi-Fi (2.4/5 GHz): DO NOT rely on SDR alone — put a Wi-Fi NIC in monitor mode (Kismet/airodump), enumerate clients, match OUI to a camera vendor, and look for a fixed device with steady high-rate uplink video. Power-cycle the suspect and watch the station drop off.

Universal physical confirm: sweep with a directional antenna or near-field probe to localize the emitter to a physical spot, then visually inspect for a baby-monitor camera/mic unit. A found monitor in a room where no infant is present is the finding — document make/model/FCC ID.

Correlate to a receiver: baby monitors are paired transmitter+parent-unit. Finding the parent/receiver unit (or evidence the feed is being watched) elevates it from 'benign leftover' to 'active surveillance.'
false_positive_overlap: 49 MHz: old cordless phones, 49 MHz walkie-talkies, RC toys/models, and wireless intercoms share the exact channels — an FM carrier here is not automatically a bug until audio-correlated.
420-430 MHz: 70 cm amateur radio, 433 MHz ISM remotes/sensors, and analog FPV video downlinks overlap; only the wide FM-video hump (not narrowband hits) points to a camera.
902-928 MHz: 900 MHz cordless phones, wireless headphones/speakers, Z-Wave, LoRa, smart meters, and industrial telemetry all live here — heavy benign traffic.

1880-1930 MHz DECT: cordless phone bases and handsets use the identical PHY (EU 1880-1900, NA UPCS 1920-1930). A DECT channel is far more likely a household phone than a bug — physical localization is essential.
2.4 GHz analog video: analog wireless CCTV, drone/FPV video, and old wireless AV senders (senders for TV) produce the same FM-video hump.
2.4 GHz FHSS: Bluetooth/BLE, wireless mice/keyboards, wireless game controllers, Zigbee, and countless proprietary IoT links flood this band — a huge false-positive pool.
2.4 GHz Wi-Fi: every phone, laptop, tablet, smart TV, Wi-Fi security camera, doorbell, and IoT device — RF layer cannot distinguish a Wi-Fi baby monitor from any of them.
5 GHz Wi-Fi: every dual-band laptop/phone, streaming stick, mesh node, and 5 GHz security camera. Radar/DFS activity in U-NII-2 can also appear.

General: a baby monitor is a LEGITIMATE device. Its RF signature is 'benign consumer electronics' by design. The TSCM finding is context (monitor present where it shouldn't be / aimed at a target), not an inherently illicit waveform.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Baby monitors are the archetypal 'hidden in plain sight' bug: legitimate, always-on, and cheap. Triage by generation. (1) ANALOG generations (49 MHz FM audio, 420/900/2.4 GHz FM video, 900 MHz FM audio) are the high-value finds — they can be DEMODULATED IN THE FIELD to plaintext audio/video, so a carrier that resolves to the target room's audio or picture is near-conclusive evidence of live surveillance. Prioritize these; they are also the ones a hostile party would repurpose precisely because they are unencrypted and receivable on any matching consumer receiver. (2) The 49 MHz generation is the single most important reason NOT to trust a stock Pluto sweep alone for this class — it is below the Pluto/B210 floor and will be MISSED entirely unless you add a VHF-capable receiver (RTL-SDR/RSP/scanner). Document this gap in the sweep report. (3) DIGITAL generations (DECT, 900 MHz/2.4 GHz FHSS, Wi-Fi) cannot be demodulated to plaintext in the field and share their band with dozens of benign devices, so they demand pattern-of-life + physical localization + (for Wi-Fi) network-layer identification. Do not call a DECT channel or a Wi-Fi burst a bug from the spectrum alone. NOTE for DECT: NA 'DECT 6.0' occupies the UPCS band 1920-1930 MHz with 5 carriers; EU DECT occupies 1880-1900 MHz with 10 carriers — sweep the correct span for the region. (4) The Wi-Fi generations blur completely into the 'Wi-Fi spy camera' class — treat them there for identification; the only baby-monitor-specific tells are OUI (VTech/Motorola/Nanit/Owlet/Cubo/Miku ranges) and a fixed device streaming steady uplink video. (5) LEGAL/CONTEXT flag: a working baby monitor pointed at a bedroom/bathroom, or a monitor whose paired parent-unit is off-premises, moves this from 'harmless leftover' toward potential unlawful interception/voyeurism — surface it to the client and, where warranted, counsel immediately rather than just logging a signal. (6) Always recover make/model/FCC ID from the physical unit; it resolves the band/PHY ambiguity instantly and supports any downstream report.

signatures.name: 49 MHz analog FM audio (legacy baby monitor)
signatures.mode: Narrowband analog FM voice, fixed channel (typ. 49.300 / 49.830 / 49.845 / 49.860 / 49.875 / 49.890 MHz), continuous carrier keyed by sound or always-on
signatures.tscm: Single fixed narrowband FM carrier in the 49.3-49.9 MHz range; demodulating with an FM receiver yields clear room audio. Shares band with old cordless phones and 49 MHz walkie-talkies/RC toys. Carrier is steady (or voice-activated: present whenever there is sound in the room). No hopping, no digital structure — the cheapest and most eavesdroppable generation. [OUT of stock Pluto range (Pluto AD9363 floor is ~325 MHz). Needs a different front end / upconverter or a wideband RTL-SDR/HF+VHF receiver. B210 also does not reach this low without a downconverter. Use a dedicated 30-500 MHz scanner or RSP-class SDR for this generation.]

signatures.name: 420 MHz analog FM composite video (legacy video monitor)
signatures.mode: Wideband analog FM video (NTSC/PAL composite over FM), continuous while camera powered; may carry FM audio subcarrier
signatures.tscm: Broad ~5-6 MHz FM video hump around 420-430 MHz — the classic cheap wireless video downlink also used by early 'FPV' and covert cameras. Demodulates to a live video frame on an analog FM-TV / vestigial receiver. Distinct from 900 MHz/2.4 GHz video only by band. Continuous, wideband, and centered — very visible on a spectrum sweep. Overlaps 70 cm amateur band and 433 MHz ISM devices, but those are narrowband; the video hump is unmistakably wide. [Comfortably inside stock Pluto range — 420 MHz sits ~95 MHz above the ~325 MHz floor, not marginal — and well within B210 range. The full 6 MHz width fits inside Pluto's 20 MHz max instantaneous bandwidth, so capture the whole hump in one grab.]

signatures.name: 900 MHz analog FM audio (analog baby monitor)
signatures.mode: Narrowband analog FM voice on a fixed 900 MHz ISM channel, continuous or voice-activated
signatures.tscm: Fixed narrowband FM carrier somewhere in the 902-928 MHz US ISM band; FM-demods to room audio. Distinguished from 900 MHz FHSS by the fact that the carrier sits still on one frequency rather than hopping. Shares band with old 900 MHz cordless phones, wireless headphones, and some SCADA/telemetry — but a static FM carrier that resolves to clear voice from a room is the tell. [Fully in stock Pluto range (902-928 MHz is well inside 325-3800 MHz) and in B210 range. Easy sweep; narrow enough that a single Pluto capture spans multiple candidate channels.]

signatures.name: 900 MHz FHSS digital audio (frequency-hopping baby monitor)
signatures.mode: Proprietary frequency-hopping spread spectrum, digital audio, hops across the full 902-928 MHz band on a pseudo-random schedule
signatures.tscm: Short digital bursts that jump around the 26 MHz-wide 900 MHz ISM band — on a persistence/max-hold waterfall this paints many narrow hits scattered across 902-928 MHz over time. No single fixed carrier to demod as audio (digital + often lightly obfuscated). Distinguished from 900 MHz analog by the hopping and by the digital burst envelope. Overlaps with 900 MHz FHSS cordless phones and some industrial telemetry — pattern-of-life and hop rate help discriminate. [Fully in stock Pluto range. Requires wideband capture (ideally the full 26 MHz) or long max-hold dwell to see the hop set; Pluto's ~20 MHz instantaneous bandwidth nearly spans it, B210's up to 56 MHz covers it in one shot.]

signatures.name: DECT 1.9 GHz digital audio (DECT/'DECT 6.0' audio monitor)
signatures.mode: DECT TDMA/TDD, GFSK, 1.728 MHz channel spacing. EU DECT: 1880-1900 MHz, 10 carriers. NA 'DECT 6.0' (UPCS band): 1920-1930 MHz, 5 carriers. Framed ~10 ms TDMA/TDD bursts.
signatures.tscm: Highly regular ~1.7 MHz-wide GFSK channel with a crisp ~10 ms TDMA frame structure — the same PHY as DECT cordless phones. On a spectrum display it is a clean rectangular channel that pulses in a fixed TDD cadence. Distinguished from Wi-Fi/2.4 GHz by band (1.88-1.93 GHz) and by the textbook DECT frame timing. Encrypted audio, so no plaintext demod. Overlaps entirely with DECT 6.0 cordless phones — the false positive is a phone base, not a bug, so physical location matters. [Fully in stock Pluto range (1.88-1.93 GHz inside 325-3800 MHz) and B210 range. Single-channel width (~1.7 MHz) is easily captured; sweep the EU 10-channel / NA 5-channel span to catch whichever carrier it parked on.]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz analog FM video (legacy 2.4 GHz video monitor)
signatures.mode: Wideband analog FM video on a fixed 2.4 GHz channel (typ. ~2414/2432/2450/2468 MHz), continuous, often with FM audio subcarrier
signatures.tscm: A broad (~15-18 MHz) continuous FM video hump parked on one of the four classic analog 2.4 GHz channels — the same waveform used by cheap analog wireless spy cameras. FM-video demodulates to a live picture. Distinct from 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi (which is bursty OFDM, not a steady wideband hump) and from 2.4 GHz FHSS (which hops). Overlaps with analog 2.4 GHz CCTV/FPV and older wireless AV senders. [In stock Pluto range but the ~18 MHz video width nearly fills Pluto's 20 MHz max instantaneous bandwidth — usable in one grab but with little margin; you may prefer to step across it or reduce sample-rate trade-offs. B210 (up to 56 MHz) captures the whole hump comfortably. 2.4 GHz is within both Pluto (3.8 GHz) and B210 (6 GHz).]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz proprietary FHSS digital audio/video (modern non-Wi-Fi monitor)
signatures.mode: Proprietary FHSS/GFSK digital audio+video (non-802.11), fast hopping across the 2.4 GHz ISM band; adaptive to avoid Wi-Fi
signatures.tscm: Digital bursts hopping across 2400-2483.5 MHz that do NOT conform to Wi-Fi channelization — the dominant modern dedicated-link video baby monitor PHY (Infant Optics, VTech, HelloBaby, etc. use proprietary 2.4 GHz FHSS, not Wi-Fi). On max-hold it fills the band with scattered narrow hits at a characteristic hop rate. Distinguished from Wi-Fi by burst shape/hop pattern and from analog 2.4 GHz video by being digital + hopping. Massive false-positive overlap with Bluetooth, BLE, wireless mice/keyboards, and other proprietary 2.4 GHz links. [In stock Pluto range and B210 range. Whole 83.5 MHz band exceeds Pluto's ~20 MHz instantaneous bandwidth — needs stepped sweep or B210's wider capture to see the full hop set. Hop discrimination usually needs a max-hold/persistence display, not a single snapshot.]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi (802.11) digital audio/video (IP/Wi-Fi baby monitor)
signatures.mode: 802.11b/g/n OFDM/DSSS, 20/40 MHz channels (1/6/11), associated to home AP, bursty uplink video stream
signatures.tscm: Standard Wi-Fi PHY — 20 MHz OFDM channel bursts on Wi-Fi channels 1/6/11 with a continuous-ish upstream video flow. INDISTINGUISHABLE at the RF layer from any other 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi camera or Wi-Fi device; you cannot tell a Wi-Fi baby monitor from a Wi-Fi spy cam or a laptop by spectrum alone. Identify by MAC OUI / SSID / traffic pattern (steady high-rate uplink from a fixed device) at the network layer, not the PHY. This is a band+behavior signature, not a unique waveform. [In stock Pluto range and B210 range for RF energy detection, but PHY demod/identification is impractical with Pluto — use a Wi-Fi NIC in monitor mode / Kismet for OUI and traffic analysis. SDR only tells you 'Wi-Fi energy is here,' not which device.]

signatures.name: 5 GHz Wi-Fi (802.11a/n/ac) digital video (dual-band Wi-Fi monitor)
signatures.mode: 802.11a/n/ac OFDM, 20/40/80 MHz channels in U-NII 1-3, associated to dual-band AP, HD video uplink
signatures.tscm: Wide OFDM Wi-Fi channels in the 5 GHz U-NII bands carrying HD video from newer dual-band Wi-Fi monitors (e.g., higher-res IP cameras/Nanit-class devices that use 5 GHz). Same identification caveat as 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi — indistinguishable from any other 5 GHz Wi-Fi client at the PHY; identify by OUI/SSID/traffic. Overlaps with every 5 GHz laptop, phone, streaming device, and Wi-Fi security camera. [OUT of range for a stock Pluto (3.8 GHz ceiling). The 5150-5875 MHz U-NII 1-3 span is WITHIN a B210's 6 GHz ceiling, so a B210 can do energy detection here. For actual device ID use a 5 GHz-capable Wi-Fi NIC. Stock Pluto cannot see this band at all.]

device_classes.device_class: DECT (Digital Enhanced Cordless Telecommunications) — cordless phones, DECT bugs/audio taps, DECT baby monitors, and DECT ULE sensors, across regional 1.88-1.93 GHz band placements plus DECT-2020 NR+
device_classes.summary: DECT is a single physical-layer family that is trivially in reach of a stock Pluto (325-3800 MHz) and a B210 — all variants live around 1.88-1.93 GHz. Classic DECT / CAT-iq / DECT ULE all share ONE on-air PHY: GFSK at 1.152 Mbit/s (~288 kHz peak deviation, modulation index ~0.5), carriers spaced 1.728 MHz, and a 24-slot TDMA/TDD frame repeating every exactly 10 ms (so bursts recur at 100 Hz / multiples). Note the ~1.728 MHz figure is the CHANNEL SPACING; a single DECT burst's occupied (-3 dB) bandwidth is narrower, roughly 1.1-1.4 MHz, so carriers do not fully fill their 1.728 MHz lane. That 10 ms TDMA heartbeat with ~1.7 MHz-wide bursts on a 1.728 MHz grid is the master DECT fingerprint and is what the matcher should key on. The genuinely DISTINCT signatures are therefore NOT per-product but per (a) REGIONAL BAND PLACEMENT — EU/RoW 1880-1900, US/Canada 1920-1930, Brazil 1910-1920, LatAm-ex-Brazil 1910-1930, Japan 1893.5-1906.1, India 1880-1930 — because that changes where the SDR tunes and detects; (b) DUTY PATTERN — a live cordless CALL is near-continuous TDMA on 1-2 carriers, an IDLE/standby base emits a low-rate dummy-bearer beacon (~every 10 ms but only a couple slots), and a DECT ULE sensor is bursty/sleepy (long silence, short DECT burst on event/keepalive); and (c) DECT-2020 NR+, which is a totally different modulation (CP-OFDM, scalable 1.728-13.824 MHz channels) sharing the same band. For TSCM: a covert DECT audio bug or a DECT baby monitor used as a room monitor looks IDENTICAL on the air to a legitimate cordless phone/base — the discriminator is location and persistence, not RF class. DECT is a favored covert-audio band precisely because sweepers who only cover 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi and analog bands miss it. Everything here is inside stock-Pluto reach; nothing needs the AD9364 mod or exceeds B210's 6 GHz ceiling.
