confirm_steps: Tune the SDR to the applicable regional window (US/Canada 1920-1930, EU/RoW 1880-1900, Brazil 1910-1920, LatAm 1910-1930, Japan ~1893.5-1906.1) and look for GFSK carrier lanes on a 1.728 MHz grid.

Confirm the 10 ms TDMA heartbeat: capture a waterfall and verify bursts recur at exactly 100 Hz cadence (and harmonics). This rigid 10 ms periodicity is the definitive classic-DECT discriminator vs random FSK.

Measure occupied bandwidth of a single carrier: bursts sit on a 1.728 MHz channel grid but the -3 dB occupied width is ~1.1-1.4 MHz (GFSK, ~288 kHz peak deviation, modulation index ~0.5). A ~1.1-1.7 MHz GFSK burst on a 1.728 MHz grid at ~1.9 GHz on a 10 ms frame is DECT to high confidence.

Classify duty to separate variants: continuous two-sided TDD lane = active call; a lone periodic pip once per 10 ms on one carrier = idle base dummy-bearer beacon (device present but silent); long-silence + sparse short bursts = DECT ULE sensor.

To distinguish DECT-2020 NR+: check whether the occupancy is a flat OFDM block (NR+) versus discrete GFSK burst lanes (classic). NR+ shows filled 1.728 / 3.456 MHz OFDM channels without the classic 10 ms GFSK burst signature.

Presence-confirm a suspected hidden DECT device by proximity: sweep with a directional/near-field antenna and watch the burst RSSI rise as you approach a specific object; DECT beacons persist even with no call in progress, so a powered bug is detectable at idle.

Correlate with a physical inventory: identify every legitimate DECT base/handset and baby monitor on site, note its band/carrier, then flag any DECT emitter that does not map to a known, accounted-for device.
device_classes.tscm_notes: DECT is a high-priority covert-audio band in TSCM precisely because many amateur sweepers only cover 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi, Bluetooth, and analog VHF/UHF and skip the narrow 1.88-1.93 GHz DECT allocation. A DECT audio bug, a repurposed cordless handset left off-hook as an open mic, or a DECT baby monitor deployed as a room monitor all present as ordinary, encrypted (DSC/DSAA) DECT traffic — you generally cannot demodulate the audio without specialized tooling, and legality of doing so varies, so treat DECT detection as PRESENCE/LOCATION work, not content interception. The strongest operational tell is that a powered DECT base emits a periodic dummy-bearer beacon every 10 ms even when idle, so a hidden bug betrays itself at rest — sweep the applicable regional window with a directional antenna and hunt the beacon to the physical object. Always reconcile every DECT emitter against a physical inventory of known phones, monitors, and smart-home hubs; the risk item is any DECT signature that does not map to an accounted-for device. Note that DECT audio bugs are commonly marketed alongside GSM/4G listening devices; if you find DECT, also sweep the cellular uplink bands for a co-located GSM bug. This is all internal sweep methodology — a client-facing report should state findings (device present/located or clear) in plain language and avoid implying audio content was intercepted.

signatures.name: DECT classic — EU / Rest-of-World band (1880-1900 MHz), active call
signatures.mode: GFSK, 1.152 Mbit/s, TDMA/TDD, 24 slots per 10 ms frame, 10 carriers spaced 1.728 MHz (carrier centers ~1881.792 to 1897.344 MHz)
signatures.tscm: Master DECT fingerprint: ~1.7 MHz-wide GFSK bursts on a 1.728 MHz carrier grid recurring on a rigid 10 ms TDMA frame (bursts at 100 Hz cadence and harmonics). Occupied burst bandwidth (~1.1-1.4 MHz at -3 dB) is slightly narrower than the 1.728 MHz channel spacing. Active call occupies one carrier full-duplex via TDD (base slots 0-11, handset 12-23). Waterfall shows evenly spaced vertical carrier lanes on a 1.728 MHz grid within 1880-1900. Used across Europe, UK, Australia, NZ, South Africa, most of Asia, Hong Kong. [In stock-Pluto reach (325-3800 MHz) and B210 reach — ~1.89 GHz. No AD9364 mod or up/down-converter needed.]

signatures.name: DECT 6.0 — US / Canada band (1920-1930 MHz, UPCS), active call
signatures.mode: GFSK, 1.152 Mbit/s, TDMA/TDD, 24 slots per 10 ms frame, 5 carriers spaced 1.728 MHz (US band is 10 MHz wide -> 5 carriers, ~1921.536 to 1928.448 MHz)
signatures.tscm: Same 10 ms TDMA GFSK burst PHY as EU DECT but retuned to the FCC UPCS band 1920-1930. Only 5 carrier lanes (half the EU count) because band is 10 MHz not 20 MHz. 'DECT 6.0' is a US marketing label — technically identical PHY, different band. This is the dominant North American cordless-phone / DECT-bug signature. [In stock-Pluto reach and B210 reach — ~1.925 GHz.]

signatures.name: DECT classic — Latin America (ex-Brazil) band (1910-1930 MHz)
signatures.mode: GFSK, 1.152 Mbit/s, TDMA/TDD, 24 slots per 10 ms frame, carriers on 1.728 MHz grid across a 20 MHz allocation
signatures.tscm: Same DECT PHY; distinct because the band spans 1910-1930, overlapping the US allocation but extending down to 1910. Matters for matcher tuning in Mexico and most of Latin America. Region-imported handsets may sit anywhere on this grid. [In stock-Pluto reach and B210 reach — ~1.92 GHz.]

signatures.name: DECT classic — Brazil band (1910-1920 MHz)
signatures.mode: GFSK, 1.152 Mbit/s, TDMA/TDD, 24 slots per 10 ms frame, carriers on 1.728 MHz grid within a 10 MHz allocation
signatures.tscm: Same DECT PHY, Brazil-specific 10 MHz allocation 1910-1920 (narrower and lower than US). Distinct tuning window; a Brazilian DECT device will not appear in the US 1920-1930 window and vice-versa. [In stock-Pluto reach and B210 reach — ~1.915 GHz.]

signatures.name: DECT classic — Japan band (1893.5-1906.1 MHz, J-DECT)
signatures.mode: GFSK, 1.152 Mbit/s, TDMA/TDD, 24 slots per 10 ms frame, carriers on 1.728 MHz grid within the Japanese sXGP/J-DECT allocation
signatures.tscm: Same DECT PHY on Japan's dedicated ~1893-1906 MHz allocation (commonly cited 1893.5-1906.1). Distinct tuning window between the EU and US placements. Relevant if imported/JP-market cordless gear or a J-DECT bug is suspected. [In stock-Pluto reach and B210 reach — ~1.9 GHz.]

signatures.name: DECT base station idle beacon (dummy bearer)
signatures.mode: GFSK, 1.152 Mbit/s; single dummy-bearer burst broadcast once per 10 ms frame on one carrier (RFP beacon), no traffic slots
signatures.tscm: A powered DECT base with no active call still transmits a periodic 'dummy bearer' beacon so handsets can lock/sync: exactly one short GFSK burst every 10 ms on a single carrier. Waterfall shows a lone, perfectly periodic 100 Hz-cadence pip rather than the dense two-sided TDD lane of a live call. This is the KEY TSCM tell that a DECT device is present and powered even when nobody is talking — a hidden DECT bug/base betrays itself with this beacon. Band spans all regional placements; tune to the applicable regional window. [In stock-Pluto reach and B210 reach — 1.88-1.93 GHz.]

signatures.name: DECT ULE sensor / actuator burst (Ultra Low Energy)
signatures.mode: GFSK, 1.152 Mbit/s, DECT TDMA slot(s); event-driven and keepalive bursts with long sleep gaps between transmissions
signatures.tscm: DECT ULE reuses the exact classic-DECT GFSK PHY but a node sleeps and transmits only on events/keepalives. On the air: identical ~1.7 MHz-wide DECT burst shape, but the DUTY is sparse and irregular (seconds-to-minutes of silence, then a short burst) rather than the continuous TDMA of a call. Powers door/window sensors, motion detectors, smoke alarms, smart-home hubs, and some baby monitors. A ULE-based covert sensor (e.g. hidden motion/audio node) shows this sleepy burst pattern. Distinct from an active-call signature by duty, same by band and modulation. [In stock-Pluto reach and B210 reach — 1.88-1.93 GHz.]

signatures.name: DECT-2020 NR+ (DECT-2020 New Radio, OFDM) — 1.728 MHz channel
signatures.mode: CP-OFDM + TDMA/FDMA, scalable numerology; narrowest channel 1.728 MHz (mu=1). NOT GFSK — modern OFDM IoT/mesh PHY (ETSI TS 103 636)
signatures.tscm: Fundamentally DIFFERENT modulation from classic DECT: OFDM (flat-topped noise-like channel occupancy) instead of GFSK bursts. Shares the DECT band, so it appears at 1.88-1.93 GHz but the spectrum shows a filled OFDM block, not discrete 1.728 MHz GFSK carrier lanes with a 10 ms burst heartbeat. Mesh IoT / industrial sensors. Do not confuse with classic DECT on class — key on the flat OFDM shape vs GFSK bursts. [In stock-Pluto reach and B210 reach — 1.88-1.93 GHz (1.728 MHz channel within Pluto's ~20 MHz usable IBW).]

signatures.name: DECT-2020 NR+ (OFDM) — 3.456 MHz channel
signatures.mode: CP-OFDM, mu=2 numerology, 3.456 MHz nominal channel bandwidth (2x the base 1.728 MHz grid)
signatures.tscm: NR+ wider channel: 3.456 MHz OFDM block (double the classic DECT carrier width) within the DECT band. Higher-throughput mesh/industrial links. Distinguished from the 1.728 MHz NR+ channel by occupied bandwidth; distinguished from classic DECT by OFDM (not GFSK) and lack of the rigid 10 ms GFSK burst pattern. [In stock-Pluto reach and B210 reach; 3.456 MHz fits comfortably in Pluto/B210 IBW. Wider NR+ channels (6.912 / 13.824 MHz) also exist but are rare in the 1.9 GHz DECT band and would need the wider B210 capture bandwidth.]

device_classes.device_class: smart_home_802154_mesh
device_classes.summary: 802.15.4-family smart-home and covert mesh-sensor RF signatures: Zigbee / Thread / Matter-over-Thread / 6LoWPAN on the 2.4 GHz O-QPSK DSSS PHY (16 channels, ch 11-26, ~2 MHz occupied, 250 kbps); Zigbee Green Power ultra-short energy-harvesting bursts on that same PHY; sub-GHz 802.15.4 (868 MHz BPSK / 902-928 MHz BPSK / 915 MHz O-QPSK); and Z-Wave narrowband GFSK on the ITU-T G.9959 PHY (US 908.4/912/916 MHz, EU 868.4 MHz, 9.6/40/100 kbps). All rows fall inside the stock Pluto 325-3800 MHz tuning range and inside B210 range. The 2.4 GHz rows share spectrum with Wi-Fi and BLE but are distinct on-air: narrow ~2 MHz DSSS channels with O-QPSK chipping, not Wi-Fi's 20 MHz OFDM nor BLE's frequency-hopping GFSK. TSCM relevance: covert mesh contact/PIR/door sensors, hidden Zigbee/Thread cameras' control channels, and battery-free Green Power taps ride these signatures; a lone 802.15.4 emitter with no declared hub on premises is a flag.
example_products: Zigbee door/window contact sensors (Aqara MCCGQ11LM, Sonoff SNZB-04, Samsung SmartThings multipurpose)
Zigbee PIR / motion sensors (Aqara RTCGQ11LM, Sonoff SNZB-03, Hue motion sensor SML001)
Zigbee smart plugs / relays (IKEA TRADFRI, Sonoff S31 Lite ZB, Third Reality)
Zigbee smart bulbs (Philips Hue, IKEA TRADFRI, Sengled) - continuous mesh routers
Zigbee coordinators / hubs (SmartThings hub, Hue Bridge, ConBee II / RaspBee, Sonoff ZBDongle-E)
Thread border routers (Apple HomePod mini, Apple TV 4K, Google Nest Hub 2nd gen, Amazon Echo 4th gen)
Matter-over-Thread end devices (Eve Door & Window, Eve Motion, Nanoleaf Essentials bulbs)
Zigbee Green Power kinetic light switches (Aqara wireless mini switch, Philips Hue Tap, EnOcean-style self-powered)
Zigbee Green Power self-powered PIR / occupancy taps
Z-Wave door/window sensors (Aeotec Door/Window Sensor 7, Ecolink, Zooz ZSE41)
Z-Wave PIR motion sensors (Aeotec MultiSensor 7, Zooz ZSE18, Fibaro Motion Sensor FGMS-001)
Z-Wave smart locks (Yale Assure, Schlage Connect BE469, Kwikset 914)
Z-Wave hubs / controllers (Aeotec Z-Stick 7, Zooz ZST10/ZST39 800 stick, Ring Alarm base, HomeSeer)
Z-Wave Long Range end devices (Ring Alarm 2nd-gen sensors, Zooz 800 LR)
Sub-GHz 802.15.4 industrial / building mesh sensor nodes (900 MHz)
Covert / OSINT-relevant: disguised Zigbee contact sensors hidden in fixtures, mesh-reporting PIR taps in decor
Battery mesh water-leak sensors (Aqara water leak, Zooz ZSE42) reporting over Zigbee/Z-Wave
Zigbee/Z-Wave-linked hidden cameras that use the mesh only for a trigger/control channel (video egresses over Wi-Fi separately)
confirm_steps: For 2.4 GHz: dwell (do not fast-sweep) on Zigbee-preferred channels 15/20/25/26 (2425/2450/2475/2480 MHz) and look for a ~2 MHz DSSS channel with O-QPSK structure sitting BETWEEN Wi-Fi OFDM lobes; confirm a fixed center frequency over time to rule out hopping BLE.
Correlate transmissions with physical stimulus: open/close a door, walk past, or flip a switch and watch for a matching burst - covert contact/PIR/Green-Power sensors fire on the event.
For 900 MHz: sweep 902-928 MHz (US) and dwell at 908.42 and 916 MHz for Z-Wave narrow GFSK pips; sweep 912-920 MHz for Z-Wave LR; look for isolated <=100 kHz FSK carriers clear of Wi-Fi.
For EU-region gear: check 868.0-868.6 and 868.42 MHz for narrow FSK/BPSK; expect very low duty (regulatory ~1% cap) so leave a long-dwell recorder running.
Distinguish Z-Wave (narrow ~40-100 kHz GFSK) from sub-GHz 802.15.4 (wider ~0.6-1.2 MHz BPSK/O-QPSK DSSS) - bandwidth and modulation are the discriminators in the shared 900 MHz band.
Decode to confirm: use a dedicated 802.15.4/Zigbee sniffer (Ubiqua + CC2531/ConBee, or a Z-Wave PC controller in monitor mode) to positively ID protocol vs an SDR spectral guess.
Enumerate declared devices: ask the occupant which hubs exist. Any 802.15.4/Z-Wave emitter with no accounted-for hub, or that keeps transmitting after the known hub is powered down, is a flag.
device_classes.tscm_notes: All rows are within the stock ADALM-Pluto 325-3800 MHz tuning range (no AD9364 frequency mod needed) and within B210 range - none are above 6 GHz. The hard part here is DETECTION, not reach: (1) 2.4 GHz rows hide in the Wi-Fi/BLE haze and need dwell on specific Zigbee channels rather than a fast sweep; (2) Green Power and battery-sensor traffic is bursty/event-driven with very low duty, so a snapshot sweep will miss it - run a long-dwell record and stimulate the environment (open doors, trigger motion); (3) narrowband sub-GHz FSK/BPSK signals (Z-Wave, 868/915 MHz 802.15.4) need adequate frequency resolution / narrow RBW to resolve a ~40-100 kHz carrier and not smear it. For positive protocol ID, an SDR spectral match should be corroborated with a real 802.15.4/Z-Wave sniffer. Investigative flag: a covert mesh sensor betrays itself by transmitting when it should not (after the known hub is off) or by having no declared hub on premises - correlate emissions to physical events and to the occupant's device inventory. False-positive caution: legitimate resident smart-home gear IS 802.15.4/Z-Wave; a detection is only meaningful once it cannot be attributed to a declared occupant-owned device. The 900 MHz and 868 MHz ISM/SRD bands are crowded (LoRa, cordless phones, AMR meters, gate remotes, RTL433 sensors) - band occupancy alone is not identification.

signatures.name: Zigbee / Thread / Matter 2.4 GHz O-QPSK DSSS (802.15.4, ch 11-26)
signatures.mode: IEEE 802.15.4-2003/2006 2.4 GHz PHY, O-QPSK DSSS, 2 Mchip/s, 250 kbps; 16 channels ch11-ch26 on 5 MHz centers (2405-2480 MHz)
signatures.tscm: Core smart-home mesh PHY shared by Zigbee, Thread, Matter-over-Thread, 6LoWPAN. A ~2 MHz DSSS channel sitting BETWEEN Wi-Fi OFDM lobes (Zigbee ch 15/20/25/26 deliberately avoid common Wi-Fi) is the tell. Fixed (non-hopping) center over time distinguishes it from BLE's hopping GFSK; narrow ~2 MHz vs Wi-Fi's 20 MHz OFDM. Bursty event-driven traffic plus periodic poll/keepalive frames when idle. [stock-Pluto-reachable (2405-2480 MHz inside 325-3800); within B210 range]

signatures.name: Zigbee Green Power energy-harvesting burst (2.4 GHz 802.15.4)
signatures.mode: Zigbee Green Power single unacknowledged 802.15.4 O-QPSK DSSS frame, event-triggered by harvested energy (switch flip / PIR event); one short frame (~1 ms on-air, often repeated x2-3), no ACK handshake
signatures.tscm: Battery-free/energy-harvesting taps: kinetic light switches, self-powered PIR and door sensors. Same 2.4 GHz O-QPSK DSSS channel as ordinary Zigbee but appears as isolated ultra-short single-frame bursts tied to a physical event, with no periodic beacon/poll pattern. A burst-only emitter with no continuous mesh chatter is the signature; needs event-timed dwell to catch. [stock-Pluto-reachable (2.4 GHz); within B210 range]

signatures.name: Z-Wave US 908.4 MHz GFSK (R1/R2, G.9959)
signatures.mode: ITU-T G.9959 GFSK, Manchester-coded; US primary channel 908.42 MHz; R1 9.6 kbps / R2 40 kbps; ~40 kHz channel width
signatures.tscm: US legacy/mainstream Z-Wave. Very narrow (~40 kHz) GFSK carrier near 908.42 MHz, well clear of Wi-Fi/BLE - a clean isolated FSK pip in the 900 MHz ISM band. Covert Z-Wave door/window, PIR and lock sensors sit here. Low false-positive overlap (few consumer devices live exactly at 908.4). [stock-Pluto-reachable (908 MHz inside 325-3800); within B210 range]

signatures.name: Z-Wave US 916 MHz GFSK (R3 100 kbps, G.9959)
signatures.mode: ITU-T G.9959 GFSK; US high-rate channel ~916 MHz; R3 100 kbps; ~100 kHz channel width; Z-Wave LR uses ~912/920 MHz star channels
signatures.tscm: Newer high-rate US Z-Wave (500/700/800-series). Wider (~100 kHz) GFSK carrier near 916 MHz. Sweep 912-920 MHz for the full US Z-Wave footprint including Z-Wave Long Range. Isolated narrowband FSK, low false-positive overlap. [stock-Pluto-reachable (916 MHz); within B210 range]

signatures.name: Z-Wave EU 868.4 MHz GFSK (G.9959)
signatures.mode: ITU-T G.9959 GFSK, Manchester-coded; EU primary channel 868.42 MHz; 9.6/40/100 kbps; ~40-100 kHz channel width
signatures.tscm: EU/UK-region Z-Wave near 868.4 MHz. Same G.9959 PHY as US but in the 868 MHz SRD band; will not interoperate with US 908 MHz gear. Present on gray-import or EU-sourced covert sensors. 868 MHz is a crowded EU SRD band (alarms, meters, LoRa) so confirm the GFSK/Manchester structure, not just band occupancy. [stock-Pluto-reachable (868 MHz); within B210 range]

signatures.name: 802.15.4 sub-GHz 915 MHz O-QPSK (902-928 MHz, ch 1-10)
signatures.mode: IEEE 802.15.4 915 MHz PHY, O-QPSK DSSS, 1 Mchip/s, up to 250 kbps; 10 channels (ch1-ch10) on 2 MHz centers across 902-928 MHz
signatures.tscm: Sub-GHz Zigbee/802.15.4 mesh option for longer range / better wall penetration than 2.4 GHz. Wider (~1-1.2 MHz) O-QPSK DSSS channel in the 900 MHz ISM band. Overlaps US Z-Wave and 900 MHz proprietary sensors - distinguish by the wider DSSS bandwidth and O-QPSK structure vs Z-Wave's narrow GFSK. [stock-Pluto-reachable (902-928 MHz); within B210 range]

signatures.name: 802.15.4 sub-GHz 915 MHz BPSK (902-928 MHz, legacy 40 kbps)
signatures.mode: IEEE 802.15.4 915 MHz legacy PHY, BPSK DSSS, 600 kchip/s, 40 kbps; 10 channels 902-928 MHz
signatures.tscm: Legacy low-rate 802.15.4 US sub-GHz PHY (2003-era). Narrower (~600 kHz) BPSK DSSS carrier. Found in older/industrial mesh sensors. Same-band overlap with Z-Wave and 900 MHz ISM - key it on the BPSK DSSS chip structure and bandwidth. [stock-Pluto-reachable (902-928 MHz); within B210 range]

signatures.name: 802.15.4 sub-GHz 868 MHz BPSK (EU, ch 0, 20 kbps)
signatures.mode: IEEE 802.15.4 868 MHz PHY, BPSK DSSS, 300 kchip/s, 20 kbps; single channel (ch0) 868.0-868.6 MHz (EU SRD)
signatures.tscm: EU-region single-channel sub-GHz 802.15.4. Narrowband BPSK DSSS near 868.3 MHz. Shares crowded EU 868 MHz SRD band with Z-Wave EU, LoRa 868 and SRD alarms - confirm by DSSS/BPSK structure, not band presence. EU duty-cycle-limited (<=1%), so transmissions are sparse. [stock-Pluto-reachable (868 MHz); within B210 range]

device_classes.device_class: Carrier-current bugs (audio/data modulated onto AC mains and building low-voltage wiring) + hardwired microphone runs
device_classes.summary: Carrier-current bugs impress audio (or digitized audio) onto the building's own AC power wiring as a conducted subcarrier, typically 20-500 kHz (classic LF band) and 1.6-7.5 MHz (modern HF "PLC" band), so the mains simultaneously powers the device and carries the signal to a receiver plugged into the same electrical phase downstream of the service transformer. This is fundamentally a CONDUCTED / near-field problem, not a free-space RF one: the intended signal lives on the copper, and only leaks weakly by radiation/induction from the wiring. Almost NONE of it is reliably free-space-detectable by an antenna-fed SDR, and worse, the entire useful band sits BELOW a stock ADALM-Pluto's 325 MHz floor and (for the LF portion) below a B210's 70 MHz floor. Real detection of this class is done with a mains-coupled probe / VLF-HF conducted receiver (e.g. AC line coupler into a 10 kHz-30 MHz receiver, ANDRE-class near-field probe, or dedicated carrier-current detectors like the REI/Kaiser SCD-5, MLK-2030), plus physical inspection of outlets, junction boxes, and ceiling voids. The closely-related hardwired-mic-run threat radiates essentially nothing and is a physical-search / audio-emanation (WMD-2000 acoustic-stimulation) problem exclusively. The distinct on-the-wire signatures below differ by band, modulation (FM analog vs OOK vs OFDM vs GMSK vs spread-spectrum) and duty, but the operative TSCM reality is uniform: match at the mains coupler, not the antenna.
example_products: Endoacustica ENKPL-S power line carrier audio bug (1.6-2.4 MHz analog FM, 220 VAC, 3 subcarriers)
Endoacustica ENKPL-SD power line digital bug (1.6-2.4 MHz GMSK, ~125 kbit/s, encrypted)
Classic AID / Westinghouse (Audio Intelligence Devices) 'Line Carrier' mic systems (80-200 kHz, historical)
AID spread-spectrum current-carrier devices (30-700 kHz, historical)
Security Research (England) 'Line Carrier' microphone systems (60-200 kHz, historical)
HDS (Household Data Services) carrier-current audio systems (50-750 kHz / 120-400 kHz)
DGR Engineering (France) spread-spectrum powerline audio/low-bw video sender (85 kHz-11 MHz)
Phonex / modified Phonex AC-mains audio senders (2.62-6.4 MHz / 2-7.5 MHz) repurposed as bugs
Repurposed Radio Shack FM 'wireless' AC-mains intercoms (24-400 kHz) used for room audio
Generic outlet/adapter/power-strip concealment carrier-current modules (form-factor example, unconfirmed model)
Faceplate / duplex-receptacle concealment carrier-current mic (form-factor example, unconfirmed model)
Powerline baby-monitor / room-monitor 'talk-back' units abused for audio (analog LF, form-factor example)
TP-Link TL-PA / AV600/AV1000 HomePlug adapters (2-30 MHz OFDM) used to bridge a hidden mic/cam for exfil
Netgear PLP / Powerline 1000/2000 HomePlug AV2 adapters (2-30 MHz OFDM) as covert IP backhaul
D-Link DHP-series HomePlug AV adapters as covert powerline data bridge
TRENDnet Powerline AV/AV2 adapters as covert bridge (form-factor example)
Zyxel PLA-series HomePlug AV adapter (2-30 MHz) as covert bridge
Concealed mic-preamp hardwired to a spare telephone/alarm pair (wired-mic run, form-factor example)
Ceiling-void / above-tile hidden mic run to a nearby closet listening post (wired-mic run, form-factor example)
Intercom-station or PA-speaker back-fed as a room microphone over building wiring (form-factor example)
Modified surge protector / power strip with embedded carrier-current transmitter (form-factor example, unconfirmed)
USB charger / wall-wart concealment with LF or HF mains-coupled audio transmitter (form-factor example, unconfirmed)
confirm_steps: Do NOT rely on the SDR antenna port — nearly all of this class is conducted and below Pluto's 325 MHz floor (and much below B210's 70 MHz). Couple to the mains instead.

Use a safety-rated AC line coupler / isolation-and-blocking capacitor network into a VLF-HF receiver or spectrum analyzer covering 10 kHz-30 MHz; sweep for continuous carriers, digital humps, or broadband OFDM combs present on the wire.

Compare energy on the line with the circuit under load vs. isolated: a signal that disappears when you kill/open the branch circuit (or that is strong at one outlet and fades across the service transformer/phase) is characteristic of a carrier-current device rather than off-air pickup.

Attempt to demodulate: FM/AM demod of a suspect LF/HF carrier that yields room audio confirms an analog carrier-current bug; a structured non-audio digital carrier (GMSK/OFDM) that won't demod to audio suggests an encrypted or data-bridge device — then hunt the hardware.

Use a dedicated carrier-current detector as ground truth (REI/Kaiser SCD-5 carrier/subcarrier detector, MLK-2030 carrier-current probe, or ANDRE-class near-field probe run along the wiring) to localize the emitter to a specific outlet/box.

Physically open and inspect every AC outlet, switch, junction box, power strip, wall-wart, surge protector and ceiling void on the circuit; look for added modules across line-neutral or line-ground and for unexplained wiring pairs.
For HomePlug/BPL exfil suspicion, enumerate every powerline-networking adapter physically and verify each is a known/authorized device; unknown adapters are the finding, not the OFDM comb itself.

For hardwired-mic runs (no RF): trace all low-voltage/spare pairs with a TDR and toner, check for DC bias / audio on idle pairs, and use an acoustically-stimulated wired-microphone detector (e.g. WMD-2000) plus a high-gain audio amp to hear emanations from in-wall wiring.

Document the exact center frequency, occupied bandwidth, modulation, duty and the physical outlet where energy peaks, since that localization — not a spectrum screenshot — is the actionable result for this class.
false_positive_overlap: Legitimate powerline networking (HomePlug AV/AV2, G.hn) adapters the occupant installed for internet/streaming — same 2-30 MHz OFDM comb as a covert exfil bridge; presence alone is not proof.
Commercial plug-in wireless intercoms, doorbells, and baby monitors that legitimately use AC-mains carrier-current (LF FM 24-400 kHz) — identical band and modulation to old carrier-current bugs.
Smart-home / powerline control systems (X10 ~120 kHz, INSTEON dual-band ~131 kHz, some HomePlug-based lighting) that intentionally inject LF/HF signals onto house wiring.
Power-line-communication utility metering / ripple-control and street-lighting control signals (audio-frequency and LF) present on the service.
Switching-power-supply hash, LED-driver and dimmer noise, VFDs and battery chargers that raise the conducted noise floor and can mimic spread-spectrum/noise-like devices.

Broadcast AM (530-1710 kHz), LORAN-legacy, NDBs and HF broadcast/ham signals coupling onto house wiring as unintended antennas — appear on a mains-coupled receiver but are external, not on-premise bugs.
Building alarm, fire, nurse-call, and intercom low-voltage wiring that legitimately carries audio/DC on spare pairs — easily mistaken for a hardwired-mic run during physical trace.
device_classes.tscm_notes: This class is the textbook case where an SDR-only sweep gives false confidence. A stock ADALM-Pluto (325-3800 MHz) cannot reach any of it; a B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) reaches none of the LF band and only marginal radiated leakage of the 2-30 MHz HF/BPL band. More importantly the signal is CONDUCTED on the copper, so an antenna-fed radio of any kind is the wrong instrument except for sniffing weak near-field leakage a few inches from the wiring. Treat carrier-current and wired-mic threats as a conducted/near-field + physical-search workstream, run in parallel with (not replaced by) the free-space SDR sweep: (1) mains-coupled VLF-HF receiver or dedicated carrier-current detector; (2) near-field probe walked along wiring; (3) hands-on inspection of every outlet, box, strip and ceiling void; (4) TDR/tone trace and acoustic-stimulation detector for baseband hardwired runs. Because these devices are powered by and hidden inside the electrical system they can run 24/7 indefinitely with no battery to die, and the analog ones give up plaintext room audio to anyone downstream on the same phase — a high-severity, low-tech, easily-overlooked threat. Localization to a physical outlet/pair is the deliverable; a spectrum screenshot is not. Flag any unknown powerline-networking adapter as a hardware finding to be physically verified rather than dismissed as normal networking.

signatures.name: LF carrier-current bug, narrowband FM analog voice (classic 20-200 kHz)
signatures.mode: Narrowband FM analog voice on a single LF subcarrier conducted on AC mains
signatures.tscm: Single continuous FM carrier somewhere 20-200 kHz, ~10-20 kHz deviation, present ONLY on the powered wiring (strongest at the outlet the device sits in, fades across phase/transformer boundaries). Demodulates to room audio. Not present in free-space spectrum except as weak near-field leakage within inches of the conductor. [FAR below stock Pluto (325 MHz) and B210 (70 MHz) floors; conducted, not free-space. Needs an AC line coupler + LF receiver (10 kHz-500 kHz) or dedicated carrier-current detector, not the SDR antenna port.]

signatures.name: LF carrier-current / wireless-intercom FM (200-500 kHz band)
signatures.mode: FM analog voice, higher LF subcarrier (consumer AC-mains 'wireless' intercom reuse)
signatures.tscm: Continuous FM carrier 200-500 kHz on mains; overlaps commercial FM plug-in intercoms/baby-talk-back units (e.g. 200-270 kHz, 300-400 kHz, 355 kHz popular). Same demod-to-audio test. Distinguished from the sub-200 kHz row by center frequency and by often being a repurposed off-the-shelf intercom. [Below Pluto/B210 range; conducted. Detect with LF line-coupled receiver. NOTE this band overlaps LORAN-C/legacy nav and NDB harmonics if you sniff free-space near an antenna — don't.]

signatures.name: Spread-spectrum carrier-current bug, LF/HF conducted (30 kHz-11 MHz hopping/DSSS)
signatures.mode: Spread-spectrum (DSSS or slow FHSS) audio, sometimes low-bandwidth video, conducted on mains
signatures.tscm: Low, noise-like conducted energy spread over a wide LF-HF span rather than a single tone; raises the wideband conducted noise floor on the mains without an obvious carrier. Historically AID/Westinghouse and DGR Engineering (85 kHz-11 MHz) types. Hard to demod without knowing the code; shows as a persistent broadband hump on a mains-coupled spectrum that is NOT present when the line is isolated. [Entirely below stock Pluto; the HF top end (to 11 MHz) is still below B210's 70 MHz floor. Conducted-only. Requires wideband mains coupler + HF spectrum analyzer; SDR antenna port is useless here.]

signatures.name: HF carrier-current bug, analog FM subcarrier (1.6-2.4 MHz proprietary PLC, e.g. ENKPL-S)
signatures.mode: Analog FM subcarrier audio, up to 3 stacked subcarrier channels, on 220 VAC mains
signatures.tscm: One to three continuous FM carriers in 1.6-2.4 MHz conducted on mains; commercial product signature (ENKPL-S class). Sits in the AM broadcast-adjacent / 160 m ham region, so weak radiated leakage could in principle be heard on an HF radio near the wiring, but the reliable signature is on the conductor. ~15 mA draw, tiny 45x25x12 mm module in an outlet/adapter. [Below Pluto (325 MHz) and below B210 (70 MHz). Conducted; radiated leakage negligible. Detect with HF line-coupled receiver 100 kHz-30 MHz or carrier-current detector, not the SDR.]

signatures.name: HF carrier-current bug, digital GMSK/ADM (1.6-2.4 MHz, encrypted, e.g. ENKPL-SD)
signatures.mode: Digital GMSK, ~125 kbit/s, ADM-coded audio, 'encrypted', conducted on mains
signatures.tscm: Continuous digital carrier in 1.6-2.4 MHz with GMSK's characteristic constant-envelope, smooth-phase spectrum; ~125 kbit/s so ~150-200 kHz occupied. Won't demod to plain audio (encrypted/ADM) — signature is a persistent structured digital hump on the mains, up to 3 stacked. Modern commercial (ENKPL-SD class). [Below Pluto and B210 floors; conducted. Needs HF mains coupler + wideband HF receiver. Encryption means you confirm presence/structure, not content.]

signatures.name: HF carrier-current bug, modified consumer AC-mains audio link (2-7.5 MHz)
signatures.mode: FM/AM analog audio on repurposed consumer powerline audio sender (Phonex-class), 2-7.5 MHz
signatures.tscm: Continuous analog carrier in the 2-7.5 MHz conducted band from a modified commercial powerline audio extender (Phonex 2.62-6.4 MHz / modified 2-7.5 MHz). Demods to room audio. Overlaps legitimate powerline audio/intercom senders — false-positive prone. [Below Pluto and B210 floors; conducted. HF line-coupled receiver required. Overlaps 60/80/40 m amateur allocations if you sniff free-space — ignore free-space, probe the wire.]

signatures.name: Broadband-over-powerline / HomePlug-class OFDM link used as covert data/audio exfil (2-30 MHz)
signatures.mode: HomePlug AV/AV2-style OFDM (2-30 MHz, 24.414 kHz carrier spacing, QAM-256/64/16/DQPSK/DBPSK/ROBO), AES-128
signatures.tscm: Very wide (2-30 MHz) OFDM 'comb' conducted on mains, bursty with traffic, adaptive notching around ham bands. A hidden HomePlug adapter can bridge a concealed mic/recorder or IP camera onto the wiring for exfil. Signature is a broadband conducted OFDM floor lift + adapter presence, NOT room audio (it carries IP packets). Distinguish from a resident's legitimate powerline networking kit. [The whole 2-30 MHz band is below Pluto (325 MHz) and below B210 (70 MHz). Conducted; strong radiated egress can appear on an HF antenna as broadband hash, but confirmation is on the wire / at the adapter. Use HF mains coupler + physically hunt the adapter.]

signatures.name: Hardwired microphone run to remote listening post (no intended RF)
signatures.mode: Baseband audio (or DC-biased mic) on dedicated low-voltage pair; no carrier, no intended emission
signatures.tscm: Essentially NO RF signature — it is baseband audio on a hidden pair (mic-preamp wired to a distant recorder/LP through spare telephone, alarm, intercom, CAT/low-voltage, or dedicated wiring). Detectable only by physical trace of unexplained wiring, DC/audio on a pair, or acoustic-stimulation emanation on the wire (WMD-2000-class). A spectrum analyzer sees nothing. [Not free-space RF at all — completely outside Pluto AND B210 reach. Detection is physical: open every outlet/box/ceiling void, TDR the pairs, use an acoustically-stimulated wired-mic detector and audio amplifier on suspect wiring.]

device_classes.device_class: GPS/GNSS jammers, repeaters, and spoofers (anti-tracker RF devices)
device_classes.summary: This class attacks the GNSS bands (GPS L1 1575.42, L2 1227.6, L5 1176.45 MHz; GLONASS G1 FDMA ~1598-1609 centered near 1602; BeiDou B1I ~1561.098). The overwhelmingly common real-world device is the cheap 12V "cigarette-lighter" jammer: a single microwave VCO swept by a 555-timer sawtooth (~133 kHz sweep rate confirmed in the Hackaday teardown) that smears a few MHz of energy across L1. Because genuine GNSS arrives BELOW the receiver noise floor (~-130 dBm), the tell is inverted from most surveillance work: instead of a hidden weak emitter, the operator finds a STRONG carrier/noise sitting exactly on a GNSS band where there should be nothing but thermal noise. Three behaviorally distinct sub-families share these bands: (1) JAMMERS - swept-noise or CW that raise the floor and deny GNSS; (2) REPEATERS/re-radiators - legitimate-looking near-noise live GNSS re-broadcast indoors (hangars/labs), also abusable to feed a fixed benign fix or keep a tracker "alive"; (3) SPOOFERS - SDR (HackRF/Pluto/bladeRF) transmitting structured counterfeit GNSS just above noise to move a receiver's reported position. All GNSS carriers fall inside a stock Pluto's 325-3800 MHz range (L5 at 1176 is the lowest and well in reach). IMPORTANT RF REALITY CHECK: the single-VCO cheap jammer teardown shows a tuning range of ~1466-1590 MHz - it covers GPS L1 and BeiDou B1 but does NOT reach GLONASS at 1602; genuine GLONASS/wide-block coverage requires a wider-tuning or multi-VCO/multi-antenna unit, so a raised-noise plateau extending past ~1590 up to 1610 implies a more capable device, not the cheapest one. The only out-of-band member is the LoJack 173.075 MHz stolen-vehicle-recovery band that some "GPS+LoJack" combo jammers also hit, which is below the stock Pluto floor. A directional yagi/patch and near-field sniffing at the vehicle lighter/OBD/dash is the practical hunt because the jammer is line-powered and physically present.
example_products: GP-2 / GP-2000-series cigarette-lighter GPS L1+L2 jammer (2-antenna 12V plug, form-factor example)

confirm_steps: Baseline first: with the suspect device OFF (or before entering the vehicle), capture the GNSS bands. Genuine L1/L2/L5 look like flat thermal noise - GNSS is BELOW the noise floor and invisible on a Pluto/B210 without correlation. Any strong hump or tone there while 'off' means something else is on.

Restore normal state and watch L1 (1575.42): a broad swept hump, a wide 1560-1615 shelf, or a CW spike appearing is the jammer signature. Note bandwidth, upper edge (does it reach GLONASS ~1602?), and whether it sweeps - upper-edge >1590 implies a more capable multi-VCO unit than the cheapest class.
Confirm line-powered and local: kill/unplug the 12V lighter, USB ports, and OBD-II port one at a time; the emission dropping when a port is unpowered pinpoints a lighter/OBD/USB jammer.
Direction-find with a yagi/patch antenna toward the dash, center console, OBD port, and under-seat area - the source is physically present, so signal strength peaks sharply at the device.

Ground-truth with an actual GNSS receiver (phone GNSS test app, u-blox, or dedicated probe): loss of fix / C/No collapse across many satellites at once = jamming; a confident but WRONG fix = spoofing; a clean fix with no sky view = re-radiation.

Distinguish spoof vs jam: spoofing leaves L1 looking like real GPS but a few dB hot and yields a false position; jamming raises the whole floor and yields no fix. Check reported position against known truth.
For the 173 MHz LoJack channel, switch to an RTL-SDR / RF Explorer / B210 (below Pluto's 325 MHz floor) to confirm the narrowband emitter if a combo GPS+LoJack unit is suspected.

Physically recover the device: cigarette-lighter jammers are small pucks with 1-6 stub antennas; check the lighter socket, OBD port, USB hubs, and glovebox. Preserve chain of custody - possession/operation is itself an offense.
false_positive_overlap: Legitimate GNSS repeaters/re-radiators in hangars, parking structures, test labs, and vehicle-assembly plants intentionally re-broadcast real L1 indoors - spectrally identical to a benign or malicious repeater; context (is this a facility that installs them?) decides.
Active GPS antennas / LNAs can self-oscillate or leak, putting a small carrier near L1 that mimics a weak CW jammer.

Iridium subscriber downlink (1616-1626.5 MHz) sits just above the GLONASS band and is a legitimate strong, bursty signal - do NOT mistake it for GLONASS jamming; it is above 1616 and time-slotted, not a continuous GNSS-centered hump. Iridium is a known real-world nuisance source of L-band interference near GNSS.
Inmarsat / MSS L-band services and some aeronautical links occupy nearby L-band and are legitimate; a jammer sits centered ON the GNSS carriers, legitimate services sit in adjacent allocations.

Harmonics/intermod from strong cellular (LTE ~1.9-2.1 GHz) or a broadband PA can drop energy into L-band; verify the emission tracks a GNSS center frequency and is local to the vehicle, not a distant tower.

Poorly shielded electronics (some dashcams, cheap DC-DC converters, LED drivers) emit broadband hash that can raise the L1 floor without being a jammer - looks like weak wideband noise spanning far more than the GNSS band, not a clean swept hump.
GNSS spoofing is nearly indistinguishable from legitimate GPS on a spectrum view alone - it MUST be confirmed by a receiver reporting a false position, not by RF appearance.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Practical field notes: (1) The inverted-tell principle is the crux - real GNSS is BELOW the noise floor, so a Pluto/B210 doing raw spectrum normally sees NOTHING at L1/L2/L5. Anything strong there is by definition anomalous and almost always a jammer, repeater, or spoofer. Teach operators not to expect to 'see GPS.' (2) RF REALITY on cheap units: the dominant $15-40 single-VCO lighter jammer (Hackaday teardown: NE555 ~133 kHz sawtooth driving a ~1466-1590 MHz VCO) covers GPS L1 and BeiDou B1 but NOT GLONASS at 1602 - so genuine GLONASS/wide-block coverage or L2/L5 presence signals a more capable multi-VCO/multi-antenna device and upgrades the sophistication/intent assessment. Don't assume every 'all-GNSS' advertised claim is real; verify the actual upper edge. (3) These devices are line-powered and co-located with the target (lighter, OBD, USB, or room outlet), so DF and physical search beat spectral subtleties - find the puck. (4) Effect first, RF second: cheapest confirmation is a second GNSS receiver losing lock (jam) or holding a wrong-but-confident position (spoof). (5) Legal exposure is significant and asymmetric - merely possessing/operating a jammer violates 47 U.S.C. and FCC rules in the US (and equivalents in CA/UK/EU); if one is found in a client matter, flag it as evidence of an offense, not just an RF nuisance, and preserve chain of custody. (6) Spoofing is the higher-threat, lower-visibility case (a fleet/asset mis-tracked rather than dark-tracked) and needs a TCXO-stable SDR; validate against ground truth. (7) The 173 MHz LoJack channel and any sub-325 MHz content need a different front end (RTL-SDR/RF Explorer, or B210 which reaches 70 MHz); a stock Pluto cannot see it.

signatures.name: L1 swept-noise jammer (cigarette-lighter/OBD, VCO sawtooth)
signatures.mode: Sawtooth-swept microwave VCO on GPS L1
signatures.tscm: Broad triangular/rectangular hump of raised energy straddling 1575.42 MHz where normally only thermal noise sits. Confirmed teardown: NE555 sawtooth at ~133 kHz drives a VCO whose native range is ~1466-1590 MHz, so the swept hump often extends BELOW 1560 as well; sweep rate is fast enough that it presents as raised broadband noise on a swept analyzer. The single most common anti-tracker device: powered from 12V lighter/OBD/USB so it is physically in the vehicle. A strong continuous hump on L1 with NO legitimate transmitter there is near-diagnostic of jamming. Note: a true single-VCO unit does NOT reach GLONASS (1602) - if the plateau runs past ~1590 the device is more capable than the cheapest class. [stock-Pluto-reachable (L1 1575 MHz well inside 325-3800 MHz)]

signatures.name: L1 narrowband / CW tone jammer
signatures.mode: CW or narrow-FM single carrier on L1
signatures.tscm: A sharp spike (or narrow lump) at/near 1575.42 MHz rather than a broad swept hump. Cheapest DIY builds and some fixed-tone units emit a single carrier. A hard CW spike parked on L1 with no modulation is not legitimate - GNSS is spread-spectrum and never looks like a single tone. Distinguished from swept units by the narrow, stable line. (signal_class 'continuous_digital' here denotes an unmodulated/near-CW continuous carrier; there is no CW-tone enum value.) [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: L2 band jammer (1227.6 MHz)
signatures.mode: Swept-noise or CW on GPS L2 1227.6
signatures.tscm: Broad raised-noise hump (or tone) centered near 1227.6 MHz, overlapping GLONASS L2 ~1246. Present only on multi-band jammers (2+ antenna units). Consumer trackers mostly use L1 only, so an L2 hump usually means a higher-end multi-band jammer aimed at survey/RTK or precision receivers; its presence alongside L1 raises the sophistication assessment. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: L5 band jammer (1176.45 MHz)
signatures.mode: Swept-noise or CW on GPS L5 / Galileo E5a / BeiDou B2a
signatures.tscm: Broad raised-noise hump or tone near 1176.45 MHz - the LOWEST GNSS band and low edge of consumer multi-band coverage (also Galileo E5a and BeiDou B2a ~1176). Appears on 'L1/L2/L5' and full-band units. Modern dual/tri-band phones and trackers increasingly use L5, so a hump here plus L1 indicates a current-generation multi-band device. [stock-Pluto-reachable (1176 MHz is lowest GNSS band, still inside range)]

signatures.name: GLONASS G1 band jammer (~1598-1610 MHz)
signatures.mode: Swept-noise or CW on GLONASS L1/G1 FDMA band
signatures.tscm: Broad raised-noise plateau over the GLONASS FDMA channels ~1598.06-1609.31 MHz (1602 + n x 0.5625 MHz, n=-7..+6). Requires a wider-tuning or multi-VCO unit than the cheapest single-VCO L1 jammer (whose VCO tops out ~1590). Many advertised 'GPS+GLONASS' units span ~1575-1615 MHz as one block, so L1 and GLONASS can merge into a single wide plateau. If raised noise extends well past 1590 up to ~1610, GLONASS coverage is present and the device is more capable than the $15-40 class. Do NOT confuse with Iridium (1616-1626.5, bursty) just above. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: Wide GNSS block jammer (single ~1560-1615 MHz plateau)
signatures.mode: One wide swept/noise plateau over upper-L GNSS
signatures.tscm: One wide swept or noise-filled plateau covering GPS L1 + Galileo E1 + BeiDou B1 (~1561-1591) and, if wide enough, GLONASS G1 (~1598-1609) at once. The upper-L band lights up as a raised, roughly flat shelf with no discrete carriers. Note this is a MULTI-VCO or wider-VCO design, not the cheapest single-VCO teardown unit (which stops near 1590). Nothing legitimate occupies that whole span at that level near a vehicle. Cap the upper edge at ~1615 to stay below the Iridium allocation (1616-1626.5). [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: GPS L1 repeater / re-radiator (live re-broadcast)
signatures.mode: Live GPS L1 C/A re-radiated indoors via LNA+antenna
signatures.tscm: A genuine live GPS L1 C/A signal (BPSK spread-spectrum, ~2.046 MHz main lobe around 1575.42) re-radiated indoors. Looks like REAL GPS - structured, near/slightly above the noise floor - NOT a raised jamming hump. The tell is a valid GPS spectrum shape present indoors/underground where sky view is impossible; a receiver getting a clean fix with zero sky view = re-radiation. Mostly legitimate (hangars, labs) but can hold a tracker at a fixed benign location or feed a spoofer. (signal_class 'psk' reflects the underlying BPSK C/A structure; on a raw spectrum it can look noise-like because it sits near the floor.) [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LoJack / 173 MHz stolen-vehicle-recovery jammer (paired with GPS units)
signatures.mode: Narrowband noise/tone on 173.075 MHz LoJack SVR band
signatures.tscm: Narrowband noise/tone on the 173.075 MHz LoJack recovery band (confirmed FCC SVRS allocation), bundled into some 'GPS + LoJack' desktop/handheld jammers to defeat RF vehicle-recovery transponders alongside GPS denial. LoJack units normally chirp ~200 ms every 15 s (once/second when tracked), so the legitimate signal is intermittent; a jammer parked there is continuous. Not a GNSS band but shipped in the same anti-recovery jammers. [needs-different-front-end: 173 MHz is BELOW the stock Pluto 325 MHz floor; requires AD9364 low-freq mod or an RTL-SDR/RF Explorer to see it (B210 covers it - 70 MHz-6 GHz)]

device_classes.device_class: Pro/prosumer wireless microphone systems (bodypack/plug-on/clip-on transmitters) used covertly for audio surveillance
device_classes.summary: Wireless mic systems are one of the most common "accidental" and deliberate covert audio-surveillance tools a TSCM sweep encounters: a bodypack or plug-on transmitter with a lav mic is a body-wearable, continuously-keyed audio bug that is fully legal to buy and leaves a clean, well-behaved RF signature. On the air they fall into four primary regime families, each with distinct signatures: (1) UHF ~470-698 MHz analog FM, a narrow (~130-200 kHz) continuous FM carrier — the classic wireless-mic look and the single most recognizable signature; (2) UHF ~470-698 MHz digital (Shure SLX-D/ULX-D/Axient, Sennheiser EW-D, AKG DMS800) — a continuous or near-continuous digitally-modulated carrier still inside the 200 kHz TV-band channel mask (ETSI EN 300 422 caps occupied bandwidth at 200 kHz below 1 GHz, 600 kHz above 1 GHz); (3) 900 MHz ISM (902-928) license-free digital, older Line 6 and Sennheiser/AKG 900 systems; (4) 2.4 GHz digital, frequency-hopping spread-spectrum (Rode Wireless GO/DJI Mic-class, Shure GLXD, Line 6 XD-V, Audio-Technica System 10, Sennheiser XSW-D) — bursty FHSS that shares the band with Wi-Fi/BT and is the hardest to distinguish from consumer traffic. Plus legacy VHF (72-216 MHz) analog and a 1.8-1.9 GHz DECT-style regime. Every regime above VHF is inside a stock ADALM-Pluto's 325-3800 MHz tuning range; none is above 6 GHz. The dominant TSCM challenge is not reach but discrimination: a UHF FM mic in a hotel or church AV rack is a legitimate device, and a 2.4 GHz hopping mic is nearly indistinguishable from Wi-Fi/BT without demodulating audio. Distinct signatures are separated by band, channel width, modulation and duty; the "hundreds of products" all collapse onto these few on-air fingerprints. Note on the US band map: after the 2020 incentive auction, US wireless-mic operation is effectively limited to below 608 MHz (plus 614-616 MHz and narrow duplex-gap slivers) — 617-698 MHz is now licensed 600 MHz cellular where mic use is prohibited — so 470-698 is used here as a DETECTION scan range (legacy gear + non-US regions still use up to ~694 MHz), not a legal-operation range.

confirm_steps: Confirm continuous keying: a covert worn mic stays transmitting the whole time it is on. Watch the carrier/hopper over 1-2 minutes — a mic streams audio nonstop (even during silence for digital), unlike PTT radios or bursty data. A signal that dies when you leave a room and returns when you re-enter tracks a person.

On UHF/VHF analog FM carriers, demodulate WFM then NFM in-app and LISTEN. If you hear clear room audio / your own footsteps / a colleague talking, it is an active analog wireless mic — this is the single most decisive confirmation and it is unencrypted by design.

Analog vs digital shape check: analog FM carrier is peaky and 'breathes' (sidebands widen with speech volume); digital mic is a flat-topped noise-like block of constant amplitude with hard edges. Use the app's persistence/waterfall to see the difference.

Physical near-field bring-up: walk a broadband/near-field detector or the SDR with a short antenna toward suspected persons/objects; a worn bodypack shows rising received power as you approach the wearer, confirming a body-worn source rather than a rack-mounted AV system.

Pilot-tone / squelch-tone hunt on analog: zoom the FFT around the carrier for a fixed sub-audible pilot spur (~32 kHz region) — presence of a deterministic pilot alongside companded FM audio is a wireless-mic fingerprint, not a random FM source.

For 2.4 GHz FHSS: run a timed hop-cadence capture. A wireless mic hops with a steady period locked to its audio frame rate and never stops while on; compare against known Wi-Fi (wide, bursty, tied to your traffic) and BLE (advertising cadence). Correlate persistence with a physical sweep.

Rule out the room's legitimate AV: check for an obvious receiver (rack, camera hot-shoe RX, presenter kit). If a receiver and its paired transmitter are accounted for and inventoried, log as authorized; an UNPAIRED transmitter with no known receiver on premises is the red flag.

Cross-band sweep: because the same product line ships in UHF, 900, 1.9 GHz and 2.4 GHz variants, sweep all four regimes (plus VHF if AD9364-modded) before clearing a space — do not clear on a single-band pass.

Watch the US band map: a strong 'mic-like' carrier above 608 MHz (up to 698) in the US is either legacy/illegal mic gear or is actually 600 MHz cellular/other service — verify before logging it as a mic; that segment is no longer licensed for mic operation.
false_positive_overlap: Legitimate venue AV: hotels, churches, courtrooms, conference centers and classrooms run banks of UHF analog/digital wireless mics — a keyed mic carrier is FAR more often authorized house AV than a bug. Inventory the room's own gear first.

UHF-TV-band overlap: 470-698 MHz also carries DTV broadcast, wireless IEM (in-ear monitor) packs, white-space devices, and (in the US 617-698 MHz) licensed 600 MHz cellular. IEMs look nearly identical (companded FM in the same band) but transmit FROM the rack TO the performer — direction and pairing distinguish them.

2.4 GHz is a swamp: Wi-Fi, Bluetooth/BLE, Zigbee, wireless keyboards/mice, drones, and consumer cameras all share 2400-2483.5 MHz. A hopping 2.4 GHz mic is genuinely hard to separate from BT/Wi-Fi without cadence analysis or audio confirmation — expect false positives here and lean on persistence + physical correlation.
900 MHz ISM overlap: 902-928 also holds cordless phones, LoRa/IoT, some baby monitors, RFID and utility telemetry — a 900 MHz digital block is not self-evidently a mic.
1.8-1.9 GHz overlap: DECT cordless phones and DECT-based room conferencing systems share the exact TDMA signature of DECT-based wireless mics; near-impossible to separate on RF alone.

VHF overlap: 72-76 MHz assistive-listening transmitters, 169-172 MHz business paging/data, and 174-216 MHz VHF-TV broadcast all share the low-VHF FM look — a VHF FM carrier is not proof of a covert mic.
IEM / assistive listening confusion: hearing-assist transmitters and IEM systems use the same companded-FM look; a continuous FM carrier is not proof of a covert mic by itself.
Pilot-tone and comb-of-carriers patterns also appear in legitimate multi-channel productions — a comb of evenly spaced UHF carriers is normal in a working AV rack.

Adjacent class (not covered here): the classic 88-108 MHz FM-broadcast-band 'spy bug' micro-transmitter and 49 MHz toy mics are a SEPARATE covert-audio device class (bare FM bug transmitter), not a wireless-mic SYSTEM — do not expect this class's fingerprints to match those; sweep the FM broadcast band under that class.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Covert-use reality: a wireless-mic bodypack or clip-on transmitter is the most 'deniable' audio bug because it is a legal, off-the-shelf pro-audio product — nothing on the RF says 'spy.' The threat model is a transmitter worn on a person, hidden in a bag/jacket, or planted near a target (taped under a table, inside a prop) with the paired receiver elsewhere. The tiny form factors matter for TSCM: Shure ADX1M micro-bodypack, Rode/DJI/Hollyland self-contained clip-ons, and onboard-recording packs (Zaxcom TRX) can be concealed easily and, in the recording case, may capture audio even with the RF link idle. Discrimination, not detection, is the whole job here: presence of a carrier is cheap; proving it is a mic vs. the venue's own AV requires (1) demodulating clear audio on analog, (2) persistence/cadence analysis on digital/FHSS, and (3) physical correlation to a wearer or a hidden object with no accounted-for receiver. Encrypted digital (SLX-D/ULX-D/Axient, EW-D, DMS800, AVX, and all the 2.4 GHz kits) yields NO clear audio — you can only prove presence and behavior, never content, from the SDR; the confirmation there is physical discovery. Legal/consent flag for the operator: in one-party-consent jurisdictions a person wearing their own mic may be lawful; a planted transmitter recording others without consent likely is not — surface any suspected unlawful interception to the client/counsel rather than adjudicating it in the field. Reach summary: the four regimes above VHF (UHF 470-698, 900 ISM, 1.8-1.9 GHz, 2.4 GHz) are ALL inside a stock ADALM-Pluto's 325-3800 MHz range; only the legacy VHF (72-216 MHz) analog mics fall below Pluto and need the AD9364 mod or a VHF front end. Nothing in this class is above 6 GHz, so the B210 covers it all; B210's larger instantaneous bandwidth mainly helps see the full 83.5 MHz of the 2.4 GHz band without sweeping. US band-plan note: post-2020 incentive auction, US mic operation is effectively below 608 MHz — 470-698 is retained here as a detection scan range for legacy/non-US gear, but a mic-shaped carrier in 617-698 MHz in the US warrants a second look (could be 600 MHz cellular). HARDWARE-UNTESTED CAVEAT: these signatures are built from published product/standards data (ETSI EN 300 422 [200 kHz below 1 GHz / 600 kHz above 1 GHz], FCC Part 74/Part 15.236, manufacturer specs), not from captures verified on this app's Pluto/B210 chain — validate center/bandwidth/duty against a live known-good mic of each regime before relying on auto-match in the field.

signatures.name: UHF analog FM wireless mic (~470-698 MHz scan; US legal op below 608 MHz)
signatures.mode: Analog wideband FM, single audio carrier with compander (companding); ~15-75 kHz peak deviation, occupied BW ~130-200 kHz per ETSI EN 300 422 (200 kHz max below 1 GHz) / FCC Part 74 mask
signatures.tscm: Single stable FM carrier that stays keyed continuously while the pack is on (not PTT). Waterfall shows a solid vertical line ~150-200 kHz wide with the characteristic FM 'breathing' of the sidebands widening/narrowing with speech loudness. Often a pilot tone (~32.768 kHz or 32.6/38 kHz sub-audible) used for squelch — a faint deterministic spur near the carrier. Demodulating WFM/NFM yields clear, un-encrypted room audio. Frequently sits on a TV-channel-aligned center; multiple mics in one venue appear as an evenly-spaced comb of carriers. [stock-Pluto-reachable (470-698 MHz well within 325-3800 MHz); trivially demodulated to audio in-app with a WFM/NFM decoder]

signatures.name: VHF analog FM wireless mic (72-216 MHz, legacy/cheap)
signatures.mode: Analog FM voice across legacy VHF sub-bands: 72-76 MHz (assistive listening, up to 1 W), 169-172 MHz (business 'traveling frequencies'), and 174-216 MHz high-band VHF (TV ch 7-13); companded, ~15-50 kHz deviation
signatures.tscm: Same continuous companded FM carrier as UHF but down in VHF. Common on very cheap/old bodypacks, karaoke, tour-guide, assistive-listening and some baby-monitor-grade mics. Continuously keyed, clear-audio on WFM/NFM demod, often drifty/unstable center compared to modern PLL UHF gear. Sub-bands cluster at 72-76, 169-172, and 174-216 MHz rather than filling the whole span. [OUT of stock-Pluto range (below 325 MHz). Needs the AD9364 mod (lowers Pluto to ~70 MHz) or a separate VHF-capable front end / downconverter. Listed for completeness — cheap legacy covert mics do live here.]

signatures.name: UHF digital wireless mic (~470-698 MHz, 200 kHz digital channel)
signatures.mode: Digital modulation (proprietary; typ. multi-carrier/QAM-like or FSK-family) inside a 200 kHz TV-band channel; Shure SLX-D/ULX-D/Axient, Sennheiser EW-D/Digital 6000, AKG DMS800; often AES-256 encrypted
signatures.tscm: Flat-topped, noise-like 'brick' ~180-200 kHz wide, sharp channel edges (unlike the peaky, breathing analog FM carrier), constant amplitude regardless of whether anyone is speaking (digital doesn't narrow with silence). No demodulable clear audio — encrypted/proprietary payload. Occupies the same TV-band real estate as analog mics, so band alone doesn't distinguish it; the flat spectral shape and constant occupancy do. Multiple units = comb of identical flat blocks. [stock-Pluto-reachable; detectable by band+bandwidth+flat-digital shape but NOT decodable to audio (proprietary/encrypted) — treat as presence-only]

signatures.name: UHF digital wireless mic — wideband / multichannel variant (~470-698 MHz, up to ~600 kHz-1 MHz aggregate)
signatures.mode: Digital WMAS-style or wideband proprietary occupying wider-than-200 kHz channel (newer wideband multichannel audio systems, some Axient/Digital 6000 wideband modes)
signatures.tscm: Wider flat digital block (roughly 300 kHz-1 MHz) than the standard 200 kHz TV-channel signature; may carry multiple audio channels in one RF block. Constant occupancy, noise-like flat top, hard channel edges. Rarer in covert use (pro touring/broadcast gear) but distinct on-air from the 200 kHz digital signature so it gets its own row. [stock-Pluto-reachable in frequency; wide block is fine for Pluto's ~20 MHz instantaneous BW, but confirm your app's FFT span covers it]

signatures.name: 900 MHz ISM digital wireless mic (902-928 MHz, license-free)
signatures.mode: Digital, license-free 900 MHz ISM; some fixed-channel, some frequency-agile/hopping (Sennheiser XSW/9000-series regional, AKG DMS, Line 6 900, various prosumer)
signatures.tscm: Digital block(s) in the 902-928 ISM band. Distinguish from UHF-TV-band gear purely by center frequency. Shares 900 ISM with cordless phones, some IoT, LoRa, and older baby monitors, so false-positive overlap is high here. May be fixed-channel (one flat block) or lightly frequency-agile (block that relocates on interference). Constant amplitude when keyed. [stock-Pluto-reachable (902-928 well within range); presence detectable, audio proprietary/not decodable]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz digital FHSS wireless mic (2400-2483.5 MHz, frequency-hopping)
signatures.mode: Digital frequency-hopping spread spectrum, license-free 2.4 GHz ISM; Rode Wireless GO/DJI Mic-class, Shure GLXD (LINKFREQ auto freq mgmt), Line 6 XD-V (DCL), Audio-Technica System 10, Sennheiser XSW-D; typ. ~1 MHz-wide hopping channels, AES/128-bit encryption common
signatures.tscm: Hopping bursts ~0.5-2 MHz wide skipping across the 2.4 GHz band, distinct from a static Wi-Fi carrier but easily confused with Bluetooth/BLE hopping and with Wi-Fi in aggregate. Persistent, regular hop cadence tied to the audio frame rate (continuous audio = steady stream of bursts even in silence, unlike bursty data). Best tell over time: a device that hops constantly and never stops for as long as it's on, co-located with a worn transmitter. Encrypted — no clear audio. Two-person kits (Rode dual) show two independent persistent hoppers. [stock-Pluto-reachable at the low edge (2.4-2.4835 GHz < 3800 MHz upper limit); wideband FHSS survey benefits from B210 (larger instantaneous bandwidth) to see the whole 83.5 MHz band at once — a stock Pluto sees it but must sweep]

signatures.name: 1.8-1.9 GHz digital wireless mic / DECT-style (1785-1805 MHz EU, 1920-1930 MHz DECT/US prosumer)
signatures.mode: Digital, DECT-based or 1.9 GHz proprietary (Sennheiser AVX 1920-1930 MHz, DECT wireless mics, Shure/Revolabs-class 1.9 GHz conference/presenter systems); TDMA framing, ~1.728 MHz DECT slots
signatures.tscm: DECT-style TDMA bursts on a ~1.728 MHz raster in the 1920-1930 MHz US UPCS/DECT 6.0 region, or 1785-1805 MHz EU wireless-mic sub-band. Regular TDMA frame structure (10 ms frames) distinguishes it. Overlaps heavily with DECT cordless phones and DECT-based room conferencing — high false-positive risk. Constant framed occupancy while active. [stock-Pluto-reachable (1.8-1.9 GHz within range); overlaps DECT cordless phone signature — correlate with a worn transmitter / physical find before calling it a mic]

device_classes.device_class: BLE item trackers (AirTag / Tile / Samsung SmartTag / Google Find My Device tags / Chipolo / Pebblebee, etc.) plus their UWB precision-finding radios
device_classes.summary: This class covers consumer "lost-item" tags and the phones/keyfobs that range to them. On the air there are really only a few PHYs: (1) Bluetooth Low Energy advertising, GFSK ~1 Msym/s, ~2 MHz occupied, transmitted on the three fixed advertising channels 37/38/39 (2402/2426/2480 MHz) — every mainstream tracker (AirTag, Tile, SmartTag, Google FMDN tags, Chipolo, Pebblebee, Eufy, Cube) uses this identical modulation; (2) the same GFSK on the 37 general-purpose DATA channels once connected/paired; (3) optional BLE Coded PHY (LE Long Range, spread GFSK) used by some newer tags/scanners; and (4) 802.15.4z HRP impulse-radio UWB for precision finding on channel 5 (6489.6 MHz) and channel 9 (7987.2 MHz), 499.2 MHz wide. CRITICAL for a spectrum matcher: the tracker "brands" (Find My, Tile, SmartTag, FMDN) are NOT distinct RF signatures — they are the SAME 2 MHz GFSK burst on ch 37/38/39. What separates them is the payload (manufacturer-data company ID / service-data UUID), which a spectrum-only tool CANNOT see — it needs a protocol-aware BLE sniffer (nRF Sniffer, Ubertooth, Sniffle) to read the advertising bytes. I list the shared GFSK air signature by advertising channel (what a Pluto/B210 can actually tune and detect), then break out the identifiable service-data tells as protocol-layer rows so the app can label a decoded advert, plus the two UWB rows flagged as at/above the B210 6 GHz edge. RANGE NOTE: all BLE is at 2.4 GHz — WELL below a stock Pluto's 325-3800 MHz upper limit, so 2.4 GHz BLE is OUT of a stock Pluto's reach and needs the AD9364 firmware mod (to ~6 GHz) or a B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz). Both UWB channels sit at/above the 6 GHz top of the B210 and are effectively out of range.

confirm_steps: Dwell on the three advertising channels (2402/2426/2480 MHz) and look for periodic ~2 MHz GFSK bursts recurring every ~1-2 s that persist as the target subject/vehicle moves between locations. A stationary owner's own tags will also show — establish a baseline with known devices powered off.

Hand off to a protocol-aware BLE sniffer to read the payload — nRF Connect app / Nordic nRF52840 nRF Sniffer, Ubertooth One, or Sniffle (TI CC1352) — and record the manufacturer/service tell: Apple 0x004C type 0x12 (Find My), Tile 0xFEED/0xFEEC, Samsung 0xFD5A, Google FMDN 0xFEAA.

Use the phone's built-in scans as a cross-check: iOS Find My 'Items Detected Near You' / 'Unknown Accessory', and Android Settings > Safety & emergency > Unknown tracker alerts (or the Find My Device 'scan now'). These decode the DULT separated-owner payload directly.

For rotating-ID tags (AirTag, FMDN, SmartTag) do NOT try to lock a fixed MAC — it rotates ~every 15 min. Instead correlate by RSSI rising/falling with proximity and by the beacon reappearing after each rotation while the target moves.

Physically localize with the RSSI gradient: sweep the antenna over seats, bags, wheel wells, bumpers, clothing, and gifts; the beacon RSSI peaks at the tag. Confirm by removing/bagging the suspected item and verifying the beacon disappears.

Trigger the tag's own tells: an AirTag separated from its owner emits an audible chirp after a period, and NFC-tapping an AirTag/most Find My tags to a phone opens a page with the serial/partial owner info — capture it for the report.

Do NOT expect to catch UWB on a Pluto or B210 — channel 5 (6489.6 MHz) is above the B210's 6 GHz edge and channel 9 (7987.2 MHz) is well out of range; UWB also only fires during an active precision-finding session, so it is not a passive-detection path.
false_positive_overlap: Every other BLE device shares the exact ch37/38/39 GFSK PHY: phones, earbuds (AirPods, Galaxy Buds), smartwatches, fitness bands, BLE beacons, retail Eddystone/iBeacon transmitters, TV remotes, medical wearables, car keyfobs, smart-home sensors. Spectrum alone CANNOT tell a tracker from any of these — payload decode is mandatory.
0xFEAA is shared between Google FMDN trackers and plain Eddystone beacons (retail/proximity marketing) — the UUID alone is not proof of a tracker; the frame type must be decoded.

AirPods, MacBooks, and any 'Find My'-enabled Apple accessory emit the same 0x004C manufacturer data as an AirTag, so an Apple-ID advert is not automatically a hidden tag — it may be the subject's own earbuds.

The 500 MHz noise-like UWB impulse can be mistaken for wideband noise or another 6-8 GHz emitter; conversely legitimate UWB (car digital keys, smart-home ranging, phones unlocking) shares the same 802.15.4z waveform.

A moving vehicle inherently carries a cloud of legitimate BLE advertisers (infotainment, TPMS-adjacent, phones), so a positive on the advertising channels in a car is expected and not by itself incriminating — you must isolate a persistent, owner-separated, following beacon.
OpenHaystack / DIY firmware can make a generic nRF52 or ESP32 dev board advertise a valid Find My payload, so a decoded Apple-format advert does not guarantee genuine Apple hardware.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Practical hierarchy for this class: the reliable, always-on detection surface is BLE advertising GFSK on 2402/2426/2480 MHz — hunt there. A stock ADALM-Pluto (325-3800 MHz) DOES reach 2.4 GHz, so it can see the GFSK bursts as IQ energy, but it cannot decode which tracker it is; you need a protocol sniffer (nRF Sniffer, Ubertooth, Sniffle) to read the manufacturer/service tell and to catch the DULT 'separated from owner' flag. Treat the brand rows above as protocol-layer labels, not separate air signatures — physically they are the same 2 MHz burst. Rotating identifiers (Apple, Google, Samsung) defeat MAC-based tracking, so localize by RSSI + movement correlation, then confirm physically (NFC tap for serial, forced chirp, bag-and-verify-disappearance). UWB (ch5 6489.6 MHz, ch9 7987.2 MHz, ~500 MHz wide) is a red herring for passive sweeping: it is above/at the B210's 6 GHz ceiling, far beyond the Pluto (even AD9364-modded to ~6 GHz), and only transmits during an active precision-finding session — it will not lead you to a hidden tag. Report language for clients should distinguish 'a tracker-format beacon was detected and decoded' (high confidence, cite the UUID/company-ID tell and the owner-separated flag) from 'BLE energy present on advertising channels' (low confidence — could be any BLE device). Finally, the leading real-world risk here is stalking/IPV: if a following owner-separated tracker is confirmed on a client's person or vehicle, treat it as a potential safety and criminal matter (surveil/stalk statutes), preserve the device and its serial/NFC data rather than destroying it, and advise the client on law-enforcement and personal-safety steps.

signatures.name: BLE advertising burst — channel 37 (2402 MHz)
signatures.mode: Bluetooth LE 1M PHY advertising, GFSK 1 Msym/s (~1 Mbps), modulation index ~0.5, ~2 MHz occupied; primary advertising channel
signatures.tscm: Short (~0.1-0.4 ms) GFSK packets hopping across the three advertising channels. Ch 37 sits at 2402 MHz, deliberately in the WiFi ch1/ch6 gap. A tracker in 'lost/offline' mode re-broadcasts roughly every 1-2 s (AirTag ~2 s); paired-but-nearby tags advertise slower. Same waveform for ALL brands — the brand is only in the payload bytes, invisible to a spectrum tool. [2.4 GHz is ABOVE a stock Pluto's 3800 MHz? No — it is at 2402 MHz which IS within 325-3800 MHz, so a STOCK Pluto CAN tune it. Correction applies to duty only. Within B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) as well.]

signatures.name: BLE advertising burst — channel 38 (2426 MHz)
signatures.mode: Bluetooth LE 1M PHY advertising, GFSK 1 Msym/s, ~2 MHz occupied; secondary advertising channel
signatures.tscm: Middle advertising channel at 2426 MHz (WiFi ch6/ch11 gap). Trackers advertise on 37, then 38, then 39 in quick succession within one advertising event, so a matcher should expect near-simultaneous energy on all three ~2 MHz slots. [2426 MHz is within a stock Pluto's 325-3800 MHz reach and within B210 range.]

signatures.name: BLE advertising burst — channel 39 (2480 MHz)
signatures.mode: Bluetooth LE 1M PHY advertising, GFSK 1 Msym/s, ~2 MHz occupied; top advertising channel
signatures.tscm: Top advertising channel at 2480 MHz, at the upper edge of the 2.4 GHz ISM band. Completes the 37/38/39 triad. Useful as a clean detection slot because it sits above most WiFi occupancy. [2480 MHz is within a stock Pluto's 325-3800 MHz reach and within B210 range.]

signatures.name: BLE data-channel GFSK (connected / paired session)
signatures.mode: Bluetooth LE 1M PHY data channels 0-36, GFSK 1 Msym/s, adaptive frequency hopping across 37 data channels (2 MHz spacing)
signatures.tscm: Once a phone connects to a tag (setup, firmware update, ring/find, config), traffic moves off the 3 advertising channels onto the 37 data channels and hops adaptively. Appears as fast 2 MHz GFSK bursts scattered across 2404-2478 MHz rather than the fixed 3-slot advertising pattern. [2.4 GHz data channels are within a stock Pluto's 325-3800 MHz reach and within B210 range. Following the hop sequence needs wideband capture / a real BLE sniffer, not narrowband Pluto tuning.]

signatures.name: BLE Coded PHY / LE Long Range advertising (S=8 125 kbps, S=2 500 kbps)
signatures.mode: Bluetooth LE Coded PHY (LE Long Range), GFSK 1 Msym/s symbol rate but FEC-spread to 125 kbps (S=8) or 500 kbps (S=2); same 2 MHz channels 37/38/39
signatures.tscm: Same 2 MHz GFSK envelope and same advertising channels, but each packet is much LONGER (coding spreads bits ~8x) so the on-air burst is stretched. Used by some newer trackers/asset tags and long-range detection scanners for extended range. A spectrum tool sees an unusually long advertising burst on 37/38/39. [2.4 GHz, within stock Pluto 325-3800 MHz and B210 range for energy detection; decode needs a Coded-PHY-capable BLE receiver.]

signatures.name: UWB precision finding — 802.15.4z HRP channel 5 (6489.6 MHz)
signatures.mode: IEEE 802.15.4z HRP impulse-radio UWB, center 6489.6 MHz, 499.2 MHz channel bandwidth, BPRF/HPRF pulse trains (PRF up to ~249.6 MHz), short two-way-ranging bursts
signatures.tscm: Very wide (~500 MHz) low-power-spectral-density impulse energy that looks noise-like on a narrowband analyzer. Only present DURING an active ranging session (phone 'Precision Finding' pointing at a tag), not continuously — the tag/phone fire short two-way-ranging exchanges. Apple U1/U2, Samsung, Google UWB tags use ch 5 and/or ch 9. [6489.6 MHz center is ABOVE the B210's 6 GHz ceiling and FAR above a stock Pluto's 3800 MHz limit — effectively OUT OF RANGE for both. Needs a >6 GHz front end / dedicated UWB radio (Qorvo/NXP) or a UWB-capable analyzer. Even the AD9364 Pluto mod (to ~6 GHz) does not reach it.]

signatures.name: UWB precision finding — 802.15.4z HRP channel 9 (7987.2 MHz)
signatures.mode: IEEE 802.15.4z HRP impulse-radio UWB, center 7987.2 MHz, 499.2 MHz channel bandwidth, BPRF/HPRF; the mandatory/most-common smartphone UWB channel
signatures.tscm: Same ~500 MHz impulse UWB but centered ~7987 MHz. Channel 9 is the widely mandated smartphone UWB channel (Apple U1/U2, recent Galaxy/Pixel). Noise-like wideband bursts only during active ranging; extremely low PSD, easy to miss without a wideband >6 GHz capture. [7987.2 MHz is WELL above the B210's 6 GHz ceiling and the Pluto's 3800 MHz limit — OUT OF RANGE for both, and above even the AD9364 mod. Requires a dedicated UWB radio or an analyzer covering 7.25-8.5 GHz.]

device_classes.device_class: Wireless HDMI / AV senders repurposed for covert video exfiltration (2.4 GHz & 5.x GHz digital WHDI/proprietary-OFDM, 5.8 GHz analog AV senders, 60 GHz WirelessHD)
device_classes.summary: This class covers consumer/prosumer wireless video links — WHDI and proprietary-OFDM "wireless HDMI" kits, cheap analog AV senders, FPV video transmitters, and 60 GHz WirelessHD — any of which can be wired to a hidden camera or spliced onto a target's HDMI/composite feed to stream a live picture out of a room. On the air they fall into a handful of genuinely distinct signatures, NOT hundreds: the RF fingerprint is band x channel width x modulation (wideband OFDM vs. analog FM-video vs. narrow FHSS) x duty. The dominant distinctions are: (1) wideband ~20-40 MHz 5 GHz OFDM digital video (WHDI / proprietary HDMI kits), (2) 2.4 GHz wideband OFDM digital video kits, (3) legacy ~18-30 MHz analog FM-video AV senders on 2.4 GHz, (4) the same on 5.8 GHz, (5) ~30 MHz analog FM FPV video transmitters spanning 5.65-5.95 GHz, and (6) 60 GHz uncompressed WirelessHD. CRITICAL REACH NOTE: every signature in this class sits ABOVE a stock PlutoSDR's 325-3800 MHz tuning range. All 2.4 GHz signatures need the AD9364 firmware mod (extends Pluto to ~70 MHz-6 GHz) or a different front end; all 5.x GHz signatures are near/at the 6 GHz ceiling and are best swept with the B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz); 60 GHz WirelessHD is entirely out of range of both radios and requires a 60 GHz down-converter / dedicated 60 GHz power sensor. The hardest part of a sweep is that these signals sit in the same ISM bands as Wi-Fi, and the OFDM variants look spectrally very similar to Wi-Fi — the tell is a CONTINUOUS, near-constant-envelope carrier (video is a persistent stream, not bursty request/response traffic) that persists even when the room's Wi-Fi clients are quiesced.
