confirm_steps: Establish a baseline FIRST: with the suspected AV link OFF (or before entering the room), record the 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz waterfalls so you know the ambient Wi-Fi/BT picture.

Hunt for CONTINUOUS occupancy: on the B210 sweep 2.4 GHz (2400-2483) and 5 GHz U-NII (5150-5850) and look for a channel that stays lit with a near-constant envelope for many seconds — video is a persistent stream, unlike bursty Wi-Fi. Note center freq and occupied bandwidth (~20 / ~40 MHz OFDM, or ~18-30 MHz FM).

Discriminate OFDM-digital vs analog-FM: analog AV senders/FPV show a peaked FM-video spectrum with discrete audio-subcarrier spikes; WHDI/HDMI kits show a flat-top OFDM block. For the analog ones, FM-demodulate a few MHz around the carrier and look for composite-video horizontal/vertical sync — recovering a picture or sync structure is a hard positive.

Rule out Wi-Fi actively: saturate or idle the room's own Wi-Fi (or take the AP offline). Legitimate Wi-Fi occupancy tracks that activity; a covert video link's occupancy does NOT drop — it keeps streaming.

Correlate with power/proximity: walk the room with a directional antenna (or near-field probe) and watch RSSI peak at a physical location — a hidden camera+sender will localize to a fixed object, not to the AP.
Check for a co-located hidden camera: pair the RF find with a lens sweep (optical/IR reflection) at the RSSI peak; the sender is only half the device.

For the 5.8-5.95 GHz FPV top channels near the SDR's 6 GHz edge, cross-check with a cheap 5.8 GHz FPV goggle/diversity receiver scanning bands A/B/E/F/R — it will lock a live FPV picture the SDR may miss at the band edge.

For 60 GHz WirelessHD, do NOT expect the SDR to see it: use a 60 GHz-capable probe/detector or a WiHD receiver as a presence check, and physically inspect for line-of-sight 60 GHz modules; document it as an SDR blind spot in the report.
false_positive_overlap: 802.11a/n/ac Wi-Fi on 5 GHz: 20/40 MHz OFDM WHDI/HDMI blocks are spectrally near-identical to Wi-Fi channels — only duty cycle (continuous vs. bursty) and non-participation in Wi-Fi contention separate them. High false-positive risk.

802.11 Wi-Fi on 2.4 GHz: 2.4 GHz digital AV kits overlap busy Wi-Fi channels; a saturated legitimate Wi-Fi stream (e.g., someone streaming video over Wi-Fi) can mimic continuous occupancy — must rule out with the AP-idle test.

Legitimate in-home wireless HDMI: many households have a wholly innocent Nyrius/IOGEAR wireless HDMI kit connecting a media box to a TV. Presence of the signature is NOT proof of surveillance — you must localize it and confirm what it is fed by.
Legitimate FPV hobby gear: a resident's drone/FPV VTX on 5.8 GHz is a lawful device; only becomes suspicious if powered, hidden, and pointed at a private space.
Baby monitors and legacy analog CCTV senders on 2.4/5.8 GHz share the analog-FM-video signature exactly — same RF, different intent.
Cordless devices, wireless game controllers, and other ISM occupants can clutter 2.4 GHz and cause spurious hits during the initial occupancy hunt.
5 GHz weather/TDWR and DFS radar events can momentarily paint the 5 GHz waterfall and be mistaken for a signal — they are pulsed, not continuous, so duty analysis separates them.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Operationally, the single most useful discriminator for this whole class is DUTY CYCLE: a live covert video feed is a continuous, near-constant-envelope emission, whereas Wi-Fi/BT traffic is bursty and tracks user activity. Build the sweep around finding persistent occupancy and then proving it does not stop when the room's own Wi-Fi is quiesced. For the analog variants (2.4/5.8 GHz AV senders and FPV VTX), FM-demodulating the carrier to recover composite-video sync is the strongest single confirmation the app can offer and should be surfaced as a one-click action. HARDWARE REALITY the report must state plainly: (1) a STOCK PlutoSDR (325-3800 MHz) cannot see ANY signature in this class — every one is above 3.8 GHz; it needs the AD9364 firmware mod to reach 2.4 GHz and is marginal at 5 GHz. (2) The B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) is the correct radio for 2.4 and 5 GHz here, but even it is near its edge at 5.9 GHz, so the very top FPV channels (5917/5945) and anything right at 6 GHz are unreliable — recommend a cheap 5.8 GHz FPV diversity receiver as an adjunct. (3) 60 GHz WirelessHD is a genuine BLIND SPOT — neither SDR can reach it; only a 60 GHz down-converter/probe or a WiHD receiver-as-detector will find it, and it must be called out as an uncovered vector so the client isn't given false assurance. Finally, an RF hit is only half a find: pair every localization with an optical/IR lens sweep at the RSSI peak, because the sender is worthless to an adversary without a camera wired to it. Do not overstate certainty in the client-facing writeup — flag each 5 GHz OFDM hit as 'consistent with wireless-video or Wi-Fi, pending duty/localization confirmation' rather than asserting surveillance.

signatures.name: WHDI / proprietary 5 GHz wireless-HDMI digital video, 20 MHz OFDM channel
signatures.mode: OFDM digital video (WHDI 5 GHz PHY / proprietary), 20 MHz mandatory mode, 16-QAM+ subcarriers, MIMO on some kits
signatures.tscm: Persistent ~20 MHz-wide near-flat-top OFDM block that stays up continuously while a source is connected (a live video stream, not bursty). Sits in U-NII 5 GHz sub-bands (5.15-5.35, 5.47-5.725, 5.725-5.85). Looks like an 802.11a/n 20 MHz channel on a waterfall but the duty cycle is the giveaway: constant occupancy, no beacon/idle gaps, no request-response burstiness. WHDI legacy kits often park mid-band and hold one channel. [Above stock Pluto 3800 MHz ceiling. Use B210 (covers to 6 GHz). AD9364-modded Pluto reaches it but with degraded performance near the top of its range; B210 strongly preferred for 5 GHz.]

signatures.name: WHDI / proprietary 5 GHz wireless-HDMI digital video, 40 MHz OFDM channel
signatures.mode: OFDM digital video, 40 MHz mandatory WHDI mode / bonded-channel proprietary kit, higher-order QAM for up to ~3 Gbps class throughput
signatures.tscm: Same as the 20 MHz WHDI signature but a ~40 MHz-wide continuous OFDM block — indistinguishable from an 802.11n/ac 40 MHz channel by shape alone. Distinguish by duty (continuous video occupancy) and by the fact that it does not participate in normal Wi-Fi contention (occupancy does not drop when you saturate the AP or when clients idle). Higher-throughput HDMI kits and 1080p60 senders favor this width. [Above stock Pluto ceiling; sweep with B210. AD9364-modded Pluto is marginal at 5 GHz and cannot instantaneously capture 40 MHz at full rate — the B210 handles the wider IQ span.]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz wireless-HDMI / digital AV sender, wideband OFDM (~20 MHz)
signatures.mode: OFDM / proprietary digital video in 2.4 GHz ISM; some kits are single-carrier wideband digital
signatures.tscm: A single continuous ~20 MHz OFDM occupancy sitting on a fixed 2.4 GHz channel (commonly parked near ch1/6/11 equivalents). Extremely easy to confuse with a busy Wi-Fi channel — the discriminator is again continuous constant-envelope occupancy of one channel with no beacon structure and no fall-off when Wi-Fi traffic stops. 2.4 GHz digital kits are chosen for wall penetration / multi-room exfil. [ENTIRELY above stock Pluto 3800 MHz ceiling AND the 2.4 GHz band is BELOW nothing — it is above Pluto's top, so stock Pluto cannot reach it. Requires AD9364 mod (to ~6 GHz) OR B210. B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) is the clean choice for 2.4 GHz.]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz analog FM composite-video AV sender (legacy 'video sender'), fixed-channel
signatures.mode: Wideband FM analog video (CVBS on FM carrier) + FM audio subcarrier(s); PLL-selectable, typically 4 channels ~2414/2432/2450/2468 MHz
signatures.tscm: Classic cheap 'video sender' fingerprint: a continuous wideband-FM carrier ~15-20 MHz wide with a characteristic FM-video spectral shape (energy concentrated around the carrier with sidebands from the video modulation, plus discrete audio subcarrier spikes usually 5.5-6.5 MHz off carrier). Demodulating FM yields a recognizable composite-video line/field sync structure — a strong positive confirmation. Occupies one of ~4 fixed channels; parks and holds. Distinctly NOT Wi-Fi-shaped (no OFDM flat-top, no packet structure). [Above stock Pluto ceiling (2.4 GHz > 3800 MHz). Needs AD9364-modded Pluto or B210. FM-video demod is the strongest confirm and only needs a few MHz of clean IQ, well within B210.]

signatures.name: 5.8 GHz analog FM composite-video AV sender, PLL fixed-channel
signatures.mode: Wideband FM analog video + FM audio subcarrier; PLL-selectable, commonly 8 channels (e.g. ~5790/5828/5847/5866 MHz), some 32-channel (4 groups of 8)
signatures.tscm: Same wideband-FM analog-video fingerprint as the 2.4 GHz sender but parked in the 5.8 GHz ISM band. Continuous ~18-22 MHz FM carrier with video sidebands and audio subcarrier spikes; FM-demod recovers a composite-video sync structure. These are marketed as higher-band, 'anti-interference' AV senders and as CCTV video links; a hidden camera wired to one gives a persistent 5.8 GHz analog picture. Not OFDM-shaped. [Above stock Pluto ceiling AND above the ~6 GHz top only for the very highest channels — 5.725-5.875 GHz is within B210's 6 GHz range but near its upper edge (expect reduced sensitivity/flatness up top). AD9364-modded Pluto is at/over its practical limit here; B210 preferred.]

signatures.name: 5.8 GHz analog FM FPV video transmitter (VTX) repurposed as exfil, ~30 MHz channel across 5.65-5.95 GHz band plan
signatures.mode: Wideband FM analog video (NTSC/PAL CVBS), 25/200/600 mW+ selectable, 40+ channels across bands A/B/E/F/R (Raceband) — e.g. TS832-class 48ch
signatures.tscm: Analog FM-video like the AV senders but with the FPV band plan: any of ~40+ discrete channels spanning ~5645-5945 MHz, ~30 MHz occupied per channel, frequently found on Raceband frequencies (5658/5695/5732/5769/5806/5843/5880/5917). Continuous carrier, FM-demod recovers composite video. A tell vs. a fixed AV sender is the exact channel center matching a known FPV table and the wider ~30 MHz occupancy. Very cheap, tiny, solder-a-camera-on modules. [Upper channels (>5.9 GHz) are AT or slightly ABOVE the B210 / AD9364 6 GHz ceiling — 5917/5945 MHz is right at the edge and may be out of clean range. Lower/mid FPV channels are reachable on B210. Stock Pluto cannot reach any of it. For the top channels you may need a 5.8 GHz FPV receiver/goggle diversity RX or a down-converter as an adjunct.]

signatures.name: 60 GHz WirelessHD (WiHD) uncompressed digital video
signatures.mode: 60 GHz EHF, single ~7 GHz-wide channel, OFDM/single-carrier uncompressed HD (4 Gbps first-gen, up to ~25 Gbps), highly directional beamformed
signatures.tscm: A ~7 GHz-wide continuous transmission in the 57-66 GHz band, extremely directional (line-of-sight, decreases sharply through walls). Used by in-room uncompressed-4K wireless HDMI kits. Effectively short-range and beam-steered, which both limits its exfil utility (must have LOS) and makes it hard to detect off-axis. [COMPLETELY OUT OF RANGE of both stock/modded Pluto (max ~6 GHz) and the B210 (max 6 GHz). Cannot be swept with this app's SDRs at all. Requires a dedicated 60 GHz front end: a 60 GHz down-converter feeding the SDR, a broadband 60 GHz power/RF detector/probe, or a WirelessHD receiver used as a presence detector. Flag as a known blind spot of the app.]

device_classes.device_class: wireless_doorbell_driveway_pir_rf
device_classes.summary: Sub-GHz ISM short-burst event transmitters used by wireless doorbells, driveway/perimeter alarms, and PIR motion chimes. On the air these are brief (tens of ms) OOK/ASK or FSK bursts on 315 MHz, 318 MHz, 390 MHz, 433.92 MHz, and in the 902-928 MHz band, fired only on a button press or a motion/beam-break event. Duty is inherently event-driven and idle-silent, which is exactly why an operator must recognize them: they look like "something transmitted, then nothing" and are overwhelmingly a benign false-positive source (the homeowner's own doorbell/driveway sensor). The TSCM concern is the exception - the same cheap 315/433.92 MHz PIR modules and door/window reed transmitters are readily repurposed as covert trip/tripwire transmitters (fire a burst when a target enters a room or opens a drawer), so the band overlaps the generic sub-GHz ISM class but the doorbell/PIR duty signature and its false-positive profile deserve an explicit call-out. Stock Pluto (325-3800 MHz) cannot see the 315/318 MHz rows without the AD9364 low-end mod or a different front end; 390/433.92 MHz and 902-928 MHz are in reach. B210 covers all of these natively.

confirm_steps: Confirm the burst is event-driven, not periodic: watch the spectrum while you physically press the suspected doorbell button or walk the driveway/beam - a correlated burst that fires on your action and is otherwise silent is the doorbell/PIR signature.

Identify the exact center frequency (315 / 318 / 390 / 433.92 / 900-band) and note whether stock Pluto could even see it - a 315/318 MHz claim requires the AD9364 low-band mod or B210; if you only have stock Pluto, state you cannot rule those bands in/out.
Classify modulation from the capture: on-off gaps = OOK, two-tone = FSK, packets jumping channels across 902-928 = FHSS. Log the matching signature row.
Count repeats and burst length: doorbell/PIR frames are typically a short pulse train repeated 3-10x over tens of ms - a genuinely continuous carrier is NOT this class and points elsewhere.

Rule benign vs covert: locate the physical emitter. If it maps to the homeowner's known doorbell button or driveway sensor, mark benign. If a 315/433.92 MHz PIR or reed burst fires on room entry / drawer or door opening with NO corresponding household doorbell/driveway device, escalate as a possible covert trip transmitter and physically search the trigger location.

Decode the frame if tooling allows (rtl_433 / URH): a recognized doorbell/driveway/PIR protocol (EV1527, PT2262, brand codes) further confirms benign; an unrecognized custom frame on entry events raises the covert-trip concern.
Note antenna reach limits in the report: 315/318 MHz below Pluto's 325 MHz floor, all rows well under 6 GHz so B210 is fine; none require above-6-GHz coverage.
false_positive_overlap: Homeowner's own wireless doorbell button and chime (315/318/433.92 MHz or 900 MHz) - the dominant benign hit
Driveway/perimeter alarm PIR and beam-break sensors (Guardline/Dakota 900 MHz, 433 MHz long-range)
TPMS tire-pressure sensors (315/433.92 MHz bursts on vehicle motion) - looks similar in duty
Car key fobs, garage/gate remotes (315/433.92 MHz OOK/rolling code)
433 MHz weather stations, temperature/soil/rain sensors (periodic, not event - distinguishable by timing)
900 MHz smart utility meters, LoRa/LoRaWAN sensors, and other 902-928 ISM telemetry
Wireless PIR nodes of legitimate home alarm systems (Honeywell/2GIG/DSC 319.5/345/433 MHz)
EV1527/PT2262-encoded generic OOK remotes for lights, fans, and outlets
device_classes.tscm_notes: This class is 95% a false-positive education problem and 5% a real threat. BENIGN DEFAULT: wireless doorbells, driveway alarms, and PIR motion chimes are ubiquitous residential/commercial gear; an idle-silent burst on 315/318/390/433.92 MHz or in 902-928 MHz that fires when someone presses a button or crosses a driveway is almost certainly the client's own device and must be logged as such, not chased as a bug. The 433.92 MHz and 900 MHz bands specifically are enormous benign pools (TPMS, weather stations, remotes, smart meters, LoRa) - never call a 433/900 burst a threat on frequency alone. COVERT-TRIP EXCEPTION (why it still matters): the exact same low-cost 315/433.92 MHz PIR modules and magnetic door/window reed transmitters used in these products are the standard building block for covert trip/tripwire transmitters - a hidden unit that keys a short burst when a target enters a room, opens a door, or opens a drawer, letting a watcher outside know movement occurred. The tell is a burst that correlates with a target's action but has NO matching household doorbell/driveway device and often an unrecognized frame. FALSE-POSITIVE OVERLAP is severe with the generic sub-GHz ISM class - this row exists mainly to give the operator the duty-cycle and correlation discipline to separate the homeowner's doorbell from a planted trip sensor. REACH CAVEAT: state plainly in any report whether the survey hardware could see 315/318 MHz - stock Pluto (325-3800 MHz) cannot without the AD9364 mod, so a "clean" result there is not authoritative on the low sub-GHz doorbell frequencies; B210 covers the whole class. Nothing in this class is above 6 GHz.

signatures.name: 315 MHz OOK doorbell/PIR event burst
signatures.mode: OOK/ASK, PWM-coded fixed or learning-code frame, single short burst per event
signatures.tscm: Idle-silent carrier that keys on only for a button press or PIR/beam-break, typically a 20-150 ms train of on-off pulses (often repeated 3-8x), narrow ~50-100 kHz occupied width, no continuous carrier. 315 MHz is the North American cousin of 433.92 MHz EU doorbells. Below stock Pluto's 325 MHz floor - needs AD9364 low-band mod or a front end that reaches 315 MHz; B210 sees it natively. Benign source: SkyLink-family (318 near here), older US doorbells, car-fob-adjacent PIR alarms. [needs-AD9364-mod]

signatures.name: 318 MHz OOK doorbell/remote event burst
signatures.mode: OOK/ASK PWM-coded frame, short burst per press/event
signatures.tscm: SkyLink's signature US frequency (TC-318 family doorbells, chimes, and driveway/entry sensors). Same idle-silent, burst-on-event behavior as the 315 MHz row but offset ~3 MHz. Distinct enough on the air to log separately. Below stock Pluto's 325 MHz floor. Benign SkyLink doorbell/driveway ecosystem is the dominant hit; the module type is also sold as a bare OOK transmitter. [needs-AD9364-mod]

signatures.name: 390 MHz OOK doorbell/gate event burst
signatures.mode: OOK/ASK coded frame, short burst
signatures.tscm: Less common US sub-GHz allocation used by some doorbells, gate/entry chimes, and Chamberlain/LiftMaster-adjacent accessories. Idle-silent, event-keyed burst. In reach of stock Pluto (above 325 MHz) and B210. Lower prior probability than 315/433 but worth a discrete row so a hit here is not misread as an unknown. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: 433.92 MHz OOK doorbell/driveway/PIR event burst
signatures.mode: OOK/ASK, PWM/Manchester coded frame (fixed-code or rolling), short burst per event, often repeated
signatures.tscm: The single most common sub-GHz event-burst signature worldwide. Wireless doorbell buttons, driveway/perimeter PIR sensors, and beam-break alarms overwhelmingly sit at 433.92 MHz. On the air: brief on-off keyed pulse train (~tens of ms, frequently sent 3-10x back to back for reliability), occupied bandwidth ~50-200 kHz, dead-silent between events. Squarely in stock Pluto and B210 range. This band is a HUGE benign false-positive pool (also TPMS, weather stations, remotes, garage fobs) - operator must correlate the burst to a physical action. TSCM exception: the same 433.92 MHz PIR/reed modules are the go-to for covert trip transmitters. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: 433.92 MHz FSK doorbell/alarm event burst
signatures.mode: 2-FSK/GFSK coded packet, short burst per event
signatures.tscm: Newer/better-quality doorbells and driveway alarms use 2-FSK instead of raw OOK for noise immunity - shows two closely spaced tones rather than pure on-off keying, but the same idle-silent, burst-on-event duty. Slightly wider occupied width than the OOK row. Distinguished from the OOK 433.92 row by modulation (spectral shape shows FSK deviation, not on/off gaps). Stock Pluto and B210 both reach it. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: 902-928 MHz FHSS doorbell/driveway event burst
signatures.mode: Frequency-hopping OOK/FSK coded packet, short burst per event, hops across the 900 MHz ISM band
signatures.tscm: Longer-range driveway alarms and premium doorbells (Guardline 915 MHz-family, Dakota Alert 900 MHz, many 1/4-mile+ perimeter sensors) use the 902-928 MHz ISM band, often frequency-hopping for range and interference immunity. On the air: brief packets appearing at different channels across the band per event, idle-silent between triggers. Wideband instantaneous survey needed to catch a hop set. In reach of stock Pluto and B210. Big benign pool (also LoRa, smart meters, cordless-adjacent gear). Guardline/Dakota driveway sensors are the archetype benign hit here. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: 902-928 MHz single-channel FSK driveway/PIR event burst
signatures.mode: Fixed-channel 2-FSK/GFSK coded packet, short burst per event
signatures.tscm: Non-hopping 900 MHz variant: a fixed narrow channel somewhere in 902-928 that keys a short FSK packet per motion/beam-break/press, then goes silent. Common in cheaper 900 MHz driveway sensors and PIR chimes that don't hop. Distinguished from the FHSS row by staying on one channel across repeated events. Stock Pluto and B210 reach it. Same benign-vs-covert-trip duality as the 433 rows. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

device_classes.device_class: Satellite messengers / trackers for covert off-grid comms and tracking (Iridium, Globalstar, Inmarsat L-band uplink emitters)
device_classes.summary: This class covers battery-powered devices that reach orbiting satellites directly on L-band mobile-satellite-service (MSS) uplinks, so they work with zero cellular/Wi-Fi infrastructure — which is exactly what makes them attractive for covert tracking and off-grid comms in a TSCM context. The three networks a stock PlutoSDR (325-3800 MHz) can actually see on their UPLINK are Iridium (1616-1626.5 MHz), Globalstar (1610-1626.5 MHz), and Inmarsat (1626.5-1660.5 MHz). All three uplinks are well inside stock-Pluto reach and inside B210 range. CRITICAL detection caveat: these are BURSTY, intermittent, low-duty-cycle emitters. A concealed asset tracker may transmit for a few tens of milliseconds once every 5-60 minutes (or only on movement), so a single spectrum snapshot will almost always miss it. Detection requires long dwell / persistent monitoring on the uplink bands, near-field antenna work, and correlation with a reporting schedule. Also critical for TSCM: you can only hear these when the hidden device actually transmits its uplink; the far more common satellite-band energy near you is legitimate GPS/GNSS (1176/1227/1575 MHz) and satphone/BGAN traffic, so band presence alone is not proof of a bug. The distinct on-air signatures are relatively few (network + link-type), but the product layer is large (dozens of trackers/messengers all share the same handful of signatures). VERIFIED against Iridium NEXT engineering statement / FCC filings, sigidwiki, Globalstar FCC report-and-order, Inmarsat/BGAN + IsatData Pro developer docs, and the IDP physical-layer manual. NOTE on one corrected error: Inmarsat IsatData Pro is OQPSK narrowband (not OFDM) and BGAN is single-carrier QPSK/16QAM TDM bearers (also not true OFDM) — this catalog previously mis-tagged them as OFDM; both are corrected to PSK here.

confirm_steps: Dwell, don't snapshot. Park the SDR on one uplink band (start 1616-1626.5 MHz for Iridium, 1610-1618.7 for Globalstar simplex, 1626.5-1660.5 for Inmarsat) and record continuously for a long window (30-60+ min). These devices burst rarely; a 1-second sweep will miss a tracker that reports every 10 minutes.

Look for the burst signature, not a steady carrier: Iridium = short narrow (~31.5 kHz) DEQPSK bursts on a 41.667 kHz raster; Globalstar = sub-second ~1.23 MHz noise-like/CDMA bumps, often repeated a few times per report; Inmarsat IsatData Pro = narrowband OQPSK bursts fixed toward one GEO direction, BGAN = a more sustained ~200 kHz bearer.

Near-field / proximity test: walk a directional or near-field antenna around the space. A concealed on-body or in-vehicle uplink emitter will spike sharply as you approach it, unlike distant legitimate satphone traffic. Suspected trackers are often on vehicles — sweep the car (wheel wells, bumpers, OBD port, seat frames) during a live report window.

Correlate timing: log burst timestamps and look for a fixed cadence (every N minutes) or motion-triggered pattern — telemetry trackers are scheduled/movement-driven, which distinguishes them from a human sending an occasional message.

Force a transmission to confirm: for a suspected two-way messenger you control/consented-to, trigger a check-in/SOS-test and watch the band light up; for a suspected covert simplex tracker, moving the vehicle/asset often triggers a report you can then catch.

Physical + power confirmation always required before calling it a bug: an L-band burst in-band is a lead, not proof. Find the device, confirm a sky-facing antenna (patch/helical), a battery or vehicle-power tap, and the network branding/FCC ID. Do not rely on RF alone.

Rule out GNSS: energy at 1176/1227/1575 MHz is GPS/GNSS RECEIVE, not a satellite uplink transmitter — do not report it as a satellite-tracker emission. Also rule out that a 1610-1626.5 spike is just a bystander's iPhone 14+ or a legitimate satphone.
false_positive_overlap: GNSS/GPS reception at 1176 (L5), 1227 (L2), 1575.42 (L1) MHz — this is the device RECEIVING, not a satellite uplink; it is the most common thing mistaken for satellite-tracker activity and must be excluded.

Legitimate Iridium/Globalstar satellite phones and inReach/ZOLEO carried by innocent users produce identical uplink signatures to a covert tracker — the signature cannot tell 'consented messenger' from 'hidden tracker'.

Ordinary iPhone 14+ and other smartphones with satellite SOS/messaging now emit in the Globalstar L-band uplink (1610-1626.5 MHz) — a spike here may just be a bystander's phone; the Band n53 S-band (2.4 GHz) side is downlink and not a device tell.
Legitimate fleet/marine/aviation telemetry (IsatData Pro, BGAN M2M, SmartOne) in commercial vehicles and vessels shares the exact class signature.

Other L-band services near the edges: aeronautical MSS, radio-astronomy protected sub-bands (e.g. 1610.6-1613.8 MHz), and general MSS traffic can put energy in 1610-1660 MHz that is not a covert device.
Iridium's rapidly-changing TDMA bursts can momentarily resemble other TDMA/frequency-hopping sources; without the 41.667 kHz raster and ~90 ms framing, do not assume Iridium.

LEO/GEO satellite DOWNLINKS and other space-to-earth signals in adjacent bands (e.g. Inmarsat/BGAN downlink 1525-1559 MHz, Iridium/Globalstar downlinks) are not device emissions and should not be flagged as a nearby bug.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Why this class matters for TSCM: satellite messengers/trackers are the go-to for covert tracking where a cellular GPS tracker would be jammed, out of coverage, or easily geofence-detected — they need no local network, work in wilderness/open-sky, and report straight to orbit. The classic threat is a magnetic or hardwired Globalstar SPOT Trace / SmartOne / Iridium-9603-based unit on a vehicle or in a bag, reporting a target's location to a third party. Two-way Iridium messengers (inReach/ZOLEO) can also be used for covert off-grid comms by a party who does not want to be on the cellular network. DETECTION REALITY: the hard part is not the frequency (all in easy Pluto reach) but the DUTY CYCLE — these emit for tens of milliseconds, minutes-to-hours apart, and only when they report or the user sends. Persistent/long-dwell monitoring and near-field antenna hunting during a live report are essential; a walk-through spectrum snapshot will miss them. Physical search of vehicles/assets during a known or forced report window is often more productive than pure RF. LEGAL/ETHICS: if a sweep turns up a satellite tracker the client did not place, treat it as potential evidence of unlawful tracking/stalking — preserve it in place where possible, photograph, document, and advise the client on law-enforcement involvement (per Matt's standing preference to surface suspected criminal exposure immediately). Chain of custody matters. HONEST LIMITS: band presence alone never confirms a covert device — satphones, legitimate fleet telemetry, and (increasingly) ordinary iPhone 14+ smartphones with satellite SOS all emit in these same L-band uplinks. Confirmation is physical, not spectral.

signatures.name: Iridium subscriber uplink burst (duplex L-band, 9601/9602/9603 SBD & voice)
signatures.mode: DEQPSK burst, 25 kBd, TDMA/FDMA on 41.667 kHz raster (240 channels); 31.5 kHz occupied; short TDMA bursts within a ~90 ms frame (each duplex slot ~8.28 ms); avg ~1.5 W in-slot
signatures.tscm: Narrow ~31.5 kHz DEQPSK burst that lands on the 240-channel raster (1616 + 0.041667*n MHz). Short TDMA bursts, not continuous. Rising/falling burst envelope on a ~90 ms cadence during an active session; a tracker check-in is a short flurry of these then silence. This is the single most common covert-tracker/messenger uplink (Garmin inReach, ZOLEO, Bivy, RockBLOCK all ride the 9603 module). [stock-Pluto-reachable (1616-1626 MHz well inside 325-3800 MHz); inside B210 range]

signatures.name: Iridium simplex messaging / ring-alert uplink (1626.0-1626.5 MHz access band)
signatures.mode: DEQPSK burst on the 12-frequency simplex access band (guard/messaging/ring-alert channels) spaced 41.667 kHz, 31.5 kHz occupied; ring-alert carrier at 1626.270833 MHz
signatures.tscm: Distinct from the main duplex raster: a dedicated 500 kHz block (1626.0-1626.5 MHz) carrying the 12 simplex channels, including the ring-alert channel at 1626.2708 MHz. Simplex/one-way telemetry bursts show up here rather than in the 1616-1626 duplex raster. Useful to separate a one-way beacon from a two-way messenger. Same DEQPSK/31.5 kHz/41.667 kHz-raster signature as the duplex band. [stock-Pluto-reachable; inside B210 range]

signatures.name: Globalstar simplex uplink (SPOT Trace / STX3 / ST100 one-way trackers)
signatures.mode: Proprietary CDMA / direct-sequence spread-spectrum burst, one-way; SPOT/STX simplex traffic sits in the ~1611.25-1618.75 MHz simplex-data portion; each report is a short repeated-burst sequence, very low duty
signatures.tscm: Wideband (~1.23 MHz) spread-spectrum energy — looks noise-like/CDMA rather than a narrow carrier, so it presents as a low, wide bump above the noise floor for a fraction of a second, then gone. Simplex trackers send the same packet multiple times for reliability, so you may catch a small cluster of short wideband bursts. No return link. This is the classic 'cheap hidden asset tracker' signature (SPOT Trace / SmartOne / STX3). [stock-Pluto-reachable (1610-1618.7 MHz), but 1.23 MHz occupied bandwidth is at/near the practical instantaneous-bandwidth edge for a clean Pluto capture — use an adequate sample rate to grab the whole channel or you will only see a slice]

signatures.name: Globalstar duplex uplink (satphone / SPOT X two-way messenger / iPhone Emergency SOS)
signatures.mode: Proprietary CDMA (~1.23 MHz channels), two-way; near-continuous during an active call/session, power-controlled
signatures.tscm: Wider, more sustained ~1.23 MHz CDMA energy during an active two-way session (voice/data), versus the sub-second bursts of the simplex tracker. Overlaps the Iridium band in the 1616-1626.5 region but is spread-spectrum/CDMA (noise-like, ~1.23 MHz wide) rather than Iridium's narrow 31.5 kHz DEQPSK bursts on a 41.667 kHz raster — the width and lack of that raster distinguishes them. Apple iPhone 14+ Emergency SOS / Messages-via-satellite uplink also lands in this Globalstar L-band uplink (the Band n53 S-band 2483.5-2495 MHz is the DOWNLINK only, so it is NOT a device-emission tell). [stock-Pluto-reachable on the L-band uplink; the S-band (2483.5-2495 MHz) side is downlink-from-satellite, not the device, so it is not a device emission]

signatures.name: Inmarsat IsatData Pro / M2M terminal uplink (data terminals, covert asset telemetry)
signatures.mode: IsatData Pro: OQPSK narrowband bursts (from-mobile subchannels ~300-3000 sym/s, tens of kHz occupied, NOT OFDM) to GEO Inmarsat-4/6; from-mobile messages up to ~6.4 KB; scheduled/event-driven bursty transmit; terminal points at a fixed GEO satellite
signatures.tscm: Sits ABOVE the Iridium/Globalstar bands (1626.5-1660.5 MHz). Because the satellite is geostationary, the terminal beam/orientation is fixed (not sweeping like LEO), and messaging is scheduled/event-driven bursts. Narrowband OQPSK carrier (tens of kHz), not a wide OFDM bearer — correction from an earlier mislabel. IsatData Pro (formerly SkyWave, now ORBCOMM IDP; IDP-680/690-class modules) is a common OEM module for hidden fleet/asset telemetry. [stock-Pluto-reachable (1626.5-1660.5 MHz inside 325-3800 MHz); inside B210 range]

signatures.name: Inmarsat BGAN broadband / IsatPhone voice uplink (portable terminals & satphones)
signatures.mode: BGAN: single-carrier QPSK/16QAM TDM bearers (~200 kHz wide, NOT OFDM), near-continuous during an active IP/voice session; IsatPhone: narrower voice-rate bursts; power-controlled to GEO
signatures.tscm: During an active BGAN data session the uplink is a more sustained ~200 kHz single-carrier bearer (vs. IsatData Pro's short narrowband scheduled bursts), fixed toward a GEO satellite. IsatPhone voice is narrower and more intermittent. Distinguishes a live broadband/voice link (someone actively communicating) from a fire-and-forget telemetry burst in the same 1626.5-1660.5 MHz band. [stock-Pluto-reachable; inside B210 range]

device_classes.device_class: cordless_phone_and_intercom_base_stations
device_classes.summary: Cordless telephone / wireless-headset / intercom / nurse-call base-and-handset RF pairs OUTSIDE the DECT (1.92-1.93 GHz) band. These are legitimate consumer/commercial devices, but a covert audio leak (a live handset left off-hook, a modified base, or a "baby-monitor"-style repurposed cordless set) presents on these same signatures, so a TSCM sweep must cover every legacy cordless allocation, not just DECT. Six distinct on-air signatures span four bands: legacy VHF analog FM (43-50 MHz), 900 MHz analog FM, 900 MHz digital spread-spectrum (DSS/FHSS), 2.4 GHz analog FM, 2.4 GHz digital spread-spectrum, and 5.8 GHz digital spread-spectrum. Reach caveats are significant: the 43-50 MHz VHF pair is far below a stock Pluto's 325 MHz floor (needs a VHF-capable front end / downconverter or an RF Explorer / RSP-class SDR); 5.8 GHz is above a stock Pluto's 3.8 GHz ceiling but inside a B210's 6 GHz range. The 900 MHz and 2.4 GHz signatures are fully in stock-Pluto reach. Note the duplex nature: base and handset transmit on separated frequencies within the band, so a sweep should expect a paired emission, not a single carrier.

900 MHz analog wireless headset base stations (call-center/office)
2.4 GHz wireless headset systems
5.8 GHz dual-band cordless handset (900/2.4 GHz base pairing)
wireless intercom base stations (900 MHz FHSS home/office intercom)
2.4 GHz wireless intercom / room-to-room intercom bases
nurse-call wireless handset/pendant base stations (facility ISM-band)

confirm_steps: Demodulate the suspect carrier as narrowband FM: legacy 43-50 MHz and 900/2.4 GHz analog cordless yield intelligible (or voice-inverted) speech — clear audio confirms an analog voice link.

Look for the DUPLEX PAIR: analog cordless transmits base and handset on separated frequencies. Confirm a second matching carrier in the paired sub-band (e.g. 43-47 MHz base + 48.76-49.99 MHz handset; or a base/handset offset within 902-928).

On a waterfall, classify the modulation: single stationary FM carrier = analog; ~1 MHz bursts hopping across the band = FHSS; wide flat ~5-80 MHz spread = DSSS/wideband. This separates the analog vs digital cordless signatures.

Check the duty cycle against a phone call: a cordless link stays up continuously for the call duration, unlike Bluetooth's short bursty pairing traffic or Wi-Fi's packet bursts — helps disambiguate 2.4/5.8 GHz FHSS cordless from Bluetooth/Wi-Fi.
For 43-50 MHz: use a VHF-capable receiver (RTL-SDR in direct-sampling mode, RSP1A, Airspy HF+, or RF Explorer) — a stock or modded Pluto cannot tune this band.
For 5.8 GHz: use the B210 (or a >6 GHz analyzer / RF Explorer 6G) — a stock Pluto tops out at 3.8 GHz and cannot see it.

Correlate with a physical walk-down: locate the base station (wall-powered, has an antenna) and confirm the emission tracks lifting/replacing a handset. A carrier that persists with all known phones on-hook is the real red flag (possible off-hook covert audio tap or modified base).
device_classes.tscm_notes: These are overwhelmingly legitimate consumer/office devices — expect false positives. The TSCM value is threefold: (1) an attacker can leave a handset off-hook or wire a hidden mic to a cordless base to exfiltrate room audio on a signature the client assumes is 'just the house phone'; (2) analog 43-50 MHz and analog 900/2.4 GHz links are UNENCRYPTED and trivially monitored from outside the premises with a scanner — a genuine eavesdropping exposure even with no bug planted; (3) 'baby-monitor'-style repurposed cordless/intercom hardware presents on these exact signatures. Do NOT treat a 2.4/5.8 GHz FHSS hit as automatically a cordless phone — overlap with Bluetooth, Wi-Fi, ZigBee, wireless HID and 2.4 GHz spy-cam control channels is heavy; confirm by modulation, duty cycle, and physical source. Reach honesty for the report: the 43-50 MHz VHF signature is OUT of stock-Pluto and AD9364-modded reach entirely (needs VHF gear); the 5.8 GHz signature is ABOVE stock-Pluto's 3.8 GHz ceiling but WITHIN B210's 6 GHz range. The 900 MHz and 2.4 GHz signatures are fully in stock-Pluto reach. Flag to the client that any surviving analog cordless phone is an open-audio liability independent of whether a bug is found.

signatures.name: Legacy VHF analog cordless phone (43-50 MHz FM base/handset pair)
signatures.mode: Analog narrowband FM voice, duplex pair: base transmits ~43.72-46.97 MHz, handset transmits ~48.76-49.99 MHz. 10 channels (1984) expanded to 25 (1995). No spread spectrum, no scrambling beyond occasional voice inversion.
signatures.tscm: A clear-audio FM carrier ~30 kHz wide that appears in TWO places at once: one in the 43-47 MHz base range and its mate in the 48.76-49.99 MHz handset range. Continuous while off-hook; demodulating either half yields intelligible speech (voice-inversion scrambling sometimes present). Sits alongside 49 MHz baby monitors, walkie-talkies and RC toys. [OUT OF stock-Pluto range (325-3800 MHz) by an order of magnitude; below AD9364 floor even modded. Requires a VHF-capable front end, an HF/VHF upconverter+SDR (RTL-SDR direct-sample / RSP1A / Airspy HF+), or an RF Explorer. B210 also cannot reach this (70 MHz floor).]

signatures.name: 900 MHz analog FM cordless phone (902-928 MHz FM pair)
signatures.mode: Analog FM voice in the 902-928 MHz ISM band, duplex base/handset pair, ~30 kHz per channel, up to ~30 channels. Earliest 900 MHz generation; clear or voice-inverted audio.
signatures.tscm: Narrow ~25-30 kHz FM carrier that demodulates directly to speech, appearing as a base/handset frequency pair within 902-928. Continuous while in use. Overlaps heavily with legitimate 900 MHz ISM traffic: wireless headsets, older baby monitors, RC links, some LoRa/metering — analog voice on demod distinguishes it. [IN stock-Pluto range (325-3800 MHz) and in B210 range.]

signatures.name: 900 MHz digital spread-spectrum cordless (DSS / FHSS, 902-928 MHz)
signatures.mode: Digital spread-spectrum cordless (DSS from ~1995, and frequency-hopping FHSS variants). Panasonic/Uniden 'digital spread spectrum' and dual-band 900 MHz+5.8 GHz sets. Hops/spreads across the 902-928 band; per-hop channel ~1 MHz.
signatures.tscm: Energy that hops or spreads across the full 902-928 band rather than a single stationary carrier; no intelligible audio on simple FM demod. On a waterfall it shows scattered ~1 MHz bursts (FHSS) or a wider spread hump (DSS). Distinguishable from analog 900 MHz by absence of a fixed demodulatable voice carrier. False-positive overlap with 900 MHz FHSS telemetry/ISM devices. [IN stock-Pluto range and B210 range. Capturing the full hop set benefits from >=20 MHz instantaneous bandwidth (B210) or wideband sweep; a narrow-BW capture will only catch fragments.]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz analog FM cordless phone (2400-2483.5 MHz analog voice)
signatures.mode: Analog / wideband-FM cordless voice in the 2.4 GHz ISM band (pre-digital and hybrid 2.4 GHz handsets). Cordless-phone channels are notably wide (5-10 MHz) and can transmit at up to ~30 dBm.
signatures.tscm: A wide (5-10 MHz) relatively continuous carrier parked somewhere in 2400-2483.5, much wider and higher-power than a 1 MHz Bluetooth hop. Demodulates to voice. Strong interferer to Wi-Fi/ZigBee on the same channel. Distinguish from Wi-Fi (bursty OFDM, 20 MHz) and from Bluetooth (1 MHz FHSS) by its continuous wideband-FM character. [IN stock-Pluto range (325-3800 MHz). Full ~80 MHz band scan exceeds Pluto's ~20 MHz instantaneous BW, so sweep in steps; B210 similar (61.44 MHz max). Individual 5-10 MHz channel fits within one capture.]

signatures.name: 2.4 GHz digital spread-spectrum cordless (DSSS / FHSS, 2400-2483.5 MHz)
signatures.mode: Digital spread-spectrum 2.4 GHz cordless: FHSS (band split into ~75 x 1 MHz hop channels) or DSSS (~82 MHz spread, ~11 overlapping channels). Includes 2.4 GHz DECT-variant handsets (~552 kbps). Panasonic KX-TG FHSS GigaRange class.
signatures.tscm: Frequency-hopping ~1 MHz bursts marching across 2400-2483.5 (FHSS) or a wide DSSS spread; no clear-audio demod. Looks Bluetooth-like on a waterfall but cordless hops are often higher power and follow a phone-call duty cycle (long continuous call vs. Bluetooth's bursty profile). Heavy false-positive overlap with Bluetooth/BLE, Wi-Fi, ZigBee, wireless mice/keyboards, and 2.4 GHz spy-cam control channels. [IN stock-Pluto and B210 range. Characterizing the hop set wants wide instantaneous BW (B210 up to 61.44 MHz) or a fast sweep; Pluto's ~20 MHz window catches a subset per dwell.]

signatures.name: 5.8 GHz digital spread-spectrum cordless (5725-5875 MHz)
signatures.mode: Digital spread-spectrum cordless voice in the 5.8 GHz ISM band (5.8 GHz handset link, often paired with a 900 MHz or 2.4 GHz base->handset direction in dual-band sets). FHSS/DSSS, digital voice, no clear-audio demod.
signatures.tscm: Hopping/spread digital energy in 5725-5875 following a call duty cycle. No intelligible FM audio. Distinguish from 5 GHz Wi-Fi (wider 20/40/80 MHz OFDM bursts, higher up in U-NII bands) by narrower hop structure and phone-call timing. Overlaps with 5.8 GHz FPV/analog-video downlinks and 5 GHz Wi-Fi. [ABOVE stock-Pluto ceiling (3800 MHz) and above even the AD9364-modded reach; NOT reachable by a stock or modded Pluto. IN B210 range (70 MHz-6 GHz) — use the B210 (or an RF Explorer 6G / other >6 GHz-capable analyzer) for this signature.]

device_classes.device_class: Non-camera Wi-Fi gadget bugs (audio-only Wi-Fi bugs, spy-pen / USB-stick Wi-Fi recorders, smart-plug / charger / adapter-disguised Wi-Fi audio recorders)
device_classes.summary: This class covers covert devices that carry a microphone (no camera) and exfiltrate audio over 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi 802.11b/g/n — live-listen streams and/or store-and-upload recorders. Physically they hide in pens, USB flash drives, USB wall chargers, mains adapters, extension cords, power banks, and fake "smart plugs." CRITICAL for a TSCM matcher: at the RF/PHY layer these are ORDINARY Wi-Fi devices. An SDR sees 802.11 OFDM/DSSS bursts on standard 2.4 GHz channels — the EXACT same air signature as a Wi-Fi spy cam, a real smart plug, a phone, or a laptop. You CANNOT distinguish an audio bug from a camera or a legitimate IoT device by band/bandwidth/modulation alone. The only physical-layer tells are behavioral: (1) TRAFFIC VOLUME — voice is ~16-256 kbps (often 8-128 kbps ADPCM/AAC/Opus), roughly 100x-1000x lower than the 1-6 Mbps a streaming camera pushes, so the device's uplink airtime/duty is low and bursty rather than a fat continuous stream; (2) DUTY PATTERN — voice-activated (VOX) recorders are silent for long stretches then burst when triggered, and store-and-forward units may go RF-silent for hours then dump a batch; (3) SETUP-MODE BEACON — nearly all briefly run a SoftAP (own SSID/beacon at ~100 ms interval) during provisioning, and factory SSIDs are a strong fingerprint. Because the discriminator is packet-rate and MAC-layer metadata, a stock Pluto/B210 doing raw IQ energy detection can locate and confirm 'a 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi emitter is here' but CANNOT by itself say audio-vs-video-vs-legit — that requires a Wi-Fi NIC in monitor mode (Kismet), a per-client airtime/throughput view, or de-authing suspects and watching which device's traffic profile matches voice. All 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi channels (2412-2472 MHz, ch 1-13, plus ch14 2484 in JP) fall inside the stock Pluto AD9364 325-3800 MHz range and inside B210 range, so tuning reach is fine; the limitation is discrimination AND instantaneous capture bandwidth (a single 20 MHz Wi-Fi channel already sits at the Pluto's practical ~20 MHz RX ceiling, and 40 MHz HT40 exceeds it), not center-frequency coverage.

confirm_steps: Do NOT try to ID audio-vs-camera from the SDR spectrum — they are identical 802.11 signatures. Instead put a Wi-Fi NIC in monitor mode (Kismet / airodump-ng) and enumerate every 2.4 GHz client + AP: capture BSSID/MAC OUI, SSID, associated channel, and especially per-client AIRTIME/THROUGHPUT.

Sort clients by uplink throughput. A camera sustains Mbps; an audio bug trickles tens-to-low-hundreds of kbps in short bursts. Flag any low-rate, always-present client that maps to no known device (phone/laptop/TV/thermostat).

Cross-check MAC OUI against the device vendor. ESP32/Espressif OUIs, generic module vendors, or an OUI that matches no furniture in the room are suspicious. Note: many bugs randomize/spoof MAC — absence of a hit is not clearance.

Force SoftAP mode: power-cycle or factory-reset a suspect gadget (unplug the mystery 'charger'/'plug'/pen and re-power) and watch for a new device-hosted SSID beaconing (~100 ms interval, factory-default or gibberish SSID, 192.168.4.1 config page). That AP appearing from an object with no business hosting a network is near-confirmation.

Physical + power correlation: audio bugs need continuous power in the target room. Inventory every always-powered object — USB chargers, wall warts, 'smart' plugs, power strips, pens left on a desk. Open/weigh/X-ray suspects; a real 5V charger has no microSD slot, no extra PCB, no mic port.

VOX test: introduce controlled sound (talk / play audio) in the room and watch monitor-mode capture for a client that begins/increases transmitting in time with the sound. A voice-activated bug will key up on audio — a legit smart plug will not.
De-auth isolation (where lawful/authorized): send a targeted deauth to a suspect client and confirm the object drops offline / re-enters SoftAP, physically tying the MAC to the object.

Rule out the cellular-fallback case: if the room 'feels bugged' but Wi-Fi is clean, sweep LTE uplink bands with the SDR and near-field probe suspect objects — a SIM-equipped recorder leaves NO 2.4 GHz trace while on 4G.

Use the SDR (Pluto/B210) for what it's good at here: near-field DF / proximity — walk the antenna to localize which object radiates the 2.4 GHz energy, then hand off to the Wi-Fi NIC + physical search for ID.
false_positive_overlap: Legitimate Wi-Fi security cameras / video doorbells / baby monitors — SAME 2.4 GHz 802.11 signature; only throughput separates them (higher for video). SDR cannot tell them apart from an audio bug.

Real smart plugs, smart bulbs, smart switches (TP-Link Kasa, Wemo, Tuya, Shelly, Sonoff) — these are LOW-throughput 2.4 GHz clients too, exactly like an audio bug's traffic profile. High false-positive risk: a bug disguised as a smart plug looks identical to a real smart plug on the air.
Voice assistants (Echo, Google Nest, Sonos), smart thermostats, smart locks, IoT sensors — low-rate 2.4 GHz clients that beacon/poll intermittently, mimicking a VOX bug's bursty pattern.
Phones, laptops, tablets, smart TVs, printers — ubiquitous 2.4 GHz OFDM emitters that dominate the band and bury a low-rate bug in the noise floor of normal traffic.
BLE: fitness trackers, earbuds, tags (AirTag/Tile), keyboards/mice — the GFSK advertising signature is indistinguishable from a bug's BLE provisioning beacon.
Neighbor / building Wi-Fi bleeding through walls — 2.4 GHz clients you can hear but that are not in the target space; wastes time if not spatially gated.
Microwave ovens, 2.4 GHz cordless phones, Zigbee/Thread hubs, wireless mouse dongles — non-Wi-Fi 2.4 GHz emitters that raise the band's energy floor and can trip a naive IQ energy detector.
Cellular fallback INVERSE case: a SIM-equipped bug produces NO 2.4 GHz signal at all, so a clean Wi-Fi sweep is a false NEGATIVE, not a clearance.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Bottom line for the matcher UI: for this class, the SDR match ('2.4 GHz 802.11 emitter present') is necessary but NOT sufficient — never let the app report 'audio bug found' from spectrum alone. The RF layer of an audio-only Wi-Fi bug is byte-for-byte the same as a Wi-Fi camera and the same as a legitimate smart plug/IoT device. Discrimination lives one layer up (MAC-layer metadata + per-client throughput + duty behavior), which needs a Wi-Fi NIC in monitor mode, not the Pluto. Also be honest about the Pluto's instantaneous bandwidth: a single 20 MHz Wi-Fi channel already sits at the Pluto's practical ~20 MHz RX ceiling and 40 MHz HT40 exceeds it, so the Pluto is a locate/energy-detect tool here, not a channel-capture/demod tool — a B210 (~56 MHz) captures a full channel but still cannot decode 802.11 without a proper NIC/stack. Frame the SDR's job honestly: (a) confirm/locate 2.4 GHz energy near a suspect object (near-field DF), (b) catch the SoftAP setup beacon, (c) sweep LTE uplinks for the cellular-fallback evasion case. Do the actual audio-vs-video-vs-legit call with Kismet/airodump throughput analysis, MAC/OUI enumeration, SoftAP forcing, VOX stimulus testing, and physical inspection of every always-powered object. The three highest-yield moves in practice: (1) inventory and open every powered gadget in the room — these bugs LIVE in chargers/plugs/pens/power strips because they need mains/USB power; (2) force SoftAP by power-cycling suspects and read the beaconed SSID; (3) run a VOX stimulus test and watch which client keys up. Assume MAC randomization/spoofing so a clean OUI list is not clearance, and remember a SIM-equipped unit gives a false-negative on any Wi-Fi-only sweep.

signatures.name: 802.11b DSSS/CCK uplink — 2.4 GHz audio exfil (legacy 1-11 Mbps)
signatures.mode: 802.11b DSSS/CCK, ~22 MHz occupied, on ch1/6/11 centers (2412/2437/2462)
signatures.tscm: Legacy DSSS/CCK spectral shape (flat-topped ~22 MHz with sinc side-lobes) rather than the flatter OFDM block of g/n — note this is DSSS, NOT OFDM, so it will not show the OFDM subcarrier structure of the g/n entries. Cheap ESP32/older modules fall back to 11b when link is weak. For an AUDIO bug the uplink airtime is TINY — short CCK bursts carrying 16-256 kbps of voice, so you see brief packets + ACKs, not a sustained fat stream. Long VOX gaps between bursts are the audio tell vs a camera's near-continuous fill. [stock-Pluto-reachable (2.4 GHz well inside 325-3800 MHz); B210 in range. 22 MHz > Pluto's ~20 MHz practical RX BW so you cannot capture the full channel in one shot — step/sweep or accept partial capture; energy detection still works. B210 (up to ~56 MHz) captures the full 22 MHz.]

signatures.name: 802.11g/n OFDM 20 MHz uplink — 2.4 GHz audio exfil (station mode, most common)
signatures.tscm: THE dominant signature — device joined the premises Wi-Fi as a station and uplinks voice. Flat ~20 MHz OFDM block, bursty. Distinguishing from a Wi-Fi CAMERA is behavioral not spectral: audio = low aggregate throughput (tens-to-low-hundreds of kbps), short packets, low airtime %, and often VOX gaps; camera = high sustained throughput (Mbps), long airtime %. Identical center freq, identical modulation, identical channel to every other Wi-Fi client — you MUST use per-client airtime/throughput (monitor-mode NIC) to separate them; raw IQ alone can't. [stock-Pluto-reachable; B210 in range. A 20 MHz channel sits right at the Pluto's practical RX BW ceiling — fine for energy detection/localization, tight-to-impractical for full capture, and you will NOT be demodulating Wi-Fi on a Pluto anyway (use a NIC for that). B210 captures the full 20 MHz comfortably.]

signatures.name: 802.11 SoftAP provisioning beacon — device's own AP during setup
signatures.mode: 802.11 beacon frames ~100 ms interval from device-hosted SoftAP (e.g. SSID like WiCardCamMic, factory default), open or WPA2
signatures.tscm: During initial pairing (and after any Wi-Fi drop / factory reset) the bug hosts its OWN access point so the installer's phone can reach its 192.168.4.1 config page. Regular ~100 ms beacon cadence + a factory-default/gibberish SSID broadcasting in a room with no legitimate AP is a HIGH-VALUE tell. A Wi-Fi scanner (phone/Kismet) reading the SSID/MAC OUI is far more diagnostic here than IQ. Catch it during install or by power-cycling a suspected device to force it back into AP mode. [stock-Pluto-reachable for periodic-beacon energy detection; B210 in range. SSID/OUI decode needs a Wi-Fi NIC, not the SDR — the SDR sees only the ~100 ms beacon energy pulses, not the frame contents.]

signatures.name: 802.11n HT40 40 MHz uplink — 2.4 GHz (bonded channel, less common on tiny bugs)
signatures.mode: 802.11n HT40 OFDM, 40 MHz bonded, center ~2422 or ~2452
signatures.tscm: Some higher-end WiFi audio recorders (and the router they associate to) use 40 MHz bonded channels. Wide ~40 MHz OFDM block spanning most of the 2.4 GHz band. For a pure audio bug this is overkill and uncommon (voice needs no bandwidth) but appears when the host AP forces HT40. Same discrimination problem: modulation identical to any n-device; audio identified only by its low throughput within the fat channel. [stock-Pluto-reachable by tuning, but 40 MHz FAR exceeds Pluto's ~20 MHz practical RX BW — you can only see a slice at a time and must sweep. B210 (up to ~56 MHz) can capture the full 40 MHz channel in one shot.]

signatures.name: BLE provisioning / companion beacon — 2.4 GHz GFSK (setup-assist on some units)
signatures.mode: Bluetooth LE GFSK advertising on ch37/38/39 (2402/2426/2480), 1-2 MHz, periodic advertising interval
signatures.tscm: Some ESP32-based and dual-radio recorders expose a BLE advertiser for phone-app provisioning alongside Wi-Fi. Narrow ~1-2 MHz GFSK bursts appearing on the three FIXED advertising channels (2402/2426/2480) at a regular adv interval — note BLE ADVERTISING does not frequency-hop across the band; only a subsequently-established BLE data CONNECTION does adaptive hopping (which is why fhss is the closest enum bucket for the device's overall BLE behavior). This is a SECONDARY signature — its presence next to a low-throughput 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi client strengthens the 'IoT gadget' hypothesis. Not itself proof of a bug (millions of legit BLE devices), but a paired BLE+low-rate-WiFi emitter in a sensitive location warrants physical inspection. [stock-Pluto-reachable (2.402-2.480 GHz in range); B210 in range. Pluto's ~20 MHz window cannot span all three adv channels (spread across ~78 MHz) at once — you watch one adv channel or step across them for burst detection. Decode/hop-follow needs dedicated BLE tooling (Ubertooth/nRF sniffer), not the SDR.]

signatures.name: 4G/LTE fallback uplink — hybrid Wi-Fi+cellular recorders (SIM-equipped)
signatures.mode: LTE SC-FDMA uplink, 1.4-20 MHz RB allocation, US bands B2/B4/B5/B12/B13/B66/B71 etc.
signatures.tscm: A minority of 'Wi-Fi' audio recorders are actually dual-mode: they prefer Wi-Fi but carry a nano-SIM and fall back to 4G so they keep exfiltrating with NO local network and NO physical access needed. When on cellular there is ZERO 2.4 GHz signature — you must sweep LTE uplink bands. Bursty SC-FDMA uplink keyed near the device while the far end is a tower. This is the dangerous evasion case: a Wi-Fi sweep alone misses it entirely. [stock-Pluto-reachable across essentially all US LTE uplinks — B71 uplink is 663-698 MHz and B12/B13 ~700 MHz, all inside 325-3800 MHz; the 617 MHz figure here is the B71 downlink floor, uplinks stay above ~663 MHz so tuning is fine. B210 in range. Discriminating a bug's LTE uplink from every phone in the building is extremely hard — this is a directional/near-field-probe + physical-search problem, not a spectral-ID problem.]

device_classes.device_class: Bluetooth Classic (BR/EDR) + Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) audio eavesdropping devices: covert earpieces, disguised earbuds/headphones with hidden recorders, BLE/BT body-worn mics, and LE Audio / Auracast broadcast bugs operating in the 2.4 GHz ISM band
device_classes.summary: This class covers any audio-surveillance device whose over-the-air footprint is a Bluetooth radio: covert in-ear earpieces, "normal-looking" earbuds/headphones with a concealed recorder or live mic, BT/BLE lav mics, and newer LE Audio / Auracast broadcast bugs. On the air they are NOT one signature. Bluetooth splits into two distinct radios - Classic BR/EDR and LE - and each has multiple sub-signatures that differ in bandwidth, modulation, channel plan, and duty. Every signature lives entirely inside 2400-2483.5 MHz. REACH NOTE: 2.4 GHz is WITHIN a stock ADALM-Pluto's 325-3800 MHz tuning range, so all rows here are reachable by stock Pluto AND B210 - the caveat for this band is the opposite of the low-band problem: at 61.44 MSPS max a B210 (56 MHz usable) or Pluto (~20 MHz stable, up to ~56 MHz hacked, USB-throughput dependent) CANNOT see the whole 83.5 MHz ISM band in one shot, so FHSS hoppers must be caught by fast sweeping or energy-detection, not a single wideband capture. Classic BT hops 1600 times/sec across 79 channels (1 MHz raster) and BLE hops across 37 data channels (2 MHz raster); you will almost never decode them with a Pluto/B210 - you detect the ENERGY SIGNATURE (hop pattern, channel raster, burst timing), not the payload. The honest TSCM reality: 2.4 GHz is the single most crowded band on earth (Wi-Fi, every BT device, Zigbee/Thread, microwave ovens, wireless mice/keyboards), so false-positive overlap is extreme and near-total. A BT audio signature alone is almost never actionable - it must be correlated with proximity, timing (only transmits when the target is present/talking), and physical inspection. This is a detection/anomaly-hunting layer, not a clean fingerprint layer.

Bluetooth car-kit / visor speakerphones left as room bugs (dual-use form-factor)
Hidden-mic USB wall chargers / power banks with BT module (form-factor example)

Airoha-chipset consumer earbuds/headsets exploitable for eavesdropping per 2025 research (CVE-2025-20700/20701/20702; affected brands include Bose, Sony, Marshall, Jabra, JBL, JLab, Beyerdynamic, Teufel, EarisMax, MoerLabs) - dual-use, firmware/BT-proximity attack vector
confirm_steps: Do NOT rely on a single spectrum hit. 2.4 GHz is saturated - treat any BT/BLE energy as a lead, not a finding, until correlated with location and timing.

Park a Pluto/B210 on BLE advertising channel 2402, 2426, or 2480 MHz and watch for the fixed-frequency A-B-C advertising triplets; enumerate every advertiser and reconcile against known devices (phones, laptops, wearables, TVs, mice/keyboards).

Also watch for extended/periodic advertising: a fixed-interval burst on a DATA channel with no connection or scan-response is the connectionless (Auracast/PAwR) tell that legacy pairing-detection misses.

Cross-check with a phone BLE scanner app (nRF Connect, LightBlue) and a Wi-Fi/BT analyzer to get MAC/name/RSSI; walk the RSSI up to physically localize the strongest unexplained emitter (proximity localization beats spectral ID here).

Use a purpose-built BT monitor (Ubertooth One, nRF52840 sniffer running Sniffle, or a commercial BT/Wi-Fi TSCM analyzer) to follow the hop and read advertising data / device names - a stock Pluto/B210 generally cannot demodulate BT payload.

Time-correlate: silence/clear the room and watch whether a suspect emitter's duty changes when someone speaks or is present. A bug that only transmits when the target is there is the anomaly; an always-on beacon is usually a benign device.

For Auracast/LE Audio suspicion, scan for broadcast sources with an Auracast assistant app or LE Audio-capable scanner and confirm any unexpected broadcaster - a room audio broadcast with no obvious source device is a red flag.

Physically inspect and RF-localize: NLJD (non-linear junction detector) to find the electronics regardless of whether it is transmitting, plus visual/physical search of earbuds, chargers, speakers, pens, glasses left in the space.
Baseline the environment on a clean day and diff: catalog every recurring BT/BLE emitter so a NEW or session-correlated emitter stands out on the next sweep.

For brand-name earbuds/headsets left in a sensitive space, treat as a live threat even if idle: the 2025 Airoha class shows a benign-looking headset can be turned into an HFP mic-listen bug by a nearby attacker - remove or power down rather than trusting RF quiet.
false_positive_overlap: Near-total: every smartphone, laptop, tablet, and smartwatch in and near the space emits BLE advertising on 2402/2426/2480 MHz constantly.
Wireless mice, keyboards, trackpads, presenters, and game controllers (many use BLE or proprietary 2.4 GHz GFSK that looks nearly identical).
All legitimate BT headphones/earbuds/speakers/car kits - the SAME signature as a covert earbud; RF alone cannot separate a spy earbud from a real one.
BLE beacons/tags: Apple AirTags, Tile, Chipolo, retail/proximity beacons, asset trackers - heavy advertising-channel traffic.
Fitness bands, hearing aids (increasingly LE Audio/Auracast), medical BLE devices, glucose monitors - legitimate periodic BLE audio/telemetry.
Wi-Fi (802.11b/g/n/ax) on the same 2400-2483.5 MHz band produces wide bursts that mask and collide with narrow BT bursts and complicate energy detection.
Zigbee / Thread / 802.15.4 smart-home devices, and microwave ovens (broadband 2.45 GHz noise) - non-BT emitters that clutter the same waterfall.
Auracast public/retail broadcasts (transit hubs, gyms, TVs, silent-disco systems) are a growing legitimate source that mimics a broadcast bug's connectionless cadence.
Extended/periodic advertising is increasingly used by benign devices (audio sharing, Find-My networks), so a connectionless periodic train is not by itself malicious.
A Pluto/B210 cannot read device identity, so distinguishing malicious from benign is done by localization/timing/inspection, NOT by the RF signature itself.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Treat this whole class as a DETECTION/ANOMALY layer, never a clean-fingerprint layer. The RF signature of a covert Bluetooth earbud is byte-for-byte the same as a legitimate one - you are hunting an out-of-place emitter, not a unique waveform. Practical Pluto/B210 workflow: (1) camp on the three BLE advertising channels (2402/2426/2480 MHz) to enumerate advertisers, since those are fixed and catchable; (2) additionally watch data channels for fixed-interval periodic/extended advertising trains (the connectionless Auracast/PAwR tell that pairing-detection misses); (3) accept that connected/hopping Classic and BLE traffic will mostly be seen as energy patterns (burst width, channel raster, periodicity), not decoded; (4) confirm with a real BT sniffer (Ubertooth/nRF52840+Sniffle) for device names/MACs, and with proximity RSSI-walking plus NLJD and physical search for localization. RF fundamentals to keep straight: Classic uses a 1 MHz channel raster (79 ch) and BLE a 2 MHz raster (3 adv + 37 data); EDR 2/3 Mbps keep the SAME 1 MHz occupied bandwidth as BR (rate comes from bits/symbol, not more spectrum), so only LE2M/LE Audio bursts show the visibly wider ~2 MHz footprint. Modern watch-items: LE Audio 2M-PHY bugs (~2 MHz-wide bursts) and Auracast BROADCAST bugs (connectionless, no pairing handshake, near-continuous ISO cadence) - Auracast in particular defeats old 'detect the pairing' logic and should be an explicit hunt step. Also relevant: 2025 Airoha-chipset research (CVE-2025-20700/20701/20702, ~29 devices across Bose, Sony, Marshall, Jabra, JBL, JLab, Beyerdynamic, Teufel, EarisMax, MoerLabs) showed mainstream earbuds/headsets can be turned into eavesdropping devices by a nearby attacker via BT link-key extraction + HFP mic-listen, requiring only ~10 m proximity - so a benign-looking brand-name earbud left in a sensitive room is a legitimate threat vector, not just purpose-built spy gear. Legal/handling note for the client report: identifying a specific person's device by MAC/name during a sweep can raise privacy issues - keep discovered identifiers internal and report findings as 'unexplained emitter localized to X location,' not as named individuals, unless counsel directs otherwise.

signatures.name: Bluetooth Classic BR (Basic Rate, GFSK) - hop energy + single-slot burst
signatures.mode: BR/EDR baseband, 1 Mbit/s GFSK, adaptive frequency hopping 1600 hops/s over 79 channels (2402-2480 MHz, 1 MHz raster)
signatures.tscm: ~1 MHz-wide GFSK bursts appearing at pseudo-random 1 MHz-raster carriers, 625 us slot timing, up to 1600 hops/sec. Access-code/header always GFSK even on EDR links. On a spectrogram: a dense scatter of narrow bursts filling the 2402-2480 band with a visible 1 MHz channel grid and AFH channel-avoidance notches where Wi-Fi sits. This is the connection-mode carrier for legacy HFP/HSP voice bugs and covert earpieces. [stock-Pluto-reachable (2.4 GHz is inside 325-3800 MHz); but 79 ch = 78 MHz span exceeds instantaneous Pluto/B210 bandwidth - detect via fast sweep or energy/hop-pattern detection, near-impossible to demod payload]

signatures.name: Bluetooth Classic EDR 2 Mbit/s (pi/4-DQPSK payload)
signatures.mode: Enhanced Data Rate 2 Mbps: GFSK access-code/header + pi/4-DQPSK payload, same 1 MSym/s symbol rate, same 79-ch AFH hop, ~1 MHz occupied BW
signatures.tscm: Same 1 MHz channel and 625 us hop timing as BR - EDR keeps the same symbol rate and 1 MHz occupied bandwidth, gaining rate purely by packing 2 bits/symbol. Within each burst the payload switches to pi/4-DQPSK after the guard band - a phase-modulated tail with a different spectral shape/higher constellation density than the GFSK header. Used by A2DP music-quality streaming in disguised-headphone recorders that also stream live. Distinguishing BR vs EDR on a Pluto/B210 requires per-burst modulation analysis, rarely practical live. [stock-Pluto-reachable; single 1 MHz burst fits in instantaneous BW, but hopping across 78 MHz and short dwell make per-burst PSK classification hard without a dedicated BT sniffer]

signatures.name: Bluetooth Classic SCO/eSCO voice link (HFP/HSP) - periodic reserved-slot duty
signatures.mode: Synchronous voice link (CVSD or mSBC/Wideband Speech), reserved slots at fixed intervals within the BR hop, continuous-while-active bidirectional audio
signatures.tscm: Distinct from A2DP: SCO/eSCO reserves slots at a regular cadence (e.g. every 6 slots) to carry a two-way voice channel - this is the classic covert-EARPIECE signature (agent listening + talking). On a waterfall it shows as a very regular, metronomic burst cadence riding the AFH hop, present only while a call/live-listen session is active. The periodicity (not the per-burst shape) is the tell. This is also the exact profile abused by the 2025 Airoha HFP mic-listen attack. [stock-Pluto-reachable; the actionable feature is the periodic burst cadence in energy-detection, not payload - visible via time-domain power on a sweeping receiver]

signatures.name: BLE 1M PHY (LE1M uncoded, GFSK) - advertising bursts on ch 37/38/39
signatures.mode: LE 1 Mbps uncoded GFSK; primary advertising PDUs on 3 fixed channels: 2402 (ch37), 2426 (ch38), 2480 (ch39)
signatures.tscm: Three fixed ~1 MHz-wide GFSK carriers at 2402/2426/2480 MHz that light up in a rapid A-B-C triplet at the advertising interval (20 ms to seconds). These sit deliberately in the gaps between Wi-Fi ch 1/6/11. ANY BLE device (including a bug in advertising/pairing/beacon mode) shows this before/at connection. A covert BLE mic or LE Audio bug is discoverable here - the three-carrier heartbeat at fixed frequencies is the single most catchable BLE tell on a Pluto/B210. [stock-Pluto-reachable and the MOST practical BLE catch: 2402/2426/2480 are fixed, so you can park on one advertising channel; but heavy false-positive overlap with every phone/wearable/beacon]

signatures.name: BLE 2M PHY (LE2M, GFSK) - LE Audio / high-throughput
signatures.mode: LE 2 Mbps uncoded GFSK, ~2 MHz occupied bandwidth, 37 data-channel hop (2 MHz raster); the workhorse PHY for LE Audio isochronous streams
signatures.tscm: Doubled symbol rate widens the occupied bandwidth to ~2 MHz per burst (visibly wider than the ~1 MHz LE1M/Classic bursts on a waterfall) - this width is the primary tell for LE Audio-capable devices. Carries CIS (unicast earbuds) and BIS (Auracast broadcast) isochronous audio. Modern LE Audio earbuds/hearing-aid-form-factor bugs default here. Bursts are periodic at the ISO interval. [stock-Pluto-reachable; ~2 MHz burst fits within Pluto/B210 instantaneous BW, so a single 2M burst is capturable, but hopping still defeats continuous follow]

signatures.name: BLE Auracast broadcast (BIS, LE Audio, connectionless)
signatures.mode: Broadcast Isochronous Stream over LE2M (or LE1M) GFSK, LC3-coded audio, connectionless one-to-many, periodic advertising train + BIS subevents hopping across data channels
signatures.tscm: Auracast is the newest and TSCM-relevant twist: a bug can BROADCAST room audio with NO pairing to unlimited receivers. Signature = periodic advertising (extended adv announcing the broadcast, see the periodic-advertising row) PLUS a very regular, near-continuous train of isochronous BIS subevent bursts hopping across data channels at a fixed ISO interval. The metronomic, always-on (while broadcasting) burst cadence - unlike bursty request/response BLE - plus LE Audio ~2 MHz width is the anomaly. No connection handshake to catch means classic pairing-detection misses it. [stock-Pluto-reachable; the strong regular ISO cadence aids energy detection, but connectionless + hopping means you confirm by cadence/anomaly, not decode. Priority hunt for modern sweeps]

device_classes.device_class: wireless_mbus_smart_utility_meter
device_classes.summary: Wireless M-Bus (wM-Bus, EN 13757-4 / OMS) is the dominant European smart-utility telemetry link for gas, water, heat, and electricity meters. From a TSCM standpoint it matters because it is a legitimate, ubiquitous, low-duty-cycle transmitter that (a) is easily mistaken for a covert device, and (b) can itself carry piggybacked exfil data inside its variable-length application payload. It has several genuinely distinct on-air signatures that the generic 863-870 MHz FSK row does not capture: S-mode uses Manchester-coded 2-FSK; T-mode uses a distinctive 3-of-6 chip-coded 2-FSK at 100 kcps; C-mode uses plain NRZ 2-GFSK sharing the same 868.95 MHz center; and N-mode is a completely separate NARROWBAND service at 169 MHz (12.5 kHz channels, 2-GFSK and 4-GFSK) that is OUT of a stock Pluto's 325-3800 MHz tuning range. A 433 MHz OMS variant also exists (Middle East / water). Because meters transmit in short intermittent bursts (seconds to tens of minutes apart), a sweep must dwell/log over time on these centers rather than rely on a single snapshot. The key TSCM discriminator: a real meter's traffic correlates with a physical utility meter on-site and repeats on a regular telemetry cadence; a device that mimics wM-Bus framing but has no corresponding meter, or transmits far more often/with larger payloads than metering warrants, is suspect.
