Kamstrup MULTICAL heat/energy meter with wM-Bus module (C1/T1)
Kamstrup flowIQ water meter (wM-Bus)
Itron Cyble RF / Intelis water and gas meters (wM-Bus)
Sensus iPERL water meter with wM-Bus
Landis+Gyr electricity meter with wM-Bus interface
Elster/Honeywell gas meter wM-Bus module
Engelmann SensoStar heat cost allocator (wM-Bus)
Techem / ista heat cost allocators and smoke detectors (868 MHz wM-Bus)
Qundis Q caloric / Q water heat-cost-allocator radios
Zenner EDC / minomess water meters (wM-Bus)
Radiocrafts RC1701HP-MBUS4 169 MHz N-mode module
Radiocrafts RC1180-MBUS / RC1701 868 MHz S/T/C module
STMicroelectronics STM32WL / S2-LP wM-Bus reference modules
Texas Instruments CC1101 / CC1120-based wM-Bus meter transceivers
Silicon Labs EZR32 / Si446x wM-Bus meter radios
Analog Devices ADF7030 / ADF7023 wM-Bus transceiver designs
NXP OL2381-based wM-Bus meter modules
Amber Wireless / Wurth AMB8465-M wM-Bus USB stick (receiver)
IMST iM871A / iM880 wM-Bus USB gateway (receiver side)
Wi-MBus / Solvimus MUC gateway collectors
Diehl IZAR RECEIVER / drive-by van collection units
Elvaco CMe series wM-Bus concentrators
Honeywell/Elster EK280 gas volume corrector with wM-Bus
Apator / Powogaz water meters with wM-Bus (Poland)
Maddalena / B METERS narrowband 169 MHz N-mode water meters
confirm_steps: Dwell/log over TIME on 868.95 MHz (T/C) and 868.30 MHz (S) with a waterfall for several minutes -- wM-Bus is bursty, so a single snapshot will miss it. Confirm short balanced FSK bursts recurring on a regular telemetry cadence.
Discriminate T-mode vs C-mode on the shared 868.95 MHz center by occupied bandwidth: ~500 kHz spread + 3-of-6 constant-weight chip pattern = T-mode; narrower ~150-200 kHz clean GFSK lobe = C-mode.
For 169 MHz N-mode, remember a STOCK ADALM-Pluto cannot tune below 325 MHz -- use a B210 (stock) or an AD9364-modded Pluto and look for very narrow 12.5 kHz channels near 169.40-169.475 MHz.

Decode to confirm identity: run rtl_433 (-f 868.95M / -f 868.3M, m_bus decoder) or a wM-Bus stack (wmbusmeters) and verify EN 13757-4 framing, manufacturer 3-letter ID, and meter serial. A valid manufacturer/serial that maps to a physical meter on-site = benign.
Physically correlate: walk down the RSSI to the emitter. It should terminate at an actual gas/water/heat/electric meter or heat-cost allocator. No corresponding meter = investigate.

Assess payload cadence and size: metering is low-rate and periodic. A wM-Bus-framed emitter that transmits far more frequently, or with anomalously large/variable payloads, is a candidate for piggybacked exfil and warrants capture + payload analysis.
false_positive_overlap: Legitimate smart water/gas/heat/electricity meters and heat-cost allocators -- these ARE wM-Bus; the signature is the device, so identity must be confirmed by decode + physical meter, not by RF alone.

Generic 863-870 MHz SRD FSK devices (the existing catalog row) share the band -- discriminate wM-Bus by its specific centers (868.30 S / 868.95 T-C), 3-of-6 or Manchester coding, and EN 13757-4 framing on decode.
Other 868 MHz ISM traffic: LoRa (chirp, not FSK -- easy to separate), IQRF, EnOcean, and proprietary alarm/sensor FSK links can look similar on a raw waterfall until decoded.
433 MHz variant overlaps a very crowded ISM band (TPMS, remote keyfobs, weather stations, garage doors, many OOK/FSK sensors) -- only the wM-Bus preamble + metering payload confirms it.
169 MHz N-mode shares the low-VHF PMR/paging/meter allocation with other narrowband services; 12.5 kHz channelization plus wM-Bus framing is the discriminator.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Benign-ubiquitous in Europe and increasingly worldwide -- expect multiple legitimate wM-Bus emitters in any building with smart utility metering (water, gas, heat-cost allocators, sometimes electricity). HIGH false-positive risk: do not flag a wM-Bus burst as a bug on sight. The real TSCM concern is twofold: (1) a covert transmitter deliberately mimicking wM-Bus framing to hide in metering traffic, and (2) a compromised/malicious meter module using its legitimate uplink to piggyback exfiltrated data inside the variable-length EN 13757-4 application payload. Both are caught the same way: decode the frames, verify the manufacturer ID + serial resolve to a real on-site meter, physically locate each emitter, and flag anything whose cadence or payload size exceeds what metering needs. Note the reach limits explicitly in any report: 169 MHz N-mode is below a stock Pluto's 325 MHz floor (needs the AD9364 mod or a B210); all 868 MHz modes and the 433 MHz variant are within stock Pluto's 325-3800 MHz range; none of these approach the 6 GHz B210 ceiling.

signatures.name: Wireless M-Bus S-mode (868.3 MHz, Manchester 2-FSK)
signatures.mode: S1/S2 stationary mode; 2-FSK, Manchester-coded, ~32.768 kcps chip / ~16.384 kbps effective, deviation approx +/-50 kHz (mod index ~0.8-1.6), center 868.30 MHz in ETSI G1 subband
signatures.tscm: Center 868.30 MHz. Manchester line coding gives a symmetric, near-DC-balanced 2-FSK spectrum with a characteristic null structure; short bursts (a frame is tens of ms) repeating on a slow telemetry cadence (minutes to hours). ~+/-50 kHz deviation. Distinct from the generic 863-870 FSK row by its fixed 868.30 center and Manchester (not raw NRZ) coding. Well inside stock Pluto range. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: Wireless M-Bus T-mode (868.95 MHz, 3-of-6 coded 2-FSK, 100 kcps)
signatures.mode: T1/T2 frequent-transmit mode; 2-FSK, 3-out-of-6 chip coding, 100 kchip/s (=> 66.6 kbit/s useful), center 868.95 MHz, ETSI G2 subband
signatures.tscm: Center 868.95 MHz, ~500 kHz occupied because of the 100 kcps chip rate. The 3-of-6 block coding produces a distinctive constant-weight chip stream (every 6-chip symbol has exactly three ones) which shows as a dense, balanced FSK burst with no long runs -- a fingerprint separating it from C-mode on the same center. Bursty short frames, meter-initiated. Distinct from the generic FSK row by chip coding + 100 kcps width. Stock-Pluto-reachable. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: Wireless M-Bus C-mode (868.95 MHz, NRZ 2-GFSK, 100 kbps)
signatures.mode: C1/C2 compact mode; 2-GFSK, plain NRZ (no chip coding), 100 kbit/s meter->other (50 kbit/s reverse), center 868.95 MHz, ETSI G2 subband
signatures.tscm: Shares the 868.95 MHz center with T-mode but is NRZ (Gaussian-filtered) so it occupies less bandwidth (~150-200 kHz) and carries the same info per burst with less energy. Spectrum is a narrower, cleaner GFSK lobe than T-mode's chip-spread lobe. Discriminate T vs C on the SAME center by occupied width and by presence/absence of the 3-of-6 constant-weight chip pattern. Bursty. Stock-Pluto-reachable. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: Wireless M-Bus N-mode narrowband (169 MHz, 2-GFSK, 12.5 kHz, 2.4 kbps)
signatures.mode: N1/N2 narrowband long-range mode, sub-bands A/B; 2-GFSK, 2.4 kbit/s in a 12.5 kHz channel; 169.40-169.475 MHz meter-reading allocation
signatures.tscm: Very narrow 12.5 kHz channels around 169.4 MHz -- unmistakably narrowband compared to the 868 MHz modes. Low 2.4 kbps rate gives high sensitivity / long range (basements, buried water meters). Slow, sparse bursts. CRITICAL: 169 MHz is BELOW a stock ADALM-Pluto's 325 MHz tuning floor, so a stock Pluto CANNOT see this without the AD9364 frequency-extension mod (Pluto tunes ~70 MHz-6 GHz once modded) or a different low-VHF front end. B210 covers 70 MHz-6 GHz and can see it stock. [needs-AD9364-mod (below stock Pluto 325 MHz floor; B210 sees it stock)]

signatures.name: Wireless M-Bus 433 MHz OMS variant (2-FSK narrowband)
signatures.mode: OMS/EN 13757-4 433 MHz profile (Middle East / high-temp water metering); 2-FSK, ~4.8-6.4 kbit/s class, within the 433.05-434.79 MHz ISM band
signatures.tscm: wM-Bus framing (same EN 13757-4 link layer) carried in the 433 MHz ISM band instead of 868/169 -- used where 868 MHz SRD is unavailable or where 433 MHz propagation/temperature behavior is preferred (Gulf water meters). Narrowband FSK bursts; discriminate from the many other 433 MHz OOK/FSK devices by the wM-Bus preamble + variable metering payload and slow telemetry cadence. Stock-Pluto-reachable (well within 325-3800 MHz). [stock-Pluto-reachable]

device_classes.device_class: imsi_catcher_downlink_indicators
device_classes.summary: Cell-site-simulator / IMSI-catcher (Stingray-class) rogue base-station DOWNLINK indicators. Unlike every other cellular row in this catalog (which watches the phone's UPLINK), this is a DEFENSIVE class that looks at the base-station-to-phone DOWNLINK: an anomalous 2G BCCH, an LTE SSB (PSS/SSS) on an unexpected EARFCN, a forced 2G-downgrade beacon, or a rogue 5G SSB. The tell is never a single tone but a *context anomaly* — a strong, clean, stationary base-station carrier that does not match the known local network (unexpected ARFCN/EARFCN/PCI, mismatched neighbor list, aggressive reselection/T3212 parameters, a 2G cell appearing where the operator has none, or two cells claiming the same identity). The SDR sees standard, spec-compliant cellular OFDM/GMSK downlink modulation; classification as hostile REQUIRES a baseline of the legitimate local RF environment (survey the site's normal cells first, then flag deviations). High false-positive overlap with legitimate macro/small cells, DAS, femtocells, and temporary COWs (cell-on-wheels). Stock Pluto (325-3800 MHz) reaches US GSM-850/PCS-1900 downlink and most mid-band LTE/5G SSB; it MISSES US low-band downlink below 325 MHz (600 MHz n71, 700 MHz not reachable) — a B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) covers all sub-6 GHz cellular downlink and is the correct front end for this class. Nothing here is above 6 GHz.

Harris Hailstorm (LTE-capable CSS)
Harris Gossamer (handheld IMSI catcher)

NeoSoft / Ability IBIS interception system

srsRAN (srsENB/srsEPC) rogue eNodeB on USRP B210 (open-source CSS)
OpenAirInterface / Open5GS rogue gNB on USRP (SA 5G catcher)
YateBTS / OpenBTS software 2G BTS on bladeRF/USRP
LimeSDR-based DIY GSM catcher
HackRF + gr-gsm passive downlink analyzer (research/DIY)
Portable 'CellHawk'-style vehicular CSS
Man-portable backpack CSS (drone/UAV-mounted dirtbox variants)
Femtocell converted to rogue mode (e.g. modified carrier femto)
Cell-on-wheels (COW) — legitimate but a common false positive
Distributed Antenna System (DAS) head-end — legitimate false positive
Carrier small cell / metrocell — legitimate false positive
confirm_steps: Baseline first: run a clean spectrum survey of the site's normal cellular downlink (GSM-850 869-894, PCS-1900 1930-1990, local LTE EARFCNs, local NR GSCNs). Record every legitimate ARFCN/EARFCN/PCI/CID and neighbor list BEFORE hunting anomalies.

Decode the downlink, not just power: use gr-gsm (2G) or srsRAN/falcon-style LTE cell search to pull ARFCN/EARFCN/PCI, CID/LAC/TAC, MIB/SIB, T3212 and reselection parameters. A raw carrier alone cannot be classified.
Flag a 2G downlink where the operator runs none, or any cell whose identity/neighbor list is absent from your baseline or from a crowd-sourced tower DB (cellmapper / OpenCellID).
Look for coercive parameters: abnormally low T3212, high cell-reselect offset, empty/mismatched neighbor list, or SIB/RRC redirect steering the phone toward 2G (redirectedCarrierInfo to a GSM ARFCN).
Correlate bands for downgrade: a suspicious LTE SIB de-prioritizing 4G/5G appearing at the same time/place as a fresh rogue GSM BCCH is a strong 2G-downgrade tell — confirm the pairing.
Check for duplicate identity: same PCI/CID from a geometry that can't be the real tower (both very strong at one spot, or a 'tower' where none is mapped).

Move and re-measure: a real macro's signal geometry changes predictably with position; a stationary vehicular catcher stays anomalously strong. Walk/drive a short transect and watch RSRP vs. expected.
Rule out legitimate temporaries: confirm no carrier COW, event small cell, DAS commissioning, or network maintenance explains the new cell before calling it hostile.

Use a B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) not a stock Pluto if you must cover US 600/700 MHz low-band downlink; stock Pluto's 325 MHz floor still reaches 850/PCS/mid-band but a B210 is the correct front end for full sub-6 coverage.

Escalate legally: if a genuine unauthorized CSS is confirmed, preserve raw IQ + decoded evidence and advise counsel — operating a CSS is a federal/legal matter and outside a TSCM sweep's remit to engage.
false_positive_overlap: Legitimate carrier macro cells (any anomaly must be judged against a real-network baseline, not in isolation)
Carrier small cells / metrocells / oDAS nodes that appear where you didn't expect a tower
Distributed Antenna Systems (DAS) in venues/buildings re-radiating operator downlink
Residential/enterprise femtocells and network extenders (legitimately create a local cell)
Cell-on-wheels (COW) deployed for events, disasters, or coverage gaps — a real temporary cell
Network maintenance / new-site commissioning temporarily changing PCIs, neighbor lists, or adding cells
Legitimate 2G still operating in regions/carriers that have not sunset GSM (a real 2G cell is not a catcher)
Roaming/border cells and cross-border carriers producing unexpected ARFCNs near edges
Repeaters/boosters and passive DAS that duplicate a real cell's identity by design
NSA-vs-SA 5G confusion (a real SA SSB with no LTE anchor can look 'lone' without being hostile)
device_classes.tscm_notes: This is the catalog's one DEFENSIVE / downlink class — it protects the client's phones rather than finding a bug on the wall, so treat it differently from the uplink bug/tracker rows. Nothing here can be classified from a spectrum snapshot alone: every signature is a *deviation from the known-good local network*, so a baseline survey of the site's real cells is mandatory before any hostile call. False-positive overlap is severe and unavoidable — legitimate macros, small cells, DAS, femtocells, carrier COWs, and network maintenance all look identical on-air; the discriminator is identity/parameter anomaly plus signal geometry, not modulation. Reach: stock Pluto (325-3800 MHz) covers US GSM-850, PCS-1900, and mid-band LTE/5G SSB, so most of this class is reachable, but for full US low-band (600 MHz n71 / 700 MHz incl. FirstNet B14) and C-band 5G above 3800 MHz you want a B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz); nothing in this class is above 6 GHz. Practically, decoding (gr-gsm, srsRAN cell search) matters more than raw sweeping here — a phone-based IMSI-catcher-detector app or a dedicated CSS-detection tool complements the SDR. Finally, a confirmed unauthorized cell-site simulator is a serious legal matter (federal spectrum + interception law); the TSCM role is to detect, preserve evidence, and refer to counsel/authorities, not to interact with or spoof the device.

signatures.name: Anomalous GSM-850 downlink BCCH (rogue 2G cell / classic Stingray)
signatures.mode: GMSK, 200 kHz GSM downlink carrier broadcasting a BCCH; flagged when ARFCN/CID/LAC/neighbor-list does not match the known local network, or a 2G cell appears where the carrier operates none
signatures.tscm: Continuous 200 kHz GMSK carrier in the 869-894 MHz US downlink block carrying a beacon/BCCH. Rogue tells: unexpected ARFCN, unusually strong/clean and perfectly stationary, empty or mismatched neighbor list, aggressively low T3212 (frequent location updates), high cell-reselect offset to trap the phone, and often stronger than the real macro it shadows. Requires a baseline of the site's real 850 downlink to call it. Stock Pluto reachable. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: Anomalous PCS-1900 downlink BCCH (rogue 2G cell, US PCS)
signatures.mode: GMSK, 200 kHz GSM downlink carrier / BCCH in the US PCS-1900 downlink block; same anomaly logic as GSM-850
signatures.tscm: Same rogue-2G signature as the 850 row but in the 1930-1990 MHz PCS downlink. Distinct on-air row because it is a different band the SDR must separately survey. Flag on unexpected ARFCN, mismatched LAC/CID/neighbor list, coercive reselection/T3212 params, or a 2G cell present where the operator runs only LTE/5G. Stock Pluto reachable. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: LTE downlink SSB (PSS/SSS) on unexpected EARFCN (rogue eNodeB / srsENB+B210 catcher)
signatures.mode: OFDM LTE downlink; center-band Synchronization Signal Block (PSS Zadoff-Chu + SSS) every 5 ms plus PBCH/MIB; flagged when the cell sits on an EARFCN/PCI/TAC that does not belong to the local network
signatures.tscm: Wideband LTE OFDM downlink (typ. 5/10/20 MHz occupied; the SSB itself is ~1.08 MHz at band center). Detector locks the PSS/SSS to recover PCI, then reads the MIB. Rogue tells: EARFCN/PCI not in the site baseline, a lone cell with no matching neighbors, MIB/SIB advertising suspicious reselection or a low-priority push toward 2G/3G, or a duplicate PCI colliding with a known real cell. Classic srsENB/Open5GS rogue-eNB on a USRP B210. Mid-band centers Pluto-reachable; low-band centers (see reach note) are not. [stock-Pluto-reachable for mid-band centers (~1700-2700 MHz, e.g. B2/B4/B66/B7); needs-AD9364-mod-or-B210 for low-band SSB below 325 MHz is N/A, but 600/700 MHz low-band centers ARE below the stock Pluto 325 MHz floor and need a B210]

signatures.name: US low-band LTE/5G downlink SSB below Pluto floor (600 MHz n71 / 700 MHz B12/B13/B14)
signatures.mode: OFDM LTE/5G-NR downlink SSB (PSS/SSS/PBCH) in US low-band; same unexpected-EARFCN/ARFCN anomaly logic, separated out purely because of SDR reach
signatures.tscm: Same rogue-downlink anomaly as the mid-band LTE row, but in US 600 MHz (n71) and 700 MHz (B12/B13/B14, incl. FirstNet B14) downlink. Broken into its own row because this band is BELOW the stock Pluto 325-3800 MHz floor at the low end and needs a wider front end. FirstNet/public-safety B14 makes an unexpected cell here especially notable. Requires local baseline to classify. [needs-AD9364-mod (stock Pluto floor is 325 MHz so 600 MHz is in reach, BUT 617-787 is fine for Pluto; the true out-of-reach US low band is 600 MHz n71 downlink at 617-652 which IS above 325 — reachable). B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) is the clean choice; stock Pluto technically reaches this whole 617-787 range]

signatures.name: Rogue 5G-NR downlink SSB on unexpected NR-ARFCN (rogue gNB, sub-6)
signatures.mode: 5G-NR OFDM downlink Synchronization Signal Block (PSS + SSS + PBCH, 4 OFDM symbols, 20 RB ~ 3.6 MHz at 30 kHz SCS), periodic (default 20 ms); flagged on unexpected NR-ARFCN/PCI/GSCN not in the local baseline
signatures.tscm: Periodic 5G SSB burst (~3.6-4.3 MHz wide, repeating ~every 20 ms) at a GSCN sync raster point. 1008 possible PCIs (3 PSS x 336 SSS). Rogue tells: NR-ARFCN/GSCN/PCI absent from the site baseline, a standalone SA cell with no matching operator neighbors, or a duplicate PCI. Sub-6 SA rogue gNBs are emerging (srsRAN/OpenAirInterface on USRP). Note real 5G is often NSA (anchored on LTE), so a lone SA SSB with no LTE anchor is itself suspicious. [stock-Pluto-reachable for FR1 mid-band (n66/n7/n77-low up to 3800 MHz); C-band above 3800 MHz needs a B210; all sub-6 within B210 range; nothing above 6 GHz here]

device_classes.device_class: body_worn_wearable_cameras
device_classes.summary: Police/consumer body-worn cameras and covert wearable cams with wireless offload or live-stream. On the air these split into: (a) 2.4/5 GHz Wi-Fi offload/live-stream (shares the same PHY as any Wi-Fi spy cam — NOT a separate cosmetic row, but the covert relevance differs because the emitter is on a moving person), (b) LTE-uplink live-stream where the bodycam itself is a continuous cellular uplink transmitter carried on-body (Axon Body 3/4 with Respond, Motorola V300/V700 LTE), and (c) the Axon Signal BLE holster/CEW-draw trigger beacon, a low-duty 2.4 GHz BLE advertising burst distinct from continuous Wi-Fi. TSCM interest is a person-worn transmitter: sustained 2.4/5 GHz Wi-Fi uplink or LTE uplink co-located with a body, or a repeating BLE Axon-Signal advertisement, can betray an active recording/streaming wearable during a sweep or meeting.

Axon Body 3 (LTE live-stream via Axon Respond)
Axon Body 2 (Wi-Fi offload, Signal-triggered)

Motorola Solutions V700 (LTE live-stream body camera)
Motorola Solutions V200 / VT100 body cameras

WatchGuard/Motorola V300 docked LTE uploader

confirm_steps: For 2.4/5 GHz Wi-Fi: capture the uplink MAC and check OUI against Axon (Axon Enterprise), Motorola Solutions, and Digital Ally vendor prefixes; correlate signal strength rising/falling with the suspected wearer's movement to separate an on-body camera from a fixed AP or the wearer's own phone.

For LTE-uplink: watch for a SUSTAINED uplink burst pattern (not idle-phone paging) that tracks with a person; use a directional antenna or near-field probe to localize the emitter to the torso/holster area rather than to a room AP or a handset in a pocket.

For Axon Signal BLE: use a BLE scanner (nRF Connect or a dedicated sniffer) to see the advertising packets and any Axon service UUID; note the ~30 ft range and correlation with a weapon-draw/CEW event, and pair the beacon with a co-located on-body Wi-Fi/LTE uplink.

Physically confirm: bodycams are overt-form but covert wearable variants hide in pens/buttons/glasses/lanyards — inspect torso, lapel, and holster line; a docked vs. worn camera changes the RF picture (docked = fixed uploader, worn = mobile emitter).

Cross-check duty cycle: continuous/sustained uplink implies active live-stream; brief periodic bursts imply store-and-offload — this distinguishes a live surveillance wearable from a passive recorder.
false_positive_overlap: 2.4/5 GHz Wi-Fi bodycam PHY is identical to every other Wi-Fi camera, AP, phone, laptop, and IoT device — band presence alone proves nothing; needs OUI + mobility correlation.

LTE-uplink bodycam is indistinguishable at the energy/duty level from the wearer's own smartphone or any nearby cellular device; only a sustained on-body uplink pattern is suggestive, never definitive.
Axon Signal BLE beacon overlaps all BLE traffic (earbuds, fitness trackers, phones, retail beacons, keyboards); a BLE hit is not a bodycam without the Axon service UUID or a co-located camera uplink.
Docked/charging bodycams uploading over Wi-Fi/LTE look like a fixed uploader and can be mistaken for a stationary camera or AP.
Legitimate on-duty law-enforcement bodycams are the dominant source of these signatures — in many contexts the correct finding is 'lawful police BWC present,' not a covert threat.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Frame this class carefully in reports: the same signatures are produced by LAWFUL law-enforcement body cameras far more often than by a covert wearable, so a hit is context-dependent — a bodycam RF signature in a police interaction is expected; the same signature in a private meeting or a family-law sweep is the finding. The only truly class-distinct rows are (1) the LTE-uplink on-body live-stream (a person acting as a continuous cellular uplink transmitter) and (2) the Axon Signal BLE holster/CEW trigger beacon; the 2.4/5 GHz Wi-Fi rows deliberately reuse the existing Wi-Fi-camera PHY and are flagged as covert-relevant variants (moving, on-body source) rather than padded duplicate signatures. Never assert a specific model from RF alone — RF gives band, bandwidth, modulation, duty, and OUI at best; physical or BLE-UUID confirmation is required. 5 GHz is out of a stock Pluto entirely (needs B210) and sits near the B210's 6 GHz ceiling; everything else (2.4 GHz, LTE uplink 698-2570 MHz, BLE band) is within stock-Pluto 325-3800 MHz reach, though BLE hop-level decode is impractical at Pluto bandwidth — treat BLE as band-presence.

signatures.name: Body-worn camera 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi offload/live-stream
signatures.mode: 802.11 b/g/n/ax OFDM/DSSS, 20 MHz channels, station uplink from a body-worn device
signatures.tscm: Shares the exact PHY of every other 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi camera/AP — do NOT treat as a unique emitter on the analyzer. Identify by MAC OUI (Axon/Motorola/Digital Ally) and by the tell that the uplink source is moving with a person rather than a fixed camera. Sustained uplink bursts (beyond beacon rate) suggest active video offload or live-stream. Stock-Pluto 325-3800 MHz covers this band; RSSI tracks with wearer movement. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: Body-worn camera 5 GHz Wi-Fi offload/live-stream
signatures.mode: 802.11 a/n/ac/ax OFDM, 20/40/80 MHz channels, UNII-1/2/3, station uplink from body-worn device
signatures.tscm: Axon Body 4 and Motorola V-series offload/stream on 5 GHz UNII bands (5150-5350, 5470-5725, 5725-5850 MHz). Same false-positive problem as any 5 GHz Wi-Fi device (phones, APs, laptops). Distinguish from the 2.4 GHz row by band and from fixed APs by mobility of the source (RSSI following a person). Out of a stock Pluto's 325-3800 MHz reach entirely; needs a B210/higher front end — 5.15-5.85 GHz sits near the top of the B210's 70 MHz-6 GHz range and is reachable there. [out-of-stock-Pluto-range; B210-reachable near 6 GHz ceiling]

signatures.name: Body-worn camera LTE-uplink live-stream (on-body cellular transmitter)
signatures.mode: LTE/5G-NR SC-FDMA uplink from a body-worn modem; sustained uplink during live-stream (Axon Respond, Motorola V300/V700 cellular)
signatures.tscm: Genuinely distinct from the Wi-Fi rows: the bodycam is itself the cellular UPLINK emitter carried on a person, streaming continuously rather than the brief bursts of an idle phone. Common uplink bands: B12/13/14 (698-798), B5/B26 (814-849), B4/B66 (1710-1780), B2/B25 (1850-1915), B30 (2305-2315), B7 (2500-2570). Huge false-positive overlap with any phone the wearer also carries — the tell is a SUSTAINED uplink burst pattern co-located with the person during suspected recording, localized to the torso with a directional/near-field probe. Uplink bands 698-2570 MHz are within stock-Pluto reach. Detect energy/duty, do not decode LTE. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: Axon Signal BLE holster/CEW-draw trigger beacon
signatures.mode: Bluetooth Low Energy advertising/GATT trigger, 2 MHz channels incl. adv channels 37/38/39 (2402/2426/2480 MHz), FHSS across 40 channels
signatures.tscm: Axon Signal Sensor (holster) and Signal Performance Power Magazine (TASER X2/X26P) emit a BLE event to wake nearby Axon body cameras within ~30 ft on weapon draw / CEW arm. On the air this is a short BLE advertising/connection burst, NOT continuous Wi-Fi — low duty, hops the BLE channel plan. Massive false-positive overlap with all BLE devices (earbuds, phones, trackers, beacons); a hit is not a bodycam without the Axon service UUID or a co-located camera uplink. Stock-Pluto covers 2.4 GHz but resolving individual BLE hops/adv packets is impractical at Pluto bandwidth — treat as band-presence, confirm with a dedicated BLE sniffer. [stock-Pluto-reachable (band only; BLE hop-level decode impractical at Pluto BW)]

device_classes.device_class: gotenna_offgrid_mesh_text_radio
device_classes.summary: goTenna encrypted off-grid mesh text radios — a Bluetooth-tethered "dead phone" relay family distinct from Meshtastic LoRa. The consumer goTenna Mesh burst-transmits GFSK in the 902-928 MHz ISM band (frequency-agile, 25 kHz channels, 0.5/1 W). The tactical goTenna Pro / Pro X / Pro X2 family instead uses AES-256-encrypted narrowband FSK in licensed VHF (142-175 MHz) and UHF (445-480 MHz) land-mobile bands — a completely separate band from both Meshtastic (CSS LoRa) and the consumer Mesh. From a TSCM standpoint these are short, bursty, low-duty data transmissions carrying PLI/position and text — easy to miss on a sweep because they are silent between bursts and, for the Pro variants, sit down in VHF/UHF where a spy-cam-focused sweep may not be looking. Band-reach caveat: the 902-928 MHz Mesh and the 445-480 MHz Pro UHF band are inside a stock ADALM-Pluto's 325-3800 MHz range; the Pro VHF band (142-175 MHz) and the European Mesh variant (868-869 MHz) fall BELOW the stock Pluto floor and need the AD9364 frequency-extension mod (or a VHF-capable front end).

confirm_steps: Watch for SHORT, low-duty narrowband FSK bursts, not a continuous carrier — dwell/record over minutes; goTenna is silent between transmissions and easy to miss on a single sweep pass.
In 902-928 MHz, look for ~25 kHz-wide GFSK bursts that appear at shifting/agile channel positions across the band (frequency-agile ISM), distinct from a fixed continuous carrier.

For the Pro variants, tune the 445-480 MHz UHF and (with AD9364 mod / VHF front end) 142-175 MHz VHF bands for very narrow (4.5-12 kHz) FSK bursts; payload is AES-256 encrypted so expect no demodulatable plaintext.
Correlate bursts with a nearby smartphone: goTenna requires a Bluetooth-paired phone — a co-located BLE link plus periodic narrowband bursts strengthens the ID.

Distinguish from Meshtastic: Meshtastic is wideband CSS/LoRa (chirp, ~250 kHz-wide sweeps) in the same 902-928 band; goTenna Mesh is narrowband GFSK (~25 kHz). If you see a chirp it is LoRa, not goTenna.

Confirm band: 142-175 MHz VHF Pro bursts are below a stock Pluto's 325 MHz floor — if you cannot see them, that is a reach limit, not absence; use the AD9364-extended Pluto or a VHF-capable receiver before concluding the band is clear.
false_positive_overlap: Meshtastic / other LoRa in the same 902-928 MHz band — but LoRa is wideband CSS chirp (~125-500 kHz), not narrowband GFSK, so the two are separable
900 MHz smart utility meters (AMI/AMR) using narrowband FSK/FHSS telemetry
Z-Wave home-automation devices (908.4 MHz US) — narrowband FSK bursts
Industrial 900 MHz telemetry/SCADA and 900 MHz FHSS cordless phones
445-480 MHz: licensed UHF business/GMRS/amateur two-way radios and their data bursts
142-175 MHz: VHF land-mobile, public-safety, MURS (151-154 MHz), and amateur data/packet — a narrowband FSK burst here is usually legitimate two-way traffic
Any generic BLE beacon nearby (goTenna needs a paired phone, but BLE alone is not diagnostic)
device_classes.tscm_notes: goTenna is a genuine off-grid covert-comms concern: it lets two parties exchange encrypted text/location with NO cellular or Wi-Fi trail, so it can support surveillance-team coordination or exfil comms that a phone-focused investigation misses. The signatures are bursty and low-duty — a snapshot sweep will very likely show nothing; you must dwell and record. False-positive overlap is significant: the 902-928 MHz ISM band is crowded with legitimate narrowband FSK/FHSS devices (smart meters, LoRa/Meshtastic, industrial telemetry, cordless-phone/keyfob traffic, Z-Wave at 908.4 MHz), and the Pro VHF/UHF bands overlap licensed land-mobile, business, MURS (151-154 MHz), and amateur radio — a narrowband FSK burst there is far more likely to be a legitimate two-way radio than a goTenna. Do not call a goTenna on band alone; corroborate with burst pattern, ~25 kHz (Mesh) vs 4.5-12 kHz (Pro) bandwidth, low duty, and a co-located Bluetooth-paired phone. Band-reach honesty: stock ADALM-Pluto (325-3800 MHz) covers the 902-928 MHz Mesh and 445-480 MHz Pro UHF band, but NOT the 142-175 MHz Pro VHF band (needs the AD9364 mod / VHF front end); all goTenna bands are well under 6 GHz so a B210 covers them fully.

signatures.name: goTenna Mesh 900 MHz ISM burst (GFSK)

signatures.tscm: Narrow (~25 kHz) FSK bursts appearing at hopping/agile positions across the 902-928 MHz ISM band; very short on-air time then silence; no continuous carrier. Consumer mesh text/location relay, Bluetooth-paired to a phone. In stock Pluto range. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

Tactical/professional variant, user-selected fixed frequency (not ISM-hopping). In stock Pluto range. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.tscm: Same narrowband encrypted FSK bursts as the Pro UHF signature but in the VHF band — a separate band entirely. Short, silent-between bursts; user-selected fixed channel. device_classes.device_class: optical_ir_covert_nonrf
device_classes.summary: Optical/IR covert devices that emit little or NO intentional RF: IR-illuminated night-vision pinhole cameras, laser/optical listening devices, and purely wired SD-card / internal-memory spy cams. HONEST FLAG: this is the SDR-BLIND class. A Pluto or B210 sweeping the RF spectrum will NOT find these devices, because their signal path is light (visible/IR/laser) or local wire-to-flash storage, not a radio transmitter. There is no legitimate transmit signature to match. They are found by OPTICAL and PHYSICAL means — lens/retro-reflection detectors, IR-viewing cameras that see 850/940 nm glow, physical search, and (for powered electronics regardless of on/off state) a non-linear junction detector (NLJD), which is an active RF-probe instrument, not a passive spectrum sweep. The only faint, UNINTENTIONAL RF these devices produce is low-level digital clock/oscillator emanation from the image sensor and on-board DVR/SD controller, plus switching-regulator (SMPS) ripple from the device's own power supply — near or below the noise floor, not designed emissions, and not reliably detectable on a stock Pluto (much of it below Pluto's 325 MHz floor). The catalog lists these as NON-MATCHABLE reference rows so the survey states plainly that a clean RF sweep does NOT clear a room of these devices. VERIFICATION: physics, Pluto 325-3800 MHz stock floor, NLJD ~888/915 MHz probe + 2nd/3rd harmonic behavior, and the named product families (Endoacustica laser mics, Axton/SCS 940 nm illuminators) were web-confirmed; the class is technically sound as written.
example_products: Non-Wi-Fi microSD 'self-recording' mini cams (clock, USB wall-charger, photo-frame, air-freshener, screw-head, alarm-clock, hook, pen form factors) sold widely on Amazon/AliExpress — record to microSD on motion (PIR), no radio (device class verified; individual listing model numbers churn constantly and are NOT asserted as SKUs)

IR940C-6 — total-invisible 940 nm IR 'charging cube' with light sensor, 6 high-power LEDs, ~30-50 ft, 5VDC (wifispycameras.com class; disguised IR illuminator example; exact SKU/spec not individually re-verified)

Wired board/pinhole cameras with 3.7 mm pinhole lens + IR lamp (industrial module class used inside covert builds; form-factor example)

Body-worn / button / spy-pen cams in local-record-only mode (SD, no live radio) (form-factor example)
Dash-cam-style covert recorders operating offline to internal storage (form-factor example)

Fiber-optic / borescope pinhole 'through-wall' lens kits feeding a hidden recorder (optical path only; form-factor example)
Two-way IR-illuminated peephole reversers / door-viewer cams recording locally (form-factor example)
confirm_steps: State the ground truth first: a passive RF spectrum sweep (Pluto or B210) does NOT clear a room of this class. If the survey only ran the SDR, the report must say wired/optical devices were NOT tested. Do not let a clean sweep read as 'no cameras.'

Dark-room optical sweep for IR illuminators: turn off all lights, let eyes adjust, and look for the faint dull-red glow of 850 nm arrays; then pan a phone camera (front camera often lacks the IR-cut filter) and/or a dedicated IR viewer across every suspected host — 850 nm shows as bright white/purple dots. For 940 nm 'total invisible' units, phone cameras are unreliable; use a proper IR viewer or IR-sensitive security camera.

Lens / retro-reflection finder: sweep the room with an optical lens-detector (ring of red LEDs + viewport). A camera's objective lens retro-reflects a bright pinpoint back at you regardless of whether it is powered or transmitting — this is the primary detector for wired SD cams. Check at multiple heights and angles; pinholes are directional.

Physical search of likely disguise hosts: clocks, USB chargers/cubes, smoke and PIR detectors, photo frames, air fresheners, alarm clocks, tissue boxes, screw heads, wall warts, DVR boxes. Open, weigh, and inspect anything that seems oddly warm, has an out-of-place pinhole, or was recently added.

NLJD pass for powered-off / non-transmitting electronics: sweep walls, furniture, and objects with a non-linear junction detector. It emits its own ~888/915 MHz (or 2.4 GHz) probe and reads 2nd/3rd harmonics of any semiconductor junction, finding the camera/DVR electronics even with no radio and even if powered off. (This is the NLJD transmitting — not the camera — so it is separate from the passive SDR survey.)

Laser-mic assessment: this is a standoff attack from OUTSIDE, so check line-of-sight from windows to nearby rooftops, windows, and parked vehicles; scan window glass with an IR viewer / laser-detector card for an invisible beam spot; recommend countermeasures (heavy curtains, window vibration/white-noise transducers) rather than expecting the SDR to hear it.
Only after optical + physical + NLJD is the class addressed. If any host is suspicious but inconclusive, bag/relocate it or power-isolate the room and re-test.
false_positive_overlap: An optical lens-finder retro-reflects off ANY lens or shiny curved surface — legitimate webcams, phone cameras, laptop cameras, eyeglasses, glossy hardware, reflective screws, jewelry, and picture-frame glass all flash back. A lens flash is a prompt to inspect, not proof of a covert cam.

Phone/IR viewers see the 850/940 nm IR LEDs of ordinary night-vision security cameras, IR remote controls, IR floodlights, some motion sensors, and IR LED illuminators — most IR dots you find are benign devices doing their job.

NLJDs respond to ALL semiconductor junctions (any electronics, and even some corroded-metal 'rusty-bolt' junctions), so a wall stud with a nail, a light switch, or a smoke detector will light it up — semiconductor 2nd-harmonic dominance vs. metal 3rd-harmonic helps but does not by itself prove a camera.

The faint CMOS/DVR clock emanation and the SMPS switching ripple, in the rare case either is detectable at all, are indistinguishable from the clock spurs and power-supply ripple of any nearby digital device (chargers, LED drivers, USB hubs, the survey laptop itself) and from ambient noise-floor comb lines.
A laser spot on glass could be a rangefinder, a leveling tool, a toy, or a reflection — confirm direction and persistence before alarming.
device_classes.tscm_notes: This is the class the SDR cannot find, and the report must say so in plain language. Wired SD-card cams transmit nothing; IR illuminators emit LIGHT (850/940 nm), not radio; laser mics use an optical beam launched from outside the room. None of these is reachable by a Pluto or B210 spectrum sweep — not because of a band limitation, but because there is no radio emission to receive. The only RF theoretically tied to them is unintended low-level clock/oscillator emanation from the sensor/DVR plus SMPS switching ripple from the device's own power supply, both near/below the noise floor, largely below the stock Pluto's 325 MHz floor (Pluto tunes 325-3800 MHz stock; 70 MHz-6 GHz only with the AD9364 firmware mod), and NOT a dependable detection at any standoff. Practically, these devices are found optically and physically: dark-room IR-glow check (with the caveat that 940 nm needs a real IR viewer, not a phone), an optical lens/retro-reflection finder for the objective lens, disciplined physical search of disguise hosts, and an NLJD to catch powered-off electronics (the NLJD is an active RF probe, transmitting ~888/915 MHz or 2.4 GHz and reading 2nd/3rd harmonics, and is separate from the passive survey). For the client deliverable: never let a clean spectrum sweep imply 'no cameras' — explicitly scope the RF survey as covering transmitting devices only, and record that wired/optical/laser threats require the optical + physical + NLJD sweep, which is a distinct line item. Surface honestly that a purely RF engagement leaves this entire class untested. VERIFICATION VERDICT: the class is technically sound as authored; corrections were additive only — added the SMPS-ripple reference row as a distinct (still non-matchable) incidental-emission mechanism, tightened the NLJD probe frequency to the confirmed ~888/915 MHz (with 2.4 GHz variant), and noted the AD9364 mod does not change the SDR-unreachable conclusion.

signatures.name: Wired SD-card / internal-memory spy cam — NO intentional RF (records locally; SDR-blind)
signatures.mode: NONE — camera writes video to a microSD card or internal flash; no radio, no Wi-Fi/BT/cellular. Nothing is transmitted for an SDR to receive. This row exists to state that plainly, not to be matched.
signatures.tscm: Absence of any RF is the point. Cannot be found by spectrum sweep. Find by: physical search of the disguise host (clock, USB charger, smoke/PIR detector, photo frame, screw-head, alarm clock, air freshener, DVR box); lens/retro-reflection detector flashing off the pinhole optic; and — for the electronics regardless of power state — an NLJD, which probes with its own ~888/915 MHz (or 2.4 GHz) transmitter and listens for 2nd/3rd harmonics of the sensor/DVR semiconductors (this is the NLJD's emission, NOT the camera's). [out-of-scope for any SDR (Pluto or B210) — no transmitted signal exists; requires optical/lens detector, IR viewer, physical search, or NLJD]

signatures.name: IR / night-vision illuminator (850 nm) — OPTICAL emission, not RF
signatures.mode: Near-infrared LIGHT at ~850 nm (~353 THz optical) from the camera's night-vision illuminator array. This is light, ~5 orders of magnitude above any radio band — a Pluto/B210 cannot see it. Listed as optical reference only.
signatures.tscm: 850 nm arrays leak a faint dull-red glow visible to the naked eye in a dark room, and show as bright white/purple points through almost any phone camera or dedicated IR viewer (silicon sensors are roughly twice as responsive at 850 nm as at 940 nm). Detect by killing the lights and looking directly, or by panning a phone/IR-viewer across suspected hosts and watching for illuminator dots. Only emits when the scene is dark and the illuminator switches on. [out-of-scope for any SDR — this is 850 nm light; use an IR-capable camera / phone camera / dark-room visual check, not the Pluto/B210]

signatures.name: Unintended CMOS-sensor / DVR clock emanation — faint, NOT a designed emission
signatures.mode: Incidental digital clock/oscillator harmonics from the image-sensor pixel clock and on-board SD/DVR controller of an otherwise non-transmitting wired cam. Low-level conducted/radiated leakage (compromising emanation), not a communications signal. Fundamentals and harmonics land unpredictably from ~1 MHz to a few hundred MHz depending on the specific chip.
signatures.tscm: Extremely weak, narrow, comb-like spurs at a device-specific clock rate and its multiples, near or below the noise floor and only at very close range (centimeters). NOT reliably detectable and NOT a designed transmission — do NOT promise a client the SDR can find a wired cam this way. Realistically this energy is what an NLJD (active probe) or a very-near-field H-field probe exploits, not a room-scale Pluto sweep. Listed for honesty about the theoretical emission, not as a practical match. [much of this comb falls BELOW a stock Pluto's 325 MHz floor (Pluto tunes 325-3800 MHz stock; 70 MHz-6 GHz only with the AD9364 firmware mod, and even then this is near-field noise-floor energy); the low-MHz fundamentals are out of stock-Pluto reach entirely, and even in-band spurs are not a dependable detection — treat as effectively SDR-unreachable]

signatures.name: Switching-regulator (SMPS/DC-DC) ripple from the cam's own power supply — incidental, NOT a designed emission
signatures.mode: Conducted/near-field switching ripple and its low-order harmonics from the buck/boost or LDO-fed DC-DC converter that powers the sensor and DVR/SD controller (or from the USB-charger-disguise host's own supply). Switching fundamentals typically ~30 kHz to ~2 MHz with harmonics stretching a few MHz higher. Incidental power-electronics leakage, not a communications signal.
signatures.tscm: A broad, drifting set of near-field ripple spurs at the converter's switching rate and multiples, present whenever the device is powered — distinct in mechanism from the pixel-clock comb above but equally undesigned and equally weak at any standoff. Indistinguishable from the SMPS ripple of every other charger, LED driver, and power brick in the room. Detectable only with a very-near-field probe touching the device, not a room-scale sweep. Listed for honesty, not as a match. [entirely BELOW a stock Pluto's 325 MHz floor (kHz-to-few-MHz) and below even the AD9364-modded 70 MHz floor — no SDR in this kit reaches it; this is a near-field-probe / physical-inspection cue only, not a spectrum-sweep detection]

device_classes.device_class: legacy_low_vhf_toy_band_audio
device_classes.summary: Legacy sub-100 MHz consumer/toy-band RF: the 26.9-27.4 MHz CB/RC "27 MHz" band and the 49.82-49.90 MHz walkie/baby-monitor/mic band. These carry both control signals (RC toys) and analog voice/audio, and any of the voice-capable variants (toy walkie-talkies, wireless "karaoke"/lapel mics, baby-monitor transmitters) can be repurposed as a cheap covert audio bug. Two application-distinct voice signatures matter most for TSCM: a 27 MHz DSB-AM voice carrier and a 49 MHz narrowband-FM continuous audio carrier. Both are ENTIRELY BELOW the stock ADALM-Pluto/AD9364 325 MHz tuning floor (325-3800 MHz) and below the USRP B210's 70 MHz floor — they cannot be seen by either stock front end. Capturing them needs the AD9364 low-band mod (extends toward ~70 MHz but still does NOT reach 27/49 MHz), an HF/low-VHF upconverter or downconverter ahead of the SDR, or a dedicated HF/6m capable receiver (e.g., RTL-SDR with upconverter, RSP-series, or a scanner). Treat these as "sweep with a separate low-band receiver" items, flagged in-app as out-of-reach. Honest false-positive note: these bands are shared with legitimate still-in-use devices (old baby monitors, kids' walkie-talkies, RC cars, cordless-phone handsets) and with CB harmonics/skip, so a detected carrier here is far more likely benign legacy consumer gear than an intentional bug — corroborate before alarming a client.
example_products: 27 MHz toy-grade RC car/truck transmitter (pistol-grip, single-channel AM)
27 MHz RC boat / RC tank / RC crane control transmitter
27 MHz color-coded crystal RC transmitter (Ch1-6, brown/red/orange/yellow/green/blue)
27 MHz toy walkie-talkie pair (kids' RadioShack-style handhelds)
27 MHz CB-band handheld/CB radio (adjacent-channel voice source)
49 MHz kids' walkie-talkie set (49.830-49.890 MHz)
49 MHz analog baby monitor transmitter unit (parent/child)
49 MHz voice-activated baby monitor with A/B channel switch
49 MHz wireless lapel/clip-on microphone (legacy karaoke/PA mic)
49 MHz wireless headset microphone (aerobics/fitness-instructor style)
49 MHz cordless telephone handset (legacy VHF cordless phone)
49 MHz cordless phone base station
49 MHz RC toy transmitter (alternate to 27 MHz band)
49 MHz wireless intercom / room monitor
Generic FCC Part 15 'FM transmitter bug' kit tuned to 49.8x MHz (hobby/spy-kit)
27 MHz single-transistor audio 'bug' hobby kit (DSB-AM)
Repurposed 49 MHz baby-monitor TX hidden as covert room-audio source
Repurposed 27/49 MHz toy walkie-talkie with PTT taped down as always-on mic
Vintage 6m/low-VHF wireless microphone body-pack (pre-UHF era)
49 MHz wireless doorbell / chime transmitter (band occupant, non-audio)
27 MHz wireless weather-station / sensor link (band occupant, non-audio)
confirm_steps: You cannot sweep 27/49 MHz with a stock Pluto or B210 — both tune well above these bands (Pluto floor 325 MHz, B210 floor 70 MHz). Use a separate low-band receiver: an RTL-SDR + HF/VHF upconverter (e.g., Ham-It-Up/converter that shifts 0-60 MHz up into RTL range), an SDRplay RSP (which tunes down to ~1 kHz / covers 27 & 49 MHz natively), or a handheld scanner covering low-VHF.

Classify by duty cycle: a CONTINUOUS carrier on a 49.8x channel is the covert-audio red flag; PTT/intermittent bursts point to a walkie-talkie or cordless handset; keyed-only-while-controlled bursts on 27 MHz point to an RC toy (control data, not voice).

Demodulate to confirm content: AM detector on 27 MHz voice channels, NBFM (~30-35 kHz dev) on 49 MHz. Intelligible room audio = live mic/monitor; command tones/pulses = RC control; open squelch hiss keyed by a handset = walkie/cordless.

Localize with a body/near-field probe or directional low-VHF antenna and signal-strength walk-down; Part 15 power is tiny (<~10 mW ERP), so a strong stable carrier means the source is inside the same room/structure.

Corroborate against legitimate legacy gear before alarming the client: ask about old baby monitors, kids' walkie-talkies, RC toys, and cordless phones on-site; power-cycle suspected consumer devices and watch whether the carrier drops.
Rule out CB skip/harmonics on 27 MHz (band is shared with CB and subject to atmospheric skip) — a signal that fades/varies with propagation is not a local bug.
false_positive_overlap: Legacy analog baby monitors (49.8x MHz) still in active use in nurseries
Children's toy walkie-talkies (27 and 49 MHz)
27 MHz RC cars/trucks/boats and other kids' RC toys (control carriers)
Legacy VHF cordless telephone handsets and bases sharing 49.82-49.90 MHz
CB radio voice and CB atmospheric skip/harmonics on the 27 MHz band
Vintage/low-cost wireless lapel, headset, and karaoke microphones on 49 MHz
Wireless doorbells, chimes, weather stations, and sensor links occupying 27/49 MHz (non-audio band occupants)
Amateur 6-meter (50 MHz) activity adjacent just above the 49 MHz band
device_classes.tscm_notes: Both bands are BELOW the reach of this app's stock Pluto (325-3800 MHz) and a stock B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) front ends, so the app should flag these signatures as 'out of tuning range - sweep with a separate low-band/HF receiver' rather than implying the Pluto can hear them. The AD9364 low-band mod referenced elsewhere in the catalog extends toward ~70 MHz but still does NOT reach 27 or 49 MHz - the honest requirement is an upconverter or an HF/low-VHF-native SDR (SDRplay RSP class) or scanner. Threat-wise, the 49.82-49.90 MHz continuous NBFM carrier is the genuinely hostile case: cheap always-on analog room-audio bugs, baby-monitor transmitters, and legacy wireless mics all live here, are trivially FM-demodulated with no encryption or hopping, and were historically rated 'extremely hostile' in classic TSCM frequency lists. But false-positive risk is high across both bands because they are saturated with still-in-service consumer gear (RC toys, kids' walkie-talkies, old cordless phones, baby monitors); a bare carrier here is more likely benign legacy hardware than an intentional bug. Always classify by duty cycle (continuous = suspicious, PTT/keyed = probably legit device), demodulate to confirm live audio, localize by field strength, and corroborate with the client's own device inventory before escalating. Never fabricate a specific bug model from a 27/49 MHz hit - report it as a band/modulation/duty signature and identify the form-factor.

signatures.name: 27 MHz DSB-AM analog voice (toy walkie / repurposed mic as covert audio)
signatures.mode: Double-sideband AM voice on 27 MHz CB/RC channels (Ch1-6: 26.995, 27.045, 27.095, 27.145, 27.195, 27.255 MHz), keyed on push-to-talk; a live/hot mic sits as a near-continuous modulated AM carrier
signatures.tscm: Discrete carriers on the 6 color-coded 27 MHz channels (most commonly Ch4 / yellow / 27.145 MHz); DSB-AM with full carrier + two ~3 kHz voice sidebands (~6-8 kHz occupied); AM envelope demodulates directly to room audio; a repurposed hot mic shows a persistent carrier rather than PTT bursts. Shares band with CB voice, so expect adjacent-channel CB and skip. BELOW stock Pluto 325 MHz floor and below B210 70 MHz floor — needs HF/low-VHF upconverter or dedicated HF receiver. [above-6GHz-out-of-range]

signatures.name: 27 MHz AM/OOK RC control carrier (children's RC toy transmitter)
signatures.mode: On-off-keyed / AM-modulated control tones on the same 6 27 MHz channels; simple RC toys send audio-tone or pulse-train commands, keyed only while a control is pressed
signatures.tscm: Carrier appears only while the toy is actively commanded (steer/throttle), giving short keyed bursts on one of the 6 fixed channels; modulation is tone/pulse command data, NOT voice, so it does not demodulate to intelligible audio (distinguishes it from the 27 MHz voice signature). Not a listening device itself, but its presence confirms band activity and can mask a co-channel bug. BELOW stock Pluto 325 MHz floor / below B210 70 MHz floor — needs HF upconverter or HF receiver. [above-6GHz-out-of-range]

signatures.name: 49 MHz narrowband-FM continuous audio carrier (wireless mic / covert audio bug / baby-monitor TX)
signatures.mode: Narrowband FM voice/audio, ~30-35 kHz deviation, on the five 49 MHz channels (49.830, 49.845, 49.860, 49.875, 49.890 MHz, plus 49.300); transmits a continuous carrier whenever powered — classic always-on room-audio signature
signatures.tscm: Persistent NBFM carrier on one of the fixed 49.8x MHz channels; ~<75 kHz occupied bandwidth; FM-demods straight to room audio with no encryption/hopping. Continuous (not PTT) presence is the covert-audio tell and matches baby-monitor transmitters and cheap lapel/karaoke mics reused as bugs. Very low power (Part 15, <~10 mW ERP), so only detectable within a few hundred metres / same-structure. Overlaps the existing baby-monitor row (49.86 MHz) — this row generalizes it to the full 49.82-49.90 covert-audio case. BELOW stock Pluto 325 MHz floor and below B210 70 MHz floor — needs low-VHF-capable receiver or upconverter. [above-6GHz-out-of-range]

signatures.name: 49 MHz AM/FM walkie-talkie / cordless-handset voice (push-to-talk)
signatures.mode: Narrowband AM or FM voice on the 49.82-49.90 MHz channels, keyed on push-to-talk (toy walkie-talkies) or activated on-hook/off-hook (legacy cordless-phone handset uplink)
signatures.tscm: Same five 49.8x MHz channels as the mic/monitor signature but appears in PTT bursts rather than continuously; toy walkie-talkies and old cordless-phone handsets share these frequencies (documented channel overlap with cordless handset TX). Intermittent keying distinguishes it from the always-on bug/monitor carrier. Legitimate legacy device in most cases — high false-positive risk. BELOW stock Pluto 325 MHz floor / below B210 70 MHz floor — needs low-VHF receiver or upconverter. [above-6GHz-out-of-range]

device_classes.device_class: acoustic_ultrasonic_covert_channel
device_classes.summary: NON-RF REFERENCE CLASS. Covert channels that ride on sound in the near-ultrasound band (~18-24 kHz) — inaudible to humans but reproducible/recordable by ordinary consumer speakers and microphones. Two families: (1) commercial ultrasonic cross-device tracking beacons ("uBeacons", SilverPush/Signal360/Lisnr lineage) embedded in TV ads, web pages, retail PA, and apps to silently link a person's phone/TV/laptop for ad attribution; (2) research/APT-grade acoustic exfiltration from air-gapped machines (Hanspach-Goetz mesh, Guri et al. Fansmitter/MOSQUITO/Ultrasonic from Ben-Gurion), where malware modulates data onto near-ultrasound emitted by speakers, headphones-as-speakers, or fans. THIS IS AUDIO, NOT RF. A Pluto or B210 sees NOTHING here — there is no electromagnetic carrier at the antenna; the energy is acoustic pressure waves in air at kHz frequencies, ~5-6 orders of magnitude below the SDR's lowest tunable RF frequency (325 MHz Pluto / 70 MHz B210). This row exists, like the optical_ir reference class, so the operator understands WHY the spectrum analyzer is silent on this threat and reaches for the correct instrument: a wideband microphone + audio spectrogram (e.g. a phone mic app, a measurement mic, or an ultrasonic-capable recorder sampling >=48 kHz, ideally 96-192 kHz) rather than the SDR. Detection is an audio-domain FFT task, not an IQ task.
example_products: SilverPush ultrasonic ad-tracking SDK (uBeacon emitter/listener, embedded in Android apps)
Signal360 (Sonic Notify) proximity/beacon audio SDK
Lisnr 'SmartTones' ultrasonic data-over-sound SDK (payments/ticketing/attribution)
Shopkick in-store ultrasonic presence beacons
Google Nearby / Chromecast ultrasonic pairing tones (legit data-over-sound, same acoustic signature)
Amazon Dash Button-era and smart-TV ACR ad beacons (uXDT-capable)
Chirp / Sonos-style ultrasonic device-pairing tones (data-over-sound)
Retail-store PA and digital-signage players injecting inaudible attribution tones
Smart-TV commercials / streaming ads carrying embedded uBeacons
Web-page JavaScript ad tags playing ultrasonic beacons through laptop/desktop speakers
Conference/venue audience-analytics 'sonic beacons'
Air-gap PoC malware: Hanspach-Goetz acoustical mesh (GUWAL-based audio modem)
Air-gap PoC malware: Guri et al. 'Ultrasonic' / MOSQUITO / Fansmitter (Ben-Gurion) — note Fansmitter uses fan RPM tones in the AUDIBLE band, still audio not RF
Commodity laptop/desktop/TV/soundbar/smart-speaker SPEAKERS acting as unwitting emitters
Smartphone microphones + any app with RECORD_AUDIO acting as unwitting receivers
Ultrasonic-capable measurement/detection gear an operator would actually use to FIND these: a >=96 kHz USB measurement mic, phone spectrogram apps, or an ultrasonic bat-detector/recorder
confirm_steps: Recognize the SDR limitation: if the client's concern is 'inaudible tones', 'they can track my phone through the TV', or air-gap leakage, the Pluto/B210 is the WRONG instrument — it will read clean because there is no RF carrier. Do not report 'no signal found' as 'all clear.'

Switch to the audio domain: capture with a microphone at the highest sample rate available. A phone spectrogram app catches ~18-22 kHz; for the 20-24 kHz air-gap class use a measurement mic or recorder sampling >=96 kHz (>=192 kHz ideal) so you don't clip content above the 22 kHz Nyquist edge of 44.1 kHz gear.

Run a real-time audio FFT/spectrogram and watch the 17-24 kHz shelf. Look for narrow tones or keyed tone-clusters sitting just above the human-hearing rolloff, especially bursts that repeat in sync with ads/media, or continuous low-bitrate keying between machines.
For a tracking-beacon concern, reproduce: play the suspect TV ad / web page / app and confirm whether a beacon appears in the 18-20 kHz band on the spectrogram; correlate timing with the media.

For an air-gap concern, sweep each room with air-gapped machines while they're powered; look for 17-24 kHz keyed tones with no legitimate audio source, and inspect endpoints for audio-jack-retasking / unexpected mic or speaker activity (software-side, not RF).

Rule out benign sources: HVAC whine, CRT/switch-mode flyback, insect/animal ultrasound, pet deterrents, and legitimate data-over-sound pairing (Chromecast, Nearby) all live in this band — confirm a data-carrying keying pattern before calling it hostile.
Document explicitly in the report that this threat is acoustic and was assessed with a microphone, so the client understands the SDR sweep did not and cannot cover it.
false_positive_overlap: Legitimate data-over-sound: Google Nearby, Chromecast/Google Home ultrasonic pairing tones, Chirp-style transfers — same 18-20 kHz acoustic signature as hostile beacons
Mobile-payment and event check-in tones (Lisnr and similar) used with user consent
HVAC and fan whine, switch-mode power supply and CRT flyback whistle in the 15-20 kHz range
Ultrasonic pest/rodent/pet deterrents and 'anti-teen' (Mosquito device) emitters
Insect and animal ultrasound (bats, some rodents) picked up by a wideband mic
Cheap-mic artifacts and aliasing: a 44.1/48 kHz recorder can fold higher tones back into band and fake a beacon
Camera/electronics coil whine and PWM backlight buzz near the top of the audible band
device_classes.tscm_notes: Include this as a REFERENCE-ONLY class in the catalog, exactly like optical_ir: it teaches the operator why the SDR is silent and what instrument to grab instead. Do not let a clean RF sweep create false assurance against 'they can hear/track me through inaudible sound.' Real, deployed threat on the tracking side (SilverPush/Signal360/Lisnr are commercial and have shipped in real apps and ads); the air-gap exfil side is largely academic PoC (Ben-Gurion, Fraunhofer) but is a legitimate concern for genuinely air-gapped, high-security environments. Frequencies are entered in MHz to satisfy the schema (0.018 MHz = 18 kHz); anyone reading the catalog must understand these rows are kHz-scale ACOUSTIC, roughly 5-6 orders of magnitude below the SDR's lowest RF frequency, so a Pluto (325-3800 MHz) and a B210 (70 MHz-6 GHz) are BOTH structurally incapable of detecting them — not a tuning gap, a wrong-physics gap. Correct tool: microphone + audio spectrogram; use >=96 kHz sampling for the 20-24 kHz air-gap variants because 44.1/48 kHz recorders Nyquist-clip above ~22-24 kHz. High false-positive overlap with legitimate data-over-sound (device pairing, mobile payments, proximity check-in) and with environmental/mechanical ultrasound; require a data-carrying keying pattern before escalating.

signatures.name: Ultrasonic tracking beacon (uBeacon / SilverPush-class cross-device tracking tone)
signatures.mode: AUDIO (near-ultrasound acoustic, NOT RF) — inaudible 18-20 kHz tone burst carrying a short ID code via FSK/OFDM-like sub-tones, emitted by TV/PC/retail speakers, recorded by phone mic + SDK
signatures.tscm: Acoustic pressure wave in air at 18-20 kHz — OUT OF RANGE of any SDR (5+ orders of magnitude below Pluto's 325 MHz / B210's 70 MHz floor). Appears only on an AUDIO spectrogram sampled >=44.1 kHz: a cluster of narrow tones in the 18-20 kHz shelf, riding just above the human hearing rolloff, keying a data payload in short bursts (often repeating every few seconds while an ad plays). SilverPush, Signal360, Lisnr, Shopkick lineage. freq fields are expressed in MHz per schema so read 0.018 MHz = 18 kHz. [NON-RF: unreachable by ANY SDR (Pluto or B210) — this is sound, not electromagnetic. Needs a microphone + audio FFT, not an antenna.]

signatures.name: Air-gap ultrasonic exfil — near-ultrasound covert mesh (Hanspach-Goetz class)
signatures.mode: AUDIO (near-ultrasound acoustic, NOT RF) — malware modulates data onto 17-20 kHz using audio modem schemes (adapted underwater/GUWAL modem), speaker-to-mic, ~20 bit/s over ~19-20 m
signatures.tscm: Sound, not RF — invisible to SDR. On an audio spectrogram: low-bitrate keyed tones in the 17-20 kHz band, persistent while exfil runs, between two air-gapped PCs in the same room/mesh. Hanspach & Goetz 2013 covert acoustical mesh network. Bit rate ~20 bps, range up to ~19-20 m. Distinguishable from ad beacons by continuous/patterned keying rather than short ad-synced ID bursts. 0.017-0.020 MHz = 17-20 kHz. [NON-RF: unreachable by SDR. Detect with a mic + spectrogram; the SDR front end has no acoustic transducer.]

signatures.name: Air-gap ultrasonic exfil — speaker-to-speaker / headphone-as-mic (Guri MOSQUITO/Ultrasonic class)
signatures.mode: AUDIO (ultrasound acoustic, NOT RF) — passive speakers/earbuds re-tasked as microphones via jack retasking; data keyed at 20-24 kHz, ~140-166 bps speaker-to-speaker
signatures.tscm: Acoustic, not RF. Ben-Gurion (Guri et al.) MOSQUITO turns headphones/earbuds into mics and does speaker-to-speaker ultrasonic comms; related work exfils at 20-20.5 kHz ~140-166 bps. On an audio spectrogram: keyed tones pushed slightly higher (20-24 kHz), often near or just beyond the Nyquist edge of a 44.1/48 kHz recorder — a mic that samples only 44.1 kHz can MISS content above ~22 kHz, so use >=96 kHz sampling to be safe. 0.020-0.024 MHz = 20-24 kHz. [NON-RF: unreachable by SDR. Requires an ultrasonic-capable mic (>=96 kHz sample rate preferred) + spectrogram; even many consumer mics roll off before 24 kHz.]

device_classes.device_class: ant_ antplus_24ghz_telemetry
device_classes.summary: ANT / ANT+ is a 2.4 GHz GFSK sport/telemetry protocol (Nordic Enhanced ShockBurst physical layer) that occupies narrow ~1 MHz channels with 1 Mbps GFSK / 160 kHz deviation, arranged 1 MHz apart across 2400-2483.5 MHz. Its distinguishing on-air trait is adaptive-isochronous TDMA: each channel wakes on a fixed period (e.g. ANT+ heart-rate at ~4.06 Hz, other profiles 4-8 Hz) and emits a very short single-packet burst in an assigned time slot, then goes silent. This periodic, time-sliced burst cadence is what separates it from BLE (2 MHz channels, adv-triplet-then-connection-hop) and from Wi-Fi (wideband OFDM). ANT+ concentrates on the 2457 MHz default channel (and 2450 MHz), so a persistent ~1 MHz GFSK carrier ticking at a metronomic sub-10 Hz rate on 2457 MHz is the classic tell. Relevant to TSCM because the same cheap ANT/ANT+ radios and Nordic nRF24-family parts are trivially repurposed for covert body-worn, low-rate telemetry / data exfil links that hide inside the enormous legitimate fitness-sensor population on 2.4 GHz. Fully within a stock ADALM-Pluto's 325-3800 MHz tuning range and well inside B210 range; no front-end mod needed. Main practical challenge is not reach but resolving a 1 MHz GFSK burst against dense 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi/BLE/Zigbee traffic and confirming the periodic isochronous cadence rather than a one-off Wi-Fi/BLE hit.
example_products: Garmin HRM-Dual / HRM-Pro / HRM-Pro Plus / HRM-600 chest heart-rate straps
Wahoo TICKR, TICKR X, TICKR FIT armband HR monitors
Polar H9 / H10 chest straps (ANT+ mode), Polar OH1/OH1+ optical armband
Scosche Rhythm24 / Rhythm+ optical armband (HR + footpod + cadence profiles)
Garmin cycling speed sensor and cadence sensor (magnetless, ANT+/BLE)
Garmin Vector / Rally pedal-based cycling power meters
Stages, Quarq, 4iiii, Power2Max crank/spider cycling power meters
Stryd running power footpod
Garmin Running Dynamics Pod / footpod (cadence, GCT, stride)
Garmin Edge / Forerunner / Fenix head units and watches acting as ANT+ display/hub
Wahoo ELEMNT / KICKR smart trainers (ANT+ FE-C)
Zwift ANT+ USB stick (via nRF24AP2) and generic ANT+ USB dongles
Nordic nRF24AP2-USB / nRF24AP2-1CH / nRF24AP2-8CH ANT modules (the reference radios attackers repurpose)
TI CC2570 / CC2571 ANT network processor chips
Suunto / Garmin foot-pods and tempe ANT+ temperature sensor
Tacx / Elite ANT+ FE-C smart trainers
Garmin tire-pressure and muscle-oxygen (Moxy) ANT+ sensors
Generic Amazon/AliExpress ANT+ chest straps (Powr Labs, CooSpo, Magene)
DIY nRF24L01+ / nRF52-based custom ANT or ShockBurst-clone body-worn logger (covert-link form factor, not a certified product)
confirm_steps: Tune the SDR to 2457 MHz (ANT+ default) and 2450 MHz first with a ~2-3 MHz span; look for a narrow ~1 MHz GFSK channel showing a metronomic short-burst tick at a fixed sub-10 Hz rate (ANT+ HR ~4.06 Hz). The regular period, not the burst itself, is the confirmation.

Confirm the carrier is STATIONARY across many bursts (ANT does not channel-hop within a session). A source that hops 1600 times/sec across the band is Bluetooth Classic FHSS, not ANT; a triplet-then-hop pattern is BLE advertising.

Measure the burst repetition period and compare to known ANT+ channel periods (e.g. 8070 counts / 32768 Hz ~= 4.06 Hz for HR). A recognizable ANT+ profile rate strongly indicates a legitimate fitness sensor; an odd non-standard period on an off-default channel raises the covert-link suspicion.

Sweep the full 2400-2483.5 MHz band on the 1 MHz grid for stationary ~1 MHz GFSK channels with periodic bursts sitting OFF the 2450/2457 MHz ANT+ defaults - those are the ones worth investigating as private/covert ANT or ShockBurst links.
Watch for a duty-pattern change: a channel that switches from evenly-spaced single-packet ticks to a dense back-to-back burst train (advanced-burst) indicates a bulk data transfer / offload event.

Cross-check against the subject: ask whether anyone present is wearing a fitness HR strap, power meter, or footpod, or has a bike computer/watch active. Correlating a detected ANT+ channel with a visible legitimate wearable resolves most false positives on the spot.

If a suspicious body-worn source is suspected, use a near-field / directional antenna and signal-strength ranging to localize whether the emitter is on a person's body versus a bystander's fitness device across the room.
false_positive_overlap: Legitimate ANT+ fitness sensors everywhere: heart-rate straps, cycling power meters, speed/cadence sensors, footpods, smart trainers, and Garmin/Wahoo head units and watches - by far the dominant source on 2457/2450 MHz.
Plain Nordic nRF24L01+ / ShockBurst links that share the identical 1 Mbps GFSK / 1 MHz-channel waveform: wireless keyboards and mice, RC/drone control links, and various 2.4 GHz IoT gadgets.
Bluetooth Classic, which also uses 1 MHz-wide 1 Mbps GFSK channels - distinguished only by its 1600 hops/sec FHSS versus ANT's stationary carrier.
BLE advertising bursts, which are periodic like ANT but use 2 MHz channels and an advertise-then-hop pattern rather than a single stationary isochronous channel.
General 2.4 GHz ISM congestion (Wi-Fi OFDM, Zigbee) that can mask or be mistaken for a 1 MHz GFSK burst on a crowded spectrum display.
device_classes.tscm_notes: Treat almost every ANT+ hit as benign by default: 2.4 GHz ANT+ is one of the most common consumer fitness-telemetry protocols on earth, and any gym-goer, cyclist, or runner in the vicinity will light up 2457/2450 MHz. The TSCM value is not in detecting ANT+ generically but in spotting the anomalous case - a stationary ~1 MHz GFSK channel with a metronomic isochronous burst cadence sitting on a non-default frequency, running with no plausible fitness device present, or offloading via burst trains. That profile fits a cheap nRF24-family part repurposed as a covert, low-rate, body-worn telemetry or data-exfil link that deliberately hides inside the legitimate ANT population. Note the false-positive minefield: ANT shares the exact 1 Mbps GFSK / 1 MHz-channel ShockBurst waveform with plain Nordic nRF24L01+ links (drones, RC gear, wireless keyboards/mice, some IoT), and is easily confused with Bluetooth Classic (also 1 MHz/1 Mbps GFSK, but FHSS). Resolve by the stationary-carrier + slow-isochronous-tick signature, not by waveform alone. Fully within a stock Pluto (325-3800 MHz) and B210 range - no AD9364 front-end mod needed - so reach is not the limiting factor; demodulating/decoding to prove it is ANT vs generic ShockBurst is the real work, and stock Pluto/B210 IQ plus rtl_433-style ANT decoders can get most of the way. Do not over-claim a covert device from a spectrum hit alone; localize and correlate with a visible wearable before flagging to a client.

signatures.name: ANT+ default-channel isochronous telemetry burst (2457 MHz)
signatures.mode: GFSK 1 Mbps, 160 kHz deviation, ~1 MHz channel; adaptive-isochronous TDMA single-packet bursts on a fixed period (ANT+ HR ~4.06 Hz; most ANT+ profiles 4-8 Hz)
signatures.tscm: The signature ANT+ tell: a narrow ~1 MHz GFSK channel parked on the 2457 MHz ANT+ default frequency, emitting one very short (~150 us) packet per period at a metronomic sub-10 Hz cadence, then silent. Constant center frequency (does NOT channel-hop like BLE) plus the regular isochronous tick distinguishes it from BLE advertising and from Wi-Fi. 2450 MHz is the common secondary ANT+ channel. Within stock Pluto 325-3800 MHz reach and B210 range. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: Generic ANT arbitrary-channel GFSK link (2400-2483.5 MHz, 1 MHz grid)
signatures.mode: GFSK 1 Mbps, 160 kHz deviation, ~1 MHz channel on 1 MHz-spaced grid; TDMA/isochronous, user-selectable RF channel (ANT frequency 0-124)
signatures.tscm: Private/proprietary ANT links (and repurposed covert links) can sit on any 1 MHz-spaced channel across the band, not just 2457/2450 MHz. Same 1 Mbps GFSK / 160 kHz-deviation ShockBurst waveform and periodic single-packet isochronous bursts, but on an operator-chosen frequency to hide off the ANT+ default. Look for a static ~1 MHz GFSK channel with a fixed short-burst period anywhere on the 1 MHz grid. Distinguish from Bluetooth Classic (also 1 MHz/1 Mbps GFSK but 1600 hops/s FHSS across 79 channels) by ANT's stationary carrier and slow isochronous tick. Within stock Pluto reach and B210 range. [stock-Pluto-reachable]

signatures.name: ANT/ANT+ high-rate burst / advanced-burst transfer (bulk payload)
signatures.mode: GFSK 1 Mbps, 160 kHz deviation, ~1 MHz channel; back-to-back burst / advanced-burst packet trains (bulk transfer) rather than single periodic packets
signatures.tscm: Distinct duty pattern from the low-rate telemetry burst: during ANT burst / advanced-burst transfers the radio sends packet trains back-to-back to move a payload (firmware, logged files, or a covert data dump), producing a short dense run of 1 MHz GFSK activity instead of an evenly-spaced tick. On the same 1 MHz channel/waveform as the telemetry signatures. This is the mode a covert body-worn logger would use to offload stored data to a nearby collector, so a normally-quiet ANT channel that suddenly shows a dense burst train is worth flagging. Within stock Pluto reach and B210 range. [stock-Pluto-reachable]
